definition: An IEEE standard for port-based network access control that requires a device to authenticate before the switch port or wireless association is allowed. It involves a supplicant, an authenticator (switch or access point) and an authentication server (usually RADIUS), using EAP methods.
examContext: Used for Wi-Fi Enterprise and wired NAC. Know the three roles and common EAP methods (EAP-TLS, PEAP). Devices that fail authentication can be denied or placed in a quarantine VLAN.
analogy: A turnstile that opens only after a guard at a desk verifies your badge.
relatedTerms: RADIUS, EAP, NAC, Port security, PEAP

detail.practicalScenario: When a laptop plugs into a wall jack, the switch port stays closed until the laptop authenticates through 802.1X to a RADIUS server. A visitor's unknown device never gets a network connection.
detail.quizQuestion: Which standard requires a device to authenticate through a RADIUS server before a switch port or Wi-Fi association is allowed?

definition: A physical card or token, often embedded with an RFID chip or magnetic stripe, that identifies its holder and is presented to a reader to unlock doors or other secured physical areas.
examContext: The exam connects access badges to tailgating risk, since someone can follow a badged employee through a door, and to cloning risk when the badge relies on weak RFID technology; often paired with access control vestibules.
analogy: Like a hotel key card that only opens the specific doors you're authorized for, rather than a single key that opens the whole building.
relatedTerms: Access control vestibule, Security guard, Tailgating, Smart card

detail.practicalScenario: Maria issues RFID access badges to all employees that are individually programmed so that warehouse staff can only badge into the warehouse, while only IT staff badges unlock the server room door.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants each employee's physical door access to be individually tracked and restricted to only the specific areas their job requires. Which control best achieves this?

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

definition: A small, secure enclosed space with two interlocking doors positioned between an unsecured and a secured area, allowing only one verified person through at a time before the second door will unlock.
examContext: Formerly called a mantrap in older materials; SY0-701 uses the term access control vestibule and tests it as the primary physical control against tailgating and piggybacking.
analogy: Like an airlock on a spaceship, where one door must seal shut before the next one will open, letting only one person through at a time.
relatedTerms: Tailgating, Security guard, Access badge

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's organization installs an access control vestibule at the server room entrance so that each employee must badge in and be individually verified between two sequential doors, preventing a second person from slipping in behind them.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to physically prevent an unauthorized person from following closely behind an authorized employee through a secured door. Which control best addresses this?

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

definition: A security control that automatically disables a user account after a specified number of consecutive failed login attempts, mitigating brute-force and password-guessing attacks.
examContext: Know account lockout policies specify a threshold, such as five failed attempts, and a lockout duration or require admin unlock; exam scenarios test balancing security against availability, since legitimate users can accidentally lock themselves out, a possible denial-of-service vector.
analogy: Like a bank vault that automatically seals itself shut after too many incorrect combination attempts, forcing a manager to come reset it.
relatedTerms: Brute force attack, Dictionary attack, Multifactor authentication

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures the Active Directory password policy to lock out any account after five consecutive failed login attempts for thirty minutes, effectively stopping an automated brute-force script from guessing employee passwords.
detail.quizQuestion: Security logs show thousands of rapid failed login attempts against a single user account from an automated script. Which control, if already configured, would have stopped the attack after a few attempts?

items.name: Length
items.detail: The strongest single factor against guessing and cracking. Favor long passphrases over short complex strings.

items.name: Complexity
items.detail: Requires mixed character types. Current NIST guidance prefers length plus a blocklist of known-bad passwords over forced complexity.

items.name: Reuse / history
items.detail: Password history stops users from recycling their last N passwords.

items.name: Expiration / maximum age
items.detail: Forces a change after a set time. Current NIST guidance says do not force routine changes unless there is evidence of compromise.

items.name: Minimum age
items.detail: Stops a user from changing the password repeatedly in one sitting to cycle back to an old one.

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Locks the account after N failed attempts. Defeats online brute force, but can be abused to lock out legitimate users (a denial of service).

items.name: Password manager
items.detail: Generates and stores unique strong passwords so users do not reuse them. Protect it with a strong master password and MFA.

items.name: Passwordless
items.detail: FIDO2 keys, passkeys and biometrics remove the shared secret that attackers phish or crack.

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Many failed logins from one account or source suggest brute force or spraying.

items.name: Concurrent session usage
items.detail: The same account logged in from several places or devices at once.

items.name: Impossible travel
items.detail: Logins from locations too far apart for the elapsed time, suggesting stolen credentials.

items.name: Blocked content
items.detail: Spikes of blocked connections or filtered downloads, which can reveal malware phoning home or users hitting malicious sites.

items.name: Resource consumption
items.detail: Unexplained CPU, memory, disk or bandwidth use, such as cryptojacking or data exfiltration.

items.name: Resource inaccessibility
items.detail: Services, files or systems suddenly unavailable: DoS, ransomware or a wiper.

items.name: Out-of-cycle logging
items.detail: Log entries or activity at unusual times, such as a batch job or admin login at 3 a.m.

items.name: Missing logs
items.detail: Gaps or deleted logs, a sign that an attacker is covering their tracks.

items.name: Published / documented
items.detail: Known IoCs and attack patterns from threat intelligence, such as a documented IP, hash or domain.

definition: Provisioning creates user accounts and assigns access based on role when someone joins or changes jobs; deprovisioning removes or disables access promptly when they leave or no longer need it. Identity systems and automation keep the process consistent.
examContext: Tied to least privilege and onboarding and offboarding. Orphaned or lingering accounts are a classic risk, so disable access promptly at termination.
analogy: Handing out and collecting building keys as staff join and leave.
relatedTerms: Least privilege, Onboarding and offboarding, Role-based access control, Identity proofing

detail.practicalScenario: When a new analyst joins, the identity system creates her accounts and adds her to the SOC role. When a contractor's engagement ends, the same system disables his accounts the same day.
detail.quizQuestion: Which process removes a departing employee's accounts and access so no orphaned credentials remain?

definition: The ability to trace actions and events back to the specific user, system, or process responsible for them, typically through logging and auditing.
examContext: Often linked with audit trails and logging questions; the exam may ask which concept holds users responsible for their actions after the fact.
analogy: Like a security camera log that lets you prove exactly who entered a room and when.
relatedTerms: Non-repudiation, Authentication, Authorization, Due care

detail.practicalScenario: Maria enables detailed audit logging on the file server so that every delete action is tied to a specific user account, allowing investigators to trace who removed a critical file.
detail.quizQuestion: After a sensitive file disappears, investigators use server logs to determine exactly which user account deleted it. This capability is an example of which concept?

definition: Gathering information by directly interacting with the target, such as port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing and vulnerability scans. It can be detected by the target's security tools.
examContext: Contrast with passive reconnaissance, which does not touch the target. It is part of the early phase of penetration testing.
analogy: Walking up to a building and trying the doors.
relatedTerms: Passive reconnaissance, Penetration testing, Vulnerability scanning, Unknown environment

detail.practicalScenario: A tester runs a port scan against the target's public servers to see which services are listening. The IDS logs the scan because it touches the target directly.
detail.quizQuestion: Which reconnaissance method involves directly probing a target with port scans and banner grabbing?

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: A zero trust control-plane concept in which a subject's access rights are continuously reevaluated using real-time context, such as location, device health, time of day, and behavior patterns, rather than being fixed once at login.
examContext: Listed by CompTIA as a control-plane element of zero trust; exam scenarios test recognizing that identity-based risk scoring changes dynamically throughout a session rather than being judged only once at the initial login.
analogy: Like a security guard who keeps re-checking your badge and behavior throughout the day, not just when you first walk in the door.
relatedTerms: Zero trust, Control plane, Risk management, Multifactor authentication, Attribute-based access control

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's identity platform flags a user session as higher risk and automatically requires step-up authentication after detecting the same account suddenly connecting from a new country on an unmanaged device mid-session.
detail.quizQuestion: A zero trust system continuously reevaluates a logged-in user's risk level, automatically prompting for additional verification after detecting a sudden change in location and device. What concept does this illustrate?

definition: A sophisticated, well-resourced threat actor, often nation-state sponsored, that gains unauthorized access to a network and remains undetected for an extended period to achieve long-term objectives.
examContext: Exam tests advanced persistent threats as characterized by stealth, patience, and significant funding, typically pursuing espionage or data theft rather than quick financial gain.
analogy: Like a spy who quietly lives in a city for years gathering secrets, rather than a burglar who grabs valuables and runs.
relatedTerms: Threat actor, Persistence, Lateral movement, Command and control, Zero-day

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team discovers malware that has been quietly collecting intellectual property from the engineering network for over a year, consistent with a nation-state-sponsored advanced persistent threat rather than an opportunistic criminal.
detail.quizQuestion: Investigators discover that a well-funded group has maintained stealthy, undetected access to a defense contractor's network for over two years, slowly exfiltrating design documents. What type of threat does this describe?

items.name: Nation-state
items.detail: Government-backed. Very high funding and sophistication, with patient long-term (APT) campaigns for espionage, sabotage and geopolitical goals.

items.name: Organized crime
items.detail: Structured criminal groups with high resources, driven by PROFIT: ransomware, fraud, theft and extortion.

items.name: Hacktivist
items.detail: Moderate skills, driven by ideology or politics. Typical acts: DDoS, website defacement, doxing and data leaks.

items.name: Unskilled attacker (script kiddie)
items.detail: Low skill and low resources. Runs pre-made tools and scripts for curiosity, bragging rights or chaos.

items.name: Insider threat
items.detail: An employee, contractor or partner with legitimate access. INTERNAL, and either malicious (revenge, profit) or unintentional (mistakes, negligence).

items.name: Shadow IT
items.detail: Staff using unapproved apps, devices or cloud services. Rarely malicious, but it creates unmanaged risk.

items.name: Attributes that separate actors
items.detail: Internal vs external; resources and funding (low to high); level of sophistication and capability (low to high).

items.name: Financial gain
items.detail: Ransom, fraud, theft of payment data or credentials to sell. The most common motive; organized crime.

items.name: Data exfiltration
items.detail: Stealing sensitive data to sell, leak or use for leverage.

items.name: Espionage
items.detail: Stealing government or corporate secrets. Nation-states and competitors.

items.name: Service disruption
items.detail: Taking systems offline (DDoS, wipers) to hurt a target or demand payment.

items.name: Blackmail
items.detail: Threatening to expose stolen or embarrassing data unless paid.

items.name: Philosophical / political beliefs
items.detail: Ideology-driven attacks. Hacktivists.

items.name: Ethical
items.detail: Authorized testing or responsible disclosure by "white hat" researchers and bug-bounty hunters.

items.name: Revenge
items.detail: Retaliation, classically a disgruntled insider.

items.name: Disruption / chaos
items.detail: Causing havoc for its own sake or for notoriety, often unskilled attackers.

items.name: War / geopolitical
items.detail: Cyber operations supporting military or state conflict.

definition: Software that automatically displays or downloads unwanted advertisements, often bundled with free programs. It can track browsing behavior, slow the system and sometimes open the door to more serious malware.
examContext: Related to PUPs and bloatware. Usually a nuisance rather than destructive, but it can degrade performance and privacy and may deliver other malicious payloads.
analogy: A pushy salesperson who follows you around the store and cannot be shaken off.
relatedTerms: Bloatware, PUP, Spyware, Malware

detail.practicalScenario: Pop-up ads begin appearing after a user installs a free PDF tool that came bundled with extra software. The bundled adware also tracks which sites the user visits.
detail.quizQuestion: Pop-up ads keep appearing after a user installs a free PDF tool that included extra bundled software. Which malware category MOST likely applies?

definition: A network or system that is physically isolated from all other networks, including the internet, with no wired or wireless connection, used to protect extremely sensitive systems from remote attack.
examContext: Know an air-gapped network as the strongest form of network isolation, often used for industrial control systems or classified environments; exam scenarios test that an air gap still requires physical and removable-media controls, since data can still cross the gap via USB drives.
analogy: Like keeping a vault in a building with no doors or windows at all; the only way in or out is for someone to physically carry something across the gap.
relatedTerms: Network segmentation, Microsegmentation, Zero trust

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's team keeps the power plant's industrial control systems on a fully air-gapped network with no physical or wireless connection to the corporate IT network, so even if office computers are compromised by malware, attackers have no network path to reach the plant's safety systems.
detail.quizQuestion: A utility company wants to ensure its industrial control systems cannot be reached by any attacker who compromises the corporate office network, even remotely. Which architecture best achieves this?

items.name: Trusted / intranet
items.detail: The internal corporate network; highest trust.

items.name: Untrusted
items.detail: The internet and anything you do not control.

items.name: Screened subnet (DMZ)
items.detail: A buffer zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS). If one is compromised, the attacker is still outside the internal network.

items.name: Extranet
items.detail: A controlled network shared with partners, suppliers or customers.

items.name: Guest network
items.detail: Isolated Wi-Fi/VLAN with internet-only access.

items.name: Management network
items.detail: A separate (often out-of-band) network used only to administer devices.

items.name: Segmentation methods
items.detail: Physical (separate hardware or an air gap), logical (VLANs and ACLs), virtual (VXLAN/overlays) and microsegmentation (per-workload policy).

items.name: North-south vs east-west
items.detail: North-south traffic enters or leaves the datacenter or network; east-west traffic moves between internal systems, which is where lateral movement happens.

definition: Adjusting detection rules, thresholds and exceptions so alerts reflect real threats, reducing false positives and alert fatigue without missing genuine incidents.
examContext: Part of alert response and remediation; compare with false positives and false negatives. Baselines and business context improve it.
analogy: Adjusting a car alarm's sensitivity so passing trucks do not set it off but a break-in does.
relatedTerms: False positive, False negative, SIEM, Log aggregation

detail.practicalScenario: The SOC receives thousands of low-value alerts each day. Analysts raise thresholds for routine admin activity and add exceptions for known scanners, so real threats stand out.
detail.quizQuestion: The SOC adjusts SIEM thresholds and adds exceptions to cut the number of meaningless alerts without missing real attacks. What is this activity?

items.name: Log aggregation
items.detail: Collect logs from many sources into one place for correlation and search.

items.name: Alerting
items.detail: Notify people or systems when events match a rule or threshold.

items.name: Alert tuning
items.detail: Adjust thresholds and rules to cut false positives without missing real attacks.

items.name: Scanning and reporting
items.detail: Regular scans and reports show trends and compliance.

items.name: Archiving
items.detail: Keep logs for the retention period required for investigations and regulations.

items.name: Quarantine
items.detail: Isolate a suspicious file, system or message until it can be investigated.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agents give deep visibility and work off-network. Agentless is easier to deploy but shallower.

definition: An allow list (whitelist) permits only explicitly approved items, such as applications, IP addresses or email senders, and blocks everything else. A deny list (blocklist) blocks specific known-bad items and allows everything else.
examContext: Allow lists follow default deny, so they are stronger but need more upkeep; deny lists are easier to run but miss unknown threats. Changes to either list are a technical implication in change management.
analogy: A guest list at a private party (allow) versus a list of banned troublemakers at the door (deny).
relatedTerms: Implicit deny, Application allow list, Firewall, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: The email gateway uses a deny list of known spam senders, while the finance VPN uses an allow list that accepts connections only from three approved office IP addresses.
detail.quizQuestion: Which approach permits only explicitly approved items and blocks everything else by default?

variants.title: Change management: technical implications and documentation

items.name: Allow lists / deny lists
items.detail: Changes may require editing the lists of approved or blocked applications, IPs or sites.

items.name: Restricted activities
items.detail: Some actions may be forbidden during a change window or freeze.

items.name: Downtime
items.detail: Planned outages that must be communicated.

items.name: Service / application restart
items.detail: A restart may be required for the change to take effect and can interrupt users.

items.name: Legacy applications
items.detail: Old software may break or not be supported after a change.

items.name: Dependencies
items.detail: Other systems and services that rely on the thing being changed.

items.name: Documentation
items.detail: Update network diagrams, policies and procedures after the change.

items.name: Version control
items.detail: Track every version of configurations and code so you can see what changed, who changed it, and roll back.

definition: A DDoS technique where the attacker sends small requests with a spoofed source address (the victim's) to servers such as open DNS, NTP or memcached that reply with much larger responses, overwhelming the victim. Reflection hides the attacker; amplification multiplies the volume.
examContext: Know reflected and amplified DDoS from the objectives. Defenses: close open resolvers, rate limiting, ingress filtering (BCP 38), scrubbing services and RTBH.
analogy: Calling a radio station while pretending to be the victim, so it blasts a huge reply to the victim's phone.
relatedTerms: DDoS, DoS, Spoofing, Botnet

detail.practicalScenario: An attacker sends tiny spoofed DNS queries to thousands of open resolvers. Each reply is dozens of times larger and is sent to the victim's IP, flooding its link with traffic that appears to come from legitimate servers.
detail.quizQuestion: A small spoofed DNS query triggers a much larger response that is sent to a victim, flooding it. What is this attack?

definition: A control that lets only approved applications run on a system and blocks everything else by default. It stops malware and unapproved software even when no signature exists for it. Also called application whitelisting.
examContext: A strong mitigation technique and hardening step on endpoints and servers, using tools such as AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control. It follows a default-deny model and needs maintenance when software changes.
analogy: A nightclub door that admits only people on the guest list, so a stranger is turned away no matter how well dressed.
relatedTerms: Allow list and deny list, Hardening, Implicit deny, Malware

detail.practicalScenario: The finance department's workstations run only the six approved applications. When an employee opens a downloaded trojan, the allow list blocks it from executing even though antivirus has never seen it.
detail.quizQuestion: Which control would stop an unknown, unapproved executable from running on a workstation even though antivirus has no signature for it?
quizOptions: C) A deny list of known malware

items.name: Segmentation
items.detail: Split the network so a compromise cannot spread freely.

items.name: Access control (ACLs and permissions)
items.detail: Restrict who and what can reach a resource.

items.name: Application allow list
items.detail: Only approved programs may run; everything else is blocked by default.

items.name: Isolation
items.detail: Separate or quarantine a risky or infected system from the rest of the environment.

items.name: Patching
items.detail: Fix known vulnerabilities.

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Protect data confidentiality at rest and in transit.

items.name: Monitoring
items.detail: Detect problems early through logging, SIEM and alerts.

items.name: Least privilege
items.detail: Grant only the access needed to do the job.

items.name: Configuration enforcement
items.detail: Automatically keep systems in line with the secure baseline.

items.name: Decommissioning
items.detail: Securely retire systems that are no longer needed, wiping data.

definition: An attack that sends forged ARP replies so other devices map the attacker's MAC address to a legitimate IP address (often the default gateway), allowing the attacker to intercept or alter traffic on the local network.
examContext: A common way to achieve an on-path position on a LAN. Defenses: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches, static ARP entries, port security and segmentation.
analogy: Someone swapping the name tag on a mailbox so the neighbor's mail is delivered to them instead.
relatedTerms: Man-in-the-middle attack, Spoofing, Network segmentation, ARP

detail.practicalScenario: A pentester on the office LAN sends forged ARP replies claiming to be the gateway. Traffic from several hosts flows through the tester's laptop, where it can be read and modified, until Dynamic ARP Inspection is enabled.
detail.quizQuestion: Which switch feature helps stop ARP poisoning?

definition: The practice of tracking hardware, software and data assets throughout their lifecycle, from acquisition and assignment through monitoring to disposal, so each has an owner, classification and security controls.
examContext: Know the lifecycle: acquisition and procurement, assignment and accounting (ownership, classification), monitoring and asset tracking (inventory, enumeration), and disposal or decommissioning (sanitization, destruction, certification, data retention).
analogy: A library catalog that records who owns each book, where it is and when it retires.
relatedTerms: Decommissioning, Data sanitization, Data destruction, Data classification, Shadow IT

detail.practicalScenario: A company keeps an inventory of every laptop and server with an owner and classification. During an incident it can instantly see which assets are affected and who is responsible for them.
detail.quizQuestion: Which practice tracks hardware, software and data from acquisition through disposal so every asset has an owner and classification?

items.name: Acquisition / procurement
items.detail: Buying and vetting hardware, software and services, including checking the supply chain.

items.name: Assignment / accounting
items.detail: Record ownership and classification so every asset has an accountable owner.

items.name: Monitoring / asset tracking
items.detail: Maintain an inventory and use enumeration to discover what is actually on the network.

items.name: Disposal / decommissioning
items.detail: Retire assets safely through sanitization or destruction, then confirm with a certificate.

items.name: Data retention
items.detail: Keep data only as long as required by policy or law, then dispose of it securely.

definition: An encryption method using a mathematically linked key pair, a public key that can be shared openly and a private key kept secret, so that data encrypted with one key can only be decrypted with the other.
examContext: SY0-701 expects you to know RSA and ECC as asymmetric algorithms and to understand that asymmetric encryption solves the key-distribution problem that symmetric encryption has, usually at the cost of speed.
analogy: Like a mailbox with a public slot anyone can drop mail into, but only the owner has the key to open the box and read it.
relatedTerms: Symmetric encryption, Public key, Private key, Key exchange, Hybrid encryption, Digital signature, Certificate

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan sets up a secure web portal where the server's public key is distributed in its certificate, allowing any client browser to encrypt a session key, while only the server's private key can decrypt it.
detail.quizQuestion: Two parties who have never communicated before need to securely establish a shared secret over an untrusted network. Which type of cryptography solves this key-distribution problem?

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

items.name: Symmetric
items.detail: One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts. Very fast, so it does the bulk data encryption. Weakness: securely sharing the key. N users need N(N-1)/2 keys.

items.name: Asymmetric
items.detail: A mathematically linked public/private key pair. Slow, so it is used for key exchange, digital signatures and certificates. Solves key distribution. N users need only 2N keys.

items.name: Hybrid
items.detail: Asymmetric crypto securely exchanges a random symmetric session key, then symmetric crypto encrypts the actual data. This is how TLS and most real systems work.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: No key (unless it is an HMAC) and no way back: a one-way function giving a fixed-length digest. Used for integrity and password storage, not for confidentiality.

items.name: Send a confidential message
items.detail: Encrypt with the RECIPIENT's PUBLIC key; only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.

items.name: Sign a message / prove authorship
items.detail: Sign with YOUR OWN PRIVATE key; anyone verifies with your public key. This gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.

items.name: Verify someone's signature
items.detail: Use the SIGNER's PUBLIC key (obtained from their certificate).

items.name: Decrypt a message sent to you
items.detail: Use YOUR OWN PRIVATE key.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: The private key never leaves its owner. The public key is shared freely. Encryption = their public key; signing = your private key.

definition: The sum of all possible points, including software, hardware, network, and human factors, where an unauthorized user could attempt to enter or extract data from a system.
examContext: Exam tests reducing the attack surface through hardening and disabling unused services and ports as a key mitigation strategy.
analogy: Like every door, window, and vent on a house, where the more there are, the more ways a burglar could try to get in.
relatedTerms: Attack vector, Hardening, Vulnerability, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: Chen disables unused network services and closes unnecessary open ports on company servers, reducing the overall attack surface available to potential intruders.
detail.quizQuestion: A systems administrator uninstalls unused software, closes unnecessary ports, and disables unneeded services on every server. What is the administrator primarily reducing?

variants.title: Common attack vectors and attack surfaces

items.name: Message-based
items.detail: Email, SMS and instant messaging carrying links, attachments or lures.

items.name: Image-based
items.detail: Malicious code or payloads hidden in image files (steganography) or malicious QR codes.

items.name: File-based
items.detail: Weaponized documents, PDFs, archives or macro-enabled Office files.

items.name: Voice call
items.detail: Vishing and pretext calls to the help desk.

items.name: Removable device
items.detail: USB drives dropped in a car park, or malicious cables.

items.name: Vulnerable software
items.detail: Unpatched client software (agent-based scanning sees it) or software that cannot host an agent (agentless scanning).

items.name: Unsupported systems
items.detail: End-of-life and end-of-support software receives no security patches.

items.name: Unsecure networks
items.detail: Open or poorly protected Wi-Fi, wired networks, and Bluetooth.

items.name: Open service ports
items.detail: Unneeded listening services that give attackers something to connect to.

items.name: Default credentials
items.detail: Factory usernames and passwords left unchanged.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Compromise through MSPs, vendors, suppliers, or tampered hardware and software updates.

items.name: Workstations and endpoints
items.detail: Install endpoint protection, enable a host firewall, patch, encrypt the disk, remove unnecessary software and bloatware, and run as a standard user.

items.name: Servers
items.detail: Minimal role-specific installs, disable unneeded services, patch, least privilege, logging and a secure baseline.

items.name: Switches and routers
items.detail: Change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH rather than Telnet, SNMPv3, port security, ACLs and firmware updates.

items.name: Cloud infrastructure
items.detail: Least-privilege IAM, MFA, no public storage buckets, encryption, logging and configuration scanning.

items.name: Mobile devices
items.detail: MDM policies, passcodes, encryption, remote wipe, app allow lists, and no sideloading.

items.name: IoT and embedded
items.detail: Change default credentials, update firmware, isolate on their own VLAN, and disable unused features.

items.name: ICS / SCADA / RTOS
items.detail: Segmentation or an air gap, strict physical security, monitoring and compensating controls, because patching is often impractical.

items.name: Common steps
items.detail: Change default passwords, disable unnecessary ports and protocols, remove unnecessary software, patch, and install endpoint protection.

items.name: Segmentation
items.detail: Split the network so a compromise cannot spread freely.

items.name: Access control (ACLs and permissions)
items.detail: Restrict who and what can reach a resource.

items.name: Application allow list
items.detail: Only approved programs may run; everything else is blocked by default.

items.name: Isolation
items.detail: Separate or quarantine a risky or infected system from the rest of the environment.

items.name: Patching
items.detail: Fix known vulnerabilities.

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Protect data confidentiality at rest and in transit.

items.name: Monitoring
items.detail: Detect problems early through logging, SIEM and alerts.

items.name: Least privilege
items.detail: Grant only the access needed to do the job.

items.name: Configuration enforcement
items.detail: Automatically keep systems in line with the secure baseline.

items.name: Decommissioning
items.detail: Securely retire systems that are no longer needed, wiping data.

definition: The specific path or method a threat actor uses to gain unauthorized access to a system, such as email, removable media, or a web application.
examContext: Exam lists common attack vectors, including email, direct access, wireless, supply chain, and social media, and expects you to identify which one a scenario describes.
analogy: Like the specific door or window a burglar used to enter a house.
relatedTerms: Attack surface, Threat actor, Phishing, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's incident response investigation determines that attackers gained initial entry through a malicious email attachment, identifying the phishing email as the attack vector used in the breach.
detail.quizQuestion: After a breach, forensic investigators determine attackers initially gained access through a compromised USB drive left in the parking lot. What does this delivery method represent?

variants.title: Common attack vectors and attack surfaces

items.name: Message-based
items.detail: Email, SMS and instant messaging carrying links, attachments or lures.

items.name: Image-based
items.detail: Malicious code or payloads hidden in image files (steganography) or malicious QR codes.

items.name: File-based
items.detail: Weaponized documents, PDFs, archives or macro-enabled Office files.

items.name: Voice call
items.detail: Vishing and pretext calls to the help desk.

items.name: Removable device
items.detail: USB drives dropped in a car park, or malicious cables.

items.name: Vulnerable software
items.detail: Unpatched client software (agent-based scanning sees it) or software that cannot host an agent (agentless scanning).

items.name: Unsupported systems
items.detail: End-of-life and end-of-support software receives no security patches.

items.name: Unsecure networks
items.detail: Open or poorly protected Wi-Fi, wired networks, and Bluetooth.

items.name: Open service ports
items.detail: Unneeded listening services that give attackers something to connect to.

items.name: Default credentials
items.detail: Factory usernames and passwords left unchanged.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Compromise through MSPs, vendors, suppliers, or tampered hardware and software updates.

definition: The process of formally verifying and vouching for the integrity, configuration, or compliance status of a system, component, or claim, often producing a signed statement that a relying party can check (e.g., remote attestation confirming a device's firmware or boot state hasn't been tampered with).
examContext: Know attestation can refer to a device cryptographically proving its boot or configuration integrity (remote attestation) or to a vendor formally vouching for compliance with a security standard; both appear in identity and third-party risk scenarios.
analogy: Like a notary stamping a document to formally certify 'I verified this is genuine,' giving anyone who sees the stamp a trustworthy, checkable claim without redoing the verification themselves.
relatedTerms: Due diligence, Due care, Governance, Digital signature, Non-repudiation

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's team enables remote attestation on all corporate laptops so that before a device can connect to the VPN, it must cryptographically prove its boot process and firmware haven't been modified, automatically blocking any laptop that fails the integrity check.
detail.quizQuestion: Before granting VPN access, a company's system requires each laptop to cryptographically prove that its boot firmware has not been altered since the last known-good state. What security process does this describe?

items.name: People
items.detail: Passwords and PINs, biometrics, smart cards and tokens, security keys, authenticator apps, MFA.

items.name: Systems and devices
items.detail: Machine certificates, 802.1X/NAC, device attestation (TPM measured boot), service accounts and API keys/secrets, IPsec certificates or pre-shared keys.

items.name: Mutual authentication
items.detail: BOTH sides prove who they are (EAP-TLS, mutual TLS, Kerberos), which defeats rogue servers and impersonation.

items.name: Internal
items.detail: Performed by the organization's own staff (an internal audit team or audit committee). Good for readiness and compliance checks; less independent.

items.name: External
items.detail: Performed by an independent third party or a regulator. More objective and credible.

items.name: Self-assessment
items.detail: The organization reviews its own controls against a checklist. Cheap and quick, but the least objective.

items.name: Regulatory examination
items.detail: An audit required by law or a regulator.

items.name: Independent third-party audit
items.detail: An outside auditor attests that controls work (for example a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certification).

items.name: Attestation
items.detail: A formal statement from an auditor or responsible party that controls are as described.

definition: An access control model that grants or denies access by evaluating a combination of attributes about the subject, the object, and the environment (such as job title, data sensitivity, device health, time of day, and location) against policy rules, rather than relying on a single fixed role.
examContext: Expect ABAC to be contrasted with RBAC on the exam: ABAC evaluates multiple attributes (user, resource, environment) for fine-grained, context-aware decisions, while RBAC grants access based on a single assigned role.
analogy: Like a nightclub bouncer who checks your age, the dress code, whether you're on the guest list, and how late it is before deciding to let you in, not just whether you hold a 'VIP' card.
relatedTerms: Role-based access control, Mandatory access control, Discretionary access control, Rule-based access control, Zero trust

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures the company's cloud access management platform so that finance employees can only open the payroll application when they are on a corporate-managed laptop, connecting from inside the country, and during normal business hours; anyone missing even one attribute is denied automatically.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital wants nurses to access patient records only when they are assigned to that patient's unit, using an approved device, and during their scheduled shift. Which access control model best fits this requirement?

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: The process of verifying that an entity, such as a user, device, or system, is who or what it claims to be.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes authentication, which proves identity, from authorization, which grants access; expect factor-based questions covering knowledge, possession, and inherence.
analogy: Like showing your ID badge at a building's front desk before anyone decides what floors you can visit.
relatedTerms: Authorization, Multifactor authentication, Biometrics, Single sign-on, Accountability

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures a VPN login to require a password plus a push notification to the employee's phone, confirming the user's identity before any resources are reached.
detail.quizQuestion: A help desk technician wants to verify that a remote employee logging in is actually who they claim to be, before deciding what files they can open. Which process is being performed first?

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

items.name: Length
items.detail: The strongest single factor against guessing and cracking. Favor long passphrases over short complex strings.

items.name: Complexity
items.detail: Requires mixed character types. Current NIST guidance prefers length plus a blocklist of known-bad passwords over forced complexity.

items.name: Reuse / history
items.detail: Password history stops users from recycling their last N passwords.

items.name: Expiration / maximum age
items.detail: Forces a change after a set time. Current NIST guidance says do not force routine changes unless there is evidence of compromise.

items.name: Minimum age
items.detail: Stops a user from changing the password repeatedly in one sitting to cycle back to an old one.

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Locks the account after N failed attempts. Defeats online brute force, but can be abused to lock out legitimate users (a denial of service).

items.name: Password manager
items.detail: Generates and stores unique strong passwords so users do not reuse them. Protect it with a strong master password and MFA.

items.name: Passwordless
items.detail: FIDO2 keys, passkeys and biometrics remove the shared secret that attackers phish or crack.

items.name: People
items.detail: Passwords and PINs, biometrics, smart cards and tokens, security keys, authenticator apps, MFA.

items.name: Systems and devices
items.detail: Machine certificates, 802.1X/NAC, device attestation (TPM measured boot), service accounts and API keys/secrets, IPsec certificates or pre-shared keys.

items.name: Mutual authentication
items.detail: BOTH sides prove who they are (EAP-TLS, mutual TLS, Kerberos), which defeats rogue servers and impersonation.

definition: A hardware or software item that generates or stores a credential used to prove identity, such as a key fob showing a rotating code, an authenticator app (TOTP) or an API or session token.
examContext: A hard token is a physical device; a soft token is an app. It is a "something you have" factor. The word "token" also means an access or session token in OAuth, so read the context.
analogy: A rotating-code key fob like the ones banks hand out.
relatedTerms: Multifactor authentication, Security key, Smart card, Single sign-on

detail.practicalScenario: An engineer uses an authenticator app that shows a new six-digit code every 30 seconds. The app is a soft token that proves she holds her registered device.
detail.quizQuestion: An authenticator app displays a six-digit code that changes every 30 seconds. What does this represent?

definition: The process of granting or denying an authenticated entity specific permissions to resources based on policy.
examContext: Exam questions often present a scenario where a user is authenticated but still denied access, testing that you recognize this as an authorization failure rather than an authentication one.
analogy: Like a hotel key card that only opens your assigned room floor, not every door in the building.
relatedTerms: Authentication, Least privilege, Role-based access control, Mandatory access control, Accountability

detail.practicalScenario: Alex sets up role-based permissions so that interns who successfully log into the network can only read shared drive folders, not modify payroll files.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee successfully logs in with correct credentials but is denied access when attempting to open the HR salary folder. Which process is responsible for that denial?

definition: Automation uses scripts and tools to perform individual tasks without manual effort; orchestration coordinates many automated tasks and systems into end-to-end workflows, as SOAR platforms do in security operations.
examContext: Benefits: efficiency, enforcing baselines, secure scaling, faster reaction time and a workforce multiplier. Drawbacks: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt and ongoing supportability.
analogy: Automation is a robot that welds one joint; orchestration is the conductor coordinating the whole assembly line.
relatedTerms: SOAR, IaC, Guard rail, Technical debt, Single point of failure

detail.practicalScenario: When the SIEM detects a compromised account, a SOAR playbook automatically disables the account, isolates the laptop, opens a ticket and notifies the analyst, all within seconds.
detail.quizQuestion: A platform automatically disables an account, isolates the host and opens a ticket when a SIEM alert fires. What is this an example of?

items.name: User provisioning
items.detail: Automatically create, change and remove accounts as people join, move and leave.

items.name: Resource provisioning
items.detail: Spin up servers, networks and cloud resources from code (infrastructure as code).

items.name: Guard rails
items.detail: Automated limits that stop risky actions before they happen.

items.name: Security groups
items.detail: Automatically apply and adjust network access rules.

items.name: Ticket creation and escalation
items.detail: Alerts automatically open tickets and escalate them if unanswered.

items.name: Enabling / disabling services and access
items.detail: Quickly turn services or accounts on or off, such as disabling a compromised account.

items.name: Continuous integration and testing
items.detail: Automatically build and test code on every change to catch problems early.

items.name: Integrations and APIs
items.detail: Connect tools so they share data and trigger each other (SOAR playbooks).

variants.title: Automation and orchestration: benefits and drawbacks

items.name: Efficiency / time saving
items.detail: Routine work is done faster and with less manual effort.

items.name: Enforcing baselines
items.detail: Every system is configured the same way, every time.

items.name: Standard infrastructure configurations
items.detail: Consistent builds reduce errors and drift.

items.name: Scaling securely
items.detail: Security grows automatically with the environment.

items.name: Employee retention
items.detail: Staff spend less time on repetitive tasks.

items.name: Reaction time
items.detail: Machines respond to incidents in seconds.

items.name: Workforce multiplier
items.detail: A small team can do the work of a much larger one.

items.name: Drawbacks
items.detail: Complexity, cost, a single point of failure (a broken script breaks everything), technical debt, and ongoing supportability.

definition: Ensuring authorized users have reliable and timely access to information and systems when needed.
examContext: Expect availability tied to denial-of-service attacks, redundancy, and fault tolerance questions; the exam tests recognizing availability-impacting incidents.
analogy: Like a 24-hour store that must stay open and stocked whenever customers want to shop.
relatedTerms: CIA triad, Fault tolerance, High availability, Failover, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures a load-balanced, multi-region web cluster so that if one data center loses power, customer traffic automatically fails over to another region without downtime.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's e-commerce site goes offline during a flash sale after being flooded with junk requests. Which element of the CIA triad was directly attacked?

definition: A hidden method of bypassing normal authentication or security controls to gain unauthorized access to a system, often installed by malware or a malicious insider.
examContext: Exam tests backdoors as providing persistent remote access, sometimes intentionally left by developers for testing and forgotten, or installed as a payload by a trojan.
analogy: Like a hidden spare key an intruder leaves under the mat after their first break-in, so they can return anytime.
relatedTerms: Trojan horse, Rootkit, Persistence, Command and control

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's security audit discovers an unauthorized remote access account quietly installed on the web server months earlier, giving attackers a standing backdoor that bypassed the normal login process entirely.
detail.quizQuestion: A forensic review finds an unauthorized hidden account configured to allow remote login that bypasses the application's normal authentication process entirely. What is this called?

definition: A predefined set of steps to reverse a change and return a system to its previous working state if the change fails or causes problems. It is normally required before a change is approved.
examContext: Part of change management alongside approvals, impact analysis, testing and a maintenance window. Also called a rollback plan. A change without a backout plan is a red flag for a change advisory board.
analogy: The way back down the mountain, planned before you start climbing.
relatedTerms: Change management, Maintenance window, Standard operating procedure, Disaster recovery

detail.practicalScenario: Before upgrading the production database, the team documents the backout plan: take a snapshot, keep the old version installed and define the exact steps and time limit for rolling back if tests fail.
detail.quizQuestion: Before approving a major database upgrade, the change advisory board asks how service will be restored if the upgrade fails. What are they asking for?

items.name: Approval process
items.detail: A formal review (often by a Change Advisory Board) before any change is made.

items.name: Ownership
items.detail: A named person responsible for the change.

items.name: Stakeholders
items.detail: Everyone affected who must be informed or consulted.

items.name: Impact analysis
items.detail: What could break, and how risky is the change?

items.name: Test results
items.detail: Proof the change works in a non-production environment first.

items.name: Backout plan
items.detail: The steps to undo the change if it fails.

items.name: Maintenance window
items.detail: A scheduled time when changes are allowed so users are least affected.

items.name: Standard operating procedure
items.detail: The documented way routine changes are performed.

definition: A copy of data or systems stored separately so it can be restored after loss, corruption, deletion or disaster. Backups are measured by how often they run (RPO), where they are stored and how long a restore takes (RTO).
examContext: Know full, incremental, differential and snapshot; onsite versus offsite; encryption; regularly testing restores; the 3-2-1 rule; and keeping at least one copy offline or immutable so ransomware cannot reach it.
analogy: A spare key kept at a friend's house.
relatedTerms: Full backup, Incremental backup, Differential backup, Snapshot, Disaster recovery, Ransomware

detail.practicalScenario: A company keeps three copies of its data: the live system, a nightly backup on local disk and an encrypted copy in another region with immutability turned on. After ransomware hits, it restores from the immutable copy.
detail.quizQuestion: Which practice BEST ensures ransomware cannot encrypt every copy of a company's backups?
quizOptions: A) Keeping an offline or immutable backup copy
B) Storing all backups on the same file server
C) Using RAID 5 on the backup server

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: A documented, approved standard set of security settings and software configurations for a system type, used as a reference point to detect unauthorized changes and ensure consistency across deployments.
examContext: Know baseline configurations are compared against current states to detect configuration drift; exam scenarios test recognizing deviation from baseline as a sign of unauthorized change or compromise.
analogy: Like a factory blueprint that every unit must match, any deviation from the blueprint signals something changed from the approved design.
relatedTerms: Hardening, Change management

detail.practicalScenario: Alex creates a baseline configuration template for all new web servers, specifying required security settings, and uses automated compliance scanning to flag any server whose running configuration has drifted from that approved baseline.
detail.quizQuestion: An automated tool flags that a production server's configuration no longer matches the organization's approved standard settings. What is this approved standard called?

variants.title: Policy, standard, procedure and guideline compared

items.name: Policy
items.detail: A high-level management statement of WHAT must be done and why. Broad, mandatory, and rarely changed (for example the Acceptable Use Policy).

items.name: Standard
items.detail: Specific, MANDATORY requirements that support a policy (passwords of 14+ characters, AES-256 for data at rest).

items.name: Procedure
items.detail: Step-by-step instructions on HOW to carry out a task (an onboarding checklist, a restore runbook).

items.name: Guideline
items.detail: Recommended best practice. ADVISORY and flexible, not mandatory.

items.name: Baseline
items.detail: The minimum secure configuration that systems must meet (see secure baseline).

items.name: Common policies
items.detail: Acceptable use, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management, password, remote access, data retention and onboarding/offboarding.

items.name: Workstations and endpoints
items.detail: Install endpoint protection, enable a host firewall, patch, encrypt the disk, remove unnecessary software and bloatware, and run as a standard user.

items.name: Servers
items.detail: Minimal role-specific installs, disable unneeded services, patch, least privilege, logging and a secure baseline.

items.name: Switches and routers
items.detail: Change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH rather than Telnet, SNMPv3, port security, ACLs and firmware updates.

items.name: Cloud infrastructure
items.detail: Least-privilege IAM, MFA, no public storage buckets, encryption, logging and configuration scanning.

items.name: Mobile devices
items.detail: MDM policies, passcodes, encryption, remote wipe, app allow lists, and no sideloading.

items.name: IoT and embedded
items.detail: Change default credentials, update firmware, isolate on their own VLAN, and disable unused features.

items.name: ICS / SCADA / RTOS
items.detail: Segmentation or an air gap, strict physical security, monitoring and compensating controls, because patching is often impractical.

items.name: Common steps
items.detail: Change default passwords, disable unnecessary ports and protocols, remove unnecessary software, patch, and install endpoint protection.

definition: An authentication factor category based on something you are, using unique physical or behavioral characteristics such as fingerprints, facial geometry, iris patterns, or voice to verify identity.
examContext: Know biometrics as a something-you-are factor, and the exam-relevant metrics: false acceptance rate, false rejection rate, and the crossover error rate where they are equal, used to judge biometric system accuracy.
analogy: Like recognizing a close friend by their face and voice instantly, without needing them to show ID or state a password.
relatedTerms: Multifactor authentication, Smart card

detail.practicalScenario: Sam deploys fingerprint scanners at the data center entrance as a biometric access control, and during testing adjusts the sensor's sensitivity to balance the false acceptance rate against the false rejection rate for optimal security without excessive employee frustration.
detail.quizQuestion: A data center wants to use a biometric fingerprint scanner for physical access control. What metric describes the point where the false acceptance rate and false rejection rate are equal?

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

items.name: Fingerprint
items.detail: Cheap and widely accepted, but can be fooled by lifted prints or fakes unless liveness detection is used.

items.name: Retina
items.detail: Scans the blood-vessel pattern at the back of the eye. Very accurate but intrusive, so uncommon.

items.name: Iris
items.detail: Scans the coloured ring around the pupil. Accurate and stable over a lifetime, and less intrusive than retina.

items.name: Facial recognition
items.detail: Convenient, but affected by lighting and angle, and spoofable with photos or masks without liveness checks.

items.name: Voice
items.detail: Affected by noise and illness; spoofable with recordings or deepfakes.

items.name: Vein / palm
items.detail: Maps the pattern of blood vessels; difficult to forge.

items.name: Gait
items.detail: A behavioral biometric based on how a person walks.

items.name: FRR (Type I)
items.detail: False Rejection Rate: a LEGITIMATE user is wrongly denied. Hurts usability.

items.name: FAR (Type II)
items.detail: False Acceptance Rate: an IMPOSTOR is wrongly allowed in. This is the dangerous one for security.

items.name: CER / EER
items.detail: Crossover (Equal) Error Rate: the point where FAR equals FRR. The LOWER the CER, the more accurate the system.

definition: A type of collision attack that exploits the mathematics of probability, which shows that finding two inputs sharing the same hash output requires far fewer attempts than brute-forcing one specific hash, named for the statistical surprise behind the birthday paradox.
examContext: Know the birthday attack as the probability-based reasoning behind why collision attacks against hash functions succeed faster than brute-force intuition would suggest, which is why hash digests need sufficient output length to resist them.
analogy: Like discovering it only takes about 23 random people in a room before two likely share the same birthday, far fewer than the 366 you'd assume are needed, because you're comparing everyone against everyone, not just against one fixed date.
relatedTerms: Collision attack, Hashing, Key stretching

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan explains to the development team why the new hashing scheme needs a long output length: a birthday attack means an attacker needs far fewer guesses than the total possible hash values to find two inputs that collide, so a short digest would be crackable much sooner than it looks.
detail.quizQuestion: A cryptographer explains that finding two inputs with matching hash values takes dramatically fewer attempts than the total number of possible hash outputs would suggest, due to simple probability math. What principle is being described?

definition: Unwanted software pre-installed by a device manufacturer or bundled with other programs. It wastes resources, may contain vulnerabilities or telemetry, and increases the attack surface.
examContext: Handled during hardening by removing unnecessary software. Related terms: PUP (potentially unwanted program) and adware.
analogy: The promotional flyers a car dealer leaves in the glove box: you did not ask for them, and they only take up space.
relatedTerms: Hardening, Attack surface, Adware, PUP, Secure baseline

detail.practicalScenario: A new laptop arrives with a dozen trial programs and a manufacturer utility that has a known vulnerability. IT's standard image removes all of them before deployment to shrink the attack surface.
detail.quizQuestion: Which hardening step addresses unneeded trial software that a manufacturer preinstalled on new laptops?

definition: A symmetric encryption algorithm that encrypts data in fixed-size chunks, such as AES's 128-bit blocks, often requiring padding and an operation mode like CBC or GCM for data that doesn't fit evenly.
examContext: Know AES as the standard block cipher; the exam may ask you to distinguish block ciphers, which use fixed-size chunks, from stream ciphers, which process data continuously bit by bit.
analogy: Like washing dishes in fixed-size batches in a dishwasher, rather than one plate at a time.
relatedTerms: Stream cipher, Symmetric encryption, Cipher suite

detail.practicalScenario: Sam selects AES-256 in GCM mode to encrypt stored customer records, taking advantage of the block cipher's fixed-size block processing plus built-in authentication to detect any tampering with the encrypted data.
detail.quizQuestion: Which type of cipher processes plaintext in fixed-size chunks, such as AES's 128-bit segments?

items.name: DES
items.detail: 56-bit key, 64-bit block. Broken by brute force decades ago; obsolete. Know it only as the "weak legacy" answer.

items.name: 3DES
items.detail: Runs DES three times (up to 168-bit key, ~112 bits effective). Slow, 64-bit blocks make it vulnerable to birthday-style attacks; deprecated and being retired.

items.name: AES
items.detail: The standard. 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Fast, hardware-accelerated (AES-NI), and used everywhere: TLS, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), disk encryption.

items.name: Blowfish
items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

items.name: ECB
items.detail: Every block is encrypted independently with the same key, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext and patterns leak through. Never use it for real data.

items.name: CBC
items.detail: Each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block before encryption, using a random IV for the first. Hides patterns, but encryption is sequential and padding-oracle attacks exist.

items.name: CFB
items.detail: Feeds the previous ciphertext back through the cipher, turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream cipher.

items.name: OFB
items.detail: Generates a keystream independent of the plaintext, so a bit error in transit affects only that bit.

items.name: CTR
items.detail: Encrypts an incrementing counter to build the keystream. Parallelizable and allows random access; the counter/nonce must never repeat with the same key.

items.name: GCM
items.detail: Counter mode plus built-in authentication (AEAD): gives confidentiality AND integrity. Fast and parallelizable; the default for AES in TLS 1.2/1.3 and WPA3.

definition: A distributed, append-only ledger technology in which transactions are grouped into cryptographically linked blocks and validated by a decentralized consensus mechanism, making records resistant to unauthorized alteration without a central authority.
examContext: Know blockchain is presented as a cryptographic solution that provides integrity and non-repudiation for a shared transaction history through decentralized consensus, rather than a tool for confidentiality.
analogy: Like a shared ledger book copied identically across hundreds of accountants' desks; to fake one entry, you'd have to secretly change every single copy at once, which is practically impossible.
relatedTerms: Hashing, Digital signature, Non-repudiation, Integrity, Encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's supply chain team implements a blockchain-based ledger to record each time a shipment changes custody between manufacturers, carriers, and warehouses, so that every party can verify the shipment's full history has not been tampered with, without needing to trust a single central database owner.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to guarantee that a shared transaction history among multiple untrusted business partners cannot be secretly altered by any single party after the fact. Which technology best supports this goal?

definition: The internal or hired group of defenders responsible for monitoring, detecting, and responding to security threats and attacks, including those simulated by a red team during an exercise.
examContext: Know the blue team consists of defenders who use SIEM, IDS/IPS, and monitoring tools to detect and respond to attacks; often contrasted with the red team on the exam.
analogy: Like the home security guards and response crew who must detect and stop the simulated intruders during a training drill.
relatedTerms: Red team, Purple team, Threat hunting

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's blue team monitors SIEM alerts throughout the red team engagement, successfully detecting the simulated attacker's lateral movement attempt within twenty minutes and isolating the affected workstation before further compromise.
detail.quizQuestion: During a red team exercise, which group is responsible for detecting and responding to the simulated attack in real time?

items.name: Red team
items.detail: OFFENSE: simulates real attackers to find weaknesses.

items.name: Blue team
items.detail: DEFENSE: monitors, detects and responds to attacks, and hardens systems.

items.name: Purple team
items.detail: Red and blue working together and sharing findings in real time to improve detection and response.

items.name: White team
items.detail: Referees and sets the rules of an exercise (scope, scoring, safety).

definition: Sending unsolicited messages or contact cards to nearby Bluetooth-enabled devices. It is more of an annoyance and does not steal data.
examContext: Contrast with bluesnarfing, which steals data. Mitigation: set Bluetooth to non-discoverable or turn it off when not in use.
analogy: Dropping unwanted flyers under windshield wipers in a parking lot.
relatedTerms: Bluesnarfing, BLE, Evil twin, War driving

detail.practicalScenario: A commuter's phone shows a spam message from an unknown nearby Bluetooth device. Nothing is copied from the phone; the sender only wanted to push a message.
detail.quizQuestion: A commuter's phone receives an unsolicited message from a nearby Bluetooth device, but no data is taken. What is this?

definition: Unauthorized access to a Bluetooth device to steal data such as contacts, calendar entries and messages, exploiting vulnerable pairing or protocol flaws.
examContext: More serious than bluejacking. Defenses: turn off Bluetooth when not in use, disable discoverable mode, patch firmware and require pairing approval.
analogy: A pickpocket quietly lifting your wallet in a crowd, compared with a prankster handing you a flyer.
relatedTerms: Bluejacking, BLE, Wireless jamming, Smishing

detail.practicalScenario: In a crowded cafe, an attacker connects to an unpatched phone over Bluetooth and copies its contact list without the owner noticing. The owner later finds the data in a phishing campaign.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker silently copies a victim's contacts over Bluetooth without consent. What attack is this?

definition: A short, sturdy vertical post installed in the ground, typically in a row, to block vehicle access to a pedestrian area or building entrance while still allowing people to walk through.
examContext: An objective 1.2 physical security control; the exam tests recognizing bollards as a vehicle-specific barrier, distinct from fencing, which blocks both people and vehicles along a full perimeter.
analogy: Like a row of concrete teeth planted outside a storefront that stop a car from driving in but let shoppers walk right past.
relatedTerms: Fencing, Access control vestibule, Security guard

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's facilities team installs a line of steel bollards along the sidewalk in front of the data center's main entrance to prevent a vehicle-ramming attack while keeping the walkway open for employees on foot.
detail.quizQuestion: After a security assessment flags the risk of a vehicle being driven into the building's lobby, which physical control should be installed to block vehicles while still allowing pedestrians to enter?

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

definition: A network of compromised, internet-connected devices known as bots that are remotely controlled by an attacker, typically used to carry out coordinated attacks such as distributed denial of service.
examContext: Exam tests botnets as directed through command-and-control infrastructure, commonly used for DDoS attacks, spam, or large-scale cryptomining.
analogy: Like a puppet master pulling the strings on thousands of zombie puppets all at once.
relatedTerms: Command and control, Malware, Cryptojacking

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's network team notices thousands of compromised IoT cameras worldwide suddenly flooding a company's web server with traffic simultaneously, all controlled remotely as part of a coordinated botnet.
detail.quizQuestion: Thousands of compromised smart devices across the globe simultaneously flood a single website with traffic on command from a remote attacker. What is this network of compromised devices called?

definition: An attack in which the attacker mimics a well-known company's logos, branding, email templates, or overall look and feel to deceive victims into trusting a fraudulent message, website, or call.
examContext: The exam treats brand impersonation as a broader deception tactic that can combine with phishing, typosquatting, or vishing; the key detail is that the attack relies on borrowed visual or verbal trust rather than any single technical method.
analogy: Like a counterfeiter printing a fake designer label onto a cheap bag, relying on the recognizable brand to earn instant trust it hasn't actually earned.
relatedTerms: Typosquatting, Phishing, Vishing, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team flags a phishing campaign that perfectly replicates a major bank's logo, email formatting, and color scheme in a message warning customers their account is locked, convincing many recipients the email is legitimate.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees receive an email that perfectly replicates a well-known software vendor's logo, formatting, and tone, asking them to confirm their license key on a linked site. Which tactic is primarily being used?

items.name: Phishing
items.detail: Mass, generic lures, usually email, that try to steal credentials or deliver malware.

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
