items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: The group of devices that receive each other's broadcast frames, in other words all devices on the same Layer 2 network. Switches forward broadcasts to every port in a VLAN, while routers do not forward them, so each VLAN and each router interface is its own broadcast domain.
examContext: Routers and VLANs split broadcast domains, while hubs and plain switches do not. Smaller broadcast domains mean less noise and a smaller area for attacks that rely on broadcasts, such as ARP poisoning and rogue DHCP servers.
analogy: Everyone within earshot of a loudspeaker announcement; walls keep it from reaching other rooms.
relatedTerms: VLAN, Switch, Router, Collision domain, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: A flat office network of 400 devices suffers from heavy broadcast traffic. The team splits it into four VLANs, and each VLAN becomes its own, smaller broadcast domain.
detail.quizQuestion: Which device does NOT forward broadcast traffic between its interfaces, and therefore separates broadcast domains?

definition: An attack method that systematically attempts every possible combination of characters or keys until the correct password or cryptographic key is found, requiring significant computational time but guaranteed to eventually succeed against an unlimited attempt budget.
examContext: Know brute force differs from dictionary attacks, which try a curated wordlist instead of every combination; mitigations include account lockout, key stretching, and strong, long passwords; the exam may ask you to identify this versus other password attacks from a description.
analogy: Like trying every single number combination on a padlock one by one until it finally opens.
relatedTerms: Account lockout, Key stretching, Dictionary attack, Credential stuffing

detail.practicalScenario: Alex notices in the authentication logs that a single account received tens of thousands of login attempts using sequentially generated password strings within an hour, and recognizes this systematic character-by-character approach as a brute force attack rather than a targeted guess.
detail.quizQuestion: Authentication logs show an account receiving tens of thousands of sequential login attempts trying every possible character combination within a short period. What type of attack does this indicate?

items.name: Length
items.detail: The strongest single factor against guessing and cracking. Favor long passphrases over short complex strings.

items.name: Complexity
items.detail: Requires mixed character types. Current NIST guidance prefers length plus a blocklist of known-bad passwords over forced complexity.

items.name: Reuse / history
items.detail: Password history stops users from recycling their last N passwords.

items.name: Expiration / maximum age
items.detail: Forces a change after a set time. Current NIST guidance says do not force routine changes unless there is evidence of compromise.

items.name: Minimum age
items.detail: Stops a user from changing the password repeatedly in one sitting to cycle back to an old one.

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Locks the account after N failed attempts. Defeats online brute force, but can be abused to lock out legitimate users (a denial of service).

items.name: Password manager
items.detail: Generates and stores unique strong passwords so users do not reuse them. Protect it with a strong master password and MFA.

items.name: Passwordless
items.detail: FIDO2 keys, passkeys and biometrics remove the shared secret that attackers phish or crack.

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: A software vulnerability that occurs when a program writes more data to a memory buffer than it was allocated to hold, potentially overwriting adjacent memory and allowing code execution.
examContext: Exam tests buffer overflow as a classic application vulnerability, mitigated through input validation, bounds checking, and secure coding practices such as data execution prevention and address space layout randomization.
analogy: Like overfilling a glass of water until it spills onto and damages the papers sitting next to it on the table.
relatedTerms: Exploit, Vulnerability, Privilege escalation

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's code review tool flags a function that fails to validate input length before copying it into a fixed-size array, a classic buffer overflow flaw that could let an attacker overwrite memory and execute arbitrary code.
detail.quizQuestion: A developer finds that a legacy application does not check the length of user input before copying it into a fixed-size memory array, potentially letting an attacker overwrite adjacent memory with malicious instructions. What vulnerability class is this?

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: A program that rewards independent researchers with money or recognition for responsibly reporting valid security vulnerabilities in an organization's systems, within defined scope and rules.
examContext: A vulnerability identification method alongside responsible disclosure programs, often run through platforms such as HackerOne or Bugcrowd. It defines scope, safe harbor and payouts.
analogy: A reward poster for anyone who finds and reports a hole in the fence.
relatedTerms: Responsible disclosure, Penetration testing, Vulnerability, Rules of engagement

detail.practicalScenario: A software company publishes a bounty policy listing which systems are in scope and what each severity pays. A researcher reports a serious flaw privately, the company fixes it and pays the reward.
detail.quizQuestion: A company pays outside researchers for privately reporting valid security flaws in its web application. What is this called?

definition: The planning and preparation that ensures an organization's critical business functions can continue operating during and after a disruptive event, encompassing policies, procedures, and resources beyond just IT systems.
examContext: Know business continuity planning is broader than disaster recovery, since it covers the whole organization's ability to keep operating including people, processes, and facilities, while disaster recovery focuses specifically on restoring IT systems; know the business impact analysis as a key supporting activity.
analogy: Like a company having a backup plan to keep serving customers from a temporary location with pen-and-paper processes even if the main office and all computers are completely unavailable.
relatedTerms: Disaster recovery, Fault tolerance, High availability

detail.practicalScenario: Sam leads a business continuity planning exercise that identifies critical functions like order processing and customer support, then establishes manual fallback procedures and an alternate work site so the company can keep serving customers even if the main office becomes unusable.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to ensure that critical customer-facing operations can continue even if its main office building becomes completely unusable for an extended period. Which type of plan addresses this broadest organizational concern?

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: A targeted social engineering attack in which an attacker compromises or convincingly spoofs a trusted email account, often an executive's, to trick an employee into wiring money, changing payment details, or disclosing sensitive information.
examContext: The exam frequently pairs BEC with whaling and invoice-fraud scenarios; a key detail is that BEC often requires no malware at all, relying purely on a convincing, well-researched impersonation of a trusted sender.
analogy: Like a con artist forging a signature on a company check, imitating the boss's handwriting well enough that the bank teller doesn't question it.
relatedTerms: Whaling, Phishing, Spear phishing, Social engineering, Pretexting

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's finance department receives an urgent email appearing to come from the CFO's exact email address requesting an immediate wire transfer to a new vendor account, which the team catches only after calling the CFO directly to verify.
detail.quizQuestion: An accounts payable employee receives an email that appears to come from the CEO's real email address, urgently requesting a wire transfer to a new account. What is this attack called?

items.name: Spear phishing

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: Forecasting and provisioning the people, technology and infrastructure needed to meet future demand so services stay available under load, growth and failure.
examContext: Covers three areas: people, technology and infrastructure. It supports availability and avoids outages caused by legitimate overload, which looks like a denial of service.
analogy: Planning enough seats, cooks and ovens for next year's dinner rush before it arrives.
relatedTerms: Scalability and elasticity, High availability, Redundancy, Business continuity

detail.practicalScenario: Before a seasonal sale, the team estimates traffic, adds servers and bandwidth and arranges extra support staff. The site stays up even when visits triple.
detail.quizQuestion: Before a seasonal sale, a team forecasts traffic and provisions extra servers, bandwidth and staff to keep services available. What is this called?

definition: Using a hidden device on a card reader, ATM or point-of-sale terminal to capture card data from the magnetic stripe, sometimes with a camera to record the PIN. The data is then used to clone cards.
examContext: Mitigate with EMV chip cards, tamper-evident seals, regular inspection of terminals, and contactless or tokenized payments. Falls under physical attacks.
analogy: A fake sleeve over the card slot that quietly copies your card as it goes in.
relatedTerms: RFID cloning, Tokenization, Shoulder surfing, Smart card

detail.practicalScenario: A cashier notices a thin overlay on a gas-pump card reader. It had been recording card numbers for days; the station adds tamper-evident seals and switches to chip-only readers.
detail.quizQuestion: A thin device fitted over a gas pump's card reader records card numbers as customers pay. What is this attack called?

definition: A digital document issued by a certificate authority that binds a public key to an identity, such as a person, server, or organization, verified through the CA's digital signature.
examContext: Know the X.509 standard and the fields it contains, such as subject, issuer, public key, and validity period; exam scenarios often involve expired or untrusted certificates causing browser warnings.
analogy: Like a notarized ID card that proves a public key truly belongs to the entity claiming it.
relatedTerms: Certificate authority, Chain of trust, Public key, Digital signature

detail.practicalScenario: Maria installs an SSL/TLS certificate issued by a trusted certificate authority on the company's web server so that visitors' browsers can confirm the site's identity and establish an encrypted connection without security warnings.
detail.quizQuestion: Users visiting a company website receive a browser warning that the site's identity cannot be verified. What is the most likely cause?
quizOptions: A) The site is using symmetric encryption
B) The site has been salted
C) The certificate is expired or untrusted
D) The private key was hashed

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

items.name: Self-signed
items.detail: Signed by its own private key, so no third party vouches for it. Free and fine for labs or internal dev, but browsers warn users and it cannot be revoked by a public CA.

items.name: Public CA-issued
items.detail: Signed by a CA that browsers and operating systems already trust. Required for public-facing sites.

items.name: Wildcard
items.detail: One certificate for *.example.com, covering every first-level subdomain. Convenient, but one stolen key exposes all of them.

items.name: SAN (Subject Alternative Name)
items.detail: One certificate that lists several specific hostnames or domains. Not to be confused with a SAN as a Storage Area Network; the exam uses both meanings.

items.name: DV / OV / EV
items.detail: Domain Validation proves only control of the domain; Organization Validation vets the company; Extended Validation is the strictest vetting.

items.name: Code signing
items.detail: Proves who published software and that it has not been altered since signing.

items.name: Machine / user / email
items.detail: Certificates that authenticate a device or a person, or sign and encrypt email (S/MIME).

items.name: Root certificate
items.detail: Self-signed certificate at the top of a chain, pre-installed in the OS/browser trust store.

definition: A trusted entity that issues, signs, and manages digital certificates, verifying the identity of certificate requestors and forming the root of trust in a public key infrastructure.
examContext: Know the CA's role in PKI, including issuing, renewing, and revoking certificates via CRL or OCSP; the exam may ask what happens when a CA itself is compromised, since all certificates it issued become untrustworthy.
analogy: Like a government passport office, it verifies your identity before issuing a document that others will trust without checking your identity themselves.
relatedTerms: Certificate, Chain of trust, Public key, Digital signature

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company sets up an internal certificate authority to issue certificates to all internal servers, allowing employee devices to automatically trust those servers without browser warnings, since the internal CA's root certificate is pre-installed on company machines.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants internal web servers to present trusted certificates to employee browsers without manual trust exceptions. What should the company deploy?

definition: A technique where an application is configured to accept only a specific certificate or public key for a given server, rather than any certificate signed by a trusted CA. It guards against rogue or compromised CAs and on-path attackers presenting fraudulent certificates.
examContext: Mobile apps commonly pin to defeat TLS interception. The drawback is operational: pinned certificates must be rotated carefully or the app breaks. Related to chain of trust and on-path attacks.
analogy: Like a bank teller who only accepts one particular signature card from you instead of any ID that looks official.
relatedTerms: Certificate, Chain of trust, Man-in-the-middle attack, Certificate authority

detail.practicalScenario: A banking app pins the bank server's public key. When an attacker on public Wi-Fi presents a fraudulent but CA-signed certificate, the app refuses the connection because the key does not match the pinned one.
detail.quizQuestion: A mobile app only accepts one specific server public key, even when another certificate is signed by a trusted CA. What is this technique called?

definition: A documented, chronological record of who collected, handled, transferred, and stored a piece of evidence, establishing that the evidence has not been altered or tampered with from collection through legal proceedings.
examContext: Know chain of custody documentation must record who collected, handled, and transferred evidence and when; any break in that chain can get evidence ruled inadmissible in court.
analogy: Like a relay race baton that every runner must sign for before and after carrying it, so there's an unbroken paper trail proving no one swapped it along the way.
relatedTerms: Incident response, Legal hold, e-Discovery, Non-repudiation, Attestation

detail.practicalScenario: Priya seizes a compromised laptop as evidence, immediately logs the date, time, her name, and a hash of the hard drive image, then has each subsequent person who handles the drive sign and date the same form, ensuring the evidence remains legally admissible if the case goes to trial.
detail.quizQuestion: During a forensic investigation, an analyst fails to document who handled a seized hard drive between collection and analysis. What is the most likely consequence?
quizOptions: A) The evidence becomes encrypted automatically
B) The evidence may be ruled inadmissible in court due to a broken chain of custody
C) The legal hold is automatically lifted
D) The e-Discovery process must restart from scratch

variants.title: Digital forensics: order of volatility and handling

items.name: Order of volatility
items.detail: Collect the MOST volatile evidence first: CPU registers and cache, then RAM (routing/ARP tables, processes), then swap/page file, then disk, then remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.

items.name: Preservation
items.detail: Use write blockers, work on forensic copies, and hash the image to prove it was not changed.

items.name: Acquisition
items.detail: A bit-for-bit disk image, a memory dump, or a snapshot. Live acquisition is needed to capture volatile data.

items.name: Chain of custody
items.detail: Documented record of who handled the evidence, when and why. Gaps can make evidence inadmissible.

items.name: Legal hold
items.detail: A mandate to preserve relevant data (stop normal deletion) because of litigation or investigation.

items.name: e-Discovery
items.detail: Identifying and collecting electronic information for legal proceedings.

items.name: Timeline and reporting
items.detail: Reconstruct events, document findings and make the report clear and reproducible.

definition: The hierarchical sequence of certificates from a root certificate authority through intermediate CAs down to an end-entity certificate, where each link is validated by the signature of the certificate above it, establishing overall trust.
examContext: Know the structure of root CA, intermediate CA, and end-entity certificate; exam scenarios test what happens if an intermediate certificate is missing, since browsers may show trust errors even if the root is valid.
analogy: Like a chain of personal introductions, you trust a stranger because someone you already trust vouches for them, who in turn was vouched for by someone even more trusted.
relatedTerms: Certificate authority, Certificate, Digital signature

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan troubleshoots a browser trust error on a company website and discovers the server is missing its intermediate certificate, breaking the chain of trust between the root CA and the site's end-entity certificate; installing the intermediate certificate resolves the warning.
detail.quizQuestion: Users report trust warnings when visiting a website, even though the site's certificate was issued by a well-known root CA. What is the most likely cause?
quizOptions: A) A missing intermediate certificate breaking the chain of trust
B) The private key was escrowed
C) The cipher suite is too weak
D) The site is using a stream cipher

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: A formal, documented process for proposing, reviewing, approving, implementing, and recording changes to IT systems, designed to minimize unintended disruptions and maintain security and stability.
examContext: Know the key elements: change request, impact analysis, approval from a change advisory board, testing, a rollback or backout plan, and documentation; exam scenarios often test recognizing an unauthorized change that skipped this process as a security risk.
analogy: Like requiring a building permit and inspection before any major renovation, ensuring changes are reviewed, approved, and documented rather than made on a whim.
relatedTerms: Baseline configuration, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan submits a formal change request to the change advisory board before modifying a production firewall rule, documenting the business justification, expected impact, testing results, and a rollback plan in case the change causes unexpected issues.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator wants to modify a production firewall rule. According to best practice, what should happen before the change is implemented?
quizOptions: A) The change should go through a formal change management approval process
B) The change should be made immediately to minimize downtime
C) The change should be tested only in production
D) The change should bypass documentation to save time

items.name: Approval process
items.detail: A formal review (often by a Change Advisory Board) before any change is made.

items.name: Ownership
items.detail: A named person responsible for the change.

items.name: Stakeholders
items.detail: Everyone affected who must be informed or consulted.

items.name: Impact analysis
items.detail: What could break, and how risky is the change?

items.name: Test results
items.detail: Proof the change works in a non-production environment first.

items.name: Backout plan
items.detail: The steps to undo the change if it fails.

items.name: Maintenance window
items.detail: A scheduled time when changes are allowed so users are least affected.

items.name: Standard operating procedure
items.detail: The documented way routine changes are performed.

variants.title: Change management: technical implications and documentation

items.name: Allow lists / deny lists
items.detail: Changes may require editing the lists of approved or blocked applications, IPs or sites.

items.name: Restricted activities
items.detail: Some actions may be forbidden during a change window or freeze.

items.name: Downtime
items.detail: Planned outages that must be communicated.

items.name: Service / application restart
items.detail: A restart may be required for the change to take effect and can interrupt users.

items.name: Legacy applications
items.detail: Old software may break or not be supported after a change.

items.name: Dependencies
items.detail: Other systems and services that rely on the thing being changed.

items.name: Documentation
items.detail: Update network diagrams, policies and procedures after the change.

items.name: Version control
items.detail: Track every version of configurations and code so you can see what changed, who changed it, and roll back.

definition: A small fixed-size value calculated from a block of data (with a simple algorithm such as a byte sum or CRC) and stored or sent alongside it, so the receiver can recalculate the value and detect accidental corruption. Checksums are not built to resist deliberate tampering, so they are weaker than cryptographic hashes.
examContext: Know that a checksum catches accidental errors (transmission noise, bad sectors) while a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 is what you compare against a vendor-published value to confirm a file was not maliciously altered. If a question is about proving authenticity or non-repudiation, a checksum is the wrong answer; think HMAC or digital signature.
analogy: Like counting the pieces in a parcel against the packing slip: it reveals a missing or damaged item, but a thief who swaps a piece and rewrites the slip would never be caught.
relatedTerms: Hashing, Digital signature, Integrity, Collision attack, Non-repudiation, CRC

detail.practicalScenario: Priya downloads a Linux ISO and runs sha256sum on it, then compares the result with the SHA-256 value on the distribution's official site. The values match, so she knows the file arrived intact and was not swapped for a tampered build. She notes that a plain CRC32 value would only have caught accidental corruption, not a deliberate substitution.
detail.quizQuestion: Which statement about a simple checksum is TRUE?
quizOptions: A) It proves who created the file
B) It detects accidental corruption but gives little protection against deliberate tampering
C) It is collision-resistant by design
D) It encrypts the data to keep it confidential

items.name: Checksum / CRC
items.detail: A small value computed from the data to catch ACCIDENTAL corruption (bit flips in transit or on disk). Fast and simple, but not secure: an attacker can alter the data and recompute a matching checksum. CRC is the common checksum algorithm (Ethernet frames, ZIP).

items.name: Cryptographic hash
items.detail: One-way function (SHA-256, SHA-3) producing a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the digest completely. Detects tampering, but anyone can recompute it, so it only proves integrity if the expected hash comes from a trusted source (e.g., the vendor's website).

items.name: HMAC
items.detail: A hash combined with a shared secret key. Proves integrity AND authenticity (only a key holder could produce it). No non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key.

items.name: Digital signature
items.detail: A hash encrypted with the sender's private key and verified with their public key. Proves integrity, authenticity AND non-repudiation. It is the strongest option because only the signer holds the private key.

definition: The foundational security model composed of Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability, used to evaluate and prioritize security controls.
examContext: Nearly every SY0-701 scenario question can be mapped back to one or more legs of the CIA triad; some questions pair it with the opposing DAD framework of disclosure, alteration, and denial.
analogy: Like a three-legged stool, where removing any one leg causes the whole thing to fall over.
relatedTerms: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, Risk management

detail.practicalScenario: Sam uses the CIA triad as a checklist when designing a new payment system, ensuring data is encrypted for confidentiality, validated with hashes for integrity, and backed up with redundancy for availability.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst is asked to evaluate a new application against the three core goals of information security. Which model should the analyst apply?

definition: A negotiated set of algorithms, including the key exchange method, bulk encryption cipher, and message authentication or hash function, that two systems agree to use to secure a TLS connection.
examContext: Know that during the TLS handshake, the client and server negotiate a cipher suite; the exam may present a cipher suite string and ask you to identify its components, such as ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384.
analogy: Like two parties agreeing on a shared language, lock type, and seal before exchanging sensitive documents, all parts must match for communication to work.
relatedTerms: Key exchange, Block cipher, Perfect forward secrecy, Asymmetric encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Priya hardens the company's web server configuration by disabling weak cipher suites and enforcing only those that use ECDHE key exchange and AES-GCM encryption, ensuring strong forward secrecy for all client connections.
detail.quizQuestion: During a TLS handshake, a client and server must agree on which combination of algorithms to use for the session. What is this negotiated combination called?

items.name: SSL 2.0 / 3.0
items.detail: Broken (SSL 3.0 fell to POODLE) and prohibited. SSL as a name survives only in casual speech; it is TLS now.

items.name: TLS 1.0 / 1.1
items.detail: Deprecated by the IETF in 2021; vulnerable to attacks such as BEAST. Disable them.

items.name: TLS 1.2
items.detail: Still widely deployed and secure when configured with ECDHE key exchange and AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM.

items.name: TLS 1.3
items.detail: Current version: faster 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy mandatory, and weak options (RC4, 3DES, SHA-1, static-RSA key exchange, CBC) removed.

definition: The process of applying a digital signature to software or code using the publisher's private key, allowing recipients to verify the software's authenticity and confirm it hasn't been altered since it was signed.
examContext: Know code signing relies on asymmetric cryptography and a trusted certificate authority, and that operating systems routinely block execution of unsigned or tampered software; a failed signature check is a classic indicator of a supply chain compromise.
analogy: Like a manufacturer sealing a product box with a tamper-evident sticker bearing their official stamp, so a customer immediately knows if anyone opened and altered the contents before it reached them.
relatedTerms: Digital signature, Certificate authority, Chain of trust, Supply chain attack

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's organization requires every internally developed application to be code signed with the company's certificate before deployment, so that endpoint protection software automatically blocks any executable whose signature is missing or fails verification, catching a tampered installer before it could run.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization's endpoint protection software automatically blocks an application installer from running because its digital signature does not match the expected publisher certificate. What security practice enabled this detection?

items.name: Self-signed
items.detail: Signed by its own private key, so no third party vouches for it. Free and fine for labs or internal dev, but browsers warn users and it cannot be revoked by a public CA.

items.name: Public CA-issued
items.detail: Signed by a CA that browsers and operating systems already trust. Required for public-facing sites.

items.name: Wildcard
items.detail: One certificate for *.example.com, covering every first-level subdomain. Convenient, but one stolen key exposes all of them.

items.name: SAN (Subject Alternative Name)
items.detail: One certificate that lists several specific hostnames or domains. Not to be confused with a SAN as a Storage Area Network; the exam uses both meanings.

items.name: DV / OV / EV
items.detail: Domain Validation proves only control of the domain; Organization Validation vets the company; Extended Validation is the strictest vetting.

items.name: Code signing
items.detail: Proves who published software and that it has not been altered since signing.

items.name: Machine / user / email
items.detail: Certificates that authenticate a device or a person, or sign and encrypt email (S/MIME).

items.name: Root certificate
items.detail: Self-signed certificate at the top of a chain, pre-installed in the OS/browser trust store.

definition: A recovery site that provides only basic space, power and cooling. The organization must bring in hardware, software and data after a disaster, so recovery takes days to weeks. It is the cheapest option.
examContext: Highest recovery time and lowest cost; suited to non-critical systems or very tight budgets.
analogy: An empty rented warehouse: you must bring in all the furniture and equipment yourself.
relatedTerms: Hot site, Warm site, Disaster recovery, Business continuity

detail.practicalScenario: A small nonprofit rents empty office space with power and cooling as a fallback. After a fire, it would need to buy and install equipment and restore data, which could take several weeks.
detail.quizQuestion: Which recovery site is the cheapest but needs days or weeks before systems are operational?

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: A cryptographic attack that attempts to find two different inputs that produce the same hash output, undermining the assumption that a hash value uniquely identifies its original data.
examContext: Know a collision attack targets hash functions specifically, not encryption algorithms; exam scenarios may describe an attacker substituting a malicious file that happens to produce the same hash digest as a legitimate one, defeating an integrity check.
analogy: Like discovering that two completely different people happen to have the exact same fingerprint, so a fingerprint scanner can no longer reliably tell them apart.
relatedTerms: Hashing, Birthday attack, Digital signature, Downgrade attack

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's security audit discovers the company's file-integrity system still relies on the outdated MD5 hashing algorithm, which researchers have already shown is vulnerable to collision attacks that let an attacker craft a malicious file sharing the same hash as a legitimate one, so Alex migrates the system to SHA-256.
detail.quizQuestion: Researchers demonstrate that two completely different files can be crafted to produce the exact same hash digest under an older hashing algorithm, defeating a system's integrity check. What type of attack does this describe?

definition: A network segment in which devices share the same medium and can interfere with each other when they transmit at the same time. A hub puts all of its ports in one collision domain, while every switch port is its own collision domain.
examContext: Mostly of historical interest (half-duplex Ethernet), but the exam contrasts hubs and switches: a switch creates one collision domain per port, and a router one per interface.
analogy: A narrow single-lane road where two cars heading in opposite directions must wait for each other.
relatedTerms: Hub, Switch, Broadcast domain

detail.practicalScenario: When the lab replaced a hub with a 24-port switch, collisions disappeared because each port became its own collision domain.
detail.quizQuestion: How many collision domains does a 24-port switch create?

definition: The infrastructure and communication channel, often abbreviated C2, that attackers use to remotely issue instructions to and receive data from compromised systems.
examContext: Exam tests command and control as central to botnets and advanced persistent threat operations; detection often involves identifying beaconing traffic to suspicious external domains or IPs.
analogy: Like a puppet master's remote control that sends commands to every puppet in the network.
relatedTerms: Botnet, Advanced persistent threat, Exfiltration, Backdoor

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's network monitoring tool identifies periodic beaconing traffic from several workstations to the same unfamiliar external IP address every five minutes, revealing an active command-and-control channel controlling the infected machines.
detail.quizQuestion: Security analysts notice several infected workstations periodically contacting the same unknown external server on a regular interval, seemingly checking in for instructions. What is this infrastructure called?

definition: An attack in which untrusted input is passed to an operating-system shell or command interpreter, letting the attacker run arbitrary commands with the application's privileges.
examContext: Prevent by avoiding shell calls, using safe APIs, validating and escaping input, and running with least privilege. Related to SQL injection but targets the OS instead of the database.
analogy: Slipping extra instructions into a note that the boss reads aloud to the staff.
relatedTerms: Input validation, SQLi, Buffer overflow, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: A web form passes the entered hostname to a ping command. An attacker enters "example.com; cat /etc/passwd" and the server returns the password file because the input was not sanitized.
detail.quizQuestion: A web form passes user input to a shell ping command, and an attacker appends "; cat /etc/passwd". What attack is this?

definition: A cloud shared by several organizations with common requirements, such as compliance obligations or a shared mission, and managed by them or a third party.
examContext: Example: government agencies sharing a compliant cloud, or hospitals sharing a healthcare-focused cloud. Costs and responsibilities are split among the members.
analogy: A co-op apartment owned and used by a group with shared needs.
relatedTerms: Public cloud, Private cloud, Hybrid cloud, Responsibility matrix

detail.practicalScenario: Several universities jointly operate a research cloud with shared security and compliance controls, splitting the costs among members who all need the same protections.
detail.quizQuestion: Several hospitals with identical compliance needs jointly operate a shared cloud. Which deployment model is this?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: An alternative control used when a primary or recommended control cannot be implemented, giving comparable protection. Example: extra monitoring, network isolation and strict ACLs for a legacy system that cannot be patched.
examContext: Used when the standard control is too costly, impractical or technically impossible (legacy, ICS and embedded systems). Common in vulnerability management and in PCI DSS exceptions. It is a stand-in, not the preferred solution.
analogy: Like a rope ladder installed because a staircase cannot be built: not the usual fix, but it still gets people safely upstairs.
relatedTerms: Control types, Preventive control, Vulnerability, Risk mitigation

detail.practicalScenario: A medical device runs an unpatchable legacy OS. Because it cannot be fixed, the security team places it on an isolated VLAN with strict firewall rules and extra monitoring to reduce the risk.
detail.quizQuestion: A vendor cannot patch a critical flaw on a legacy device, so the security team isolates it on its own VLAN with strict firewall rules and extra monitoring. What type of control is this?

items.name: Preventive
items.detail: Stops an incident BEFORE it happens: firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, patching, MFA.

items.name: Deterrent
items.detail: Discourages attackers by raising the perceived risk: warning signs, visible cameras and guards, lighting, policies with consequences.

items.name: Detective
items.detail: Finds and alerts to an incident as or after it happens: IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, CCTV, audits, motion sensors.

items.name: Corrective
items.detail: Limits damage and restores things AFTER an incident: restoring from backup, patching a hole, incident response, quarantining malware.

items.name: Compensating
items.detail: A substitute control used when the primary control is not feasible, giving equivalent protection: for example extra monitoring and network isolation for a legacy system that cannot be patched.

items.name: Directive
items.detail: Tells people what they must or must not do: policies, procedures, standards, signs such as "authorized personnel only."

items.name: Examples
items.detail: Firewall = technical + preventive. Security guard = physical + preventive/deterrent. CCTV = physical + detective. Acceptable use policy = managerial + directive. Backups = technical + corrective. Awareness training = operational + preventive.

definition: Meeting the requirements of the laws, regulations, standards and contracts that apply to an organization, and being able to demonstrate it through reporting, monitoring and audits.
examContext: Know the consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license and contractual impacts. Monitoring includes due diligence and due care, attestation and acknowledgement, and automation.
analogy: Following the building code and keeping the inspection certificates to prove it.
relatedTerms: Governance, Due diligence, Due care, Attestation, Regulated data

detail.practicalScenario: A payment processor performs regular scans, keeps evidence of its controls and files compliance reports. When a regulator asks for proof, it can show that it met every requirement.
detail.quizQuestion: Which term describes an organization meeting the requirements of applicable laws, regulations and standards, and proving it?

definition: An indicator in which the same account is active in multiple places or on multiple devices at the same time, which may reveal shared or stolen credentials.
examContext: Seen in authentication and VPN logs; many systems limit concurrent sessions. Context matters because legitimate users may use several devices.
analogy: The same house key opening two different doors at the same moment.
relatedTerms: Indicators of malicious activity, Impossible travel, Credential stuffing, Session hijacking

detail.practicalScenario: A contractor's VPN account shows active sessions from two different countries at once. Because policy allows only one session per user, the second login is flagged and the credentials are reset.
detail.quizQuestion: The same user account is active on two different continents at the same time. What indicator is this?

definition: Ensuring information is not disclosed to unauthorized individuals, entities, or processes.
examContext: SY0-701 tests confidentiality as one leg of the CIA triad; expect scenario questions asking which control, such as encryption or access lists, best preserves it.
analogy: Like a sealed envelope that only the addressee can open.
relatedTerms: CIA triad, Integrity, Availability, Encryption, Data classification

detail.practicalScenario: Maria encrypts customer Social Security numbers stored in the database and restricts the decryption key to the finance team, ensuring that even if a backup file is stolen, the data inside remains unreadable.
detail.quizQuestion: A hospital wants to ensure that only authorized nurses can view patient diagnosis records, even if the file is intercepted in transit. Which security principle is the hospital primarily trying to uphold?

definition: A situation in which a vendor, employee or assessor has competing interests that could bias their judgment, such as a consultant recommending products that they also sell.
examContext: A vendor-selection consideration and one reason for separation of duties and independent audits.
analogy: A referee who also owns one of the teams.
relatedTerms: Vendor assessment, Separation of duties, Due diligence, Right-to-audit clause

detail.practicalScenario: The consultant hired to recommend a firewall also earns commissions from one vendor. The company chooses an independent assessor to avoid a conflict of interest.
detail.quizQuestion: A consultant who advises a company on which security product to buy also earns commissions from one of the vendors. What is this?

definition: A method of packaging an application and its dependencies into a lightweight, isolated unit (a container) that shares the host operating system's kernel, enabling consistent, portable deployment across environments without the overhead of a full virtual machine.
examContext: Expect exam questions to test that containers share the host OS kernel (making them more lightweight than VMs) and that a container escape vulnerability can therefore expose the underlying host, unlike a VM escape, which affects the hypervisor.
analogy: Like shipping goods in standardized cargo containers that can be loaded onto any ship, train, or truck without repacking; the container, not the goods, defines portability.
relatedTerms: Virtualization, Microservices, Serverless computing, Hardening, Attack surface

detail.practicalScenario: Alex packages the company's web application into a container with only the exact libraries it needs, allowing the same image to run identically in development, testing, and production while shrinking the attack surface compared to the old full-VM deployment.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team wants to deploy an application consistently across environments while minimizing resource overhead compared to full virtual machines. Which technology should they use?

definition: The incident response phase in which the team limits the spread and impact of an incident, for example by isolating hosts, disabling accounts or blocking malicious IP addresses, before removing the cause.
examContext: Comes after analysis and before eradication. Short-term containment stops the damage quickly; long-term containment lets systems operate safely until clean-up. Preserve evidence while containing.
analogy: Closing fire doors so the fire cannot spread while firefighters work.
relatedTerms: Eradication, Incident response, Isolation, Lessons learned

detail.practicalScenario: After finding malware beaconing from three servers, the team blocks the command-and-control address, disconnects the hosts and disables the compromised account. The spread stops before anyone starts cleaning.
detail.quizQuestion: During an incident, a team disconnects infected servers and blocks the attacker's IP address to stop the spread. Which response phase is this?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: The four ways security controls are grouped by what they are made of or who operates them: technical (technology), managerial (policy and oversight), operational (carried out by people) and physical (tangible barriers and devices).
examContext: CompTIA asks you to classify a control twice: by CATEGORY and by TYPE. The category answers "what kind of control is it?"; the type answers "what does it do?". A firewall is technical + preventive, an awareness program is operational + preventive, and a policy is managerial + directive.
analogy: Like sorting tools by material (metal, plastic, wood), separately from sorting them by job (cutting, measuring, fastening).
relatedTerms: Control types, Technical control, Managerial control, Operational control, Physical control

detail.practicalScenario: A security manager builds a control inventory. Firewalls and encryption go under technical, the acceptable use policy under managerial, quarterly phishing training under operational, and badge readers and fences under physical. Each entry is then tagged with its type (preventive, detective and so on) to find gaps.
detail.quizQuestion: A company requires every employee to complete security awareness training delivered by its staff. Which control CATEGORY best describes the training?

variants.title: Control categories (WHAT the control is made of)

items.name: Technical
items.detail: Implemented with technology: firewalls, encryption, antivirus, ACLs, MFA, IDS/IPS.

items.name: Managerial (administrative)
items.detail: Policies, risk assessments, security planning and oversight: the "paperwork" that governs how security is managed.

items.name: Operational
items.detail: Carried out day to day by PEOPLE: security awareness training, guards, change and patch procedures, backups performed by staff.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tangible barriers and devices: locks, fences, bollards, cameras, badge readers, vestibules, lighting.

items.name: Tip
items.detail: The category describes what it is or who runs it. The TYPE (preventive, detective and so on) describes what it does. One control has both: a firewall is a technical, preventive control.

definition: In zero trust architecture, the logical layer where access policies are defined and access decisions are made; it houses the Policy Engine, the Policy Administrator, adaptive identity evaluation, and threat scope reduction.
examContext: CompTIA explicitly groups adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control, the Policy Administrator, and the Policy Engine under the control plane; expect a matching or diagram question separating this from the data plane.
analogy: Like the air traffic control tower that decides which planes may land, as opposed to the runway and gates where planes actually move.
relatedTerms: Zero trust, Policy Engine, Policy Administrator, Adaptive identity, Threat scope reduction, Data plane

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's team centralizes all access-decision logic, identity risk scoring, and policy rules into a dedicated control plane platform, keeping decision-making logically separate from the systems that actually carry user traffic.
detail.quizQuestion: Which zero trust layer is responsible for defining policy, evaluating identity risk, and housing the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator?

definition: The six functions a security control can perform: preventive (stop it), deterrent (discourage it), detective (spot it), corrective (fix it afterward), compensating (stand in for a missing control) and directive (tell people what to do).
examContext: Learn them by timing: preventive acts before, detective during or after, corrective after the damage. Deterrent influences attackers' behavior, directive influences employees' behavior, and compensating substitutes for a control you cannot use. One control can fit more than one type, such as a visible CCTV camera (detective and deterrent).
analogy: Like the roles in a fire plan: sprinklers prevent, warning signs deter, alarms detect, the fire crew corrects, a temporary barrier compensates, and the evacuation rules direct.
relatedTerms: Control categories, Preventive control, Deterrent control, Detective control, Corrective control, Compensating control, Directive control

detail.practicalScenario: Reviewing a new data center, an auditor labels each control: mantrap (preventive), "monitored premises" signs (deterrent), motion sensors (detective), backup restoration (corrective), extra monitoring on an unpatchable system (compensating), and the visitor policy (directive).
detail.quizQuestion: An IDS that generates an alert when it spots a port scan is MOST accurately described as which control type?

items.name: Preventive
items.detail: Stops an incident BEFORE it happens: firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, patching, MFA.

items.name: Deterrent
items.detail: Discourages attackers by raising the perceived risk: warning signs, visible cameras and guards, lighting, policies with consequences.

items.name: Detective
items.detail: Finds and alerts to an incident as or after it happens: IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, CCTV, audits, motion sensors.

items.name: Corrective
items.detail: Limits damage and restores things AFTER an incident: restoring from backup, patching a hole, incident response, quarantining malware.

items.name: Compensating
items.detail: A substitute control used when the primary control is not feasible, giving equivalent protection: for example extra monitoring and network isolation for a legacy system that cannot be patched.

items.name: Directive
items.detail: Tells people what they must or must not do: policies, procedures, standards, signs such as "authorized personnel only."

items.name: Examples
items.detail: Firewall = technical + preventive. Security guard = physical + preventive/deterrent. CCTV = physical + detective. Acceptable use policy = managerial + directive. Backups = technical + corrective. Awareness training = operational + preventive.

definition: A control that limits the damage of an incident and restores systems to normal after it has occurred, such as restoring from backups, patching after exploitation, incident response and quarantining malware.
examContext: "Correct" means fix it AFTER. Backups used for restoration and incident response actions are corrective. Patching can be preventive (before an exploit) or corrective (after one), so watch the timing in the question.
analogy: The repair crew and fire extinguisher: they act after something has gone wrong to put things right.
relatedTerms: Preventive control, Detective control, Compensating control, Incident response

detail.practicalScenario: After ransomware encrypts a file server, the team isolates the host, rebuilds it and restores data from clean backups. These actions repair damage that has already happened, so they are corrective controls.
detail.quizQuestion: Which action is a CORRECTIVE control?
quizOptions: B) Restoring data from a clean backup after ransomware

definition: An attack in which previously breached username and password pairs from one service are automatically tried against other, unrelated services, exploiting the common practice of password reuse across multiple accounts.
examContext: Know credential stuffing relies on data breaches from other sites rather than guessing, exploiting password reuse; the standard mitigation tested on the exam is MFA and unique passwords, often via a password manager, since the credentials themselves are already technically valid.
analogy: Like a thief who finds a master list of house addresses paired with keys stolen from one neighborhood, then tries each key at houses in a completely different neighborhood, betting that some homeowners reused the same lock.
relatedTerms: Brute force attack, Multifactor authentication, Dictionary attack

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's security team detects a credential stuffing attack when thousands of login attempts use valid username and password combinations leaked from an unrelated third-party breach, and responds by forcing a password reset and enforcing MFA for all affected accounts.
detail.quizQuestion: A company notices a surge of successful logins using username and password combinations that match a password dump from an unrelated website's breach months earlier. What attack does this describe, and what is the best mitigation?
quizOptions: A) Brute force attack; mitigated by account lockout
B) Dictionary attack; mitigated by key stretching
C) Credential stuffing; mitigated by MFA and unique passwords
D) Replay attack; mitigated by nonces

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: The unauthorized use of a victim's computing resources to mine cryptocurrency, typically without the owner's knowledge or consent.
examContext: Exam tests cryptojacking as causing performance degradation, such as high CPU usage and overheating, rather than data theft, often delivered through browser scripts or malware.
analogy: Like a stranger secretly plugging their own appliance into your outlet and running up your electric bill.
relatedTerms: Malware, Botnet

detail.practicalScenario: Sam notices that a fleet of company servers is running at near full CPU utilization overnight with no legitimate workload, and investigation reveals hidden mining software silently generating cryptocurrency for an attacker.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees report that their workstations have become unusually slow and the fans run constantly, and IT discovers hidden software using the CPUs to mine cryptocurrency for an unknown third party. What is this attack called?

definition: A part of the internet reachable only with special software such as Tor, hosting hidden sites and markets where stolen credentials, malware and exploits are bought and sold.
examContext: A threat intelligence source: monitoring it can reveal leaked credentials and attacker chatter. Distinguish from the deep web, which is merely unindexed content such as intranets.
analogy: A back-alley market that is not on any street map.
relatedTerms: Threat intelligence, OSINT, Credential stuffing, Indicator of compromise

detail.practicalScenario: A threat-intelligence service alerts a company that thousands of its employees' credentials are for sale on a dark web forum. The company forces password resets and enables MFA before the logins are abused.
detail.quizQuestion: A company monitors hidden forums accessed through Tor for sales of its stolen credentials. Which intelligence source is this?

definition: Data stored on a persistent medium such as a disk, database, backup tape or removable drive, as opposed to moving across a network or being processed in memory.
examContext: Protect with full-disk, file or database encryption, access controls and secure storage. A stolen laptop or a lost USB stick is the classic data-at-rest risk.
analogy: Documents sitting in a locked filing cabinet.
relatedTerms: Data in transit, Data in use, Encryption, FDE

detail.practicalScenario: The HR database is stored on encrypted volumes and backups are written to encrypted tape. If a drive is stolen from the data center, the data on it stays unreadable.
detail.quizQuestion: Customer records stored on a database server's disks are in which data state?

variants.title: Data states and how to protect each

items.name: At rest
items.detail: Stored on disk, in a database, on backups or removable media. Protect with full-disk, file or database encryption, access controls and secure storage.

items.name: In transit (in motion)
items.detail: Moving across a network. Protect with TLS, IPsec, VPN, SSH and WPA3.

items.name: In use
items.detail: Being processed in memory or by the CPU. The hardest state to protect: secure enclaves, memory encryption, access controls, and locking screens.

items.name: General methods
items.detail: Encryption, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation, permission restrictions and geographic restrictions (geofencing).

definition: The process of organizing data into categories, such as Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted, based on its sensitivity and the impact its exposure would have, enabling appropriate handling and protection controls to be applied.
examContext: Know common classification tiers and that classification drives which controls, such as encryption, access restrictions, and retention, apply to a given dataset; exam scenarios test matching data types to appropriate classification levels and controls.
analogy: Like sorting mail into bins labeled Public, Internal, Confidential, and Top Secret, so each bin automatically determines who's allowed to open and read it.
relatedTerms: Data masking, Mandatory access control, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's organization classifies customer social security numbers as Restricted data, automatically triggering encryption-at-rest requirements and strict access logging, while marketing brochures are classified as Public with no special handling needed.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to ensure that highly sensitive customer data automatically receives stricter encryption and access controls than general marketing materials. What process should be implemented first?

items.name: Public
items.detail: Safe to disclose; no harm.

items.name: Private / internal
items.detail: For internal use only.

items.name: Sensitive
items.detail: Disclosure could cause harm or embarrassment.

items.name: Confidential
items.detail: Disclosure would cause serious harm; protected by contract or law.

items.name: Restricted
items.detail: The most tightly controlled, with very limited access.

items.name: Critical
items.detail: Essential to operations; loss or alteration would be severe.

items.name: Government scheme
items.detail: Unclassified, then Confidential, Secret and Top Secret, in rising order of damage if disclosed.

items.name: Data types
items.detail: Regulated (PII, PHI, payment data), trade secrets, intellectual property, legal information and financial information. Data may be human-readable or non-human-readable (binary, encoded).

definition: Under privacy regulations such as GDPR, the entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data, deciding why and how personal data is collected and used, and that bears primary legal responsibility for compliance.
examContext: Know the data controller decides the purpose and means of processing personal data and bears primary legal accountability, while the data processor only acts on the controller's instructions; exam scenarios describe a business relationship and ask you to identify each role.
analogy: Like a restaurant owner who decides what's on the menu and how the kitchen operates; they set the purpose and rules, even if they hire an outside catering company to actually cook some dishes.
relatedTerms: Data processor, Right to be forgotten, Data sovereignty, Privacy, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's company collects customer email addresses to send marketing newsletters and decides exactly what data to collect and why, making the company the data controller, while the separate email-sending platform it hires only processes that data according to Chen's instructions.
detail.quizQuestion: A retail company decides what customer personal data to collect and why it will be used, then hires a third-party marketing firm to send emails using that data under the retailer's instructions. Under privacy regulations like GDPR, what role does the retail company hold?

items.name: Data owner
items.detail: A senior person ACCOUNTABLE for a dataset. Decides its classification and who may access it.

items.name: Data controller
items.detail: Decides WHY and HOW personal data is processed (GDPR term). Carries the primary legal responsibility.

items.name: Data processor
items.detail: Processes personal data ON BEHALF of the controller, following its instructions (a payroll or cloud vendor).

items.name: Data custodian
items.detail: Handles the TECHNICAL side: storage, backups, access controls and protection.

items.name: Data steward
items.detail: Looks after data QUALITY and the correct labeling and use of data under policy.

items.name: Data subject
items.detail: The individual the personal data is about.

items.name: DPO
items.detail: Data Protection Officer: oversees privacy compliance (GDPR).

definition: The role responsible for the day-to-day technical handling of data, including storage, backup, encryption, and recovery, carried out according to the classification and rules set by the data owner.
examContext: Know the data custodian is typically an IT or infrastructure role implementing technical controls, such as backup schedules and access permissions, defined by the data owner's classification; the exam tests distinguishing this hands-on role from the accountable owner role.
analogy: Like a bank vault manager who physically stores, backs up, and protects the valuables inside according to rules the vault's owner set, without deciding who's allowed to own an account in the first place.
relatedTerms: Data owner, Data steward, Data classification, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Sam, a database administrator, acts as the data custodian for the customer records database, configuring nightly encrypted backups and access permissions exactly according to the classification level and rules that the data owner in the business unit established.
detail.quizQuestion: A database administrator configures daily encrypted backups and sets technical access permissions on a customer database, strictly following the classification rules established by the business unit that owns the data. What role is the administrator performing?

definition: Physically destroying storage media so data cannot be recovered, using methods such as shredding, pulverizing, incineration or degaussing (for magnetic media). Paper is shredded or pulped.
examContext: Used when media will not be reused or holds highly sensitive data. Degaussing does not work on SSDs. A certificate of destruction provides evidence for audits.
analogy: Burning the whiteboard instead of wiping it.
relatedTerms: Data sanitization, Decommissioning, Data retention, Asset management

detail.practicalScenario: A defense contractor sends failed SSDs to a shredding service that pulverizes them into fragments and returns a certificate of destruction for the audit file.
detail.quizQuestion: Which method does NOT reliably destroy data on a solid-state drive?

items.name: Acquisition / procurement
items.detail: Buying and vetting hardware, software and services, including checking the supply chain.

items.name: Assignment / accounting
items.detail: Record ownership and classification so every asset has an accountable owner.

items.name: Monitoring / asset tracking
items.detail: Maintain an inventory and use enumeration to discover what is actually on the network.

items.name: Disposal / decommissioning
items.detail: Retire assets safely through sanitization or destruction, then confirm with a certificate.

items.name: Data retention
items.detail: Keep data only as long as required by policy or law, then dispose of it securely.

items.name: Overwriting (wiping)
items.detail: Writes patterns over the data so it cannot be recovered. The drive can be reused.

items.name: Cryptographic erase
items.detail: Destroys the encryption key of a self-encrypting or fully encrypted drive, making the data unreadable instantly.

items.name: Secure erase / purge
items.detail: A built-in drive command that removes data at the firmware level. Stronger than a simple delete or format.

items.name: Degaussing
items.detail: A powerful magnetic field wipes magnetic media (HDDs and tapes). It does NOT work on SSDs.

items.name: Shredding / pulverizing
items.detail: Physically destroys media into small pieces. Works for any media.

items.name: Incineration
items.detail: Burning the media completely.

items.name: Pulping (paper)
items.detail: Paper is shredded then broken down into pulp.

items.name: Certification
items.detail: A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents what was destroyed, when and how, for audit and compliance.

items.name: Remember
items.detail: A normal delete or quick format does NOT remove data. Sanitization lets you reuse the media; destruction does not.

definition: Data moving between systems across a network, such as an email, a web request or a file transfer. Also called data in motion.
examContext: Protect with TLS, IPsec, VPNs, SSH and WPA3. Packet sniffing and on-path attacks are the main threats. Do not confuse with data at rest (stored) or data in use (being processed).
analogy: A letter in the mail truck: it is safest inside a sealed envelope (encryption).
relatedTerms: Data at rest, Data in use, Encryption, Man-in-the-middle attack

detail.practicalScenario: Employees upload files to a cloud service over HTTPS. TLS protects the data while it crosses the internet, so someone sniffing the Wi-Fi at a coffee shop sees only encrypted traffic.
detail.quizQuestion: Which control primarily protects data in transit?

examContext: Protect with secure enclaves, confidential computing, memory encryption, strong access controls and locking screens. Homomorphic encryption is an emerging option.
analogy: A document open on your desk: it is out of the cabinet and readable while you work on it.
relatedTerms: Data at rest, Data in transit, Secure enclave, Homomorphic encryption
