definition: A set of tools and processes that monitor, detect, and block the unauthorized transmission or exfiltration of sensitive data outside an organization's network, whether via email, USB devices, or cloud uploads.
examContext: Know DLP solutions can be network-based, endpoint-based, or cloud-based, and typically work by scanning content for patterns, such as credit card or SSN formats, or data classification tags; exam scenarios often involve blocking an employee from emailing sensitive files externally.
analogy: Like a vigilant mailroom clerk who checks every outgoing package for sensitive documents and refuses to ship any that violate company policy.
relatedTerms: Data classification, Exfiltration

detail.practicalScenario: Chen deploys a DLP solution that automatically blocks an employee's attempt to email a spreadsheet containing unmasked customer credit card numbers to a personal Gmail account, generating an alert for the security team to investigate.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee attempts to email a file containing customer credit card numbers to their personal email account, and the action is automatically blocked with an alert sent to security. Which technology performed this action?

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Reversible with the right key. Protects confidentiality of data at rest and in transit.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: One-way. Used to verify integrity and store passwords; the original cannot be recovered.

items.name: Masking
items.detail: Replaces part of a value with placeholder characters (****-****-****-1234) for display, testing or training.

items.name: Tokenization
items.detail: Swaps a sensitive value for a random surrogate token; the real value lives only in a secured vault. Common for payment cards (shrinks PCI DSS scope).

items.name: Obfuscation
items.detail: Making data or code hard to understand (scrambling, renaming variables). Weak on its own: "security through obscurity."

items.name: Steganography
items.detail: Hides the very EXISTENCE of data inside another file such as an image or audio clip.

definition: The person, typically a senior business role, with ultimate accountability for a specific set of data, responsible for assigning its classification level and approving who may access or use it.

Scenario questions often name a business executive as the owner, not an IT administrator.
analogy: Like a company's chief librarian who decides which books are restricted versus public and sets the rules for who may check them out, without personally shelving or repairing every book.
relatedTerms: Data custodian, Data steward, Data classification, Data controller, Governance

definition: The policy-driven practice of keeping data for a defined period to meet legal, regulatory and business needs, then securely disposing of it. Keeping data too long raises risk and cost; deleting too soon can violate the law.
examContext: Tied to legal hold (suspends normal deletion), privacy laws that demand data minimization, and sanitization at end of life. Retention periods come from regulations such as tax and financial record rules.
analogy: A document-shredding schedule: keep tax records for the required years, then destroy them.
relatedTerms: Legal hold, Data classification, e-Discovery, Data destruction

items.name: Assignment / accounting
items.detail: Record ownership and classification so every asset has an accountable owner.

items.name: Monitoring / asset tracking
items.detail: Maintain an inventory and use enumeration to discover what is actually on the network.

items.detail: Retire assets safely through sanitization or destruction, then confirm with a certificate.

items.name: Data retention
items.detail: Keep data only as long as required by policy or law, then dispose of it securely.

definition: The process of removing data from storage media so it cannot be recovered, while still allowing the media to be reused, for example by overwriting, cryptographic erase or secure erase.
examContext: Distinguish from destruction, which physically destroys the media. A normal delete or quick format does NOT sanitize. NIST SP 800-88 describes clear, purge and destroy levels.
analogy: Wiping a whiteboard thoroughly so it can be used again, whereas destruction is shredding the whiteboard.
relatedTerms: Data destruction, Decommissioning, Data retention, Asset management

detail.practicalScenario: Before reissuing laptops, IT runs a secure erase that overwrites every sector and records the result. The laptops return to service, and the stored data cannot be recovered.
detail.quizQuestion: IT wants to reuse hard drives but ensure the old data cannot be recovered. Which process should they use?

items.name: Overwriting (wiping)
items.detail: Writes patterns over the data so it cannot be recovered. The drive can be reused.

items.name: Cryptographic erase
items.detail: Destroys the encryption key of a self-encrypting or fully encrypted drive, making the data unreadable instantly.

items.name: Secure erase / purge
items.detail: A built-in drive command that removes data at the firmware level. Stronger than a simple delete or format.

items.name: Degaussing
items.detail: A powerful magnetic field wipes magnetic media (HDDs and tapes). It does NOT work on SSDs.

items.name: Shredding / pulverizing
items.detail: Physically destroys media into small pieces. Works for any media.

items.name: Incineration
items.detail: Burning the media completely.

items.name: Pulping (paper)
items.detail: Paper is shredded then broken down into pulp.

items.name: Certification
items.detail: A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents what was destroyed, when and how, for audit and compliance.

items.name: Remember
items.detail: A normal delete or quick format does NOT remove data. Sanitization lets you reuse the media; destruction does not.

definition: The concept that data is subject to the laws and governance structures of the country or jurisdiction in which it is physically collected or stored.
examContext: Exam tests data sovereignty in the context of cloud computing, where storing data in a foreign data center may subject it to that country's legal requirements.
analogy: Like a visitor abroad who must follow local laws, even if those laws differ from their home country's rules.
relatedTerms: Privacy, Governance, Data classification

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's company selects a cloud region located within a specific jurisdiction specifically to ensure customer data remains subject to that region's privacy laws rather than a different country's rules.
detail.quizQuestion: A multinational company must ensure that customer data collected in one country stays stored on servers located within that same region to comply with local law. Which concept does this requirement reflect?

definition: A role focused on the quality, accuracy, context, and proper usage of data within a specific business domain, ensuring data is labeled, defined, and used appropriately according to the data owner's policies.
examContext: Know the data steward focuses on data quality, labeling, and appropriate day-to-day usage within a business context, which the exam distinguishes from the data custodian's more technical storage and backup focus, even though both act under the data owner's classification decisions.
analogy: Like a museum curator who ensures every exhibit is correctly labeled, categorized, and displayed appropriately for its context, distinct from the building's security team that physically locks and protects the artifacts overnight.
relatedTerms: Data owner, Data custodian, Data classification

detail.practicalScenario: Maria serves as the data steward for the company's customer relationship database, regularly reviewing records to ensure fields are accurately labeled and consistently defined across departments, while the technical backups and encryption of that same database remain the data custodian's responsibility.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee regularly reviews a shared customer database to ensure fields are accurately labeled, consistently defined, and used appropriately across departments, but does not manage its technical backups or encryption. Which role best matches this responsibility?

items.name: Data owner
items.detail: A senior person ACCOUNTABLE for a dataset. Decides its classification and who may access it.

items.name: Data controller
items.detail: Decides WHY and HOW personal data is processed (GDPR term). Carries the primary legal responsibility.

items.name: Data processor
items.detail: Processes personal data ON BEHALF of the controller, following its instructions (a payroll or cloud vendor).

items.name: Data custodian
items.detail: Handles the TECHNICAL side: storage, backups, access controls and protection.

items.name: Data steward
items.detail: Looks after data QUALITY and the correct labeling and use of data under policy.

items.name: Data subject
items.detail: The individual the personal data is about.

items.name: DPO
items.detail: Data Protection Officer: oversees privacy compliance (GDPR).

definition: The individual whom personal data is about (a GDPR term). Data subjects have rights over their data, including access, correction, portability and erasure.
examContext: Distinguish from the controller (decides why and how data is processed), the processor (processes it on the controller's behalf) and the DPO. The right to be forgotten is a data subject right.
analogy: The patient in a doctor's records: it is their information, even though the clinic holds it.
relatedTerms: Data controller, Data processor, Right to be forgotten, Privacy

detail.practicalScenario: A customer emails a retailer asking to see all personal data it holds and to have it deleted. Under GDPR, she is exercising her rights as a data subject, and the retailer must respond within the legal deadline.
detail.quizQuestion: Under GDPR, what is the term for the person whose personal data is collected and processed?

definition: A wireless attack that sends forged deauthentication frames to disconnect clients from an access point, causing denial of service or forcing reconnections so the attacker can capture the WPA handshake or lure users to an evil twin.
examContext: Possible because management frames were unauthenticated in older Wi-Fi. 802.11w protected management frames, mandatory in WPA3, mitigate it.
analogy: Someone repeatedly shouting "meeting over" in the host's name to send everyone home.
relatedTerms: Evil twin, WPA3, Wireless jamming, WIPS

detail.practicalScenario: Devices on the guest Wi-Fi keep disconnecting every few seconds. A wireless scan shows a flood of forged deauthentication frames, and the attacker is capturing handshakes each time the clients reconnect.
detail.quizQuestion: Which feature mitigates forged deauthentication frames on a wireless network?

definition: The controlled process of retiring a system, device or application at end of life, including removing it from inventory and networks, revoking access and certificates, and sanitizing or destroying stored data.
examContext: A mitigation technique and part of asset disposal. Forgotten, unmanaged systems become attack surface. Document it, often with a certificate of sanitization or destruction.
analogy: Properly closing and emptying a rented storage unit instead of just walking away.
relatedTerms: Asset management, Data sanitization, Data destruction, Attack surface

detail.practicalScenario: When retiring an old file server, IT removes it from the domain and monitoring, revokes its certificates, wipes the disks and records the disposal in the asset inventory with a certificate of sanitization.
detail.quizQuestion: Which process includes removing an end-of-life server from the network, revoking its access and wiping its data?

definition: Factory-set usernames and passwords (such as admin/admin) that ship with devices and software and are widely published. Leaving them unchanged lets attackers log in with no hacking at all.
examContext: Changing default passwords is a core hardening step. IoT devices and network gear are common victims, as in the Mirai botnet.
analogy: The factory-set combination on a new lock that everyone already knows.
relatedTerms: Hardening, Misconfiguration, Botnet, Attack surface

detail.practicalScenario: An attacker scans the internet for cameras that still accept admin/admin and takes control of hundreds of them for a botnet. The vendor now forces a unique password at first setup.
detail.quizQuestion: Attackers log in to a new router using the username and password printed in the manufacturer's public manual. Which weakness is this?

definition: The router address on a device's own subnet that it sends traffic to when the destination is on another network. Without a correct default gateway, a device can talk to local devices but not to the internet.
examContext: It is usually the router's LAN interface. A rogue DHCP server can hand out a malicious gateway, and ARP poisoning can impersonate the real one; both give the attacker an on-path position. Troubleshooting rule: local works but the internet does not, so check the gateway.
analogy: The mailbox at the end of your street: anything not for a neighbor goes there to be sent on.
relatedTerms: Router, IP address, Subnet, ARP poisoning, Man-in-the-middle attack

detail.practicalScenario: A new PC can open files on the office server but cannot browse the internet. The technician finds that its default gateway field is blank, and the problem disappears once the router's address is entered.
detail.quizQuestion: A PC can reach other devices on its own network but not the internet. Which setting should be checked first?

definition: A layered security strategy that uses multiple, overlapping controls so that if one layer fails, others still protect the asset.
examContext: Expect questions describing several layered controls working together, such as a firewall plus IDS plus endpoint protection plus training, and asking you to name the strategy.
analogy: Like a castle with a moat, walls, and guards, where an attacker who gets past one obstacle still faces more.
relatedTerms: Network segmentation, Firewall, Zero trust, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: Priya deploys a perimeter firewall, an internal intrusion detection system, endpoint antivirus, and employee phishing training together, so that a single bypassed control does not lead directly to a breach.
detail.quizQuestion: A company implements a firewall, network segmentation, endpoint detection, and security awareness training all at once rather than relying on a single tool. Which concept best describes this approach?

definition: A control that identifies and signals an incident while it is happening or after it has occurred, but does not stop it, such as IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, audits, motion sensors and CCTV.
examContext: "Detect" means find it. An IDS is detective while an IPS is preventive. Log monitoring, audits and motion sensors are detective. Do not pick detective when the control actually blocks the activity.
analogy: A smoke alarm: it cannot put the fire out, but it tells you there is one.
relatedTerms: Preventive control, Corrective control, Deterrent control, Control types

detail.practicalScenario: The SOC sees an alert from its SIEM when an account logs in from two countries within an hour. The alert does not block anything, but it reveals the suspicious activity so analysts can respond.
detail.quizQuestion: Which of the following is a DETECTIVE control?

items.name: Preventive
items.detail: Stops an incident BEFORE it happens: firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, patching, MFA.

items.name: Deterrent
items.detail: Discourages attackers by raising the perceived risk: warning signs, visible cameras and guards, lighting, policies with consequences.

items.name: Detective
items.detail: Finds and alerts to an incident as or after it happens: IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, CCTV, audits, motion sensors.

items.name: Corrective
items.detail: Limits damage and restores things AFTER an incident: restoring from backup, patching a hole, incident response, quarantining malware.

items.name: Compensating
items.detail: A substitute control used when the primary control is not feasible, giving equivalent protection: for example extra monitoring and network isolation for a legacy system that cannot be patched.

items.name: Directive
items.detail: Tells people what they must or must not do: policies, procedures, standards, signs such as "authorized personnel only."

items.name: Examples
items.detail: Firewall = technical + preventive. Security guard = physical + preventive/deterrent. CCTV = physical + detective. Acceptable use policy = managerial + directive. Backups = technical + corrective. Awareness training = operational + preventive.

definition: A control meant to discourage an attacker from trying by raising the perceived risk or effort, without necessarily blocking anything, such as warning signs, visible cameras, guards, lighting and publicized penalties.
examContext: Deterrents influence behavior; they do not physically stop anyone. A "monitored by CCTV" sign or a visible guard is deterrent. A visible camera is also detective, and a sign can also be treated as directive, so read the wording of the question.
analogy: A "Neighborhood Watch" sign: it does not lock the door, but a burglar may choose an easier house.
relatedTerms: Preventive control, Detective control, Directive control, Video surveillance

detail.practicalScenario: A retailer places visible cameras and "You are being recorded" signs at its entrance. Shoplifters often move on to easier targets, even though nothing physically stops them from entering.
detail.quizQuestion: A company posts signs warning that the premises are monitored and trespassers will be prosecuted. Which control TYPE best describes the signs?

items.name: Preventive
items.detail: Stops an incident BEFORE it happens: firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, patching, MFA.

items.name: Deterrent
items.detail: Discourages attackers by raising the perceived risk: warning signs, visible cameras and guards, lighting, policies with consequences.

items.name: Detective
items.detail: Finds and alerts to an incident as or after it happens: IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, CCTV, audits, motion sensors.

items.name: Corrective
items.detail: Limits damage and restores things AFTER an incident: restoring from backup, patching a hole, incident response, quarantining malware.

items.name: Compensating
items.detail: A substitute control used when the primary control is not feasible, giving equivalent protection: for example extra monitoring and network isolation for a legacy system that cannot be patched.

items.name: Directive
items.detail: Tells people what they must or must not do: policies, procedures, standards, signs such as "authorized personnel only."

items.name: Examples
items.detail: Firewall = technical + preventive. Security guard = physical + preventive/deterrent. CCTV = physical + detective. Acceptable use policy = managerial + directive. Backups = technical + corrective. Awareness training = operational + preventive.

definition: A password-guessing attack that uses a curated list of common words, phrases, and previously leaked passwords rather than trying every possible character combination, exploiting the fact that many users choose predictable passwords.
examContext: Know a dictionary attack is faster but less exhaustive than brute force since it only tries likely candidates; strong, complex, non-dictionary-word passwords and key stretching are the standard mitigations tested on the exam.
analogy: Like a thief trying only the most common PIN codes, such as 1234 or a birthday pattern, instead of every possible four-digit combination, because those guesses are far more likely to work quickly.
relatedTerms: Brute force attack, Key stretching, Salting

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's penetration test uses a dictionary attack loaded with the ten thousand most common leaked passwords against the company's login portal, successfully cracking several employee accounts that used simple, predictable passwords.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester successfully gains access to several accounts within minutes by trying a curated list of the most commonly used passwords, rather than every possible combination. What technique was used?

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: A backup that copies all data changed since the last FULL backup. Each differential grows larger until the next full backup, but a restore needs only the last full backup plus the most recent differential.
examContext: A middle ground: slower and larger than incremental, but a faster restore. Example: after a Sunday full, Wednesday's differential contains everything changed Monday through Wednesday.
analogy: Keeping a running list of every change since the last full copy, so you only ever need the original plus the latest list.
relatedTerms: Full backup, Incremental backup, Backup, Snapshot

detail.practicalScenario: A full backup runs on Sunday and a differential runs each night. When data is lost on Thursday morning, the admin restores only the Sunday full and Wednesday's differential.
detail.quizQuestion: A full backup runs on Sunday followed by nightly differentials. Data is lost on Thursday morning. What is needed to restore?
quizOptions: C) Sunday full plus every daily differential
D) Sunday full plus Wednesday's differential

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: The discipline of collecting, preserving, analyzing and presenting digital evidence in a legally defensible way, using techniques such as disk imaging, memory capture and timeline analysis.
examContext: Know chain of custody, legal hold, order of volatility, write blockers, and hashing to prove an image has not changed. Key phases include acquisition, preservation, analysis and reporting.
analogy: Crime-scene investigation for computers.
relatedTerms: Chain of custody, Order of volatility, Legal hold, e-Discovery, Hashing

detail.practicalScenario: After a suspected insider theft, the investigator images the employee's laptop with a write blocker, hashes the image, documents each handoff and analyzes the copy, never the original.
detail.quizQuestion: An investigator creates a bit-for-bit copy of a suspect's drive using a write blocker and hashes it to prove it was not altered. Which discipline is this?

variants.title: Digital forensics: order of volatility and handling

items.name: Order of volatility
items.detail: Collect the MOST volatile evidence first: CPU registers and cache, then RAM (routing/ARP tables, processes), then swap/page file, then disk, then remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.

items.name: Preservation
items.detail: Use write blockers, work on forensic copies, and hash the image to prove it was not changed.

items.name: Acquisition
items.detail: A bit-for-bit disk image, a memory dump, or a snapshot. Live acquisition is needed to capture volatile data.

items.name: Chain of custody
items.detail: Documented record of who handled the evidence, when and why. Gaps can make evidence inadmissible.

items.name: Legal hold
items.detail: A mandate to preserve relevant data (stop normal deletion) because of litigation or investigation.

items.name: e-Discovery
items.detail: Identifying and collecting electronic information for legal proceedings.

items.name: Timeline and reporting
items.detail: Reconstruct events, document findings and make the report clear and reproducible.

definition: A cryptographic mechanism that uses a sender's private key to sign a hash of a message, allowing anyone with the sender's public key to verify the message's integrity and authenticity, and providing non-repudiation.
examContext: SY0-701 ties digital signatures directly to non-repudiation; know the process is hash-then-sign-with-private-key, and verification uses the signer's public key.
analogy: Like a wax seal pressed with a unique personal signet ring, anyone can verify it's authentic, but only you can create it.
relatedTerms: Hashing, Public key, Private key, Non-repudiation, Certificate, Asymmetric encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Alex signs a financial transaction approval email using his private key so that recipients can use his public key to confirm the message truly came from him and was not altered, preventing him from later denying he sent it.
detail.quizQuestion: A company needs to ensure that an executive cannot later deny having authorized a wire transfer request sent by email. Which control provides this assurance?

items.name: Checksum / CRC
items.detail: A small value computed from the data to catch ACCIDENTAL corruption (bit flips in transit or on disk). Fast and simple, but not secure: an attacker can alter the data and recompute a matching checksum. CRC is the common checksum algorithm (Ethernet frames, ZIP).

items.name: Cryptographic hash
items.detail: One-way function (SHA-256, SHA-3) producing a fixed-length digest; any change to the input changes the digest completely. Detects tampering, but anyone can recompute it, so it only proves integrity if the expected hash comes from a trusted source (e.g., the vendor's website).

items.name: HMAC
items.detail: A hash combined with a shared secret key. Proves integrity AND authenticity (only a key holder could produce it). No non-repudiation, because both sides hold the same key.

items.name: Digital signature
items.detail: A hash encrypted with the sender's private key and verified with their public key. Proves integrity, authenticity AND non-repudiation. It is the strongest option because only the signer holds the private key.

items.name: Send a confidential message
items.detail: Encrypt with the RECIPIENT's PUBLIC key; only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.

items.name: Sign a message / prove authorship
items.detail: Sign with YOUR OWN PRIVATE key; anyone verifies with your public key. This gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.

items.name: Verify someone's signature
items.detail: Use the SIGNER's PUBLIC key (obtained from their certificate).

items.name: Decrypt a message sent to you
items.detail: Use YOUR OWN PRIVATE key.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: The private key never leaves its owner. The public key is shared freely. Encryption = their public key; signing = your private key.

definition: A control that instructs or compels people to behave in a certain way, such as policies, standards, procedures and mandatory signage. It directs behavior rather than technically enforcing it.
examContext: Directive means it tells people what to do (policies, procedures, "authorized personnel only" signs). It is one of the six control types in SY0-701 (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive).
analogy: The rules posted at a swimming pool: they tell you how to behave but do not physically stop you.
relatedTerms: Control types, Security policy, Managerial control, Deterrent control

detail.practicalScenario: HR distributes an acceptable use policy that states what employees may and may not do with company systems. The policy guides behavior but does not technically block anything, so it is a directive control.
detail.quizQuestion: A company publishes an acceptable use policy telling employees what they may and may not do with company systems. Which control TYPE is this?

items.detail: Stops an incident BEFORE it happens: firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, patching, MFA.

items.name: Deterrent
items.detail: Discourages attackers by raising the perceived risk: warning signs, visible cameras and guards, lighting, policies with consequences.

items.name: Detective
items.detail: Finds and alerts to an incident as or after it happens: IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, CCTV, audits, motion sensors.

items.name: Corrective
items.detail: Limits damage and restores things AFTER an incident: restoring from backup, patching a hole, incident response, quarantining malware.

items.name: Compensating
items.detail: A substitute control used when the primary control is not feasible, giving equivalent protection: for example extra monitoring and network isolation for a legacy system that cannot be patched.

items.name: Directive
items.detail: Tells people what they must or must not do: policies, procedures, standards, signs such as "authorized personnel only."

items.name: Examples
items.detail: Firewall = technical + preventive. Security guard = physical + preventive/deterrent. CCTV = physical + detective. Acceptable use policy = managerial + directive. Backups = technical + corrective. Awareness training = operational + preventive.

definition: An attack that manipulates file path input with sequences such as ../ to access files and directories outside the intended web root, potentially reading configuration files or password stores. Also called path traversal.
examContext: Mitigate with input validation, canonicalizing paths, running the web server with least privilege and keeping sensitive files outside the web root.
analogy: Asking the librarian for a book but adding directions that lead you into the staff-only archive.
relatedTerms: Input validation, Command injection, Least privilege, SQLi

detail.practicalScenario: A request for /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd returns the server's password file. The developers fix the bug by normalizing the path and rejecting any file outside the allowed folder.
detail.quizQuestion: A request containing ../../etc/passwd retrieves system files from a web server. What attack is this?

definition: The specific process and procedures for restoring IT systems, data, and infrastructure after a disruptive event, typically measured by recovery time objective and recovery point objective targets.
examContext: Know recovery time objective, how long until systems are back up, and recovery point objective, how much data loss measured in time is acceptable, cold, since these are classic calculation-style exam questions; disaster recovery is the IT-focused subset of business continuity.
analogy: Like a backup generator and a pre-rehearsed plan to get the power and systems in a building running again as fast as possible after an outage, with a clear target for how quickly and how much data can be restored.
relatedTerms: Business continuity, Fault tolerance, High availability

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's disaster recovery plan specifies a four-hour recovery time objective and a fifteen-minute recovery point objective for the order database, so after a data center outage, her team restores operations within four hours while losing no more than fifteen minutes of transaction data.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization's disaster recovery plan states that after an outage, no more than 15 minutes of data can be lost. Which metric does this describe?

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: An access control model in which the owner of a resource decides who is granted access and what permissions they receive, offering flexibility but less centralized consistency than other models.
examContext: Know DAC is common in general-purpose operating systems, such as standard Windows or Linux file permissions, where the file owner can grant or revoke access to others at their own discretion; contrasted with MAC's centrally enforced labels.
analogy: Like a homeowner who personally decides which friends get a copy of their house key, rather than a landlord dictating who's allowed in.
relatedTerms: Mandatory access control, Role-based access control

detail.practicalScenario: Alex creates a shared folder on his workstation and personally grants read and write access to two specific colleagues working on the same project, exercising the discretionary access control model built into the operating system's file permissions.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee creates a project folder on a shared drive and personally chooses which specific coworkers can read or edit its contents. Which access control model does this represent?

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: False information that is deliberately created and spread with the intent to deceive, manipulate public opinion, or damage a person's or organization's reputation.
examContext: The exam distinguishes disinformation as intentional deception, in contrast with misinformation, which lacks deceptive intent; watch for scenarios involving coordinated campaigns, such as fake social media accounts, used to damage a company's reputation or influence public perception.
analogy: Like a rival planting a fake, damaging news story on purpose, knowing it's false, specifically to manipulate how people feel.
relatedTerms: Misinformation, Social engineering, Brand impersonation

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's threat intelligence team traces a coordinated wave of fake social media accounts deliberately spreading fabricated claims about a data breach that never occurred, timed to damage the company's stock price right before an earnings call.
detail.quizQuestion: A threat intelligence team discovers a coordinated network of fake accounts deliberately spreading fabricated claims about a company breach that never happened, timed to hurt its stock price. What is this attack best classified as?

definition: Blocking access to malicious or unwanted domains at the DNS resolution step, so the connection is never made, using threat intelligence and category lists.
examContext: Works for every device that uses the filtering resolver and stops many phishing and malware domains early. Can be bypassed by DNS over HTTPS or other resolvers unless controlled.
analogy: Removing the dangerous addresses from the phone book so nobody can dial them.
relatedTerms: Web filter, DNS, DNSSEC, Pharming

detail.practicalScenario: The company points all devices at a filtering DNS service. When a user clicks a phishing link, the lookup returns a block page and the request never reaches the malicious server.
detail.quizQuestion: Which control stops a connection to a malicious site by refusing to resolve its domain name?

items.name: URL / domain block and allow lists
items.detail: Explicitly permit or deny named sites. Precise, but must be maintained.

items.name: Content categorization
items.detail: Sites are sorted into categories (gambling, adult, malware) and whole categories are blocked.

items.name: Reputation filtering
items.detail: Blocks sites with a poor trust score based on threat intelligence, newly registered domains and past abuse.

items.name: Agent-based
items.detail: Software on the endpoint enforces policy wherever the device is, even off the corporate network.

items.name: Centralized proxy
items.detail: All web traffic is forced through one gateway that applies the policy; users on the network are covered without agents.

items.name: DNS filtering
items.detail: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at name resolution, before a connection is made.

definition: An attack that inserts forged DNS records into a resolver's cache so users asking for a legitimate domain are given the attacker's IP address and redirected to malicious sites. Also called DNS cache poisoning.
examContext: Mitigated by DNSSEC (signed records), patched resolvers, source port and query ID randomization, and DNS filtering. It is also the technique behind many pharming attacks.
analogy: Altering the phone book at the library so the pizza place's number rings a scammer instead.
relatedTerms: Pharming, DNSSEC, DNS, Spoofing

detail.practicalScenario: After a vulnerable resolver's cache is poisoned, the company's domain resolves to an attacker's server for hours. Enabling DNSSEC validation later prevents the unsigned forged records from being accepted.
detail.quizQuestion: Which control helps ensure DNS responses are authentic and have not been forged?

definition: A cryptographic attack in which an attacker forces a connection to abandon a strong, modern encryption protocol in favor of an older, weaker one that is easier to break, then exploits that weaker protocol's flaws.
examContext: Grouped with collision and birthday attacks as a cryptographic attack category; know the classic example is forcing a TLS connection down to an outdated, vulnerable protocol version or cipher suite, which is why disabling legacy protocol support is the standard mitigation.
analogy: Like convincing a bank to communicate with you using an old, easily picked lock instead of its current high-security vault door, then picking that old lock.
relatedTerms: Collision attack, Birthday attack, Man-in-the-middle attack, Cipher suite, Perfect forward secrecy

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's vulnerability scan flags that the company's web server still accepts outdated TLS 1.0 connections, confirming it's vulnerable to a downgrade attack where an on-path attacker could force a browser's connection down to that weak protocol before intercepting the traffic, so she disables every protocol version older than TLS 1.2.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker intercepts the start of a TLS handshake and forces the client and server to negotiate an outdated, vulnerable encryption protocol instead of the strongest one both support. What is this attack called?

items.name: SSL 2.0 / 3.0
items.detail: Broken (SSL 3.0 fell to POODLE) and prohibited. SSL as a name survives only in casual speech; it is TLS now.

items.name: TLS 1.0 / 1.1
items.detail: Deprecated by the IETF in 2021; vulnerable to attacks such as BEAST. Disable them.

items.name: TLS 1.2
items.detail: Still widely deployed and secure when configured with ECDHE key exchange and AEAD ciphers such as AES-GCM.

items.name: TLS 1.3
items.detail: Current version: faster 1-RTT handshake, forward secrecy mandatory, and weak options (RC4, 3DES, SHA-1, static-RSA key exchange, CBC) removed.

items.name: ARP poisoning
items.detail: Forged ARP replies map the attacker's MAC to another host's IP, putting the attacker on-path. Fix: Dynamic ARP Inspection, static entries.

items.name: DNS poisoning
items.detail: Forged records are injected into a resolver's cache so users are sent to attacker sites. Fix: DNSSEC, patched resolvers.

items.name: MAC flooding
items.detail: Fills a switch's CAM table so it floods traffic out of every port, letting the attacker sniff. Fix: port security.

items.name: MAC spoofing
items.detail: Adopting another device's MAC address to evade filtering or impersonate it. Fix: 802.1X, port security.

items.name: VLAN hopping
items.detail: Switch spoofing or double tagging to reach other VLANs. Fix: disable trunk negotiation, change the native VLAN, prune unused ports.

items.name: On-path (MITM)
items.detail: The attacker sits between two parties to read or alter traffic. Fix: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, mutual authentication.

items.name: Session hijacking
items.detail: Stealing or guessing a session token to impersonate a logged-in user. Fix: TLS, secure and HttpOnly cookies, short sessions.

items.name: SSL stripping
items.detail: Downgrades a victim's HTTPS session to HTTP. Fix: HSTS.

items.name: Replay
items.detail: Captured valid data is re-sent later. Fix: nonces, timestamps and expiring tokens.

items.name: Spoofing
items.detail: Forging an address or identity (IP, MAC, email, caller ID). Fix: ingress/egress filtering, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, authentication.

definition: The reasonable and responsible actions an organization takes to protect its assets, based on what a prudent entity would do in similar circumstances.
examContext: Exam tests due care as the follow-through step after due diligence, meaning actually implementing the protections that the research identified as necessary.
analogy: Like actually installing the smoke detectors and fire extinguisher after learning your building code requires them.
relatedTerms: Due diligence, Governance, Risk management, Accountability

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's company, after learning through an audit that patches were overdue, immediately rolls out the missing security updates across all servers to act responsibly on that finding.
detail.quizQuestion: After an audit reveals unpatched vulnerabilities, a CISO ensures the patches are applied within the week and documents the remediation. Which concept does this action demonstrate?

items.name: Vendor selection
items.detail: Perform due diligence, check for conflicts of interest, and review financial stability and security posture.

items.name: Vendor assessment
items.detail: Penetration testing, a right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments and supply chain analysis.

items.name: Questionnaires
items.detail: Standardized security questionnaires the vendor completes.

items.name: Agreements
items.detail: SLA, MSA, SOW, NDA and similar contracts that set expectations and responsibilities.

items.name: Vendor monitoring
items.detail: Continual review of the vendor's performance, security and compliance throughout the relationship.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: Written limits on what testing a third party may do.

definition: The ongoing research and investigation an organization performs before making a decision, such as vetting a vendor's security practices before signing a contract.
examContext: Exam distinguishes due diligence, the research done beforehand, from due care, the act of following through on that knowledge; often tested with vendor risk management scenarios.
analogy: Like reading all the reviews and inspecting a used car thoroughly before deciding to buy it.
relatedTerms: Due care, Risk management, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's procurement team conducts a thorough security audit and reviews a cloud vendor's compliance reports before signing a multi-year contract, confirming the vendor meets requirements.
detail.quizQuestion: Before signing a contract with a new cloud provider, a company reviews the vendor's audit reports, certifications, and security questionnaire responses. Which concept does this research represent?

items.name: Vendor selection
items.detail: Perform due diligence, check for conflicts of interest, and review financial stability and security posture.

items.name: Vendor assessment
items.detail: Penetration testing, a right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments and supply chain analysis.

items.name: Questionnaires
items.detail: Standardized security questionnaires the vendor completes.

items.name: Agreements
items.detail: SLA, MSA, SOW, NDA and similar contracts that set expectations and responsibilities.

items.name: Vendor monitoring
items.detail: Continual review of the vendor's performance, security and compliance throughout the relationship.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: Written limits on what testing a third party may do.

definition: The practice of searching through an organization's or individual's discarded trash to recover sensitive documents, hardware, or information.
examContext: Exam tests dumpster diving as a reconnaissance technique, with mitigation being proper shredding and secure disposal policies.
analogy: Like a treasure hunter sifting through someone's garbage looking for discarded bank statements.
relatedTerms: Social engineering, Shoulder surfing

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's security assessment finds unshredded printouts containing employee names and partial account numbers in the office recycling bin, exposing a weakness an attacker could exploit through dumpster diving.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester retrieves discarded printed memos and old hard drives from an organization's outdoor trash bins to gather information for a social engineering campaign. What technique is this?

definition: A method of testing an application for security vulnerabilities by executing it and observing its actual behavior, inputs, and outputs while it runs, rather than examining its source code.
examContext: Know dynamic analysis tests the running application itself, often able to catch runtime issues like session-handling flaws that a static review of source code alone would miss; the two techniques are complementary, not competing.
analogy: Like taste-testing the dish while it's actually cooking on the stove, rather than just reading over the recipe beforehand.
relatedTerms: Static code analysis, Sandboxing, Penetration testing

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's QA team runs the web application in a staging environment and feeds it a barrage of malformed and unexpected inputs while monitoring its live responses, catching a session-handling flaw that only appears while the application is actually executing, something the earlier static source code scan never flagged.
detail.quizQuestion: A QA team executes a web application in a test environment and feeds it unexpected inputs while observing its live runtime behavior to uncover vulnerabilities. What testing approach does this describe?

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

definition: The process of identifying, collecting, preserving, and producing electronically stored information (ESI) in response to litigation, regulatory inquiries, or investigations.
examContext: Know e-Discovery is the process of identifying, collecting, and producing electronically stored information for litigation or investigation, and that it typically follows a legal hold.
analogy: Like a librarian tasked with finding every book, note, and sticky tab in a massive archive that mentions a specific topic, then handing a complete, organized copy to the lawyers.
relatedTerms: Legal hold, Chain of custody, Data classification, Incident response

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's team uses specialized e-Discovery software to search across years of archived emails and file shares for every message mentioning a specific contract dispute, then exports the results with metadata intact so outside counsel can review them for an upcoming lawsuit.
detail.quizQuestion: A company has been served with a lawsuit and must locate, collect, and produce all relevant emails and documents from its systems for the opposing counsel's review. Which process does this describe?

variants.title: Digital forensics: order of volatility and handling

items.name: Order of volatility
items.detail: Collect the MOST volatile evidence first: CPU registers and cache, then RAM (routing/ARP tables, processes), then swap/page file, then disk, then remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.

items.name: Preservation
items.detail: Use write blockers, work on forensic copies, and hash the image to prove it was not changed.

items.name: Acquisition
items.detail: A bit-for-bit disk image, a memory dump, or a snapshot. Live acquisition is needed to capture volatile data.

items.name: Chain of custody
items.detail: Documented record of who handled the evidence, when and why. Gaps can make evidence inadmissible.

items.name: Legal hold
items.detail: A mandate to preserve relevant data (stop normal deletion) because of litigation or investigation.

items.name: e-Discovery
items.detail: Identifying and collecting electronic information for legal proceedings.

items.name: Timeline and reporting
items.detail: Reconstruct events, document findings and make the report clear and reproducible.

definition: A computer system with a dedicated function built into a larger device, such as a printer, smart TV, medical device or vehicle controller, usually running fixed firmware with limited resources.
examContext: Security challenges: inability to patch, weak defaults, long lifespans and too little compute for security agents. Defenses: segmentation, compensating controls and monitoring.
analogy: The tiny computer in a microwave: it does one job and nobody expects to update it.
relatedTerms: RTOS, IoT, ICS, SCADA, Compensating control, Hardening

detail.practicalScenario: A hospital's infusion pumps run old embedded firmware that the vendor no longer updates. The team places them on an isolated VLAN with strict firewall rules because they cannot be patched.
detail.quizQuestion: Which of the following is the MOST common security challenge with embedded systems such as medical devices?
quizOptions: A) Difficulty patching or updating them
B) Constant internet exposure by design

items.name: ICS
items.detail: Industrial Control Systems: control physical processes such as power, water and manufacturing.

items.name: SCADA
items.detail: A kind of ICS that supervises geographically spread sites (pipelines, power grids) with HMIs and field controllers.

items.name: RTOS
items.detail: Real-Time Operating System: guarantees predictable timing, used in safety-critical embedded devices.

items.name: Embedded system
items.detail: Dedicated hardware and firmware for one job (printers, car controllers, medical devices). Often hard to patch.

items.name: IoT
items.detail: Internet-connected devices, frequently with weak defaults and no update path.

items.name: Constraints
items.detail: Limited power and compute, long lifecycles, inability to patch, and availability or safety taking priority over everything else.

items.name: Typical defenses
items.detail: Segmentation or air gaps, compensating controls, monitoring and strict physical security.

definition: The process of wrapping data in a header (and sometimes a trailer) at each layer as it moves down the stack: data becomes a segment, then a packet, then a frame, then bits. The receiver reverses the process, which is called de-encapsulation.
examContext: Know the data unit names (data, segment, packet, frame, bits) and what each layer adds: ports at Layer 4, IP addresses at Layer 3 and MAC addresses at Layer 2. Tunneling and VPNs also encapsulate packets inside other packets.
analogy: Putting a letter in an envelope, the envelope in a shipping box and the box on a truck: each wrapper adds its own label.
relatedTerms: OSI, TCP, IP, VPN, IPSec

detail.practicalScenario: When a laptop sends a web request, the application data gets a TCP header (a segment), then an IP header (a packet), then an Ethernet header and trailer (a frame) before it is sent as signals.
detail.quizQuestion: At which layer does encapsulation add the IP header, turning a segment into a packet?

definition: The process of converting plaintext data into unreadable ciphertext using an algorithm and key, so that only authorized parties with the correct key can convert it back to its original form.
examContext: SY0-701 Domain 1.4 expects you to know encryption as the core mechanism for protecting data at rest, in transit, and in use; be ready to distinguish it from hashing, which is one-way and not reversible.
analogy: Like sealing a letter in a locked box that only the intended recipient has the key to open.
relatedTerms: Symmetric encryption, Asymmetric encryption, Hashing, Hybrid encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Maria configures full-disk encryption on all company laptops so that if a device is lost or stolen, the data on it remains unreadable without the recovery key, satisfying the organization's data-at-rest protection policy.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to ensure that data on stolen laptops cannot be read by unauthorized parties. Which control should be implemented?
quizOptions: A) Hashing the hard drive contents

items.name: Symmetric
items.detail: One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts. Very fast, so it does the bulk data encryption. Weakness: securely sharing the key. N users need N(N-1)/2 keys.

items.name: Asymmetric
items.detail: A mathematically linked public/private key pair. Slow, so it is used for key exchange, digital signatures and certificates. Solves key distribution. N users need only 2N keys.

items.name: Hybrid
items.detail: Asymmetric crypto securely exchanges a random symmetric session key, then symmetric crypto encrypts the actual data. This is how TLS and most real systems work.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: No key (unless it is an HMAC) and no way back: a one-way function giving a fixed-length digest. Used for integrity and password storage, not for confidentiality.

items.name: Full-disk
items.detail: Everything on the drive, including the OS (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS). Protects a lost or stolen device; data is exposed once the system is unlocked and running.

items.name: Partition / volume
items.detail: One partition or logical volume is encrypted while others stay in the clear.

items.name: File / folder
items.detail: Individual files (EFS, GPG, 7-Zip AES). Protects specific data even from other users of the same machine.

items.name: Database
items.detail: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) encrypts the database files; column- or record-level encryption protects individual fields such as SSNs.

items.name: Transport / communication
items.detail: Protects data in motion: TLS, IPsec, SSH, WPA3. The data is not necessarily encrypted at the other end.

variants.title: Data states and how to protect each

items.name: At rest
items.detail: Stored on disk, in a database, on backups or removable media. Protect with full-disk, file or database encryption, access controls and secure storage.

items.name: In transit (in motion)
items.detail: Moving across a network. Protect with TLS, IPsec, VPN, SSH and WPA3.

items.name: In use
items.detail: Being processed in memory or by the CPU. The hardest state to protect: secure enclaves, memory encryption, access controls, and locking screens.

items.name: General methods
items.detail: Encryption, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation, permission restrictions and geographic restrictions (geofencing).

definition: Short-lived credentials, tokens or certificates created on demand for a single task or session that expire automatically, so there is no long-term secret for attackers to steal.
examContext: Used in PAM, cloud IAM and DevOps; they reduce the window of exposure and the reliance on static secrets.
analogy: A one-day visitor badge that stops working at closing time.
relatedTerms: Just-in-time access, Password vaulting, PAM, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: A deployment pipeline requests a temporary cloud credential that is valid for 15 minutes. If the credential leaks in a log file, it is already useless by the time anyone could abuse it.
detail.quizQuestion: A pipeline receives a cloud credential that expires automatically after 15 minutes. What type of credential is this?

definition: The incident response phase in which the root cause is removed from the environment: deleting malware, closing exploited vulnerabilities, rebuilding compromised systems and resetting credentials.
examContext: Comes after containment and before recovery. If the root cause is not removed, the attacker or malware can return.
analogy: Removing every trace of the infestation, not just the visible bugs.
relatedTerms: Containment, Incident response, Lessons learned, Persistence

detail.practicalScenario: With the spread contained, the team removes the malware, patches the exploited vulnerability, rebuilds the affected servers from clean images and resets all passwords that may have been exposed.
detail.quizQuestion: In which incident response phase are malware removed, vulnerabilities patched and compromised systems rebuilt?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: A rogue wireless access point configured with the same SSID as a legitimate network so victims connect to it, letting the attacker eavesdrop, capture credentials or launch on-path attacks.
examContext: Different from a generic rogue AP, which is any unauthorized AP. Defenses: WPA3 or 802.1X with certificate validation, WIDS/WIPS, a VPN on public Wi-Fi and user awareness.
analogy: A fake ATM placed next to the real one that looks identical but records your PIN.
relatedTerms: Rogue access point, Man-in-the-middle attack, Deauthentication attack, WIDS

detail.practicalScenario: At an airport, an attacker creates a network named "Airport_Free_WiFi", identical to the real one. Travelers connect to the stronger signal and the attacker captures their unencrypted traffic and login pages.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker sets up an access point named "Airport_Free_WiFi" next to the real one to capture traffic from travelers. What is this?

definition: The unauthorized transfer or theft of data from a system or network to a location controlled by an attacker.
examContext: Exam tests exfiltration as typically the final goal in a data breach, often detected through data loss prevention tools monitoring for unusual outbound data transfers.
analogy: Like a spy smuggling stolen documents out of a building in a hidden briefcase.
relatedTerms: Command and control, Data loss prevention, Advanced persistent threat, Steganography

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's data loss prevention system alerts on an unusually large encrypted file being uploaded to a personal cloud storage account late at night, which investigation confirms was an attacker exfiltrating stolen customer records.
detail.quizQuestion: A data loss prevention tool flags a large, encrypted file being uploaded from a finance workstation to an unfamiliar external cloud storage account in the middle of the night. What stage of an attack does this most likely represent?

definition: A specific piece of code, technique, or method used to take advantage of a vulnerability to cause unintended behavior.
examContext: Exam often presents a proof-of-concept code scenario and asks you to label it as the exploit versus the underlying vulnerability it targets.
analogy: Like the specific lockpick tool used to open an unlocked door, as opposed to the weak lock itself.
relatedTerms: Vulnerability, Zero-day, Threat actor, Buffer overflow

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's red team writes a proof-of-concept exploit that leverages an unpatched buffer overflow vulnerability to gain remote code execution on a test server.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester uses a publicly available script that takes advantage of a known unpatched flaw to gain shell access to a server. What is this script an example of?

items.name: Application
items.detail: Memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (TOCTOU) and malicious updates.

items.name: Operating system
items.detail: Unpatched or misconfigured OS components and services.

items.name: Web-based
items.detail: SQL injection, XSS and other flaws in web applications.

items.name: Hardware / firmware
items.detail: Flaws in firmware or silicon, plus end-of-life and legacy devices that can no longer be patched.

items.name: Virtualization
items.detail: VM escape (breaking out to the hypervisor or other VMs), resource reuse (data left in reassigned memory or storage), and VM sprawl.

items.name: Cloud-specific
items.detail: Misconfigured storage, over-permissive IAM roles, exposed APIs and weak tenant isolation.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Weaknesses introduced through a service provider, hardware provider or software provider.

items.name: Cryptographic
items.detail: Weak or outdated algorithms, short keys and poor key management.

items.name: Misconfiguration
items.detail: Open permissions, default settings and unnecessary services or protocols.

items.name: Mobile device
items.detail: Side loading and jailbreaking/rooting bypass the platform's security model.

items.name: Zero-day
items.detail: A flaw unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists yet.

definition: An independent examination of an organization's controls by a third party or regulator that provides objective assurance, such as a SOC 2 audit, a regulatory examination or an ISO 27001 certification audit.
examContext: More credible than internal audits and sometimes legally required. It results in an attestation or report.
analogy: The official health inspector, not the owner.
relatedTerms: Internal audit, Self-assessment, Attestation, Compliance

detail.practicalScenario: An independent firm audits a SaaS provider's controls over several months and issues a SOC 2 Type II report that customers can rely on during their own vendor assessments.
detail.quizQuestion: An independent firm examines a company's controls and issues a SOC 2 report. What type of audit is this?

items.name: Internal
items.detail: Performed by the organization's own staff (an internal audit team or audit committee). Good for readiness and compliance checks; less independent.

items.name: External
items.detail: Performed by an independent third party or a regulator. More objective and credible.

items.name: Self-assessment
items.detail: The organization reviews its own controls against a checklist. Cheap and quick, but the least objective.

items.name: Regulatory examination
items.detail: An audit required by law or a regulator.

items.name: Independent third-party audit
items.detail: An outside auditor attests that controls work (for example a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certification).

items.name: Attestation
items.detail: A formal statement from an auditor or responsible party that controls are as described.

definition: A design principle where a system defaults to an unlocked, permissive state upon failure, prioritizing availability and safety over security.
examContext: Commonly tested with fire-exit scenarios where life safety codes require doors to unlock during power failure, even though it reduces security. The objectives contrast it with fail-closed (the same idea as fail secure).
analogy: Like fire doors that automatically unlock in an emergency so people are never trapped inside.
relatedTerms: Fail secure, Availability

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's facility team configures emergency exit doors to unlock automatically during a fire alarm, prioritizing occupant safety even though it temporarily removes access control.
detail.quizQuestion: A building's fire exit doors automatically unlock whenever the fire alarm triggers, allowing occupants to evacuate freely. Which principle does this represent?

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

definition: A design principle where a system defaults to a locked-down, denying state upon failure, prioritizing security over availability. Also called fail-closed.
examContext: The SY0-701 objectives name the pair "fail-open" and "fail-closed", so treat fail secure and fail-closed as the same thing. Exam often contrasts fail secure, where doors lock on power loss, with fail open, where doors unlock on power loss, in physical security scenarios.
analogy: Like a bank vault door that automatically locks shut if the power goes out, keeping intruders from walking in.
relatedTerms: Fail open, Implicit deny, Availability

detail.practicalScenario: Sam configures the data center's electronic door locks to remain locked during a power outage, accepting that employees may be briefly inconvenienced in exchange for preventing unauthorized entry.
detail.quizQuestion: During a power failure, a company's server room door automatically locks and remains shut, preventing anyone from entering until backup power restores the badge system. Which design principle is in effect?

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

definition: The automatic process of switching to a redundant or standby system, server, or network component the moment the primary one fails or becomes unavailable, minimizing service disruption.
examContext: Know failover is the mechanism or event itself, the switch, while high availability and fault tolerance are the broader goals or properties it helps achieve; exam scenarios describe a primary system going down and traffic automatically shifting to a backup.
analogy: Like a backstage understudy who steps onto the stage the instant the lead actor becomes unable to perform, so the show continues without the audience noticing a gap.
relatedTerms: High availability, Fault tolerance, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures a failover cluster for the company's database so that if the primary database server crashes, the standby replica automatically takes over within seconds, and application connections are redirected with minimal disruption to users.
detail.quizQuestion: A primary database server unexpectedly crashes, and within seconds a standby replica automatically takes over processing all requests. What is this automatic switch called?

items.name: Active-active
items.detail: Every node serves traffic at once: best use of capacity, but losing a node reduces total capacity.

items.name: Active-passive
items.detail: A standby node idles until the active node fails. Simpler and predictable, but the standby capacity is unused.

items.name: Round robin
items.detail: Requests go to servers in rotation. Weighted round robin sends proportionally more to stronger servers.

items.name: Least connections
items.detail: The next request goes to the server with the fewest active connections.

items.name: Source IP hash / persistence
items.detail: The same client keeps going to the same server (sticky sessions), which matters when the server holds session state.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 balancers route on IP and port; Layer 7 balancers route on content such as URL, cookies or headers.

items.name: Redundancy
items.detail: Duplicate components (disks, power supplies, links, servers) so a single failure does not stop service.

items.name: Fault tolerance
items.detail: The system keeps operating, with no interruption, when a component fails (RAID, dual power, clustering).

items.name: High availability
items.detail: Designing for maximum uptime (for example "five nines" = 99.999%), usually using redundancy, failover and load balancing.

items.name: Failover
items.detail: Switching automatically from a failed component to a standby.

items.name: Resilience
items.detail: The ability to absorb a disruption and recover quickly.

items.name: Scalability vs elasticity
items.detail: Scalability: the ability to handle growth. Elasticity: automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes.

items.name: Single point of failure
items.detail: Any one component whose failure takes the whole service down. Redundancy exists to remove these.

definition: A failure to detect a real threat or vulnerability, so a genuine problem is reported as clean.
examContext: More dangerous than a false positive because it creates false assurance. Reduce it with layered detection, up-to-date signatures and more than one scanning method.
analogy: A smoke alarm that stays silent during a real fire.
relatedTerms: False positive, Alert tuning, Vulnerability scanning, IDS

detail.practicalScenario: A signature-based scanner reports a server as clean, but a pentester later exploits an unpatched flaw on it that the scanner missed. The scan result was a false negative.
detail.quizQuestion: A vulnerability scan reports a server as clean, but a real exploitable flaw exists that the scanner missed. What is this called?

items.name: Credentialed
items.detail: The scanner logs in with an account, so it sees patch levels, configuration and local vulnerabilities. More accurate, with fewer false positives.

items.name: Non-credentialed
items.detail: An outside-in view, like an attacker. Finds exposed services but may miss internal weaknesses and produces more false positives.

items.name: Intrusive vs non-intrusive
items.detail: Intrusive scans actively try to exploit and can disrupt systems; non-intrusive scans only probe and identify.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agent-based: software on the host reports continuously, even for roaming devices. Agentless: the scanner connects over the network.

items.name: Active vs passive
items.detail: Active sends probes; passive listens to traffic and infers what exists without touching it.

items.name: Scan vs pen test
items.detail: A scan is automated and lists KNOWN weaknesses without exploiting them. A pen test is largely manual and exploits weaknesses to prove real impact.

items.name: False positive / false negative
items.detail: False positive: reported but not real (wastes time). False negative: a real flaw that was missed (dangerous).

definition: An alert or scan result that reports a problem that does not actually exist, such as a legitimate file flagged as malware or a vulnerability reported on a system that is already patched.
examContext: Wastes analyst time and causes alert fatigue; reduce it with tuning and credentialed scans. Contrast with a false negative (a real threat that is missed), which is more dangerous.
analogy: A smoke alarm triggered by burnt toast.
relatedTerms: False negative, Alert tuning, Vulnerability scanning, Indicator of compromise

detail.practicalScenario: A vulnerability scanner reports a critical flaw on a web server, but the analyst checks and finds the patch was already installed. The finding is recorded as a false positive and the scan settings are adjusted.
detail.quizQuestion: A scanner reports a critical vulnerability that, after manual checking, does not actually exist. What is this called?

items.name: Credentialed
items.detail: The scanner logs in with an account, so it sees patch levels, configuration and local vulnerabilities. More accurate, with fewer false positives.

items.name: Non-credentialed
items.detail: An outside-in view, like an attacker. Finds exposed services but may miss internal weaknesses and produces more false positives.

items.name: Intrusive vs non-intrusive
items.detail: Intrusive scans actively try to exploit and can disrupt systems; non-intrusive scans only probe and identify.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agent-based: software on the host reports continuously, even for roaming devices. Agentless: the scanner connects over the network.

items.name: Active vs passive
