items.detail: Weaknesses introduced through a service provider, hardware provider or software provider.

items.name: Cryptographic
items.detail: Weak or outdated algorithms, short keys and poor key management.

items.name: Misconfiguration
items.detail: Open permissions, default settings and unnecessary services or protocols.

items.name: Mobile device
items.detail: Side loading and jailbreaking/rooting bypass the platform's security model.

items.name: Zero-day
items.detail: A flaw unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists yet.

definition: A technique in which a file system or database writes intended changes to a log (the journal) before applying them, so after a crash or power loss it can replay or roll back incomplete operations and return to a consistent state.
examContext: Provides integrity and fast recovery after crashes (NTFS, ext4, database transaction logs). It is not a replacement for backups.
analogy: A ship's logbook: even if the crew is interrupted, the log shows what was in progress.
relatedTerms: Backup, Replication, Integrity, Fault tolerance

detail.practicalScenario: A server loses power mid-write. On reboot, the journaled file system replays the log and finishes or discards the half-completed changes, so the volume is consistent without a long repair.
detail.quizQuestion: Which technique records pending changes in a log so a file system can recover to a consistent state after a crash?

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: A hardened, tightly monitored intermediary server that administrators must connect through to reach devices on a more sensitive or isolated network segment, rather than connecting to those devices directly.
examContext: Know a jump server centralizes and logs all administrative access into a sensitive network zone through one hardened chokepoint, instead of exposing every internal device's management interface directly to administrators' workstations.
analogy: Like requiring every visitor to check in at a single, guarded front desk before being escorted into a secure wing of a building, rather than letting people walk in through any door.
relatedTerms: Network segmentation, Air-gapped network, Zero trust, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: Sam reconfigures network access so that administrators can no longer RDP directly into servers on the isolated management VLAN; instead, they must first authenticate to a hardened jump server, which logs every session before relaying the connection onward.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants all administrative connections into an isolated server management network to pass through a single, heavily logged and monitored chokepoint rather than connecting to each server directly. What should they deploy?

definition: An access control approach that grants users elevated or privileged permissions only for a limited, specific time window when needed to perform a task, automatically revoking the access afterward rather than leaving standing privileges active at all times.
examContext: Know just-in-time access ties to least privilege and privileged access management by granting elevated rights only for a limited time window tied to a specific task, then automatically revoking them, eliminating always-on standing privileges.
analogy: Like a hotel key card that only works for your checkout day and the specific room you booked, instead of a master key that works on every door forever.
relatedTerms: Least privilege, Zero trust, Role-based access control, Privilege escalation, Attribute-based access control

detail.practicalScenario: Sam configures the privileged access management system so that when an administrator needs to patch a production database, they must request elevated access, which is automatically approved for exactly one hour and then revoked, rather than administrators holding permanent standing admin rights.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants administrators to receive elevated database permissions only for the exact duration of an approved maintenance task, with the access automatically revoked afterward. Which approach best satisfies this requirement?

items.name: Just-in-time permissions
items.detail: Privilege is granted only when needed and removed automatically afterwards, so no one holds standing admin rights.

items.name: Password vaulting
items.detail: Privileged credentials are stored encrypted in a vault, checked out by approved users, and rotated after use.

items.name: Ephemeral credentials
items.detail: Short-lived credentials or tokens created on demand for a single task or session, so there is nothing long-lived to steal.

items.name: Session recording
items.detail: Privileged sessions are monitored and recorded for audit and forensics.

items.name: Least privilege / separation of duties
items.detail: Give only the access needed, and split sensitive tasks across people so no single person can complete fraud alone.

definition: A ticket-based network authentication protocol, the default in Windows Active Directory domains. A client proves its identity once to the Key Distribution Center (KDC) and receives a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT), which it later presents to obtain service tickets, so the password never crosses the network again and both sides authenticate each other.
examContext: Know the pieces: KDC (authentication service plus ticket granting service), TGT, service ticket, port 88, and mutual authentication. Kerberos needs synchronized clocks (default tolerance is 5 minutes), so clock skew is a classic failure cause. Do not confuse it with RADIUS or TACACS+, which handle network access and device administration.
analogy: Like a theme park: you show ID once at the gate for a wristband (the TGT), then flash the wristband at each ride to get a ride ticket without proving who you are again.
relatedTerms: Single sign-on, Federation, Authentication, Multifactor authentication, Pass-the-hash, KDC, TGT

detail.practicalScenario: In Dana's Windows domain, she logs in at 8 a.m. and the domain controller (the KDC) hands her a TGT. When she opens a file share, her PC silently exchanges the TGT for a service ticket, so she never retypes her password. One laptop whose clock was 20 minutes off could not authenticate until time sync was fixed.
detail.quizQuestion: Users in a Windows domain sign in once and then reach many services without re-entering credentials, using time-limited tickets issued by a KDC. Which protocol is this?

definition: An arrangement in which copies of cryptographic keys are held in trust by a third party, allowing authorized recovery of encrypted data, for example by law enforcement or a company, under defined conditions.
examContext: Exam questions test the trade-off: key escrow enables data recovery if an employee loses their key or leaves the company, but introduces a risk if the escrow agent itself is compromised.
analogy: Like giving a spare house key to a trusted neighbor in case you get locked out, convenient, but it means someone else could also get in.
relatedTerms: Private key, Certificate authority, Key stretching

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's organization requires all employees' disk-encryption recovery keys to be stored with a designated key escrow service, so that IT can still access an encrypted laptop's data if an employee forgets their passphrase or leaves the company unexpectedly.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee forgets the passphrase to their encrypted laptop and no backup exists. Which practice, if implemented beforehand, would have allowed IT to recover the data?

items.name: Certificate (X.509)
items.detail: A signed document binding a public key to an identity. Holds the subject, issuer, serial number, validity dates, public key and the CA's signature.

items.name: Certificate authority (CA)
items.detail: The trusted issuer that signs certificates. Everyone relying on the certificate must trust the CA.

items.name: Root vs intermediate CA
items.detail: The root CA is self-signed, the trust anchor, and is usually kept OFFLINE. Intermediate CAs are signed by the root and issue the day-to-day certificates; compromise of one can be contained and revoked.

items.name: Registration authority (RA)
items.detail: Verifies requesters' identities on the CA's behalf; it does not sign certificates itself. Careful: CompTIA's acronym list also uses RA for "Recovery Agent" (see the Recovery agent row below).

items.name: CSR
items.detail: Certificate Signing Request: the applicant's public key and identity details, signed with their private key, sent to the CA. The private key never leaves the applicant.

items.name: CRL
items.detail: A CA-published list of revoked certificate serial numbers. Downloaded periodically, so it can be stale and large.

items.name: OCSP
items.detail: Real-time query to ask "is this one certificate still valid?". OCSP stapling lets the web server attach a fresh signed OCSP response to the TLS handshake, which is faster and more private.

items.name: Key escrow
items.detail: A trusted third party holds a copy of private keys so data can be recovered if the owner loses theirs (or for lawful access).

items.name: Recovery agent
items.detail: A designated role authorized to recover encrypted data when a user's key is lost, using escrowed keys or a recovery certificate (for example an EFS or BitLocker recovery agent).

definition: A method or protocol, such as Diffie-Hellman, that allows two parties to securely establish a shared secret key over an untrusted channel without ever transmitting the key itself.
examContext: Know Diffie-Hellman (DHE/ECDHE) as the standard key exchange protocol used in TLS, and that it underpins perfect forward secrecy when ephemeral keys are used.
analogy: Like two people publicly mixing paint colors in a way that lets each independently arrive at the same final secret shade, without ever revealing their individual starting colors to an eavesdropper.
relatedTerms: Asymmetric encryption, Perfect forward secrecy, Symmetric encryption, Cipher suite

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the company's VPN concentrator to use Diffie-Hellman key exchange so that remote workers' devices and the VPN gateway can agree on a shared symmetric session key without ever sending that key across the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: Two systems need to establish a shared symmetric session key over the internet without ever transmitting the key itself. Which process accomplishes this?

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: The size of a cryptographic key in bits. Longer keys create a larger keyspace and make brute force harder, but strength also depends on the algorithm: a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as a 3072-bit RSA key.
examContext: Know typical minimums: AES-128 or AES-256, RSA 2048 or more (3072+ preferred), ECC 256 or more. Longer keys cost more CPU, so there is a performance trade-off. Do not compare bit lengths across algorithm families; symmetric and asymmetric keys are not equivalent bit for bit.
analogy: Like the number of dials on a combination lock: more dials make guessing every combination far harder, but they also take longer to open.
relatedTerms: Symmetric encryption, Asymmetric encryption, Brute force attack, Key stretching

detail.practicalScenario: An audit flags a web server using a 1024-bit RSA certificate. The admin reissues it with a 2048-bit key, accepting slightly slower handshakes in exchange for a much larger keyspace that meets current guidance.
detail.quizQuestion: Which change makes a brute-force attack against an encryption key MORE difficult?
quizOptions: A) Shortening the key to speed up encryption
B) Reusing the same key for all files
D) Using a longer key from a strong algorithm

definition: A metric that signals increasing exposure to risk before an incident occurs, such as the number of unpatched critical systems, failed logins or overdue access reviews.
examContext: Used in risk reporting and monitoring with defined thresholds. Contrast with key performance indicators (KPIs), which measure performance rather than rising risk.
analogy: A rising engine-temperature gauge warning of a possible breakdown.
relatedTerms: Risk register, Risk assessment, Risk tolerance, Indicator of compromise

detail.practicalScenario: The CISO tracks the count of critical vulnerabilities older than 30 days. When the number crosses the agreed threshold, it triggers a review because the exposure is growing.
detail.quizQuestion: The number of critical vulnerabilities left unpatched for over 30 days is tracked monthly and triggers a review when it rises. What is this metric?

items.name: Qualitative
items.detail: Uses descriptive ratings (high / medium / low) on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix. Quick and subjective.

items.name: Quantitative
items.detail: Uses numbers and currency to calculate expected loss. More objective, but needs good data.

items.name: SLE
items.detail: Single Loss Expectancy = Asset Value (AV) x Exposure Factor (EF). The cost of ONE incident.

items.name: ARO
items.detail: Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.

items.name: ALE
items.detail: Annualized Loss Expectancy = SLE x ARO. Compare it with the annual cost of a control to see if the control pays for itself.

items.name: Worked example
items.detail: A laptop worth $2,000 (AV) with 100% EF has an SLE of $2,000. If theft is expected once every two years (ARO 0.5), ALE = $1,000 a year, so a $300 a year tracking service is worth buying.

items.name: Assessment frequency
items.detail: Ad hoc (as needed), recurring (scheduled), one-time (for a project) or continuous (ongoing monitoring).

items.name: Key risk indicators
items.detail: Metrics that signal rising risk before an incident, such as the number of unpatched critical systems.

definition: A technique that repeatedly processes a password or key through a hashing algorithm many times, or uses an intentionally resource-intensive function like PBKDF2, bcrypt, or Argon2, to slow down brute-force and dictionary attacks.
examContext: SY0-701 pairs key stretching with salting as password-storage best practices; know specific algorithm names such as bcrypt, PBKDF2, and Argon2 as likely answer choices.
analogy: Like deliberately making a lock take ten extra seconds to turn, unnoticeable for the legitimate owner, but hugely time-consuming for someone trying thousands of keys.
relatedTerms: Salting, Hashing, Brute force attack, Dictionary attack

detail.practicalScenario: Maria migrates the authentication database from a single round of SHA-1 hashing to bcrypt with a high work factor, dramatically increasing the computational cost required for an attacker to crack stolen password hashes.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to make stolen password hashes significantly more time-consuming to crack via brute force, without changing the underlying passwords. What should they implement?

items.name: MD5
items.detail: 128-bit digest. Broken: practical collision attacks exist, so never use it where security matters. Still seen for quick, non-security file checks.

items.name: SHA-1
items.detail: 160-bit digest. Deprecated: collisions were demonstrated in 2017. Browsers and CAs no longer accept SHA-1 certificates.

items.name: SHA-2 (SHA-256 / SHA-512)
items.detail: The current workhorse family (224/256/384/512-bit digests). SHA-256 is the most common choice for file integrity, certificates and signatures.

items.name: SHA-3
items.detail: Standardized in 2015 using a different internal design (Keccak) from SHA-2. Not a replacement forced by SHA-2 weakness; it is a structurally different fallback.

items.name: RIPEMD
items.detail: Open-design 160-bit hash (RIPEMD-160), an alternative to the SHA family; best known for use in Bitcoin address generation.

items.name: bcrypt / PBKDF2 / Argon2
items.detail: NOT general-purpose hashes: these are deliberately slow password-hashing / key-stretching functions with built-in salting. Use them to store passwords, never plain SHA or MD5.

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: A type of spyware that records every keystroke a user types, often used to capture passwords, credit card numbers, and other sensitive input.
examContext: Exam tests keyloggers as existing in both software and hardware forms, including a physical device plugged between a keyboard and a computer; recognize both forms.
analogy: Like an invisible person standing behind you writing down every letter you type.
relatedTerms: Spyware, Malware

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security sweep finds a small USB hardware device plugged in between a public kiosk's keyboard and computer, secretly recording every password typed by unsuspecting users.
detail.quizQuestion: Investigators find a small, unfamiliar hardware device connected between a reception desk keyboard and the computer, found to be recording all typed input. What is this device?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A penetration test (white box) in which the tester receives full knowledge of the target, including network diagrams, source code and credentials, so testing is efficient and thorough.
examContext: Also called white box; it mimics an insider or an attacker who has already gathered information. Compare partially known (gray box) and unknown (black box).
analogy: An inspector given the building's blueprints and keys.
relatedTerms: Partially known environment, Unknown environment, Penetration testing, Rules of engagement

detail.practicalScenario: The client gives the testers network diagrams, source code and admin accounts so they can find deep flaws quickly without spending days on discovery.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester is given network diagrams, source code and credentials before testing. Which type of test is this?

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: Techniques attackers use to move through a network from one compromised system to another after gaining initial access, in search of additional resources or higher-value targets.
examContext: Exam tests lateral movement as a post-exploitation technique, often following initial access and preceding data exfiltration; linked to pass-the-hash attacks.
analogy: Like a burglar who, once inside one apartment, uses connecting hallways to sneak into neighboring units.
relatedTerms: Pivoting, Privilege escalation, Persistence, Pass-the-hash, Advanced persistent threat

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's SOC detects an attacker who, after compromising a single receptionist's workstation, is using stolen credentials to connect to file servers and other employee machines across the same network segment.
detail.quizQuestion: After compromising a low-level workstation, an attacker uses harvested credentials to log into several other employee workstations and file servers across the same network segment in search of valuable data. What is this activity called?

definition: A switch that can also route between VLANs or subnets at high speed in hardware, combining Layer 2 switching and Layer 3 routing in one device.
examContext: Common in enterprise cores for inter-VLAN routing, usually with ACLs between the VLANs. Distinguish it from a regular Layer 2 switch, which cannot route between networks.
analogy: A receptionist who also runs the mailroom, so notes between floors need no trip to a separate building.
relatedTerms: Switch, Router, VLAN, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: A company puts staff, guests and servers in separate VLANs. A Layer 3 switch routes between them and applies ACLs, so guests can reach only the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: Which device can both forward frames by MAC address and route packets between VLANs in hardware?

definition: The principle of granting users, processes, or systems only the minimum access rights necessary to perform their job functions.
examContext: Commonly tested with scenarios describing over-privileged accounts; the exam expects you to recommend reducing permissions to the minimum required.
analogy: Like giving a janitor keys only to the supply closets they clean, not to the executive offices.
relatedTerms: Separation of duties, Need to know, Role-based access control, Zero trust

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan reviews a developer's account and removes domain admin rights, leaving only the specific server permissions needed for deployments, reducing the blast radius if that account is compromised.
detail.quizQuestion: An auditor finds that a marketing employee's account has full administrative rights to the entire domain, far beyond what their role requires. Which principle has been violated?

items.name: Just-in-time permissions
items.detail: Privilege is granted only when needed and removed automatically afterwards, so no one holds standing admin rights.

items.name: Password vaulting
items.detail: Privileged credentials are stored encrypted in a vault, checked out by approved users, and rotated after use.

items.name: Ephemeral credentials
items.detail: Short-lived credentials or tokens created on demand for a single task or session, so there is nothing long-lived to steal.

items.name: Session recording
items.detail: Privileged sessions are monitored and recorded for audit and forensics.

items.name: Least privilege / separation of duties
items.detail: Give only the access needed, and split sensitive tasks across people so no single person can complete fraud alone.

definition: A legal obligation requiring an organization to preserve all forms of relevant information, including electronic records, when litigation, investigation, or audit is reasonably anticipated, suspending normal data retention or destruction schedules.
examContext: Know that once a legal hold is issued, routine data retention and destruction policies (like auto-deleting old emails) must be suspended for the affected data, regardless of the normal schedule.
analogy: Like a 'do not discard' sticky note slapped on a box in storage the moment a lawsuit is filed, overriding the usual rule that boxes older than a year get thrown out.
relatedTerms: e-Discovery, Chain of custody, Data classification, Incident response

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's legal department issues a litigation hold notice after receiving a lawsuit threat, and the IT team immediately suspends the automatic 90-day email purge policy for the named employees' mailboxes so none of the potentially relevant messages are destroyed before the case concludes.
detail.quizQuestion: A company anticipates litigation and its legal department issues a notice requiring certain employee data to be preserved. What must the IT department do in response?
quizOptions: A) Immediately encrypt all affected data
B) Begin the e-Discovery review process without legal approval
C) Transfer the data to a third-party processor
D) Suspend routine deletion and retention policies for the relevant data

variants.title: Digital forensics: order of volatility and handling

items.name: Order of volatility
items.detail: Collect the MOST volatile evidence first: CPU registers and cache, then RAM (routing/ARP tables, processes), then swap/page file, then disk, then remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.

items.name: Preservation
items.detail: Use write blockers, work on forensic copies, and hash the image to prove it was not changed.

items.name: Acquisition
items.detail: A bit-for-bit disk image, a memory dump, or a snapshot. Live acquisition is needed to capture volatile data.

items.name: Chain of custody
items.detail: Documented record of who handled the evidence, when and why. Gaps can make evidence inadmissible.

items.name: Legal hold
items.detail: A mandate to preserve relevant data (stop normal deletion) because of litigation or investigation.

items.name: e-Discovery
items.detail: Identifying and collecting electronic information for legal proceedings.

items.name: Timeline and reporting
items.detail: Reconstruct events, document findings and make the report clear and reproducible.

definition: The post-incident review in which the team analyzes what happened, how well the response worked and what to improve, then updates plans, controls and training. It includes root cause analysis and a written report.
examContext: The final phase of the incident response process and a key input to continuous improvement. Hold it soon after the incident, in a blameless way.
analogy: A sports team reviewing game film after the match.
relatedTerms: Incident response, RCA, Containment, Eradication

detail.practicalScenario: A week after an incident, the team meets to review the timeline. They find that a missing alert delayed detection, add a new detection rule and update the playbook.
detail.quizQuestion: After an incident is resolved, the team meets to review what went wrong and update plans and controls. Which phase is this?

items.name: 1. Preparation
items.detail: Policies, an incident response plan, trained team, tools, contact lists and playbooks, all ready BEFORE an incident.

items.name: 2. Detection
items.detail: Spotting events through monitoring, alerts and user reports.

items.name: 3. Analysis
items.detail: Validating whether it is a real incident, how big it is and what is affected, then prioritizing.

items.name: 4. Containment
items.detail: Stopping the spread: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block IPs. Short-term first, then long-term.

items.name: 5. Eradication
items.detail: Removing the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, reset credentials.

items.name: 6. Recovery
items.detail: Restoring from clean backups, validating, and watching for recurrence.

items.name: 7. Lessons learned
items.detail: A post-incident review and root cause analysis; update the plan and controls.

items.name: NIST view
items.detail: NIST SP 800-61 compresses these into four: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity.

definition: Strategically placed illumination around a facility's exterior and entrances that deters intruders by removing concealment and improves the effectiveness of guards and cameras after dark.
examContext: The exam treats lighting as a low-cost deterrent control often listed alongside fencing and bollards; remember it primarily works by eliminating hiding spots and improving visibility for other controls like guards and cameras.
analogy: Like a porch light that discourages a prowler simply by removing the shadows they'd otherwise hide in.
relatedTerms: Video surveillance, Security guard, Fencing

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's facilities team installs motion-activated floodlights around every loading dock and dark corner of the parking lot, removing the shadowed areas that previously made the camera footage useless at night.
detail.quizQuestion: A security review finds that nighttime camera footage around a building's rear entrance is too dark to identify anyone. Which control would most directly improve this situation?

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

items.name: Infrared (PIR)
items.detail: Detects the body heat of a person moving through its field of view. Common in motion-activated lights and alarms.

items.name: Pressure
items.detail: Detects weight or force on a floor mat, tile or fence line, so it triggers when someone steps or climbs.

items.name: Microwave
items.detail: Emits microwave energy and detects changes in the reflection caused by movement. Covers a large area and can sense through thin walls.

items.name: Ultrasonic
items.detail: Emits high-frequency sound and detects movement from changes in the reflected waves. Good for enclosed rooms.

items.name: Video / camera
items.detail: Records or analyzes images; paired with motion detection to alert on activity.

items.name: Role in security
items.detail: All of these are DETECTIVE controls. The response (alarm, lights, recording) can add a deterrent or corrective effect.

definition: A technique that distributes network or application traffic across multiple servers to optimize resource use, maximize throughput, minimize response time, and avoid overloading any single server.
examContext: Know load balancers also contribute to high availability and fault tolerance, since if one server fails, traffic is redirected to healthy servers; common algorithms include round-robin and least-connections.
analogy: Like a store manager directing customers to whichever checkout line is shortest, so no single cashier gets overwhelmed while others sit idle.
relatedTerms: High availability, Failover, Fault tolerance, Proxy server

detail.practicalScenario: Sam deploys a load balancer in front of the web application's four server instances, distributing incoming customer traffic evenly so that no single server becomes overwhelmed during a traffic surge, and automatically rerouting traffic if one instance goes down.
detail.quizQuestion: During a major sale event, a company's website receives ten times its normal traffic. Which solution distributes requests across multiple backend servers to prevent any single server from being overwhelmed?

items.name: Forward proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of CLIENTS. Users' outbound requests go through it for content filtering, caching, logging and anonymity. Clients are configured to use it.

items.name: Reverse proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of SERVERS. Outside clients talk to the proxy, which forwards to the back end. Used for load balancing, TLS offloading, caching and hiding server details.

items.name: Transparent proxy
items.detail: Intercepts traffic inline without any client configuration, so users do not know it is there.

items.name: Caching proxy
items.detail: Stores copies of frequently requested content to save bandwidth and speed responses.

items.name: Active-active
items.detail: Every node serves traffic at once: best use of capacity, but losing a node reduces total capacity.

items.name: Active-passive
items.detail: A standby node idles until the active node fails. Simpler and predictable, but the standby capacity is unused.

items.name: Round robin
items.detail: Requests go to servers in rotation. Weighted round robin sends proportionally more to stronger servers.

items.name: Least connections
items.detail: The next request goes to the server with the fewest active connections.

items.name: Source IP hash / persistence
items.detail: The same client keeps going to the same server (sticky sessions), which matters when the server holds session state.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 balancers route on IP and port; Layer 7 balancers route on content such as URL, cookies or headers.

items.name: Redundancy
items.detail: Duplicate components (disks, power supplies, links, servers) so a single failure does not stop service.

items.name: Fault tolerance
items.detail: The system keeps operating, with no interruption, when a component fails (RAID, dual power, clustering).

items.name: High availability
items.detail: Designing for maximum uptime (for example "five nines" = 99.999%), usually using redundancy, failover and load balancing.

items.name: Failover
items.detail: Switching automatically from a failed component to a standby.

items.name: Resilience
items.detail: The ability to absorb a disruption and recover quickly.

items.name: Scalability vs elasticity
items.detail: Scalability: the ability to handle growth. Elasticity: automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes.

items.name: Single point of failure
items.detail: Any one component whose failure takes the whole service down. Redundancy exists to remove these.

definition: Collecting logs from many systems into a central repository so they can be searched, correlated and retained, typically using a SIEM or log management platform.
examContext: The foundation of SIEM detection and of investigations; it also protects logs from tampering on a compromised host. Part of security monitoring.
analogy: Bringing the footage from every security camera into one control room.
relatedTerms: Syslog, SIEM, Missing logs, Alert tuning

detail.practicalScenario: The company forwards firewall, server and application logs to a central SIEM. When an attacker wipes the local logs on a compromised server, the aggregated copy still shows what happened.
detail.quizQuestion: Which practice sends logs from many systems to one central location for correlation, search and tamper-resistant retention?

variants.title: Log and data sources for investigations

items.name: Firewall logs
items.detail: Allowed and denied connections, source/destination IPs and ports.

items.name: Application logs
items.detail: Application events, errors and user actions.

items.name: Endpoint logs
items.detail: Events from EDR or the host: process starts, file and registry changes.

items.name: OS-specific security logs
items.detail: Windows Event Log (Security, System, Application) or Linux auth.log and syslog: logons, privilege use and policy changes.

items.name: IDS / IPS logs
items.detail: Detected and blocked attack signatures and anomalies.

items.name: Network logs
items.detail: Router and switch logs, NetFlow, DNS and proxy logs.

items.name: Metadata
items.detail: Data about data: file timestamps, EXIF in photos, email headers.

items.name: Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards
items.detail: Aggregated views that spot trends and help prioritize.

items.name: Packet captures
items.detail: A full copy of traffic for deep analysis (PCAP files).

items.name: Log aggregation
items.detail: Collect logs from many sources into one place for correlation and search.

items.name: Alerting
items.detail: Notify people or systems when events match a rule or threshold.

items.name: Alert tuning
items.detail: Adjust thresholds and rules to cut false positives without missing real attacks.

items.name: Scanning and reporting
items.detail: Regular scans and reports show trends and compliance.

items.name: Archiving
items.detail: Keep logs for the retention period required for investigations and regulations.

items.name: Quarantine
items.detail: Isolate a suspicious file, system or message until it can be investigated.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agents give deep visibility and work off-network. Agentless is easier to deploy but shallower.

definition: Malicious code intentionally inserted into a system that remains dormant until triggered by a specific condition, such as a date or an event.
examContext: Exam tests logic bombs as often planted by disgruntled insiders, triggered by conditions like a termination date appearing in HR records.
analogy: Like a landmine buried and forgotten until someone's footstep, or a specific date, sets it off.
relatedTerms: Insider threat, Malware, Persistence

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's forensic team discovers code hidden in the payroll system set to delete all records automatically if the disgruntled developer's employee ID was ever removed from the active directory, a logic bomb meant to trigger upon his termination.
detail.quizQuestion: A former employee's code is discovered that was designed to silently delete critical database tables only if his own user account was ever deactivated. What type of malicious code is this?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A 48-bit hardware address, written as six pairs of hex digits such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E, assigned to a network interface and used at Layer 2 to deliver frames on the local network. It can be changed or spoofed in software.
examContext: Switches use MAC addresses and routers use IP addresses. Attacks: MAC spoofing (impersonating a device) and MAC flooding (overflowing a switch table). MAC filtering is weak security because addresses are easy to copy, while port security limits the MAC addresses per port. Remember that the acronym MAC can also mean Mandatory Access Control or Message Authentication Code.
analogy: A name tag: it identifies you at the front desk, but it does not say where you live.
relatedTerms: IP address, Switch, MAC flooding, Spoofing, Port security, ARP poisoning

detail.practicalScenario: A cafe's Wi-Fi only admits registered MAC addresses. An attacker sniffs an allowed device's address, sets his own laptop to use it and joins the network, which shows why MAC filtering is not strong security.
detail.quizQuestion: Which identifier is burned into a network card and used by switches to deliver frames on the local network?

definition: An attack that floods a switch with frames carrying fake source MAC addresses to overflow its CAM table, causing the switch to fail open and broadcast traffic out of all ports so the attacker can sniff it.
examContext: Mitigate with port security (limit the number of MAC addresses per port) and sticky MAC. A Layer 2 attack grouped with ARP poisoning and VLAN hopping.
analogy: Flooding a receptionist with fake visitor names until she stops checking the list and lets everyone wander the halls.
relatedTerms: ARP poisoning, VLAN hopping, Port security, MAC

detail.practicalScenario: A switch suddenly sends all traffic out of every port after its address table fills with thousands of spoofed entries, letting an attacker capture other users' traffic. Port security with a per-port MAC limit prevents it.
detail.quizQuestion: A switch begins sending all traffic out of every port after its address table is filled with spoofed entries. What attack occurred?

definition: A scheduled period, usually during low usage, in which planned changes, patching and maintenance are allowed so disruption to users and the business is minimized.
examContext: Change management requires scheduling within an approved maintenance window and communicating downtime to stakeholders. It is a business process element of change control.
analogy: Road repairs scheduled overnight so that daytime traffic is not disrupted.
relatedTerms: Change management, Backout plan, Patch management, High availability

detail.practicalScenario: The team applies server patches only on Sunday between 2 and 4 a.m., when usage is lowest, and notifies all stakeholders in advance. If a patch fails, the backout plan runs inside the same window.
detail.quizQuestion: To reduce business impact, a team applies server patches only between 2 and 4 a.m. on Sundays. What is this scheduled period called?

items.name: Approval process
items.detail: A formal review (often by a Change Advisory Board) before any change is made.

items.name: Ownership
items.detail: A named person responsible for the change.

items.name: Stakeholders
items.detail: Everyone affected who must be informed or consulted.

items.name: Impact analysis
items.detail: What could break, and how risky is the change?

items.name: Test results
items.detail: Proof the change works in a non-production environment first.

items.name: Backout plan
items.detail: The steps to undo the change if it fails.

items.name: Maintenance window
items.detail: A scheduled time when changes are allowed so users are least affected.

items.name: Standard operating procedure
items.detail: The documented way routine changes are performed.

definition: A vulnerability in which an attacker compromises a software update mechanism or vendor build process to deliver malware inside what appears to be a legitimate patch.
examContext: A supply chain risk illustrated by tampered updates. Mitigate with code signing and signature verification, hash checks, staged rollouts and vendor risk management.
analogy: A poisoned package delivered by a trusted courier.
relatedTerms: Supply chain attack, Code signing, Patch management, Hashing

detail.practicalScenario: A software vendor's build server is breached and a signed-looking update containing a backdoor reaches thousands of customers. Customers who verify signatures and stage updates to a test group detect it early.
detail.quizQuestion: Attackers compromise a vendor's update server so that a legitimate-looking patch installs a backdoor on customers' systems. Which vulnerability type is this?

definition: Any software intentionally designed to cause damage, disrupt operations, or gain unauthorized access to a computer system.
examContext: Exam uses malware as the umbrella term; expect you to classify specific types such as ransomware, spyware, and rootkits as subcategories of malware.
analogy: Like a general term for sickness, which covers many diseases including the flu, a cold, and chickenpox.
relatedTerms: Ransomware, Spyware, Rootkit, Virus, Worm, Trojan horse

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's antivirus software quarantines a file downloaded from an email attachment after detecting signatures matching known malicious code designed to corrupt system files.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst needs a single term to describe viruses, worms, ransomware, and spyware collectively in an incident report. Which term should be used?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: An attack in which a threat actor secretly intercepts and potentially alters communications between two parties who believe they are communicating directly with each other. CompTIA's current objectives call this an on-path attack.
examContext: CompTIA now lists this as an "on-path" attack, so expect either name. Exam tests man-in-the-middle attacks through examples like rogue access points, ARP spoofing, and SSL stripping; mitigations include strong encryption and certificate validation.
analogy: Like a dishonest mail carrier who secretly opens, reads, and possibly alters letters between two people before resealing and delivering them.
relatedTerms: Replay attack, Encryption, Certificate authority

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's security team discovers a rogue Wi-Fi access point in the office lobby that was silently intercepting and relaying traffic between employee laptops and the real company network, capturing login credentials along the way.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker sets up a rogue wireless access point with the same name as the corporate network, silently relaying traffic between victims and the real network while capturing their credentials. What type of attack is this?

items.name: ARP poisoning
items.detail: Forged ARP replies map the attacker's MAC to another host's IP, putting the attacker on-path. Fix: Dynamic ARP Inspection, static entries.

items.name: DNS poisoning
items.detail: Forged records are injected into a resolver's cache so users are sent to attacker sites. Fix: DNSSEC, patched resolvers.

items.name: MAC flooding
items.detail: Fills a switch's CAM table so it floods traffic out of every port, letting the attacker sniff. Fix: port security.

items.name: MAC spoofing
items.detail: Adopting another device's MAC address to evade filtering or impersonate it. Fix: 802.1X, port security.

items.name: VLAN hopping
items.detail: Switch spoofing or double tagging to reach other VLANs. Fix: disable trunk negotiation, change the native VLAN, prune unused ports.

items.name: On-path (MITM)
items.detail: The attacker sits between two parties to read or alter traffic. Fix: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, mutual authentication.

items.name: Session hijacking
items.detail: Stealing or guessing a session token to impersonate a logged-in user. Fix: TLS, secure and HttpOnly cookies, short sessions.

items.name: SSL stripping
items.detail: Downgrades a victim's HTTPS session to HTTP. Fix: HSTS.

items.name: Replay
items.detail: Captured valid data is re-sent later. Fix: nonces, timestamps and expiring tokens.

items.name: Spoofing
items.detail: Forging an address or identity (IP, MAC, email, caller ID). Fix: ingress/egress filtering, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, authentication.

definition: A control that governs how security is planned, organized and overseen, such as policies, risk assessments, security planning, vendor reviews and audits. Also called an administrative control.
examContext: Think paperwork and oversight: risk assessments, policies, standards, procedures and security program management. Many managerial controls are directive (policies) or detective (audits, risk assessments). Do not confuse with operational controls, which are carried out by staff day to day.
analogy: The company rulebook and the board's oversight, rather than the locks on the doors.
relatedTerms: Control categories, Directive control, Operational control, Risk assessment

detail.practicalScenario: The CISO commissions an annual risk assessment and revises the information security policy. Neither activity touches a system directly, but both steer how security is run, which makes them managerial controls.
detail.quizQuestion: Which of the following is an example of a MANAGERIAL control?

variants.title: Control categories (WHAT the control is made of)

items.name: Technical
items.detail: Implemented with technology: firewalls, encryption, antivirus, ACLs, MFA, IDS/IPS.

items.name: Managerial (administrative)
items.detail: Policies, risk assessments, security planning and oversight: the "paperwork" that governs how security is managed.

items.name: Operational
items.detail: Carried out day to day by PEOPLE: security awareness training, guards, change and patch procedures, backups performed by staff.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tangible barriers and devices: locks, fences, bollards, cameras, badge readers, vestibules, lighting.

items.name: Tip
items.detail: The category describes what it is or who runs it. The TYPE (preventive, detective and so on) describes what it does. One control has both: a firewall is a technical, preventive control.

definition: An access control model where a central authority assigns data classification labels, such as Confidential or Top Secret, and users are granted access only if their security clearance matches or exceeds that label, with users unable to alter permissions themselves.
examContext: Know MAC is used in high-security, military, and government environments, such as SELinux; the key distinguishing fact is that regular users cannot change permissions at all, since only a central administrator or system enforces access based on labels.
analogy: Like a classified government document stamped Top Secret, no matter who physically holds it, only people with the matching security clearance level are permitted to read it.
relatedTerms: Discretionary access control, Role-based access control, Data classification

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's government agency implements mandatory access control so that documents labeled Secret can only be opened by users whose account clearance is set to Secret or higher, and no file owner, regardless of position, can grant access to someone without the matching clearance.
detail.quizQuestion: A government system enforces access so that only users with a matching or higher security clearance level can open documents labeled Secret, and individual file owners cannot override this. Which access control model is in use?

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: A code execution technique in which an attacker inserts malicious instructions directly into the memory space of a running, legitimate process, causing that process to execute the attacker's code under its own trusted identity and privileges.
examContext: Know memory injection as an application-based vulnerability where malicious code runs inside a trusted, already-running process's memory rather than as its own file, which is exactly why it evades antivirus tools that only scan files on disk.
analogy: Like a con artist slipping a forged page into the middle of an already-signed, notarized contract, so the fake page carries the same authority as the legitimate document.
relatedTerms: Buffer overflow, Privilege escalation, Rootkit, Dynamic code analysis

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's endpoint detection tool flags the normally harmless svchost.exe process making unexpected outbound connections; her investigation finds an attacker used memory injection to insert malicious code straight into the running process's address space, so no new file ever appeared on disk for antivirus to catch.
detail.quizQuestion: A trusted Windows system process is observed making unusual outbound network connections, yet a full disk and file scan finds no malicious executable anywhere on the system. Which technique most likely explains this behavior?

definition: Data that describes other data, such as file creation and modification times, authorship, GPS coordinates in photos (EXIF) and email headers. It is valuable in investigations and can also leak sensitive information.
examContext: Has both forensic and OSINT value; scrub it before publishing documents. Part of the data sources used in investigations.
analogy: The label on a file folder: it tells you about the contents without opening it.
relatedTerms: Digital forensics, OSINT, Chain of custody, Log aggregation

detail.practicalScenario: Investigators use a document's metadata to show it was created on a former employee's laptop three days before they resigned. A photo posted online also reveals the location where it was taken.
detail.quizQuestion: Which type of data, such as a file's creation time and author, describes other data and is useful in forensic investigations?

variants.title: Log and data sources for investigations

items.name: Firewall logs
items.detail: Allowed and denied connections, source/destination IPs and ports.

items.name: Application logs
items.detail: Application events, errors and user actions.

items.name: Endpoint logs
items.detail: Events from EDR or the host: process starts, file and registry changes.

items.name: OS-specific security logs
items.detail: Windows Event Log (Security, System, Application) or Linux auth.log and syslog: logons, privilege use and policy changes.

items.name: IDS / IPS logs
items.detail: Detected and blocked attack signatures and anomalies.

items.name: Network logs
items.detail: Router and switch logs, NetFlow, DNS and proxy logs.

items.name: Metadata
items.detail: Data about data: file timestamps, EXIF in photos, email headers.

items.name: Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards
items.detail: Aggregated views that spot trends and help prioritize.

items.name: Packet captures
items.detail: A full copy of traffic for deep analysis (PCAP files).

definition: A granular form of network segmentation, common in virtualized and cloud environments, that enforces security policies down to the individual workload or application level, often using software-defined networking rather than physical network boundaries.
examContext: Know microsegmentation as a zero trust architecture building block, enabling very fine-grained east-west traffic control within a data center, beyond what traditional VLAN-based segmentation offers.
analogy: Like giving every single room in a building its own lock and access list, instead of just locking the building's front door and a few floor entrances.
relatedTerms: Network segmentation, Zero trust

detail.practicalScenario: Sam implements microsegmentation in the company's virtualized data center so that each application workload has its own explicit traffic policy, preventing a compromised virtual machine from communicating laterally with unrelated workloads even within the same subnet.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud architect wants to enforce security policies at the individual workload level within a data center, preventing lateral movement between virtual machines on the same subnet. Which approach best achieves this?

items.name: Trusted / intranet
items.detail: The internal corporate network; highest trust.

items.name: Untrusted
items.detail: The internet and anything you do not control.

items.name: Screened subnet (DMZ)
items.detail: A buffer zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS). If one is compromised, the attacker is still outside the internal network.

items.name: Extranet
items.detail: A controlled network shared with partners, suppliers or customers.

items.name: Guest network
items.detail: Isolated Wi-Fi/VLAN with internet-only access.

items.name: Management network
items.detail: A separate (often out-of-band) network used only to administer devices.

items.name: Segmentation methods
items.detail: Physical (separate hardware or an air gap), logical (VLANs and ACLs), virtual (VXLAN/overlays) and microsegmentation (per-workload policy).

items.name: North-south vs east-west
items.detail: North-south traffic enters or leaves the datacenter or network; east-west traffic moves between internal systems, which is where lateral movement happens.

definition: An architectural approach that structures an application as a collection of small, independently deployable services, each handling a specific business function and communicating over well-defined APIs (often REST or messaging), rather than one monolithic codebase.
examContext: Know the trade-off the exam tests: microservices improve fault isolation and independent scaling/patching of each service, but expand the attack surface since every service and its interfaces must be individually authenticated and secured.
analogy: Like a restaurant kitchen split into separate stations, grill, salad, dessert, each run independently, instead of one cook trying to do everything at a single station.
relatedTerms: Containerization, Serverless computing, Virtualization, Attack surface

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's team breaks apart their aging monolithic e-commerce application into separate microservices for inventory, payments, and user accounts, each with its own authentication and deployment pipeline, so a bug in the inventory service can be patched and redeployed without taking down checkout.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization splits a single large application into many small, independently deployable services that communicate over APIs. What is the primary security trade-off introduced by this architecture?
quizOptions: A) It increases the attack surface since each service and interface must be secured individually
B) It eliminates the need for authentication between services
C) It removes the need for patch management
D) It guarantees data at rest is automatically encrypted

definition: Incorrect or insecure settings in software, devices or cloud services, such as open storage buckets, default accounts, unnecessary services or overly broad permissions, that expose systems to attack.
examContext: One of the most common causes of breaches, covering default credentials and unhardened systems. Prevent with secure baselines, configuration scanning, infrastructure as code and change control.
analogy: Leaving the vault door ajar: the vault is strong, but someone set it up wrong.
relatedTerms: Hardening, Secure baseline, Default credentials, Vulnerability

detail.practicalScenario: A cloud storage bucket holding customer files is accidentally set to public. Nobody exploited a software bug; the data was simply exposed by the setting.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud storage bucket holding customer data is accidentally set to public access. Which vulnerability type is this?

definition: False or inaccurate information that is spread regardless of whether the person sharing it intends to deceive; in a security context it can still damage trust, cause panic, or influence decisions even without malicious intent.
examContext: The exam distinguishes misinformation, false information spread without necessarily intending to deceive, from disinformation, deliberately false information spread to deceive; both fall under the influence-campaign concepts tested in objective 2.2.
analogy: Like a rumor that spreads through an office because someone genuinely misunderstood a memo, not because anyone meant to lie.
relatedTerms: Disinformation, Social engineering, Brand impersonation

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's communications team notices employees are sharing an outdated internal memo as if it reflects current policy, unintentionally spreading inaccurate information that the team must quickly correct with an official clarification.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee shares an outdated security memo on the company chat, genuinely believing it still reflects current policy, causing confusion about proper procedures. What best describes this spread of false information?

definition: Gaps, cleared or deleted entries in log files, often a sign that an attacker or insider is covering their tracks. Logging pipelines can also fail for benign reasons, so gaps need investigation.
examContext: Attackers commonly clear logs after compromise. Protect logs with centralized aggregation (SIEM), write-once storage and integrity monitoring.
analogy: Torn-out pages in a ledger.
relatedTerms: Indicators of malicious activity, Log aggregation, SIEM, FIM

detail.practicalScenario: During an investigation, analysts notice that the web server's local logs stop for two hours during the suspected intrusion. The SIEM copy shows the real activity, proving the attacker tried to erase evidence.
detail.quizQuestion: Analysts find a two-hour gap in a server's security logs during a suspected intrusion. What indicator does this represent?

definition: Using services from more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in, improve resilience and choose the best service for each need, at the cost of added complexity in security, identity and visibility.
examContext: An architecture consideration that supports platform diversity and resilience but demands consistent IAM, policy and monitoring across providers (often with a CASB).
analogy: Shopping at several supermarkets so one closure does not leave you without food.
relatedTerms: Hybrid cloud, Public cloud, Platform diversity, Responsibility matrix

detail.practicalScenario: A company runs its main application on one cloud provider and keeps its disaster-recovery copy on another. An outage at one provider no longer takes down the service, but the team must manage two sets of security controls.
detail.quizQuestion: A company spreads workloads across two different cloud providers to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages. What is this approach called?

definition: An authentication method requiring two or more independent verification factors from different categories, such as something you know, something you have, something you are, or somewhere you are, before granting access.
examContext: Know the factor categories and that combining two items from the same category, such as a password plus a PIN, does not count as true MFA; exam scenarios test identifying valid versus invalid factor combinations.
analogy: Like an ATM requiring both your physical card, something you have, and your PIN, something you know, before dispensing cash, one alone isn't enough.
relatedTerms: Biometrics, Smart card, Single sign-on, Authentication

detail.practicalScenario: Maria enables multifactor authentication on all remote VPN logins, requiring employees to enter their password plus a one-time code from an authenticator app, so a stolen password alone can no longer grant an attacker access.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to ensure that a stolen password alone cannot be used to log into the corporate VPN. Which control should be required?

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

items.name: Fingerprint
items.detail: Cheap and widely accepted, but can be fooled by lifted prints or fakes unless liveness detection is used.

items.name: Retina
items.detail: Scans the blood-vessel pattern at the back of the eye. Very accurate but intrusive, so uncommon.

items.name: Iris
items.detail: Scans the coloured ring around the pupil. Accurate and stable over a lifetime, and less intrusive than retina.

items.name: Facial recognition
items.detail: Convenient, but affected by lighting and angle, and spoofable with photos or masks without liveness checks.

items.name: Voice
items.detail: Affected by noise and illness; spoofable with recordings or deepfakes.

items.name: Vein / palm
items.detail: Maps the pattern of blood vessels; difficult to forge.

items.name: Gait
items.detail: A behavioral biometric based on how a person walks.

items.name: FRR (Type I)
items.detail: False Rejection Rate: a LEGITIMATE user is wrongly denied. Hurts usability.

items.name: FAR (Type II)
items.detail: False Acceptance Rate: an IMPOSTOR is wrongly allowed in. This is the dangerous one for security.

items.name: CER / EER
items.detail: Crossover (Equal) Error Rate: the point where FAR equals FRR. The LOWER the CER, the more accurate the system.

items.name: HOTP
items.detail: HMAC-based, COUNTER-based: each use advances a counter, so a code stays valid until it is used and can drift out of sync. No built-in expiry.

items.name: TOTP
items.detail: Time-based: the code is derived from the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so it expires quickly. What authenticator apps use; needs reasonably accurate clocks.

items.name: SMS / voice code
items.detail: Delivered over the phone network. Weakest option: vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, and discouraged by NIST.

items.name: Push notification
items.detail: Approve a prompt on your phone. Convenient, but vulnerable to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) when users approve out of annoyance.

items.name: Hard vs soft token
items.detail: A hard token is a physical device that displays or generates codes; a soft token is an app on a phone.

items.name: Security key (FIDO2 / WebAuthn)
items.detail: Public-key based and bound to the website's origin, so it resists phishing. The strongest everyday option.

definition: A threat actor sponsored or directed by a government, with large budgets, advanced tools and patience. Goals include espionage, sabotage of critical infrastructure and political or military advantage, often pursued through advanced persistent threat campaigns.
examContext: Highest resources and sophistication of any actor; motivations are espionage, war and geopolitical aims. Classic examples are APT groups. Contrast with hacktivists (ideology) and organized crime (profit).
analogy: A professional intelligence agency with a huge budget and a long-term mission, as opposed to a lone burglar.
relatedTerms: Advanced persistent threat, Threat actor, Hacktivist, Organized crime, Zero-day

detail.practicalScenario: A defense contractor discovers that attackers lived in its network for 14 months, quietly stealing blueprints with custom malware and zero-day exploits. Analysis points to a state-sponsored group pursuing espionage.
detail.quizQuestion: A well-funded group uses custom malware and zero-day exploits over many months to steal defense designs. Which threat actor type is MOST likely?

definition: A restriction that limits access to information to only those individuals whose job duties require it, even if they already hold sufficient clearance.
examContext: Exam distinguishes need to know, which is information-specific, from least privilege, which is access-rights-specific; often tested together with classified data handling.
analogy: Like a hospital where even a doctor with full clearance only pulls up charts for patients actively under their care.
relatedTerms: Least privilege, Separation of duties, Data classification, Confidentiality

detail.practicalScenario: Alex, who holds a high security clearance, is still denied access to a classified project file because her current assignment does not require that specific information.
detail.quizQuestion: A cleared employee with top-level security clearance is denied access to a classified file because the project is unrelated to her duties. Which principle justifies this restriction?

definition: A number from 0 to 65,535 that identifies a specific service or application on a device so incoming traffic reaches the right program. An IP address plus a port is called a socket, and ports 0 to 1023 are the well-known ports.
examContext: Open ports are attack surface, so close what you do not use. Know the ranges and common ports (22, 53, 80, 443, 3389). A port scan classifies each port as open, closed or filtered. Do not confuse this with the physical ports on a switch.
analogy: The apartment number inside a building: the IP address gets traffic to the building and the port gets it to the right apartment.
relatedTerms: TCP, UDP, Attack surface, Hardening, Implicit deny, Firewall

detail.practicalScenario: A server listens on port 443 for secure web traffic and on port 22 for administrator logins. A firewall rule allows 443 from anywhere but allows 22 only from the administrators' network.
detail.quizQuestion: What does a port number identify?
quizOptions: A) The physical cable connected to a switch
B) The specific service or application on a device that should receive the traffic
C) The manufacturer of a network card
D) The geographic location of a server

definition: The practice of dividing a network into smaller, isolated subnetworks, typically using VLANs or firewalls, to contain breaches, reduce the attack surface, and enforce access control between zones.
examContext: Know segmentation as a core defense-in-depth and containment strategy, frequently paired with the principle of least privilege; exam scenarios often involve isolating sensitive systems, such as payment processing or SCADA, from the general network.
analogy: Like dividing a ship into watertight compartments so that a hull breach in one section doesn't sink the entire vessel.
relatedTerms: Microsegmentation, Defense in depth, Firewall

detail.practicalScenario: Maria segments the company's network so that point-of-sale terminals sit on an isolated VLAN separate from general office workstations, ensuring that a malware infection on an employee's laptop cannot directly reach payment card systems.
detail.quizQuestion: A security architect wants to ensure that a malware infection on a general office workstation cannot spread to the payment card processing systems. Which strategy should be implemented?

items.name: Trusted / intranet
items.detail: The internal corporate network; highest trust.

items.name: Untrusted
items.detail: The internet and anything you do not control.

items.name: Screened subnet (DMZ)
items.detail: A buffer zone between the internet and the internal LAN that hosts public-facing servers (web, mail, DNS). If one is compromised, the attacker is still outside the internal network.

items.name: Extranet
items.detail: A controlled network shared with partners, suppliers or customers.

items.name: Guest network
items.detail: Isolated Wi-Fi/VLAN with internet-only access.

items.name: Management network
items.detail: A separate (often out-of-band) network used only to administer devices.

items.name: Segmentation methods
items.detail: Physical (separate hardware or an air gap), logical (VLANs and ACLs), virtual (VXLAN/overlays) and microsegmentation (per-workload policy).

items.name: North-south vs east-west
items.detail: North-south traffic enters or leaves the datacenter or network; east-west traffic moves between internal systems, which is where lateral movement happens.
