definition: A hardware device inserted inline on a physical network link that passively copies all passing traffic to a monitoring port, allowing full visibility for analysis without affecting the original data flow.
examContext: Know a network tap is a hardware-based, passive, and generally more reliable alternative to port mirroring for capturing all traffic, including at full line rate and even malformed packets, often used for IDS or IPS sensor placement.
analogy: Like splicing a wire to attach a listening device that duplicates every signal passing through, without interrupting the original connection.
relatedTerms: Port mirroring

detail.practicalScenario: Priya installs a network tap between the core switch and the internet-facing router so that the intrusion detection system receives a complete, unaltered copy of all traffic for analysis, even during high-traffic periods when switch resources are constrained.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team needs to guarantee capture of 100% of traffic on a critical link, including during periods of high switch CPU utilization, for an IDS sensor. Which solution is most reliable for this purpose?

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

definition: The assurance that an entity cannot deny having performed an action such as sending a message or completing a transaction.
examContext: Tied closely to digital signatures and audit logs; the exam expects you to identify non-repudiation as the control that prevents a sender from denying authorship.
analogy: Like a signed receipt, where the signature proves you received the package and you cannot later claim you did not.
relatedTerms: Digital signature, Authentication, Integrity, Accountability

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan requires all contract approvals to be digitally signed with the employee's private key, so an executive cannot later deny having approved a wire transfer.
detail.quizQuestion: A finance director claims she never authorized a large payment, but the transaction log shows her digital signature attached to the request. Which security concept allows the organization to refute her claim?

definition: A "number used once": a value that must never repeat with the same key. Nonces and initialization vectors make every encryption or authentication operation unique, so identical plaintexts yield different ciphertexts and captured messages cannot be replayed.
examContext: Reusing a nonce with the same key in counter mode or GCM can completely break confidentiality. Nonces also appear in challenge-response authentication, where a fresh random value defeats replay attacks.
analogy: Like a single-use ticket number: the venue accepts each number once, so a photocopied ticket is rejected.
relatedTerms: IV, Replay attack, Block cipher, Session key

detail.practicalScenario: A server sends a random challenge (a nonce) that the client must include in its signed reply. When an attacker replays an old captured reply, the server rejects it because the nonce inside has already been used.
detail.quizQuestion: Which value, used only once, helps prevent replay attacks in authentication protocols?

definition: A technique used to deliberately make code, data, or communications difficult to understand or analyze, often to evade detection or reverse engineering.
examContext: Exam tests obfuscation as a technique malware authors use to evade signature-based detection, distinct from steganography, which hides the existence of data rather than just making it unreadable.
analogy: Like scrambling the words of a note so that even if someone finds it, they cannot easily read what it says.
relatedTerms: Steganography, Malware

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's malware analysis team spends extra hours deobfuscating heavily scrambled and renamed variable names in a malicious script before they can understand what the code actually does.
detail.quizQuestion: A malware sample uses heavily scrambled variable names and encoded strings specifically to make it harder for antivirus signatures and analysts to understand its function. What technique is being used?

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Reversible with the right key. Protects confidentiality of data at rest and in transit.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: One-way. Used to verify integrity and store passwords; the original cannot be recovered.

items.name: Masking
items.detail: Replaces part of a value with placeholder characters (****-****-****-1234) for display, testing or training.

items.name: Tokenization
items.detail: Swaps a sensitive value for a random surrogate token; the real value lives only in a secured vault. Common for payment cards (shrinks PCI DSS scope).

items.name: Obfuscation
items.detail: Making data or code hard to understand (scrambling, renaming variables). Weak on its own: "security through obscurity."

items.name: Steganography
items.detail: Hides the very EXISTENCE of data inside another file such as an image or audio clip.

definition: Infrastructure that an organization owns and operates in its own facilities, giving full control over hardware and data but also full responsibility for security, maintenance, power and capacity.
examContext: Contrast with cloud: highest control, higher capital cost and slower scaling, with the organization responsible for the entire stack including physical security.
analogy: Cooking at home: total control of the kitchen, but you buy and clean everything.
relatedTerms: Private cloud, Public cloud, Hybrid cloud, Air-gapped network

detail.practicalScenario: A defense contractor runs its servers in its own locked data center. It controls every layer, but it must also patch, power, cool and physically secure everything itself.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization runs all servers in its own data center and is responsible for hardware, power and physical security. Which deployment is this?

definition: The HR and IT processes that bring new staff into an organization (accounts, access, equipment, training, policy acknowledgment) and that remove access and recover assets when they leave.
examContext: A governance procedure. Offboarding must revoke access immediately, recover devices and review data. Lingering access enables insider threats.
analogy: Checking guests into and out of a hotel, including collecting the keys.
relatedTerms: Account provisioning and deprovisioning, Insider threat, Least privilege, Security awareness training

detail.practicalScenario: On day one, a new hire signs the acceptable use policy, completes security training and receives only the access her role needs. On her last day, IT disables her accounts and collects her laptop and badge.
detail.quizQuestion: Which step is MOST important during offboarding to reduce insider risk?
quizOptions: A) Immediately revoking the employee's access and recovering assets
B) Waiting 30 days before disabling accounts
C) Letting the employee keep a copy of their data
D) Reusing the account for the replacement

definition: A distributed, transparent record of transactions that is replicated across many nodes and visible to all participants, with new entries validated by consensus rather than a single central authority; the foundational structure behind most blockchain implementations.
examContext: The exam connects open public ledger directly to blockchain as the underlying concept; know that its integrity comes from decentralization and consensus, making it extremely difficult for any single party to secretly alter past records.
analogy: Like a shared notebook that thousands of people hold identical copies of simultaneously, so no one person can secretly erase or alter a past entry without everyone else noticing the mismatch.
relatedTerms: Blockchain, Non-repudiation, Hashing, Digital signature

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's supply chain team adopts a blockchain built on an open public ledger so that every participant, from manufacturer to retailer, can independently verify a product's full shipping history without trusting any single company's internal database.
detail.quizQuestion: A consortium of companies wants a shared transaction record that no single member can secretly alter, with every participant able to independently verify its history. What underlying structure provides this?

definition: A control carried out day to day by people rather than by technology, such as security awareness training, guard patrols, change and patch procedures, and incident response drills.
examContext: Operational means executed by staff in daily operations. It is the category most often confused with managerial (policy and oversight). Training programs and routine procedures are the classic operational examples.
analogy: Like the nightly routine a building crew follows: walking the halls, checking doors and logging problems.
relatedTerms: Control categories, Managerial control, Security awareness training, Technical control

detail.practicalScenario: Each quarter the security team runs phishing-awareness sessions and a tabletop exercise, and the IT staff follow the patching schedule. These are people-driven, repeated activities, so they are operational controls.
detail.quizQuestion: Which of the following is an example of an OPERATIONAL control?
quizOptions: A) A bollard in front of the entrance
C) A written information security policy
D) Quarterly security awareness training for staff

variants.title: Control categories (WHAT the control is made of)

items.name: Technical
items.detail: Implemented with technology: firewalls, encryption, antivirus, ACLs, MFA, IDS/IPS.

items.name: Managerial (administrative)
items.detail: Policies, risk assessments, security planning and oversight: the "paperwork" that governs how security is managed.

items.name: Operational
items.detail: Carried out day to day by PEOPLE: security awareness training, guards, change and patch procedures, backups performed by staff.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tangible barriers and devices: locks, fences, bollards, cameras, badge readers, vestibules, lighting.

items.name: Tip
items.detail: The category describes what it is or who runs it. The TYPE (preventive, detective and so on) describes what it does. One control has both: a firewall is a technical, preventive control.

definition: A process of identifying information that adversaries could piece together, then protecting it through habits such as not oversharing on social media, clean desk practices and controlling who needs to know what (OPSEC).
examContext: A security awareness topic: avoid discussing sensitive details publicly and protect small pieces of information that reveal larger secrets.
analogy: Not announcing your vacation dates on social media.
relatedTerms: Security awareness training, Need to know, Social engineering, Insider threat

detail.practicalScenario: Staff at a defense contractor are told not to post photos of badges, project names or travel plans online. Adversaries can combine small details to learn about sensitive work.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees are told not to post project names or travel plans online because adversaries could combine small details. Which practice is this?

items.name: Phishing campaigns
items.detail: Simulated phishing to teach users to recognize attacks and to measure click and report rates.

items.name: Reporting suspicious messages
items.detail: Give users an easy way to report (a report button), and respond to the reports.

items.name: Anomalous behavior recognition
items.detail: Recognize risky behavior (unsafe habits), unexpected behavior (out of pattern) and unintentional behavior (honest mistakes).

items.name: User guidance topics
items.detail: Policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threats, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, and hybrid/remote work.

items.name: Development and execution
items.detail: Create the content, deliver it (computer-based, in person, gamified), and keep it relevant.

items.name: Reporting and monitoring
items.detail: Initial training at onboarding, recurring refreshers, and tracking completion rates and metrics.

definition: The sequence in which digital evidence should be collected, from the most volatile (lost fastest) to the least: CPU registers and cache, RAM, swap, disk, remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.
examContext: Collect the most volatile first. A typical exam answer: memory before disk. Based on RFC 3227.
analogy: Photographing melting ice sculptures before the stone ones.
relatedTerms: Digital forensics, Chain of custody, Legal hold, e-Discovery

detail.practicalScenario: An investigator arriving at a compromised server captures the RAM first, then the network connections, and only afterward images the disk, because a power cycle would erase the memory.
detail.quizQuestion: According to the order of volatility, which evidence should be collected FIRST from a running compromised system?

variants.title: Digital forensics: order of volatility and handling

items.name: Order of volatility
items.detail: Collect the MOST volatile evidence first: CPU registers and cache, then RAM (routing/ARP tables, processes), then swap/page file, then disk, then remote logs and monitoring data, then archival media and backups.

items.name: Preservation
items.detail: Use write blockers, work on forensic copies, and hash the image to prove it was not changed.

items.name: Acquisition
items.detail: A bit-for-bit disk image, a memory dump, or a snapshot. Live acquisition is needed to capture volatile data.

items.name: Chain of custody
items.detail: Documented record of who handled the evidence, when and why. Gaps can make evidence inadmissible.

items.name: Legal hold
items.detail: A mandate to preserve relevant data (stop normal deletion) because of litigation or investigation.

items.name: e-Discovery
items.detail: Identifying and collecting electronic information for legal proceedings.

items.name: Timeline and reporting
items.detail: Reconstruct events, document findings and make the report clear and reproducible.

definition: Structured criminal groups that run cyber attacks as a business to make money, using ransomware, fraud, data theft, extortion and the sale of stolen data or network access. They have substantial resources and often specialized roles.
examContext: The primary motive is financial gain. Typical activities: ransomware, business email compromise, credential theft and carding. Resources are higher than hacktivists but generally lower than nation-states.
analogy: A corporation whose product is crime, complete with specialists, suppliers and customer service.
relatedTerms: Threat actor, Ransomware, Business email compromise, Nation-state actor, Hacktivist

detail.practicalScenario: A ransomware gang encrypts a hospital's systems, steals patient data as extra leverage and demands cryptocurrency. It runs a negotiation portal and recruits affiliates who share the profits.
detail.quizQuestion: A well-resourced group runs ransomware campaigns and sells stolen data to make money. Which threat actor type is this?

definition: Log entries or activity occurring at unusual times or outside normal patterns, such as an administrator logging in at 3 a.m. or a scheduled job running at an odd hour.
examContext: One of the objective 2.4 indicators. Baselines of normal behavior make it detectable; investigate for stolen accounts and insider threats.
analogy: A janitor's key card used at the bank at 3 a.m. when the janitor only works evenings.
relatedTerms: Indicators of malicious activity, Time-of-day restrictions, Insider threat, Missing logs

detail.practicalScenario: The SIEM notes a database administrator account running large exports at 3 a.m. on a Sunday, when no maintenance is scheduled. The unusual timing triggers an investigation that finds a compromised account.
detail.quizQuestion: A database administrator account runs large data exports at 3 a.m. on a Sunday, outside any scheduled maintenance. Which indicator is this?

definition: A basic firewall technique that inspects individual packets' header information, such as source and destination IP, port, and protocol, against a static rule set, allowing or denying each packet independently without tracking connection state.
examContext: Know this is the simplest and fastest but least secure firewall type since it cannot detect attacks that rely on connection context or payload content; often contrasted with stateful inspection on the exam.
analogy: Like a mail sorter who only checks the address on the envelope and nothing about the sender's history or the letter's contents before deciding to deliver or discard it.
relatedTerms: Firewall, Stateful inspection

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures a border router's access control list to perform basic packet filtering, dropping any packets from known malicious source IP ranges based solely on header information, before traffic even reaches the main firewall.
detail.quizQuestion: A router is configured to allow or deny traffic based solely on source IP, destination IP, and port number in each packet's header, without tracking any connection history. What type of filtering is this?

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

definition: A penetration test (gray box) in which the tester receives limited information, such as a normal user account or part of the network layout.
examContext: It balances realism and efficiency and simulates a malicious insider or an attacker who already has a foothold.
analogy: An inspector who has a visitor's pass and a floor plan of just one wing.
relatedTerms: Known environment, Unknown environment, Penetration testing, Insider threat

detail.practicalScenario: The testers are given a standard employee account and told the IP range of the corporate network. They start from there, simulating an attacker who has phished one user.
detail.quizQuestion: A pentester is given a standard user account and limited network details before starting. Which type of test is this?

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: An attack technique in which a threat actor captures a hashed password and uses it directly to authenticate to a system without needing to crack it into plaintext.
examContext: Exam tests pass-the-hash as exploiting how some authentication protocols accept the hash itself as proof of identity, enabling lateral movement without the actual password.
analogy: Like a thief who steals the wax seal stamp itself, so they can forge your seal on documents without ever learning your actual signature.
relatedTerms: Lateral movement, Hashing, Credential stuffing

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's penetration test extracts a cached password hash from a compromised workstation's memory and uses it directly to authenticate to a file server, never needing to actually crack the hash into plaintext.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester extracts a cached credential hash from a workstation's memory and uses it directly to log into another server, without ever converting it to a plaintext password. What attack technique is this?

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: Gathering information about a target without interacting with its systems, using public sources such as OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings and search engines like Shodan.
examContext: Hard for the target to detect. Contrast with active reconnaissance, which touches the target.
analogy: Studying a building from public photos and records without ever approaching it.
relatedTerms: Active reconnaissance, OSINT, Penetration testing, Unknown environment

detail.practicalScenario: Before touching anything, a tester reads the company's job postings, WHOIS data and social media to learn about its technologies and staff. The target never sees any traffic from the tester.
detail.quizQuestion: A tester learns about a target solely from WHOIS records, job postings and social media without sending any traffic to it. Which method is this?

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: A tool that generates, stores and fills strong unique passwords for each account, protected by one strong master password and ideally MFA, so users do not reuse or memorize passwords.
examContext: A best-practice defense against credential stuffing and password reuse. The risk is a single point of compromise, so protect the master password with MFA.
analogy: A secure keyring holding a different key for every door.
relatedTerms: Credential stuffing, Password policy, Multifactor authentication, Passwordless authentication

detail.practicalScenario: An employee stops reusing one password and lets the company password manager create a unique 20-character password for every site. When one site is breached, the leaked password works nowhere else.
detail.quizQuestion: Which tool BEST helps users avoid reusing the same password across sites?

definition: The set of rules that governs how passwords are created and managed, covering length, complexity, history (reuse), expiration (age), lockout and storage.
examContext: Know the settings: minimum length, complexity, history, maximum and minimum age, and lockout threshold. Modern NIST guidance favors length and breached-password blocklists over forced complexity and routine expiry.
analogy: House rules about how strong each lock must be and how often it may be changed.
relatedTerms: Account lockout, Password manager, Multifactor authentication, Passwordless authentication, Key stretching

detail.practicalScenario: The policy requires 14-character passwords, blocks passwords found in breach lists, remembers the last 12 passwords and locks the account after five failed attempts.
detail.quizQuestion: Which password policy setting prevents users from cycling back to a recently used password?

definition: A password attack in which an attacker tries one commonly used password, such as 'Spring2024!', against many different user accounts, rather than many passwords against a single account, in order to stay under account lockout thresholds.
examContext: The exam directly contrasts this with a dictionary attack: password spraying tries one or a few common passwords across many accounts to stay under lockout thresholds, while a dictionary attack tries many candidate passwords against a single account.
analogy: Like a thief trying the single most common key on every door down an entire hallway, instead of trying every key on their keyring against just one door.
relatedTerms: Dictionary attack, Brute force attack, Account lockout, Credential stuffing

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's SOC notices one failed login attempt on hundreds of different corporate accounts within the same hour, all using the password 'Welcome2024', and recognizes this low-and-slow pattern as password spraying designed to stay below the five-attempt lockout threshold on any single account.
detail.quizQuestion: Security logs show a single common password being attempted once against hundreds of different user accounts over the course of an hour, with no account receiving more than one attempt. What attack technique does this best describe?

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: Storing privileged and shared credentials in an encrypted vault where users must check them out, with access logged, passwords rotated automatically and sessions sometimes recorded. A core privileged access management feature.
examContext: Part of PAM along with just-in-time access and ephemeral credentials. It prevents sharing and hard-coding of administrator passwords.
analogy: A bank safe-deposit box with a sign-out sheet.
relatedTerms: PAM, Just-in-time access, Ephemeral credentials, Least privilege

detail.practicalScenario: Administrators no longer know the domain admin password. They request it from the vault, which logs the checkout, records the session and rotates the password immediately after use.
detail.quizQuestion: Which PAM feature stores privileged passwords in an encrypted repository, logs each checkout and rotates the password afterward?

definition: An authentication method that verifies a user's identity using a factor other than a memorized password, such as a biometric scan, a hardware security key, or a cryptographic certificate stored on a trusted device.
examContext: Know passwordless authentication eliminates password-based risks entirely, such as brute force, dictionary, and credential stuffing attacks, by relying instead on possession- or biometric-based factors.
analogy: Like unlocking your front door with your fingerprint instead of a key you could lose, forget, or have copied.
relatedTerms: Biometrics, Smart card, Multifactor authentication, Identity proofing

detail.practicalScenario: Sam rolls out passwordless authentication for the company's laptops, letting employees log in with a fingerprint scan paired with a hardware security key instead of a typed password, eliminating the risk of credential stuffing attacks against those device logins entirely.
detail.quizQuestion: A company replaces typed passwords on its laptops with a combination of fingerprint scans and hardware security keys for login. What has the company implemented?

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

items.name: HOTP
items.detail: HMAC-based, COUNTER-based: each use advances a counter, so a code stays valid until it is used and can drift out of sync. No built-in expiry.

items.name: TOTP
items.detail: Time-based: the code is derived from the current time window (usually 30 seconds), so it expires quickly. What authenticator apps use; needs reasonably accurate clocks.

items.name: SMS / voice code
items.detail: Delivered over the phone network. Weakest option: vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception, and discouraged by NIST.

items.name: Push notification
items.detail: Approve a prompt on your phone. Convenient, but vulnerable to MFA fatigue (prompt bombing) when users approve out of annoyance.

items.name: Hard vs soft token
items.detail: A hard token is a physical device that displays or generates codes; a soft token is an app on a phone.

items.name: Security key (FIDO2 / WebAuthn)
items.detail: Public-key based and bound to the website's origin, so it resists phishing. The strongest everyday option.

items.name: Length
items.detail: The strongest single factor against guessing and cracking. Favor long passphrases over short complex strings.

items.name: Complexity
items.detail: Requires mixed character types. Current NIST guidance prefers length plus a blocklist of known-bad passwords over forced complexity.

items.name: Reuse / history
items.detail: Password history stops users from recycling their last N passwords.

items.name: Expiration / maximum age
items.detail: Forces a change after a set time. Current NIST guidance says do not force routine changes unless there is evidence of compromise.

items.name: Minimum age
items.detail: Stops a user from changing the password repeatedly in one sitting to cycle back to an old one.

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Locks the account after N failed attempts. Defeats online brute force, but can be abused to lock out legitimate users (a denial of service).

items.name: Password manager
items.detail: Generates and stores unique strong passwords so users do not reuse them. Protect it with a strong master password and MFA.

items.name: Passwordless
items.detail: FIDO2 keys, passkeys and biometrics remove the shared secret that attackers phish or crack.

definition: The systematic process of identifying, testing, acquiring, and deploying software updates to fix vulnerabilities and bugs, typically governed by a formal policy that balances security urgency against system stability.
examContext: Know the typical patch management lifecycle of identifying, testing in a non-production environment, deploying, and verifying, and that emergency or out-of-band patching applies to actively exploited zero-days.
analogy: Like a scheduled maintenance program for a fleet of vehicles, ensuring every car gets necessary safety recalls applied in a controlled, tested manner rather than haphazardly.
relatedTerms: Vulnerability scanning, Hardening, Change management

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's IT team tests a critical security patch in a staging environment before rolling it out to production servers during the next scheduled maintenance window, following the organization's formal patch management policy.
detail.quizQuestion: A critical vulnerability is disclosed in widely used software. Before deploying the vendor's patch organization-wide, what should the IT team do first according to best practice?
quizOptions: A) Deploy immediately to all production systems
B) Wait for the next annual maintenance cycle
C) Test the patch in a non-production environment first
D) Disable the affected software permanently

items.name: Confirmation
items.detail: Verify findings and weed out false positives and false negatives.

items.name: Prioritization
items.detail: Rank by CVSS, exploitability, asset criticality, exposure and business impact.

items.name: Remediation
items.detail: Patch, change configuration, or segment the system.

items.name: Compensating control
items.detail: When you cannot fix the flaw (legacy system, patch unavailable), add another control that reduces the risk.

items.name: Exception / exemption
items.detail: A documented, approved decision to leave a vulnerability unfixed for a stated reason and period.

items.name: Insurance / transfer
items.detail: Shift part of the financial impact to a third party.

items.name: Validation
items.detail: Rescan, audit, and verify that the fix worked and nothing broke.

items.name: Reporting
items.detail: Share trends and metrics with owners and leadership.

definition: An authorized, simulated attack against a system or network performed by security professionals to actively exploit identified vulnerabilities and assess real-world exploitability, going beyond simple detection to demonstrate actual impact.
examContext: Know the phases of reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation, and reporting, along with the different knowledge levels of black box, white box, and gray box; the rules of engagement document and written authorization are critical exam points.
analogy: Like hiring a professional burglar to actually try breaking into your building, with permission, to prove whether the locks you installed can really be defeated.
relatedTerms: Vulnerability scanning, Red team, Exploit

detail.practicalScenario: Priya hires an external firm to conduct a penetration test against the company's customer portal, with a signed rules-of-engagement document specifying scope and timing, and the testers successfully exploit an unpatched vulnerability to demonstrate real-world risk to leadership.
detail.quizQuestion: Leadership wants concrete proof that a known vulnerability could actually be exploited by a real attacker, not just a theoretical risk score. Which activity provides this evidence?

items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

items.name: Credentialed
items.detail: The scanner logs in with an account, so it sees patch levels, configuration and local vulnerabilities. More accurate, with fewer false positives.

items.name: Non-credentialed
items.detail: An outside-in view, like an attacker. Finds exposed services but may miss internal weaknesses and produces more false positives.

items.name: Intrusive vs non-intrusive
items.detail: Intrusive scans actively try to exploit and can disrupt systems; non-intrusive scans only probe and identify.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agent-based: software on the host reports continuously, even for roaming devices. Agentless: the scanner connects over the network.

items.name: Active vs passive
items.detail: Active sends probes; passive listens to traffic and infers what exists without touching it.

items.name: Scan vs pen test
items.detail: A scan is automated and lists KNOWN weaknesses without exploiting them. A pen test is largely manual and exploits weaknesses to prove real impact.

items.name: False positive / false negative
items.detail: False positive: reported but not real (wastes time). False negative: a real flaw that was missed (dangerous).

definition: A property of key-exchange protocols where each session uses a unique ephemeral key, so that even if a server's long-term private key is later compromised, previously captured encrypted sessions cannot be decrypted.
examContext: Know that PFS is achieved through ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchanges such as DHE or ECDHE; exam scenarios ask why past captured traffic remains safe even after a key compromise.
analogy: Like using a different, one-time disposable lock for every single shipment, so that stealing today's master key doesn't open yesterday's shipments.
relatedTerms: Key exchange, Asymmetric encryption, Cipher suite

detail.practicalScenario: Chen configures the organization's VPN to use ECDHE for every new session, ensuring that even if an attacker later steals the gateway's private key, none of the previously recorded encrypted sessions can be retroactively decrypted.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst wants to ensure that previously captured encrypted traffic cannot be decrypted even if the server's private key is compromised in the future. Which property should the key exchange protocol provide?

items.name: RSA
items.detail: Based on factoring large primes. Can encrypt, sign, and exchange keys. 2048-bit is the minimum today (3072+ recommended). Slow, so it protects small things such as session keys.

items.name: DSA
items.detail: Digital signatures ONLY: it cannot encrypt or exchange keys.

items.name: ECC
items.detail: Elliptic-curve math gives equal strength with far smaller keys (a 256-bit ECC key is roughly as strong as 3072-bit RSA). Ideal for mobile, IoT and low-power devices.

items.name: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
items.detail: Key EXCHANGE only: two parties derive the same shared secret over an untrusted channel without ever sending it. Unauthenticated DH is open to man-in-the-middle.

items.name: DHE / ECDHE
items.detail: The "E" means ephemeral: a fresh key pair for every session, which provides perfect forward secrecy. ECDHE is the elliptic-curve version and is the preferred TLS key exchange.

items.name: ECDSA
items.detail: DSA over elliptic curves: signatures only, with small keys. Used in modern TLS certificates and in Bitcoin.

definition: Techniques attackers use to maintain long-term access to a compromised system even after reboots, credential changes, or initial detection attempts.
examContext: Exam tests persistence mechanisms like scheduled tasks, registry run keys, and new admin accounts; closely tied to advanced persistent threat behavior.
analogy: Like a burglar who installs their own hidden spare key so they can get back in even after you change the main lock.
relatedTerms: Backdoor, Advanced persistent threat, Rootkit, Privilege escalation

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's incident responders find that attackers created a hidden scheduled task that re-installs their malware every time the server reboots, ensuring continued access even after the initial infection is removed.
detail.quizQuestion: Even after a compromised server is rebooted and the original malware file is deleted, attackers regain access because a hidden scheduled task silently reinstalls their tool. What technique allowed this continued access?

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: An attack that silently redirects users from a legitimate website to a fraudulent one, typically by poisoning DNS or altering a hosts file, so victims reach the fake site even when they type the correct address.
examContext: Differs from phishing because no lure or click is required. Defenses: DNSSEC, secure DNS, endpoint protection and checking certificates.
analogy: Someone secretly swapping the road signs so you drive to a fake store even though you followed your usual route.
relatedTerms: Phishing, DNS poisoning, Typosquatting, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Customers type the bank's correct address but land on an identical-looking fake that harvests logins. Investigation shows a compromised DNS server returning the attacker's IP address.
detail.quizQuestion: Users who type a bank's correct address are redirected to a fraudulent site because DNS records were altered. What is this attack?

definition: A social engineering attack that uses fraudulent emails or messages, often impersonating a trusted source, to trick victims into revealing information or installing malware.
examContext: The most commonly tested social engineering attack; exam variants like spear phishing, whaling, vishing, and smishing are differentiated by target specificity and medium.
analogy: Like a fake letter from your bank asking you to mail back your account number.
relatedTerms: Spear phishing, Whaling, Vishing, Smishing, Social engineering, Pretexting

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's email gateway flags a mass email claiming to be from a shipping company, which links to a fake login page designed to harvest employee credentials.
detail.quizQuestion: Thousands of employees across different companies receive an identical email claiming their package delivery failed, with a link to a fake tracking site requesting login credentials. What is this attack called?

items.name: Phishing
items.detail: Mass, generic lures, usually email, that try to steal credentials or deliver malware.

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: A controlled exercise in which an organization sends fake phishing messages to employees to measure how many click or report them, and uses the results to target training.
examContext: Part of awareness campaigns. Track click and report rates and use the results for learning rather than punishment.
analogy: A fire drill for email.
relatedTerms: Security awareness training, Phishing, Spear phishing, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Each month, the security team sends a realistic fake invoice email to staff. Those who click get an instant teaching page, and the team tracks how many people report it.
detail.quizQuestion: Security staff send fake phishing emails to employees to measure who clicks and who reports them. What is this?

items.name: Phishing campaigns
items.detail: Simulated phishing to teach users to recognize attacks and to measure click and report rates.

items.name: Reporting suspicious messages
items.detail: Give users an easy way to report (a report button), and respond to the reports.

items.name: Anomalous behavior recognition
items.detail: Recognize risky behavior (unsafe habits), unexpected behavior (out of pattern) and unintentional behavior (honest mistakes).

items.name: User guidance topics
items.detail: Policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threats, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, and hybrid/remote work.

items.name: Development and execution
items.detail: Create the content, deliver it (computer-based, in person, gamified), and keep it relevant.

items.name: Reporting and monitoring
items.detail: Initial training at onboarding, recurring refreshers, and tracking completion rates and metrics.

definition: A tangible barrier or device that protects facilities, equipment and people, such as locks, fences, bollards, badge readers, access control vestibules, cameras, lighting and guards.
examContext: Physical controls are things you can touch. They can also be tagged with a type: locks and bollards are preventive, cameras and motion sensors are detective, and signs or visible guards are deterrent.
analogy: The castle walls and drawbridge: obstacles in the real world rather than rules or software.
relatedTerms: Control categories, Access control vestibule, Bollard, Video surveillance, Fencing

detail.practicalScenario: A warehouse adds bollards at the loading dock, badge readers on doors and cameras in the aisles. Each one is a physical device in the real world, so all of them are physical controls.
detail.quizQuestion: Which of the following is a PHYSICAL control?

variants.title: Control categories (WHAT the control is made of)

items.name: Technical
items.detail: Implemented with technology: firewalls, encryption, antivirus, ACLs, MFA, IDS/IPS.

items.name: Managerial (administrative)
items.detail: Policies, risk assessments, security planning and oversight: the "paperwork" that governs how security is managed.

items.name: Operational
items.detail: Carried out day to day by PEOPLE: security awareness training, guards, change and patch procedures, backups performed by staff.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tangible barriers and devices: locks, fences, bollards, cameras, badge readers, vestibules, lighting.

items.name: Tip
items.detail: The category describes what it is or who runs it. The TYPE (preventive, detective and so on) describes what it does. One control has both: a firewall is a technical, preventive control.

definition: Devices that detect physical presence, motion or pressure to trigger alarms, lighting or recording. Common types are infrared (heat), pressure, microwave and ultrasonic sensors.
examContext: Know what each senses: infrared (PIR) detects body heat, pressure detects weight on a floor or mat, microwave detects motion from reflected microwave energy (and can see through thin walls), and ultrasonic detects motion from reflected sound waves. They are detective controls.
analogy: The motion-activated lights and alarms of a building, but each sensor "feels" a different thing: heat, weight, microwaves or sound.
relatedTerms: Detective control, Video surveillance, Lighting, Physical control

detail.practicalScenario: A data center installs infrared sensors in the corridors, pressure mats at the cage doors and ultrasonic sensors inside the server hall. Any trigger after hours raises an alarm in the security office.
detail.quizQuestion: Which type of sensor detects an intruder by sensing body heat?

items.name: Infrared (PIR)
items.detail: Detects the body heat of a person moving through its field of view. Common in motion-activated lights and alarms.

items.name: Pressure
items.detail: Detects weight or force on a floor mat, tile or fence line, so it triggers when someone steps or climbs.

items.name: Microwave
items.detail: Emits microwave energy and detects changes in the reflection caused by movement. Covers a large area and can sense through thin walls.

items.name: Ultrasonic
items.detail: Emits high-frequency sound and detects movement from changes in the reflected waves. Good for enclosed rooms.

items.name: Video / camera
items.detail: Records or analyzes images; paired with motion detection to alert on activity.

items.name: Role in security
items.detail: All of these are DETECTIVE controls. The response (alarm, lights, recording) can add a deterrent or corrective effect.

definition: A post-exploitation technique in which an attacker uses a compromised system as a relay point to reach and attack other systems that would otherwise be unreachable.
examContext: Exam tests pivoting as specifically using a foothold device to bridge into isolated or segmented network zones, distinct from general lateral movement between peer systems.
analogy: Like a spy who takes over a guard's post specifically to access a restricted wing they could not otherwise reach.
relatedTerms: Lateral movement, Privilege escalation, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's red team compromises a dual-homed jump server in the DMZ and uses it as a relay to route traffic into an isolated internal network segment that has no direct route from the internet.
detail.quizQuestion: A red team member compromises a server that has a network connection into an otherwise isolated finance subnet, and routes further attack traffic through that server to reach systems that are not directly accessible from outside. What technique is being demonstrated?

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: Plaintext is data in its readable, unencrypted form; ciphertext is the unreadable result produced by applying an encryption algorithm and key to it. Decryption reverses the process using the correct key.
examContext: Basic vocabulary used across cryptography questions. Encryption provides confidentiality by turning plaintext into ciphertext, but a hash is not ciphertext because it cannot be reversed.
analogy: Plaintext is a message written in your own language; ciphertext is the same message scrambled into a code that only the key holder can read.
relatedTerms: Encryption, Symmetric encryption, Asymmetric encryption, Hashing

detail.practicalScenario: A laptop's disk holds only ciphertext. When Maria enters her BitLocker PIN, the system derives the key and converts sectors back to plaintext in memory. If the laptop is stolen, a thief sees nothing but ciphertext.
detail.quizQuestion: What is the term for the unreadable output of an encryption algorithm?

definition: Using different operating systems, hardware vendors, software and technologies across the environment so a single vulnerability or failure does not affect every system. It avoids a technology monoculture.
examContext: A resilience technique with the trade-off of higher complexity and cost. Also called technology diversity.
analogy: Planting several crop varieties so one disease cannot wipe out the whole harvest.
relatedTerms: Geographic dispersion, Redundancy, Multi-cloud, Defense in depth

detail.practicalScenario: A firm runs its primary firewalls from one vendor and its internal firewalls from another. A flaw in one product cannot open the whole network because the second layer uses different code.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization uses firewalls from two different vendors so one product's flaw cannot compromise every layer. What concept is this?

definition: A documented set of conditional steps and decision points that guide a response team through handling a specific type of security incident, covering who does what and under which conditions.
examContext: Know a playbook is the human-readable decision-tree document, the what-to-do-and-when, while a runbook is the step-by-step technical procedure that actually carries those steps out; the exam may describe one and ask you to distinguish it from the other.
analogy: Like a football team's playbook that outlines the decision logic for different game situations, who covers what and when, without itself running the actual plays.
relatedTerms: Runbook, Incident response, Tabletop exercise

detail.practicalScenario: Alex writes a ransomware playbook that lays out exactly which stakeholders must be notified, in what order, and the decision criteria for whether to isolate a segment or shut it down entirely, giving the incident response team a clear decision tree to follow during the actual event.
detail.quizQuestion: A document outlines the decision points and responsible roles for handling a ransomware incident, such as when to notify legal counsel versus when to isolate a network segment, but does not itself contain the technical commands to execute those actions. What is this document called?

definition: The zero trust control-plane component that takes the Policy Engine's decision and generates the session-specific instructions or credentials that establish or tear down the communication path at the Policy Enforcement Point.
examContext: Know that the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator both live in the control plane and work as a pair; the Administrator is specifically the one that communicates the decision to the enforcement point, while the Engine makes the decision itself.
analogy: Like a judge's clerk who takes the ruling and issues the official paperwork telling the courtroom bailiff whether to open or lock the doors.
relatedTerms: Zero trust, Policy Engine, Policy Enforcement Point, Control plane

detail.practicalScenario: After the Policy Engine approves Jordan's access request, the Policy Administrator generates a short-lived authentication token and signals the Policy Enforcement Point to open a secure session between Jordan's laptop and the internal application.
detail.quizQuestion: Once a zero trust Policy Engine approves an access request, which component is responsible for communicating that decision and establishing the session with the enforcement point?

definition: The zero trust data-plane component that acts as the actual gatekeeper, allowing, monitoring, or terminating the connection between a subject and a resource strictly based on the decision handed down by the Policy Administrator.
examContext: This is a heavily tested diagram-labeling term; remember the PEP sits in the data plane, not the control plane, and is the enforcement mechanism, distinct from the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator that make the decision.
analogy: Like the bailiff standing at the courtroom door who only opens it after receiving the clerk's signed order, never deciding the case themselves.
relatedTerms: Zero trust, Policy Engine, Policy Administrator, Data plane, Implicit trust zone

detail.practicalScenario: Sam deploys a Policy Enforcement Point in front of the payroll application so that every connection attempt is physically allowed or blocked at that gateway, strictly following the instructions issued by the Policy Administrator.
detail.quizQuestion: In a zero trust model, which component is physically responsible for allowing or blocking a connection to a resource, acting strictly on instructions from the control plane?

definition: The zero trust control-plane component that evaluates an access request against policy rules, threat intelligence, and contextual data about the subject and device, then renders the actual grant, deny, or revoke decision.
examContext: CompTIA's zero trust diagram places the Policy Engine in the control plane alongside the Policy Administrator; expect questions that ask you to distinguish the component that decides (Policy Engine) from the one that enforces (Policy Enforcement Point).
analogy: Like a judge who reviews the evidence and renders a verdict, but doesn't personally escort anyone out of the courtroom.
relatedTerms: Zero trust, Policy Administrator, Policy Enforcement Point, Control plane, Adaptive identity

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the organization's zero trust Policy Engine to cross-reference a laptop's patch status, the user's role, and real-time threat intelligence feeds before deciding whether a request to access the finance server should be approved.
detail.quizQuestion: In a zero trust architecture, which component evaluates the subject's identity, device posture, and contextual risk signals against policy to decide whether to grant, deny, or revoke access?

definition: A switch feature, also called SPAN, that copies traffic from one or more source ports to a designated destination port for monitoring, allowing network analysis tools to observe traffic without a dedicated inline tap device.
examContext: Know port mirroring is a software or switch-configuration-based alternative to a network tap; it can drop packets under heavy load since it competes for switch processing resources, which the exam may test as a limitation.
analogy: Like a photocopier making a duplicate of every piece of mail passing through a sorting office and sending the copies to a separate inspection desk.
relatedTerms: Network tap

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan configures port mirroring on the access switch to send a copy of all VLAN traffic to a packet analyzer connected to the monitoring port, enabling network troubleshooting without purchasing additional tap hardware.
detail.quizQuestion: A network administrator needs a low-cost way to send a copy of switch traffic to a packet analyzer for troubleshooting, using existing switch features rather than new hardware. What should be configured?

variants.title: Active vs passive, inline vs tap/monitor

items.name: Inline (active)
items.detail: The device sits directly in the traffic path, so it CAN block or modify traffic. It adds latency and is a single point of failure. Examples: firewall, IPS, WAF.

items.name: Tap / monitor (passive)
items.detail: The device receives a COPY of traffic, so it cannot block anything but also cannot disrupt the network. Examples: IDS, packet capture, NetFlow collector.

items.name: Network tap
items.detail: Dedicated hardware inserted in the cable that copies every frame (including errors) without dropping any. Reliable, but costs money and must be physically installed.

items.name: SPAN / port mirror
items.detail: A switch feature that copies traffic from chosen ports to a monitoring port. Cheap and flexible, but may drop packets under heavy load.

items.name: Fail-open vs fail-closed
items.detail: If an inline device fails it can let traffic through (fail-open: favors availability) or block everything (fail-closed / fail-secure: favors security). Safety systems such as door locks have their own version of the choice.

definition: A switch feature that restricts which devices can use a port by limiting the number of MAC addresses or specifying the allowed ones, and then shuts down or restricts the port when the rule is violated. It defends against MAC flooding and unauthorized devices.
examContext: Related to 802.1X and NAC; includes sticky MAC addresses and violation modes (shutdown, restrict, protect). Also disable unused switch ports.
analogy: A parking garage that only admits registered license plates, and at most one car per space.
relatedTerms: MAC flooding, 802.1X, NAC, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: An admin configures each access port to allow one learned MAC address. When someone plugs in a rogue switch and floods the port with fake addresses, the port shuts down automatically and an alert is sent.
detail.quizQuestion: Which switch feature limits the MAC addresses allowed on a port and can shut the port down on a violation?

definition: A social engineering technique in which an attacker fabricates a believable scenario or false identity to manipulate a victim into divulging information or granting access.
examContext: Exam tests pretexting as creating a false narrative or identity, such as posing as an auditor or new vendor, to build trust before the actual request.
analogy: Like a fake inspector who shows up with a clipboard and uniform, inventing a story to get past the front desk.
relatedTerms: Social engineering, Phishing, Vishing, Tailgating

detail.practicalScenario: Maria poses as a new IT contractor over the phone, inventing a detailed backstory about a scheduled system migration to convince the help desk to reset an executive's password.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker calls the help desk claiming to be a traveling executive who lost phone access, providing a fabricated but convincing backstory to get a password reset. What technique is being used?
