items.name: Authority
items.detail: People obey someone who appears to hold power (a CEO, an auditor, the police).

items.name: Intimidation
items.detail: Threats or pressure push a victim to comply ("your account will be closed").

items.name: Urgency / scarcity
items.detail: A deadline or limited supply stops people from thinking carefully.

items.name: Consensus / social proof
items.detail: People copy what others seem to be doing ("everyone else already completed this").

items.name: Familiarity / liking
items.detail: People help those they like or feel they know.

items.name: Trust
items.detail: Rapport built over time lowers suspicion.

items.name: Best defense
items.detail: Security awareness training, a no-exceptions verification process, and a culture where staff can safely say "let me check."

definition: A control that stops an incident from happening in the first place by blocking or avoiding the threat, such as firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, MFA, patching and training.
examContext: "Prevent" means stop it BEFORE it happens. If a control only alerts, it is detective, not preventive. Typical examples on the exam: firewall rules, IPS in line, door locks, bollards, access control vestibules and account lockout.
analogy: A seat belt or a deadbolt: it works before anything bad happens.
relatedTerms: Detective control, Corrective control, Deterrent control, Control types

detail.practicalScenario: A company enforces MFA on its VPN and applies least privilege on file shares. Both measures are meant to stop unauthorized access before it can occur, so they are preventive controls.
detail.quizQuestion: Which action is a PREVENTIVE control?
quizOptions: B) Enforcing MFA on the VPN

items.name: Preventive
items.detail: Stops an incident BEFORE it happens: firewalls, locks, least privilege, encryption, patching, MFA.

items.name: Deterrent
items.detail: Discourages attackers by raising the perceived risk: warning signs, visible cameras and guards, lighting, policies with consequences.

items.name: Detective
items.detail: Finds and alerts to an incident as or after it happens: IDS, SIEM alerts, log reviews, CCTV, audits, motion sensors.

items.name: Corrective
items.detail: Limits damage and restores things AFTER an incident: restoring from backup, patching a hole, incident response, quarantining malware.

items.name: Compensating
items.detail: A substitute control used when the primary control is not feasible, giving equivalent protection: for example extra monitoring and network isolation for a legacy system that cannot be patched.

items.name: Directive
items.detail: Tells people what they must or must not do: policies, procedures, standards, signs such as "authorized personnel only."

items.name: Examples
items.detail: Firewall = technical + preventive. Security guard = physical + preventive/deterrent. CCTV = physical + detective. Acceptable use policy = managerial + directive. Backups = technical + corrective. Awareness training = operational + preventive.

definition: The protection of personal information from unauthorized collection, use, or disclosure, respecting an individual's right to control their own data.
examContext: SY0-701 ties privacy to regulations and roles like data controller and data processor; expect questions distinguishing privacy, which concerns personal data rights, from confidentiality, which concerns general information protection.
analogy: Like curtains on your windows, where you decide who gets to see into your personal life.
relatedTerms: Data sovereignty, Confidentiality, Data classification, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's organization appoints a data privacy officer to ensure customer consent is obtained before personal data is collected, in compliance with applicable privacy regulations.
detail.quizQuestion: A company must obtain explicit customer consent before collecting personal data and must allow customers to request deletion of their records. Which concept primarily governs these requirements?

definition: A cloud environment used by a single organization, hosted on its own premises or by a provider, offering greater control, customization and isolation at higher cost.
examContext: Often chosen for regulated data that needs strong control. The organization carries more of the operational and security responsibility.
analogy: A single-family home: everything is yours, and so is the maintenance.
relatedTerms: Public cloud, Hybrid cloud, Community cloud, On-premises

detail.practicalScenario: A bank builds a private cloud in its own data centers to run sensitive workloads, gaining cloud-style automation while keeping complete control of hardware and data location.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants cloud-style services but dedicated to its own use for strict control over regulated data. Which deployment model fits?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: The secret half of an asymmetric key pair that must be protected and never shared, used to decrypt data encrypted with the matching public key or to create digital signatures.
examContext: Exam scenarios test what happens when a private key is compromised, since all communications and signatures tied to it become untrustworthy and the certificate must be revoked; know it is often stored securely in hardware like a TPM or HSM.
analogy: Like the only key to your personal safe, if someone else gets a copy, every secret you locked away is compromised.
relatedTerms: Public key, Asymmetric encryption, Digital signature, Key escrow, Certificate authority

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan discovers that a server's private key may have been exposed in a misconfigured backup, so she immediately requests certificate revocation from the CA and generates a new key pair to prevent attackers from impersonating the server.
detail.quizQuestion: A server's private key is suspected to have been compromised in a data breach. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
quizOptions: D) Revoke the certificate and generate a new key pair

items.name: Send a confidential message
items.detail: Encrypt with the RECIPIENT's PUBLIC key; only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.

items.name: Sign a message / prove authorship
items.detail: Sign with YOUR OWN PRIVATE key; anyone verifies with your public key. This gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.

items.name: Verify someone's signature
items.detail: Use the SIGNER's PUBLIC key (obtained from their certificate).

items.name: Decrypt a message sent to you
items.detail: Use YOUR OWN PRIVATE key.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: The private key never leaves its owner. The public key is shared freely. Encryption = their public key; signing = your private key.

definition: The act of exploiting a vulnerability, design flaw, or misconfiguration to gain elevated access rights beyond what was originally granted.
examContext: Exam distinguishes vertical privilege escalation, gaining higher-level rights such as moving from user to admin, from horizontal privilege escalation, accessing another user's same-level data.
analogy: Like a hotel guest finding a way to upgrade their key card from a standard room to the master key that opens every door.
relatedTerms: Lateral movement, Rootkit, Exploit, Vulnerability

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's penetration test shows that a standard user account can exploit a misconfigured service to execute commands as the system administrator, demonstrating a critical privilege escalation flaw.
detail.quizQuestion: A penetration tester, starting with only standard user credentials, exploits a misconfigured scheduled task to execute commands with full administrator rights. What is this technique called?

definition: An intermediary system that sits between clients and external servers, forwarding requests and responses on their behalf, which can provide caching, content filtering, anonymity, and an additional layer of inspection.
examContext: Know the difference between forward proxies, which protect and control internal clients accessing the internet, and reverse proxies, which protect and distribute load for internal servers receiving external requests.
analogy: Like a personal assistant who takes your requests, makes the calls on your behalf, and relays back only the relevant results, so the outside party never talks directly to you.
relatedTerms: Firewall, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan deploys a forward proxy server so that all employee internet traffic is filtered and logged for policy compliance, while a separate reverse proxy sits in front of internal web servers to distribute incoming client requests and hide internal server details.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to filter and log all employee web traffic before it reaches the internet, while also hiding the internal structure of its web servers from external users. Which combination of devices accomplishes both goals?
quizOptions: B) A network tap and port mirror
C) Forward and reverse proxy servers

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

items.name: Forward proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of CLIENTS. Users' outbound requests go through it for content filtering, caching, logging and anonymity. Clients are configured to use it.

items.name: Reverse proxy
items.detail: Sits in front of SERVERS. Outside clients talk to the proxy, which forwards to the back end. Used for load balancing, TLS offloading, caching and hiding server details.

items.name: Transparent proxy
items.detail: Intercepts traffic inline without any client configuration, so users do not know it is there.

items.name: Caching proxy
items.detail: Stores copies of frequently requested content to save bandwidth and speed responses.

items.name: URL / domain block and allow lists
items.detail: Explicitly permit or deny named sites. Precise, but must be maintained.

items.name: Content categorization
items.detail: Sites are sorted into categories (gambling, adult, malware) and whole categories are blocked.

items.name: Reputation filtering
items.detail: Blocks sites with a poor trust score based on threat intelligence, newly registered domains and past abuse.

items.name: Agent-based
items.detail: Software on the endpoint enforces policy wherever the device is, even off the corporate network.

items.name: Centralized proxy
items.detail: All web traffic is forced through one gateway that applies the policy; users on the network are covered without agents.

items.name: DNS filtering
items.detail: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at name resolution, before a connection is made.

definition: A cloud deployment in which a provider such as AWS, Azure or Google Cloud owns and operates shared, multi-tenant infrastructure and delivers it to many customers over the internet.
examContext: Lowest upfront cost and high scalability, with the shared responsibility model. Data sovereignty and tenant isolation are common concerns.
analogy: An apartment building: a shared structure, but your own locked unit.
relatedTerms: Private cloud, Hybrid cloud, Community cloud, Responsibility matrix, Multi-cloud

detail.practicalScenario: A startup hosts its web app on a public cloud, paying only for the compute it uses and relying on the provider to maintain the data centers while it secures its own data and identities.
detail.quizQuestion: Which cloud deployment model uses shared, multi-tenant infrastructure operated by a provider for many customers?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: The openly shareable half of an asymmetric key pair, used by others to encrypt data meant for the key owner or to verify a digital signature created with the matching private key.
examContext: Remember the public key is distributed freely, often via a certificate, while the private key must remain secret; exam questions frequently test which key is used for which operation.
analogy: Like a padlock you hand out freely to anyone who wants to send you a locked box, only you hold the key that opens it.
relatedTerms: Private key, Asymmetric encryption, Certificate, Digital signature, Key exchange

detail.practicalScenario: Sam publishes his public key on the company's internal key server so that colleagues can encrypt sensitive emails addressed to him, knowing only his corresponding private key can decrypt them.
detail.quizQuestion: Which key should be distributed openly to allow others to send encrypted messages to a specific recipient?

items.name: Send a confidential message
items.detail: Encrypt with the RECIPIENT's PUBLIC key; only the recipient's private key can decrypt it.

items.name: Sign a message / prove authorship
items.detail: Sign with YOUR OWN PRIVATE key; anyone verifies with your public key. This gives integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.

items.name: Verify someone's signature
items.detail: Use the SIGNER's PUBLIC key (obtained from their certificate).

items.name: Decrypt a message sent to you
items.detail: Use YOUR OWN PRIVATE key.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: The private key never leaves its owner. The public key is shared freely. Encryption = their public key; signing = your private key.

definition: A collaborative function where red team and blue team members actively share techniques, findings, and insights in real time, aiming to improve detection and response capabilities faster than siloed exercises would.
examContext: Know purple team isn't a separate standing team but a collaborative approach bridging red and blue teams; the exam may ask which team maximizes knowledge transfer between attackers and defenders.
analogy: Like having the attacking and defending coaches sit together during the game, explaining their moves to each other in real time so both sides learn faster.
relatedTerms: Red team, Blue team

detail.practicalScenario: Alex organizes a purple team session where the red team walks the blue team through each attack technique immediately after executing it, allowing the defenders to tune their SIEM detection rules in real time based on direct attacker feedback.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants its attackers and defenders to collaborate in real time, sharing techniques immediately to improve detection rules faster. What approach does this describe?

items.name: Red team
items.detail: OFFENSE: simulates real attackers to find weaknesses.

items.name: Blue team
items.detail: DEFENSE: monitors, detects and responds to attacks, and hardens systems.

items.name: Purple team
items.detail: Red and blue working together and sharing findings in real time to improve detection and response.

items.name: White team
items.detail: Referees and sets the rules of an exercise (scope, scoring, safety).

definition: A risk analysis approach that rates risks with descriptive categories such as high, medium and low (often on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix) based on expert judgment instead of numerical values.
examContext: Fast and cheap but subjective. Contrast with quantitative analysis, which uses numbers (SLE, ARO, ALE).
analogy: Rating restaurants with stars rather than measuring their exact costs.
relatedTerms: Quantitative risk analysis, Risk assessment, Risk register, Heat map

detail.practicalScenario: A workshop rates each risk as high, medium or low for likelihood and impact and plots them on a heat map. No dollar figures are calculated, which keeps the exercise quick.
detail.quizQuestion: A team rates risks as high, medium or low on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix without calculating dollar values. Which approach is this?

items.name: Qualitative
items.detail: Uses descriptive ratings (high / medium / low) on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix. Quick and subjective.

items.name: Quantitative
items.detail: Uses numbers and currency to calculate expected loss. More objective, but needs good data.

items.name: SLE
items.detail: Single Loss Expectancy = Asset Value (AV) x Exposure Factor (EF). The cost of ONE incident.

items.name: ARO
items.detail: Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.

items.name: ALE
items.detail: Annualized Loss Expectancy = SLE x ARO. Compare it with the annual cost of a control to see if the control pays for itself.

items.name: Worked example
items.detail: A laptop worth $2,000 (AV) with 100% EF has an SLE of $2,000. If theft is expected once every two years (ARO 0.5), ALE = $1,000 a year, so a $300 a year tracking service is worth buying.

items.name: Assessment frequency
items.detail: Ad hoc (as needed), recurring (scheduled), one-time (for a project) or continuous (ongoing monitoring).

items.name: Key risk indicators
items.detail: Metrics that signal rising risk before an incident, such as the number of unpatched critical systems.

definition: A risk analysis approach that uses numerical values and formulas, such as SLE, ARO and ALE, to estimate the expected financial loss from risks and compare it with the cost of controls.
examContext: SLE = AV x EF and ALE = SLE x ARO. It needs good data. It is used to justify security spending by showing whether a control costs less than the loss it prevents.
analogy: Pricing out exactly what a flood would cost per year and comparing it with the price of flood insurance.
relatedTerms: Qualitative risk analysis, Risk assessment, Risk, Risk management

detail.practicalScenario: A server worth $50,000 with an exposure factor of 40% has an SLE of $20,000. If the event is expected once every four years (ARO 0.25), the ALE is $5,000, so a $1,000-a-year control is clearly worthwhile.
detail.quizQuestion: An analyst calculates SLE and ALE in dollars to decide whether a $1,000-a-year control is cost-effective. Which approach is this?

items.name: Qualitative
items.detail: Uses descriptive ratings (high / medium / low) on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix. Quick and subjective.

items.name: Quantitative
items.detail: Uses numbers and currency to calculate expected loss. More objective, but needs good data.

items.name: SLE
items.detail: Single Loss Expectancy = Asset Value (AV) x Exposure Factor (EF). The cost of ONE incident.

items.name: ARO
items.detail: Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.

items.name: ALE
items.detail: Annualized Loss Expectancy = SLE x ARO. Compare it with the annual cost of a control to see if the control pays for itself.

items.name: Worked example
items.detail: A laptop worth $2,000 (AV) with 100% EF has an SLE of $2,000. If theft is expected once every two years (ARO 0.5), ALE = $1,000 a year, so a $300 a year tracking service is worth buying.

items.name: Assessment frequency
items.detail: Ad hoc (as needed), recurring (scheduled), one-time (for a project) or continuous (ongoing monitoring).

items.name: Key risk indicators
items.detail: Metrics that signal rising risk before an incident, such as the number of unpatched critical systems.

definition: Cryptographic approaches that use quantum mechanical properties (such as photon polarization in quantum key distribution) or are designed to resist attacks from quantum computers, aiming to secure communications against both classical and future quantum-based cryptanalysis.
examContext: Know that quantum computing is presented as an emerging threat capable of breaking current asymmetric algorithms like RSA, and that the recommended mitigation is migrating toward quantum-resistant (post-quantum) cryptographic algorithms before that capability matures.
analogy: Like sealing a letter in an envelope that visibly tears itself apart the instant anyone peeks inside, so both sender and receiver instantly know if eavesdropping occurred.
relatedTerms: Asymmetric encryption, Key exchange, Perfect forward secrecy, Hashing, Encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's organization begins inventorying every system that relies on RSA key exchange after a vendor briefing on quantum computing risk, and starts a multi-year migration plan toward quantum-resistant algorithms so that encrypted data captured today cannot be decrypted retroactively once quantum computers mature.
detail.quizQuestion: A CISO is concerned that sensitive data encrypted today could be decrypted in the future once sufficiently powerful quantum computers exist. Which strategy most directly addresses this long-term risk?
quizOptions: A) Migrating to quantum-resistant cryptographic algorithms

definition: Isolating a suspicious file, device or message in a restricted area so it cannot harm other systems while it is investigated or cleaned.
examContext: Used by antivirus, email gateways and NAC, where non-compliant devices are placed in a remediation VLAN. A containment and response action.
analogy: Isolating a sick patient away from the rest of the ward.
relatedTerms: Isolation, Containment, NAC, Malware

detail.practicalScenario: The antivirus tool moves a suspicious attachment into quarantine so it cannot run, and the NAC platform places a laptop with outdated patches into a restricted VLAN until it is updated.
detail.quizQuestion: An email gateway moves a suspicious attachment to a restricted area where it cannot run until it is reviewed. What is this action?

items.name: Log aggregation
items.detail: Collect logs from many sources into one place for correlation and search.

items.name: Alerting
items.detail: Notify people or systems when events match a rule or threshold.

items.name: Alert tuning
items.detail: Adjust thresholds and rules to cut false positives without missing real attacks.

items.name: Scanning and reporting
items.detail: Regular scans and reports show trends and compliance.

items.name: Archiving
items.detail: Keep logs for the retention period required for investigations and regulations.

items.name: Quarantine
items.detail: Isolate a suspicious file, system or message until it can be investigated.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agents give deep visibility and work off-network. Agentless is easier to deploy but shallower.

definition: A vulnerability that arises when the outcome of a process depends on the timing or sequence of two or more operations, allowing an attacker to manipulate the gap between them to produce an unintended result.
examContext: Know the classic example is a time-of-check to time-of-use pattern, already tested in this app as the TOCTOU acronym, where an attacker changes a resource's state in the brief window between when a program checks a condition and when it acts on it; the fix is making that check-then-act sequence atomic.
analogy: Like switching out a product's price tag right after a cashier checks it but before they actually ring it up, exploiting the brief gap between the check and the action.
relatedTerms: Buffer overflow, Privilege escalation, Memory injection

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's code review finds that a file-transfer utility checks a user's permissions and then, a split second later, performs the actual file operation; a tester proves the file can be swapped in that gap, so Jordan rewrites the routine to lock the check and the action together as a single atomic step.
detail.quizQuestion: A tester demonstrates that swapping a file during the brief interval between a program's permission check and its actual access to that file grants unauthorized read access. Which vulnerability class does this exploit?

items.name: SQL injection
items.detail: Attacker input is run as part of a database query to read, change or delete data. Fix: parameterized queries / prepared statements, input validation, least-privilege DB accounts.

items.name: XSS
items.detail: Injects script into a page that OTHER users view, so it runs in their browsers (steals sessions or cookies). Fix: output encoding, input validation, Content Security Policy.

items.name: CSRF
items.detail: Tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site that trusts it. Fix: anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies.

items.name: SSRF
items.detail: Makes the SERVER send requests to internal resources (such as the cloud metadata service) on the attacker's behalf. Fix: destination allow lists, network controls.

items.name: Command injection
items.detail: Attacker input is passed to an operating-system shell. Fix: avoid shell calls, validate and escape input.

items.name: Directory traversal
items.detail: Uses ../ sequences to read files outside the web root. Fix: canonicalize paths and restrict file permissions.

items.name: Buffer overflow
items.detail: Writing past the end of a memory buffer to crash the program or run attacker code. Fix: bounds checking, ASLR, DEP, safe languages.

items.name: Race condition (TOCTOU)
items.detail: Exploits the gap between checking a condition (time of check) and using it (time of use). Fix: atomic operations and locking.

items.name: Key difference
items.detail: XSS attacks the USER through a trusted site; CSRF abuses the user's logged-in SESSION; SSRF abuses the SERVER's trust in itself.

definition: A large pre-computed lookup table of password hashes and the plaintexts that produce them, letting an attacker reverse unsalted hashes almost instantly instead of computing each guess. Adding a unique salt to every password makes rainbow tables useless.
examContext: The standard answer to "how do you defeat rainbow tables?" is salting (plus key stretching with bcrypt or PBKDF2). Rainbow tables are for OFFLINE cracking of stolen hashes, unlike online brute force, which is rate-limited by the service.
analogy: Like a reverse dictionary built in advance: instead of working out each answer from scratch, you simply look the hash up.
relatedTerms: Salting, Hashing, Key stretching, Brute force attack, Dictionary attack

detail.practicalScenario: After a breach, attackers hold a table of unsalted MD5 password hashes and match them against a pre-built rainbow table, recovering thousands of passwords within minutes. The company later moves to per-user salts and bcrypt, which makes the same table worthless.
detail.quizQuestion: Which control MOST directly defeats pre-computed rainbow table attacks against a stolen password database?
quizOptions: A) Encrypting the database with a shared key
B) Adding a unique random salt to each password before hashing
C) Forcing password changes every 30 days

definition: Malware that encrypts a victim's files or locks their system, demanding payment, usually in cryptocurrency, in exchange for restoring access.
examContext: Exam tests ransomware heavily, including double-extortion tactics that combine encryption with a threat to leak data, and the recommendation to maintain offline backups rather than pay the ransom.
analogy: Like a kidnapper who locks up your valuables in a safe and demands money for the combination.
relatedTerms: Malware, Exfiltration, Cryptojacking

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's hospital network discovers that patient record files have been encrypted overnight, with a ransom note demanding cryptocurrency payment for the decryption key, forcing a shift to paper-based operations.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees arrive to find all files on the shared drive encrypted, with a note demanding cryptocurrency payment for the decryption key. What type of malware caused this?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A group of security professionals who simulate real-world adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures against an organization's defenses in an authorized offensive security exercise, testing detection and response capabilities.
examContext: Know that the red team represents offense, the blue team represents defense, and the purple team represents collaboration between both; exam scenarios test identifying which team performs which role.
analogy: Like a military unit practicing as the enemy force in a training exercise to test how well the home base's defenses hold up.
relatedTerms: Blue team, Purple team, Penetration testing

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan leads a red team engagement simulating a sophisticated phishing and lateral movement campaign against the company's network to test whether the security operations center can detect and respond before reaching critical systems.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization hires a group to simulate real-world attacker techniques against its own network to test detection capabilities. What is this group called?

items.name: Red team
items.detail: OFFENSE: simulates real attackers to find weaknesses.

items.name: Blue team
items.detail: DEFENSE: monitors, detects and responds to attacks, and hardens systems.

items.name: Purple team
items.detail: Red and blue working together and sharing findings in real time to improve detection and response.

items.name: White team
items.detail: Referees and sets the rules of an exercise (scope, scoring, safety).

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: Duplicating critical components, such as disks, power supplies, network links, servers or sites, so a failure of one does not cause an outage.
examContext: A core availability concept: RAID, dual power supplies, NIC teaming, clustering and multiple ISPs. Redundancy removes single points of failure.
analogy: A spare tire and a second driver on a long road trip.
relatedTerms: Single point of failure, High availability, Fault tolerance, Failover, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: A hospital installs two power supplies in each server, two network switches and two internet providers. When one switch dies, traffic keeps flowing over the other.
detail.quizQuestion: Which design principle uses duplicate components so that one failure does not cause an outage?

items.name: Redundancy
items.detail: Duplicate components (disks, power supplies, links, servers) so a single failure does not stop service.

items.name: Fault tolerance
items.detail: The system keeps operating, with no interruption, when a component fails (RAID, dual power, clustering).

items.name: High availability
items.detail: Designing for maximum uptime (for example "five nines" = 99.999%), usually using redundancy, failover and load balancing.

items.name: Failover
items.detail: Switching automatically from a failed component to a standby.

items.name: Resilience
items.detail: The ability to absorb a disruption and recover quickly.

items.name: Scalability vs elasticity
items.detail: Scalability: the ability to handle growth. Elasticity: automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes.

items.name: Single point of failure
items.detail: Any one component whose failure takes the whole service down. Redundancy exists to remove these.

definition: Data whose handling is controlled by law, regulation or industry standard, such as personally identifiable information (PII), protected health information (PHI) and payment card data. Mishandling can bring fines and legal action.
examContext: Know the matching regimes: PHI is HIPAA, cardholder data is PCI DSS, personal data of EU residents is GDPR, and financial reporting data is SOX. Regulated data usually needs stricter classification, encryption and retention rules.
analogy: Like hazardous cargo: the law dictates how it must be labeled, stored, moved and disposed of.
relatedTerms: PII, PHI, Data classification, Data sovereignty, Data controller

detail.practicalScenario: A clinic stores patient records and must follow HIPAA, so it encrypts the data, restricts access by role and logs every access. Treating the records as ordinary files would put it in violation.
detail.quizQuestion: Patient medical records that must be protected under HIPAA are an example of which data type?

items.name: Public
items.detail: Safe to disclose; no harm.

items.name: Private / internal
items.detail: For internal use only.

items.name: Sensitive
items.detail: Disclosure could cause harm or embarrassment.

items.name: Confidential
items.detail: Disclosure would cause serious harm; protected by contract or law.

items.name: Restricted
items.detail: The most tightly controlled, with very limited access.

items.name: Critical
items.detail: Essential to operations; loss or alteration would be severe.

items.name: Government scheme
items.detail: Unclassified, then Confidential, Secret and Top Secret, in rising order of damage if disclosed.

items.name: Data types
items.detail: Regulated (PII, PHI, payment data), trade secrets, intellectual property, legal information and financial information. Data may be human-readable or non-human-readable (binary, encoded).

definition: An attack in which a valid data transmission, such as an authentication token or session packet, is intercepted and maliciously retransmitted to trick the receiving system into granting unauthorized access or repeating an action.
examContext: Know that replay attacks are mitigated with timestamps, sequence numbers, session tokens, and nonces; a classic exam scenario involves a captured login packet being resent later to gain access.
analogy: Like recording someone saying a one-time entry password at a guarded door, then playing back the recording later to trick the guard into letting you in.
relatedTerms: Man-in-the-middle attack, Perfect forward secrecy

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team implements time-based nonces and session tokens in the API authentication flow, so that if an attacker intercepts and retransmits a captured request packet, the server rejects it as stale and refuses to process the duplicate action.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker captures a legitimate authentication packet and retransmits it later to gain unauthorized access to a system. Which control is specifically designed to prevent this?
quizOptions: A) Timestamps and nonces to detect retransmitted packets

items.name: ARP poisoning
items.detail: Forged ARP replies map the attacker's MAC to another host's IP, putting the attacker on-path. Fix: Dynamic ARP Inspection, static entries.

items.name: DNS poisoning
items.detail: Forged records are injected into a resolver's cache so users are sent to attacker sites. Fix: DNSSEC, patched resolvers.

items.name: MAC flooding
items.detail: Fills a switch's CAM table so it floods traffic out of every port, letting the attacker sniff. Fix: port security.

items.name: MAC spoofing
items.detail: Adopting another device's MAC address to evade filtering or impersonate it. Fix: 802.1X, port security.

items.name: VLAN hopping
items.detail: Switch spoofing or double tagging to reach other VLANs. Fix: disable trunk negotiation, change the native VLAN, prune unused ports.

items.name: On-path (MITM)
items.detail: The attacker sits between two parties to read or alter traffic. Fix: TLS with certificate validation, HSTS, mutual authentication.

items.name: Session hijacking
items.detail: Stealing or guessing a session token to impersonate a logged-in user. Fix: TLS, secure and HttpOnly cookies, short sessions.

items.name: SSL stripping
items.detail: Downgrades a victim's HTTPS session to HTTP. Fix: HSTS.

items.name: Replay
items.detail: Captured valid data is re-sent later. Fix: nonces, timestamps and expiring tokens.

items.name: Spoofing
items.detail: Forging an address or identity (IP, MAC, email, caller ID). Fix: ingress/egress filtering, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, authentication.

definition: Continuously or periodically copying data from one system or site to another so a current duplicate is available. It can be synchronous (waits for the copy) or asynchronous (the copy follows slightly later). It improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.
examContext: Replication is not a backup: ransomware or accidental deletion replicates too. Synchronous replication means zero data loss but needs low latency; asynchronous allows a small amount of data loss.
analogy: A live mirror: every change you make appears in the reflection, including your mistakes.
relatedTerms: Backup, High availability, Disaster recovery, Journaling, RAID

detail.practicalScenario: A company replicates its database to a second site every few seconds. When ransomware encrypts the primary, the encrypted data replicates too, so the team must restore from an earlier point-in-time backup instead.
detail.quizQuestion: Which statement about data replication is TRUE?
quizOptions: A) It always requires tape media
B) It can copy corruption or ransomware encryption to the replica
C) It removes the need to plan an RPO
D) It protects against accidental deletion because the copy is separate

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: The risk that remains after controls and mitigations have been applied. It must be within the organization's risk appetite and tolerance or be explicitly accepted by the risk owner.
examContext: Inherent risk reduced by the effectiveness of controls equals residual risk. It is never zero.
analogy: The risk left after wearing a seat belt and having airbags: you could still be hurt.
relatedTerms: Inherent risk, Risk mitigation, Risk acceptance, Risk tolerance, Risk appetite

detail.practicalScenario: After deploying MFA and patching, the likelihood of account takeover drops sharply. The small remaining risk is the residual risk, which the risk owner reviews and formally accepts.
detail.quizQuestion: What is the risk that remains after security controls have been applied?

items.name: Avoid
items.detail: Stop the risky activity entirely (discontinue a product, do not enter a market).

items.name: Mitigate
items.detail: Reduce the likelihood or the impact with controls (patching, firewalls, training).

items.name: Transfer
items.detail: Shift the financial impact to someone else (cyber insurance, outsourcing, contractual indemnity). Accountability usually stays with you.

items.name: Accept
items.detail: Knowingly live with the risk, typically when the cost of controls exceeds the likely loss. Document it as an exception or exemption, within risk appetite.

items.name: Inherent vs residual
items.detail: Inherent risk exists BEFORE controls. Residual risk is what remains AFTER controls and must be within tolerance.

items.name: Risk appetite postures
items.detail: Expansionary (accepts more risk to grow), conservative (low risk), neutral (balanced).

definition: A virtualization and cloud vulnerability in which memory, storage or other resources released by one tenant are reassigned to another without being fully cleared, so leftover data can be exposed.
examContext: Mitigate by zeroing memory and wiping storage on release, encrypting volumes, and relying on strong tenant isolation.
analogy: Checking into a hotel room where the previous guest's notes are still in the drawer.
relatedTerms: Virtualization, VM escape, Data sanitization, Encryption

detail.practicalScenario: A newly provisioned cloud disk still contains fragments of another customer's data because it was not wiped on release. The provider changes its process to zero storage before reassigning it.
detail.quizQuestion: A cloud tenant finds leftover data from a previous customer on newly allocated storage. Which vulnerability is this?

definition: A documented breakdown of which security tasks and controls are handled by a cloud service provider versus the customer, with the exact split varying depending on whether the service is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
examContext: Also called the shared responsibility model; know that the customer's share of responsibility grows moving from SaaS to PaaS to IaaS, since the provider manages less of the stack, and scenario questions often ask who is responsible for a specific failure, such as a misconfigured setting.
analogy: Like renting an apartment where the landlord is responsible for the building's structure and fire alarms, but you're responsible for locking your own door and not leaving your windows open.
relatedTerms: Governance, Due diligence, Risk management, Virtualization, Containerization

detail.practicalScenario: Maria reviews the cloud provider's responsibility matrix before migrating to an IaaS platform and confirms that while the provider secures the physical data center and hypervisor, her own team remains fully responsible for patching the guest operating systems and configuring the firewall rules.
detail.quizQuestion: A company migrates a database server to an Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) cloud platform. According to the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating system running on that virtual server?
quizOptions: A) Neither party, it is automated

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: A practice in which a researcher privately reports a discovered vulnerability to the vendor and allows time to fix it before publishing details, so users are protected.
examContext: Contrast with full disclosure (public immediately). Part of vulnerability management; many organizations publish a disclosure policy so researchers know how to report.
analogy: Telling a store owner about an unlocked back door instead of announcing it to the neighborhood.
relatedTerms: Bug bounty program, Vulnerability, Zero-day, Penetration testing

detail.practicalScenario: A researcher finds a flaw in a router, emails the vendor privately and agrees to wait 90 days. The vendor ships a patch and then the researcher publishes the details, so users can already be protected.
detail.quizQuestion: A researcher privately reports a flaw to the vendor and waits for a fix before publishing the details. What is this practice called?

definition: Copying the data from an RFID badge or tag onto another card so the clone can open doors or gain access. Low-frequency proximity cards often have no encryption, so attackers can read them from a short distance.
examContext: A physical attack listed in the objectives. Mitigations: encrypted smart cards, RFID-blocking sleeves, MFA at sensitive doors, and monitoring badge logs.
analogy: A photocopy of a key that works as well as the original.
relatedTerms: Access badge, Smart card, RFID, Tailgating

detail.practicalScenario: An attacker brushes past an employee with a hidden reader, captures the badge data and writes it to a blank card. The cloned card opens the server-room door, and the log shows the real employee's name.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker reads an employee's proximity badge from a short distance and writes the data to a blank card. What attack is this?

definition: A privacy right, codified in regulations like the GDPR, that allows an individual to request the erasure of their personal data from an organization's systems when the data is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing was unlawful, subject to certain legal exceptions.
examContext: Know the right to be forgotten (right to erasure) is a GDPR-based privacy right letting individuals request deletion of their personal data, and that organizations must have a documented process to verify and honor such requests.
analogy: Like asking a store to shred every copy of your old membership application and purchase history once you no longer want them keeping it on file.
relatedTerms: Data controller, Data processor, Privacy, Data sovereignty, Data classification

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's company receives a formal request from a former customer in the EU invoking the right to be forgotten, so Jordan's team verifies the request, locates every system storing that customer's personal data, and permanently erases it while documenting the deletion to prove compliance.
detail.quizQuestion: A former customer in the European Union formally requests that a company permanently delete all of their personal data from its systems, citing GDPR. Which privacy right is the customer exercising?

definition: A contract provision that lets a customer audit a vendor's security controls, processes and compliance, either directly or through an independent assessor.
examContext: A key third-party risk control, commonly written into master service agreements. It complements questionnaires and independent assessments.
analogy: A clause that lets you inspect the caterer's kitchen before and during your event.
relatedTerms: Vendor assessment, Supply chain attack, MSA, Due diligence

detail.practicalScenario: The contract with a cloud hosting provider includes a right-to-audit clause. After an incident at the vendor, the customer's auditors review its access controls and logs on site.
detail.quizQuestion: Which contract provision lets a customer inspect a vendor's security controls and compliance?

items.name: Vendor selection
items.detail: Perform due diligence, check for conflicts of interest, and review financial stability and security posture.

items.name: Vendor assessment
items.detail: Penetration testing, a right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments and supply chain analysis.

items.name: Questionnaires
items.detail: Standardized security questionnaires the vendor completes.

items.name: Agreements
items.detail: SLA, MSA, SOW, NDA and similar contracts that set expectations and responsibilities.

items.name: Vendor monitoring
items.detail: Continual review of the vendor's performance, security and compliance throughout the relationship.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: Written limits on what testing a third party may do.

definition: The potential for loss or damage when a threat exploits a vulnerability, typically expressed as a function of likelihood and impact.
examContext: Exam tests qualitative versus quantitative risk assessment and formulas like annualized loss expectancy; know that risk is the combination of threat and vulnerability, not either alone.
analogy: Like the overall chance of getting into a car accident, which depends on both how dangerous the road is and how worn your tires are.
relatedTerms: Threat, Vulnerability, Risk management, Exploit

detail.practicalScenario: Sam calculates that a server with a known vulnerability facing active exploitation attempts represents a high risk, prioritizing it over a theoretical vulnerability with no known threat targeting it.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst combines the likelihood of a flood with the potential financial impact to a data center to decide how much insurance coverage to purchase. What is the analyst calculating?

items.name: Mitigate
items.detail: Reduce the likelihood or the impact with controls (patching, firewalls, training).

items.name: Transfer
items.detail: Shift the financial impact to someone else (cyber insurance, outsourcing, contractual indemnity). Accountability usually stays with you.

items.name: Accept
items.detail: Knowingly live with the risk, typically when the cost of controls exceeds the likely loss. Document it as an exception or exemption, within risk appetite.

items.name: Inherent vs residual
items.detail: Inherent risk exists BEFORE controls. Residual risk is what remains AFTER controls and must be within tolerance.

items.name: Risk appetite postures
items.detail: Expansionary (accepts more risk to grow), conservative (low risk), neutral (balanced).

items.name: Qualitative
items.detail: Uses descriptive ratings (high / medium / low) on a likelihood-versus-impact matrix. Quick and subjective.

items.name: Quantitative
items.detail: Uses numbers and currency to calculate expected loss. More objective, but needs good data.

items.name: SLE
items.detail: Single Loss Expectancy = Asset Value (AV) x Exposure Factor (EF). The cost of ONE incident.

items.name: ARO
items.detail: Annualized Rate of Occurrence: how many times per year the event is expected.

items.name: ALE
items.detail: Annualized Loss Expectancy = SLE x ARO. Compare it with the annual cost of a control to see if the control pays for itself.

items.name: Worked example
items.detail: A laptop worth $2,000 (AV) with 100% EF has an SLE of $2,000. If theft is expected once every two years (ARO 0.5), ALE = $1,000 a year, so a $300 a year tracking service is worth buying.

items.name: Assessment frequency
items.detail: Ad hoc (as needed), recurring (scheduled), one-time (for a project) or continuous (ongoing monitoring).

items.name: Key risk indicators
items.detail: Metrics that signal rising risk before an incident, such as the number of unpatched critical systems.

definition: A decision to knowingly tolerate a risk without further treatment, usually because the cost of controls exceeds the potential loss or the risk is within tolerance. It should be documented as an exception or exemption approved by the risk owner.
examContext: It must be a conscious, documented decision within risk appetite, not simply ignoring the risk.
analogy: Choosing to drive an old car without collision coverage because the repairs would cost less than the premiums.
relatedTerms: Risk transference, Risk avoidance, Risk mitigation, Risk appetite, Risk tolerance

detail.practicalScenario: A legacy lab server holds only public test data. The owner signs an exception form accepting the unpatched risk because the cost of replacing it far exceeds any loss.
detail.quizQuestion: Management signs a documented exception to leave a low-impact risk unaddressed because controls would cost more than the loss. Which risk response is this?

examContext: The exam frequently tests the difference between risk appetite (the broad, strategic amount of risk leadership is willing to accept) and risk tolerance (the specific, measurable acceptable variation for one risk); don't mix these up.
analogy: Like a company deciding in general 'we're willing to take calculated risks to innovate quickly,' setting the overall attitude before anyone looks at the specifics of any one project.
relatedTerms: Risk tolerance, Risk register, Risk management, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's executive leadership documents a risk appetite statement declaring the company is 'risk-averse' toward customer data but 'risk-tolerant' toward adopting new productivity tools, giving department heads a strategic compass for the specific risk decisions they make day to day.
detail.quizQuestion: Senior leadership issues a broad statement defining how much risk the organization is generally willing to accept in pursuit of its business objectives. What is this statement called?
