items.name: Risk appetite postures
items.detail: Expansionary (accepts more risk to grow), conservative (low risk), neutral (balanced).

definition: Shifting the financial impact of a risk to a third party, for example through cyber insurance, outsourcing or contractual indemnification. Responsibility and reputational harm usually stay with the organization.
examContext: One of four risk responses (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept). Buying cyber insurance is the classic example, and it is also an architecture consideration for cloud services.
analogy: Buying car insurance: the insurer pays for damage, but you still have the accident.
relatedTerms: Risk acceptance, Risk avoidance, Risk mitigation, Risk management

detail.practicalScenario: A company buys a cyber insurance policy that covers breach costs. A ransomware incident still disrupts operations, but the insurer pays much of the recovery bill.
detail.quizQuestion: A company buys cyber insurance to cover the financial cost of a potential data breach. Which risk response is this?

items.name: Avoid
items.detail: Stop the risky activity entirely (discontinue a product, do not enter a market).

items.name: Mitigate
items.detail: Reduce the likelihood or the impact with controls (patching, firewalls, training).

items.name: Transfer
items.detail: Shift the financial impact to someone else (cyber insurance, outsourcing, contractual indemnity). Accountability usually stays with you.

items.name: Accept
items.detail: Knowingly live with the risk, typically when the cost of controls exceeds the likely loss. Document it as an exception or exemption, within risk appetite.

items.name: Inherent vs residual
items.detail: Inherent risk exists BEFORE controls. Residual risk is what remains AFTER controls and must be within tolerance.

items.name: Risk appetite postures
items.detail: Expansionary (accepts more risk to grow), conservative (low risk), neutral (balanced).

definition: Any wireless access point connected to a network without authorization, whether planted by an attacker or installed by a well-meaning employee, creating an unmonitored back door around the perimeter.
examContext: Detect with WIDS/WIPS and wireless surveys; prevent with 802.1X and port security on switches. An evil twin is a special case that imitates a legitimate SSID.
analogy: An unlocked side door added by an employee because the front door was inconvenient.
relatedTerms: Evil twin, WIDS, WIPS, Shadow IT

detail.practicalScenario: A manager plugs a personal Wi-Fi router into an office network jack so her team can use their phones. The router has no security controls, so anyone in the parking lot can reach the internal network.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee plugs a personal Wi-Fi router into an office network jack. What is this device?

definition: An access control model that assigns permissions to users based on their job role within an organization, rather than to each individual separately, simplifying administration as users are added, moved, or removed.
examContext: Know RBAC is the most common enterprise access model, tied closely to least privilege and separation of duties; exam scenarios test recognizing RBAC when permissions are described as tied to job function or title.
analogy: Like a hospital where a badge marked Nurse automatically grants access to the medication room, regardless of which specific nurse is wearing it.
relatedTerms: Mandatory access control, Discretionary access control, Least privilege, Attribute-based access control, Rule-based access control

detail.practicalScenario: Maria redesigns the file server permissions so that access is granted based on department roles like HR Manager or Finance Analyst rather than to individual employee accounts, so that when someone changes jobs internally, their access automatically updates with their new role assignment.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants new employees to automatically receive the correct system permissions based on their job title, and wants access to update automatically when someone changes departments. Which access control model fits this need?

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: The foundational, inherently trusted hardware, firmware, or cryptographic component, such as a TPM, from which an entire chain of trust is built, used to verify that each subsequent layer of boot code or software has not been tampered with.
examContext: The exam ties root of trust to secure boot and attestation processes; know it is the starting anchor that must itself be trustworthy, since everything else in the chain of trust is verified relative to it.
analogy: Like the foundation of a building: every floor built on top is only as trustworthy as that original foundation being solid and untampered with.
relatedTerms: Chain of trust, Attestation, Secure enclave, Certificate authority

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's organization enables secure boot on all company laptops, relying on a hardware root of trust embedded in the TPM chip to verify that the bootloader and operating system haven't been tampered with before the device finishes starting up.
detail.quizQuestion: A laptop's secure boot process verifies each stage of startup code against the previous stage, all ultimately anchored to one trusted hardware component. What is this foundational anchor called?

variants.title: TPM vs HSM vs KMS vs secure enclave

items.name: TPM
items.detail: Trusted Platform Module: a chip on a single device's motherboard that stores keys bound to that machine. Powers BitLocker, measured/secure boot and attestation.

items.name: HSM
items.detail: Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance, card or cloud service that generates, stores and uses keys at scale. FIPS 140 validated; used by CAs, banks and payment systems.

items.name: KMS
items.detail: Key Management System/Service: software (often cloud) that manages the key lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, store). Frequently backed by an HSM.

items.name: Secure enclave
items.detail: An isolated, protected area inside a processor for sensitive operations and data (biometric templates, keys), walled off even from the main OS.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: One laptop's disk encryption: TPM. A datacenter-wide key store or signing service: HSM. Managing and rotating keys centrally: KMS.

definition: Malware designed to gain and maintain privileged, root or administrator level access to a system while actively hiding its presence from users and security tools.
examContext: Exam tests rootkits as operating at a low level, such as kernel mode, to evade detection, often requiring specialized tools or a full operating system reinstall to remove.
analogy: Like a secret passage hidden behind a bookshelf that lets an intruder come and go without anyone noticing.
relatedTerms: Backdoor, Privilege escalation, Persistence, Malware

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's forensic investigation reveals that standard antivirus scans show the server as clean, yet a kernel-level rootkit is hiding malicious processes from the operating system's own reporting tools.
detail.quizQuestion: A security tool cannot detect any malicious files, yet the server exhibits odd behavior, and a specialized offline scan reveals hidden processes operating with kernel-level privileges. What type of malware is this?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A Layer 3 device that connects different networks and forwards packets between them by reading the destination IP address and choosing the best next hop from its routing table. It does not forward broadcasts, so it separates broadcast domains.
examContext: Router means Layer 3 and IP addresses. It is usually the default gateway and may also perform NAT, ACL filtering and VPN termination. Hardening: change defaults, disable unused services, restrict management with ACLs, filter spoofed addresses at the edge and authenticate routing updates.
analogy: A mailroom that sends mail between different buildings using their street addresses.
relatedTerms: Switch, Default gateway, Routing table, Subnet, Network segmentation, Firewall

detail.practicalScenario: A branch office router has one interface in the office LAN and another toward the provider. When a PC requests a website, the router reads the destination IP address, finds its default route and forwards the packet to the provider's router.
detail.quizQuestion: Which device connects two different IP networks and chooses the next hop using the destination IP address?

definition: The list of networks a router knows about, with the next hop or interface used to reach each one. The router matches the destination IP address to the most specific entry, and a default route (0.0.0.0/0) catches everything else.
examContext: Entries come from directly connected networks, static routes or dynamic routing protocols such as OSPF and BGP. Forged routing updates and route hijacking attack the table, so authenticate routing protocols and filter the routes you accept.
analogy: A road atlas the router checks for every packet to decide the next turn.
relatedTerms: Router, Default gateway, Subnet, Network segmentation

detail.practicalScenario: A packet for 10.5.0.9 arrives at the router. It matches the entry for 10.0.0.0/8 and is forwarded to the next hop listed there. A packet for a public website matches only the default route and goes to the provider.
detail.quizQuestion: Which entry in a router's table is used when no more specific route matches the destination?

definition: An access control model that grants or restricts access based on a predefined set of system-enforced rules (often if-then logic), such as firewall ACLs or time-of-day restrictions, applied uniformly regardless of the specific user's identity or role.
examContext: The exam expects you to distinguish rule-based access control (static, administrator-defined if-then rules like firewall ACLs, applied the same way to everyone) from role-based access control, even though both are casually abbreviated 'RBAC.'
analogy: Like a parking garage gate that only lifts for cars between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m.; the rule applies to every vehicle equally, no matter who is driving.
relatedTerms: Role-based access control, Attribute-based access control, Mandatory access control, Discretionary access control, Firewall

detail.practicalScenario: Sam writes a firewall rule set stating that any traffic from the guest Wi-Fi VLAN destined for the internal file server subnet is automatically dropped, no matter which device or user is connecting, enforcing network segmentation through static rules rather than user identity.
detail.quizQuestion: A network administrator configures a firewall so that any connection attempt to the internal database port from outside the corporate IP range is automatically blocked, regardless of who initiates it. This is an example of which access control model?

items.name: DAC · discretionary
items.detail: The resource OWNER decides who gets access (via ACLs). Flexible, but users can pass permissions on, so it is the weakest. Examples: NTFS and Linux file permissions.

items.name: MAC · mandatory
items.detail: The SYSTEM enforces access from security labels and clearances; neither users nor owners can override it. Strictest; military and government. Example: SELinux.

items.name: RBAC · role-based
items.detail: Permissions belong to roles (job functions) and users inherit them. Scales well and supports least privilege and separation of duties.

items.name: Rule-based
items.detail: Fixed rules apply to everyone regardless of identity: firewall ACLs, "only from the office network," time-of-day restrictions. Not the same as role-based.

items.name: ABAC · attribute-based
items.detail: Decisions use attributes of the user, the resource and the context (department = HR AND device is managed AND business hours). Most granular and flexible; the engine behind zero-trust policies.

items.name: Quick cue
items.detail: Owner decides = DAC. Labels and clearances = MAC. Job role = RBAC. Conditions or schedules = rule-based. Many attributes = ABAC.

definition: The written agreement that defines the scope, permitted techniques, timing, targets, communication and authorization for a penetration test or red team exercise.
examContext: Never test without it: it is the permission slip. It limits legal liability and prevents damage, and it includes emergency contacts and what is out of scope.
analogy: A contract telling the movers which rooms they may enter and what they may touch.
relatedTerms: Penetration testing, Red team, Known environment, Unknown environment

detail.practicalScenario: Before a pentest begins, the client and testers sign rules of engagement that list the permitted IP ranges, testing hours and a contact for emergencies. Production databases are marked out of scope.
detail.quizQuestion: Which document defines the scope, permitted techniques and timing of a penetration test?

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: A detailed, step-by-step set of technical instructions, often automated or scripted, that carries out a specific task or response action consistently every time it's executed.
examContext: Contrast with a playbook: a runbook is the concrete, often automated execution layer, the exact script or steps that isolate a host and collect forensic artifacts, while the playbook is the higher-level decision logic that determines when to trigger it.
analogy: Like a detailed step-by-step appliance repair manual that tells a technician exactly which screws to remove and in what order, rather than just explaining when a repair is needed.
relatedTerms: Playbook, Incident response, Change management

detail.practicalScenario: Priya automates the account-compromise runbook so that once triggered, it executes the exact scripted sequence every time: disable the account, force a password reset, revoke active session tokens, and notify the user, with no step left to manual interpretation.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team creates an automated script that, once triggered, executes an identical scripted sequence every time: disabling a compromised account, revoking its sessions, and resetting its password. What is this automated procedure called?

definition: The practice of adding a unique random value to data, typically a password, before hashing it, so that identical inputs produce different hash outputs, defeating precomputed rainbow table attacks.
examContext: Expect scenario questions about why two users with the same password have different stored hashes, the answer is salting; know it is used alongside hashing, not as a replacement for it.
analogy: Like adding a unique secret ingredient to each recipe so that even identical dishes taste slightly different and can't be mass-produced from a single stolen recipe card.
relatedTerms: Hashing, Key stretching, Brute force attack, Dictionary attack

detail.practicalScenario: Priya updates the authentication system to add a unique random salt to every user password before hashing, ensuring that even if two employees choose the identical password, their stored hash values are completely different.
detail.quizQuestion: A security audit reveals that users with identical passwords have identical password hashes stored in the database, making the system vulnerable to rainbow table attacks. What should be implemented?

items.name: Brute force
items.detail: Tries every possible combination. Online (against a login) or offline (against stolen hashes). Defeated by long passwords, lockouts and key stretching.

items.name: Dictionary
items.detail: Tries a list of common words and leaked passwords; a hybrid attack adds mutations (Password1!).

items.name: Password spraying
items.detail: Tries a FEW common passwords against MANY accounts, staying under lockout thresholds.

items.name: Credential stuffing
items.detail: Replays username/password pairs leaked from OTHER breaches, betting on password reuse. Defeated by MFA and unique passwords.

items.name: Rainbow table
items.detail: Pre-computed hash-to-password lookup tables for fast offline cracking. Defeated by SALTING.

items.name: Pass-the-hash
items.detail: Uses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate directly, with no cracking required.

items.name: Online vs offline
items.detail: Online attacks hit a live service and trigger lockouts and alerts. Offline attacks crack stolen hashes at GPU speed without detection; the defense is strong hashing (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2) with salts.

definition: The practice of running an untrusted application, file, or piece of code in an isolated environment, separated from the host system and production network, so that any malicious behavior it exhibits cannot affect the real environment.
examContext: Know sandboxing as both a malware-analysis technique, safely detonating a suspicious file, and a development practice, isolating untested code; exam scenarios often describe a suspicious attachment being opened in an isolated environment first.
analogy: Like testing a questionable chemical reaction inside a sealed fume hood instead of out in the open lab, so if something goes wrong, the damage stays contained.
relatedTerms: Containerization, Virtualization, Dynamic code analysis, Static code analysis

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security team routes every email attachment flagged as suspicious into an isolated sandbox environment first, where the file can be opened and observed safely; when one attachment attempts to contact a known command-and-control server, the sandbox contains the connection and the real network is never exposed.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants to safely observe what a suspicious email attachment actually does when opened, without risking any harm to production systems. What technique should they use?

definition: Scalability is a system's ability to handle a growing workload by adding resources; elasticity is the ability to add and remove resources automatically as demand rises and falls. Cloud platforms are valued for both.
examContext: Architecture considerations include scalability, resilience, cost, responsiveness and ease of deployment. Elasticity is automatic and dynamic, while scalability is the capacity to grow.
analogy: Scalability is a restaurant with room to add tables; elasticity is tables that appear for the dinner rush and vanish afterward.
relatedTerms: Capacity planning, Public cloud, High availability, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: An online store's application automatically launches extra servers during a flash sale and shuts them down afterward, so it pays only for what it uses and never runs out of capacity.
detail.quizQuestion: A web application automatically adds servers during a sale and removes them when demand falls. Which cloud property is this?

items.name: Redundancy
items.detail: Duplicate components (disks, power supplies, links, servers) so a single failure does not stop service.

items.name: Fault tolerance
items.detail: The system keeps operating, with no interruption, when a component fails (RAID, dual power, clustering).

items.name: High availability
items.detail: Designing for maximum uptime (for example "five nines" = 99.999%), usually using redundancy, failover and load balancing.

items.name: Failover
items.detail: Switching automatically from a failed component to a standby.

items.name: Resilience
items.detail: The ability to absorb a disruption and recover quickly.

items.name: Scalability vs elasticity
items.detail: Scalability: the ability to handle growth. Elasticity: automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes.

items.name: Single point of failure
items.detail: Any one component whose failure takes the whole service down. Redundancy exists to remove these.

definition: A network segment, formerly called a DMZ, placed between the internet and the internal network and protected by firewalls. It hosts public-facing servers such as web, mail and DNS so that a compromise does not give direct access to the internal LAN.
examContext: CompTIA now uses the term screened subnet. Know the placement: internet, external firewall, screened subnet, internal firewall, internal LAN.
analogy: A hotel lobby: visitors can come in without being able to wander into the staff offices.
relatedTerms: DMZ, Firewall, Network segmentation, Security zone

detail.practicalScenario: A company places its public web server in a screened subnet. If the server is compromised, the internal firewall still blocks the attacker from reaching the employee network and databases.
detail.quizQuestion: Where should a public-facing web server be placed to limit exposure of the internal network if it is compromised?
quizOptions: B) Directly on the internal LAN
D) On the same VLAN as the database

definition: A documented, minimum set of security configurations that a system must be brought to and kept at, covering the steps to establish, deploy, and maintain that hardened starting state across every instance of that system type.
examContext: Know the exam frames secure baselines as a lifecycle, establish the standard, deploy it consistently to new systems, then maintain it over time, which distinguishes it from a one-time baseline configuration snapshot used only for drift detection.
analogy: Like a restaurant chain's standard recipe and setup checklist that every new location must be built to match and is regularly re-inspected against, not just measured once on opening day.
relatedTerms: Baseline configuration, Hardening, Patch management, Sandboxing

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan builds a secure baseline image for every new cloud server the company deploys, defining exactly which services run and which ports stay open, then schedules automated compliance checks that re-verify every running instance still matches that maintained baseline each week.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization defines a standard, hardened configuration that every new server must be built from, and then continuously re-verifies existing servers against that same standard over time. What security practice best describes this establish-deploy-maintain lifecycle?

items.name: Workstations and endpoints
items.detail: Install endpoint protection, enable a host firewall, patch, encrypt the disk, remove unnecessary software and bloatware, and run as a standard user.

items.name: Servers
items.detail: Minimal role-specific installs, disable unneeded services, patch, least privilege, logging and a secure baseline.

items.name: Switches and routers
items.detail: Change default credentials, disable unused ports, use SSH rather than Telnet, SNMPv3, port security, ACLs and firmware updates.

items.name: Cloud infrastructure
items.detail: Least-privilege IAM, MFA, no public storage buckets, encryption, logging and configuration scanning.

items.name: Mobile devices
items.detail: MDM policies, passcodes, encryption, remote wipe, app allow lists, and no sideloading.

items.name: IoT and embedded
items.detail: Change default credentials, update firmware, isolate on their own VLAN, and disable unused features.

items.name: ICS / SCADA / RTOS
items.detail: Segmentation or an air gap, strict physical security, monitoring and compensating controls, because patching is often impractical.

items.name: Common steps
items.detail: Change default passwords, disable unnecessary ports and protocols, remove unnecessary software, patch, and install endpoint protection.

definition: A browser cookie marked with attributes, such as Secure and HttpOnly, that restrict it to being transmitted only over encrypted HTTPS connections and block it from being accessed by client-side scripts, reducing the risk of theft.
examContext: Know the Secure attribute forces HTTPS-only transmission and HttpOnly blocks JavaScript access to the cookie, which directly mitigates session hijacking via cross-site scripting; exam scenarios may describe a stolen session cookie and ask which attribute would have prevented it.
analogy: Like sealing a letter in a tamper-evident envelope that can only be opened through one trusted mail slot, instead of leaving it as an open postcard anyone passing by could read or swap.
relatedTerms: Input validation, Encryption, Man-in-the-middle attack

detail.practicalScenario: Priya configures the web application's session cookies with both the Secure and HttpOnly attributes set, so the cookie is never sent over an unencrypted connection and a cross-site scripting payload injected by an attacker can no longer read or steal it through JavaScript.
detail.quizQuestion: After a cross-site scripting vulnerability is discovered, an attacker is unable to read a user's session cookie through injected JavaScript. Which cookie attribute most likely prevented this?

definition: An isolated, hardware-based area of a processor that stores and processes sensitive data, such as encryption keys and biometric templates, separately from the main operating system so it remains protected even if the OS is compromised.
examContext: The exam ties secure enclave to protecting cryptographic keys and biometric data at the hardware level; it serves a similar purpose to a TPM but typically refers to a dedicated secure co-processor on mobile devices and modern CPUs.
analogy: Like a small, windowless vault inside a bank that stays locked and separate even if someone takes over the entire rest of the building.
relatedTerms: Root of trust, Key escrow, Biometrics, Attestation

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's mobile app stores users' fingerprint templates inside the device's secure enclave rather than in regular app storage, ensuring the biometric data stays protected even if the phone's operating system is later compromised by malware.
detail.quizQuestion: A mobile device manufacturer wants fingerprint data and encryption keys to remain protected even if the main operating system is fully compromised by malware. Where should this sensitive data be stored?
quizOptions: A) In an encrypted database file
D) In an implicit trust zone

variants.title: TPM vs HSM vs KMS vs secure enclave

items.name: TPM
items.detail: Trusted Platform Module: a chip on a single device's motherboard that stores keys bound to that machine. Powers BitLocker, measured/secure boot and attestation.

items.name: HSM
items.detail: Hardware Security Module: a tamper-resistant appliance, card or cloud service that generates, stores and uses keys at scale. FIPS 140 validated; used by CAs, banks and payment systems.

items.name: KMS
items.detail: Key Management System/Service: software (often cloud) that manages the key lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke, store). Frequently backed by an HSM.

items.name: Secure enclave
items.detail: An isolated, protected area inside a processor for sensitive operations and data (biometric templates, keys), walled off even from the main OS.

items.name: Rule of thumb
items.detail: One laptop's disk encryption: TPM. A datacenter-wide key store or signing service: HSM. Managing and rotating keys centrally: KMS.

definition: A program that teaches employees to recognize and respond to threats such as phishing, social engineering and unsafe behavior, and to follow security policies. It includes initial onboarding training and recurring refreshers.
examContext: Elements: phishing campaigns, anomalous behavior recognition, user guidance (policies, password management, removable media, remote work) and reporting and monitoring. It is an operational, preventive control.
analogy: Teaching everyone in the building how to spot a stranger and what to do about it.
relatedTerms: Phishing simulation, Social engineering, Situational awareness, Operational security, Insider threat

detail.practicalScenario: New hires complete security training in their first week and every employee takes a refresher each year. The program tracks completion and click-rates and targets extra coaching where results are weak.
detail.quizQuestion: Which control teaches employees to recognize phishing and follow security policies?

items.name: Phishing campaigns
items.detail: Simulated phishing to teach users to recognize attacks and to measure click and report rates.

items.name: Reporting suspicious messages
items.detail: Give users an easy way to report (a report button), and respond to the reports.

items.name: Anomalous behavior recognition
items.detail: Recognize risky behavior (unsafe habits), unexpected behavior (out of pattern) and unintentional behavior (honest mistakes).

items.name: User guidance topics
items.detail: Policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threats, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, and hybrid/remote work.

items.name: Development and execution
items.detail: Create the content, deliver it (computer-based, in person, gamified), and keep it relevant.

items.name: Reporting and monitoring
items.detail: Initial training at onboarding, recurring refreshers, and tracking completion rates and metrics.

definition: A trained person physically stationed at a facility to monitor access, verify identities, patrol the premises, and respond to security incidents in real time.
examContext: The exam notes guards provide a flexible, judgment-based control that can adapt to unexpected situations, unlike fixed controls such as fencing or badge readers, but they add cost and remain subject to human error or social engineering.
analogy: Like a lifeguard who doesn't just watch a sign saying no swimming, but actively observes, judges situations, and intervenes when something looks wrong.
relatedTerms: Access control vestibule, Access badge, Tailgating, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's building staffs a security guard at the main lobby desk who checks every visitor's identification against a pre-approved list and physically escorts guests who lack a valid access badge.
detail.quizQuestion: Which physical security control is best suited to exercise real-time judgment, such as questioning an unfamiliar person who lacks a badge but claims to be a new employee?

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

definition: A recommended practice that offers advice and flexibility but is not mandatory, such as suggestions for building memorable passphrases or choosing a secure Wi-Fi network.
examContext: The key word is optional or advisory. Policies and standards are mandatory; guidelines are best-practice recommendations that staff may adapt.
analogy: A "tips for hikers" leaflet: helpful advice, but nobody is forced to follow it.
relatedTerms: Security policy, Security standard, Security procedure, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: The security team circulates a guideline that suggests using a password manager and avoiding public USB charging ports. Staff are encouraged but not required to follow it.
detail.quizQuestion: Which type of document is advisory rather than mandatory?

variants.title: Policy, standard, procedure and guideline compared

items.name: Policy
items.detail: A high-level management statement of WHAT must be done and why. Broad, mandatory, and rarely changed (for example the Acceptable Use Policy).

items.name: Standard
items.detail: Specific, MANDATORY requirements that support a policy (passwords of 14+ characters, AES-256 for data at rest).

items.name: Procedure
items.detail: Step-by-step instructions on HOW to carry out a task (an onboarding checklist, a restore runbook).

items.name: Guideline
items.detail: Recommended best practice. ADVISORY and flexible, not mandatory.

items.name: Baseline
items.detail: The minimum secure configuration that systems must meet (see secure baseline).

items.name: Common policies
items.detail: Acceptable use, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management, password, remote access, data retention and onboarding/offboarding.

definition: A physical hardware authenticator, usually a USB, NFC or Bluetooth device using FIDO2/WebAuthn public-key cryptography, that proves possession and is bound to the legitimate website, resisting phishing.
examContext: A "something you have" factor and a strong MFA option (such as a YubiKey). It is phishing-resistant because it checks the site's origin before responding.
analogy: A physical key that only fits your own front door and refuses to turn in a fake lock.
relatedTerms: Multifactor authentication, Passwordless authentication, Smart card, Authentication token

detail.practicalScenario: Employees log in with a password and then touch a USB security key. When a convincing phishing page asks for the code, the key refuses to respond because the site is not the real one.
detail.quizQuestion: Which MFA method uses a hardware device with public-key cryptography that resists phishing by verifying the website?

definition: A high-level, management-approved document that states what the organization requires to protect its information and systems, and why. Policies are broad, mandatory and change infrequently; standards, procedures and guidelines supply the detail.
examContext: Know the hierarchy: policy (what and why) leads to standard (specific mandatory requirements), procedure (how, step by step) and guideline (optional advice). Examples include the acceptable use, information security, BCP/DR, incident response and data retention policies.
analogy: A country's constitution: broad principles from which more detailed laws and rules follow.
relatedTerms: Security standard, Security procedure, Security guideline, Governance, Directive control

detail.practicalScenario: The board approves an information security policy that requires all sensitive data to be protected. IT then writes standards (approved encryption algorithms) and procedures (how to encrypt a laptop) that implement it.
detail.quizQuestion: Which document gives the broad, mandatory statement of an organization's security intent and rarely changes?

definition: Step-by-step instructions for performing a specific task consistently, such as onboarding a user, restoring from backup or responding to a phishing report.
examContext: Procedures describe HOW. They support policies and standards, are used for training and audits, and are sometimes called SOPs or runbooks.
analogy: A recipe: ordered steps that produce the same result every time.
relatedTerms: Security policy, Security standard, Standard operating procedure, Runbook

detail.practicalScenario: The help desk follows a documented procedure to reset a locked account: verify the caller's identity, check the ticket, reset the password, force a change at next login and log the action.
detail.quizQuestion: A checklist tells the help desk exactly how to reset a locked account, step by step. What is this document?

definition: A specific, mandatory requirement that supports a policy, such as minimum password length, approved encryption algorithms or required configuration baselines.
examContext: Standards say exactly WHAT level or technology must be used, while procedures say HOW to do the task. If it is mandatory and specific (for example, "AES-256 for data at rest"), it is a standard.
analogy: The building code that says exactly how thick the walls must be, supporting the general law that buildings must be safe.
relatedTerms: Security policy, Security procedure, Security guideline, Baseline configuration

detail.practicalScenario: To support the data protection policy, the security team publishes a standard that all laptops must use AES-256 full-disk encryption and passwords must be at least 14 characters.
detail.quizQuestion: A document states that all laptops must use AES-256 full-disk encryption. What is it?

items.detail: Acceptable use, information security, business continuity, disaster recovery, incident response, SDLC, change management, password, remote access, data retention and onboarding/offboarding.

definition: A logical or physical area of a network grouped by trust level and function, such as trusted internal, untrusted internet, screened subnet, guest and management, with controls enforced where zones meet.
examContext: The basis of segmentation and zero trust. Traffic between zones passes through a firewall. Zero trust adds implicit trust zones and policy enforcement points.
analogy: Areas of an airport: public, ticketed and secure airside, each with its own checkpoint.
relatedTerms: Screened subnet, Network segmentation, Zero trust, Implicit trust zone, Microsegmentation

detail.practicalScenario: The network team defines zones for servers, employees, guests and building systems. Firewalls between the zones allow only the traffic each one needs, so a compromised guest laptop cannot reach the servers.
detail.quizQuestion: A network is divided into areas by trust level, with firewalls controlling traffic between them. What are these areas called?

definition: A review in which an organization evaluates its own controls and compliance against a checklist or framework, usually quickly and cheaply, without independent verification.
examContext: The least objective form of assessment; common for PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaires and quick gap checks.
analogy: Grading your own exam.
relatedTerms: Internal audit, External audit, Gap analysis, Compliance

detail.practicalScenario: A small merchant completes a PCI DSS self-assessment questionnaire, answering each requirement itself. No outside party verifies the answers.
detail.quizQuestion: A small company completes a compliance checklist by evaluating its own controls, without outside verification. What is this?

items.name: Internal
items.detail: Performed by the organization's own staff (an internal audit team or audit committee). Good for readiness and compliance checks; less independent.

items.name: External
items.detail: Performed by an independent third party or a regulator. More objective and credible.

items.name: Self-assessment
items.detail: The organization reviews its own controls against a checklist. Cheap and quick, but the least objective.

items.name: Regulatory examination
items.detail: An audit required by law or a regulator.

items.name: Independent third-party audit
items.detail: An outside auditor attests that controls work (for example a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certification).

items.name: Attestation
items.detail: A formal statement from an auditor or responsible party that controls are as described.

definition: A digital certificate signed with its own private key rather than by a trusted certificate authority. It can enable encryption but gives no third-party validation of identity, so browsers and clients show warnings unless the certificate is manually trusted.
examContext: Acceptable for internal labs and development, risky for production or public sites because anyone can generate one and there is no chain of trust. Root CA certificates are also self-signed, but they are deliberately pre-installed in trust stores.
analogy: Like a handwritten ID card you made for yourself: it names you, but nobody official vouches for it.
relatedTerms: Certificate, Certificate authority, Chain of trust, Root of trust

detail.practicalScenario: A developer starts a test web app with a self-signed certificate. Browsers warn that the connection is not trusted because no public CA vouches for it. Before launch, the team buys a CA-issued certificate instead.
detail.quizQuestion: A browser warns that a site's certificate was not issued by a recognized authority but by the site itself. What type of certificate is this?

definition: A control that divides critical tasks among multiple people so that no single individual can complete a sensitive process alone.
examContext: Exam scenarios often involve fraud prevention in financial processes, where one person requests a payment and another approves it; recognize this as separation of duties, not least privilege.
analogy: Like requiring two keys turned simultaneously to launch a missile, so no one person can act alone.
relatedTerms: Least privilege, Need to know, Accountability, Governance

detail.practicalScenario: Chen restructures the accounts payable process so that the employee who creates a vendor invoice is different from the employee who approves payment, preventing a single person from creating and cashing a fraudulent invoice.
detail.quizQuestion: A company requires that the employee who initiates a wire transfer request cannot be the same employee who approves it. Which security principle does this enforce?

items.name: Just-in-time permissions
items.detail: Privilege is granted only when needed and removed automatically afterwards, so no one holds standing admin rights.

items.name: Password vaulting
items.detail: Privileged credentials are stored encrypted in a vault, checked out by approved users, and rotated after use.

items.name: Ephemeral credentials
items.detail: Short-lived credentials or tokens created on demand for a single task or session, so there is nothing long-lived to steal.

items.name: Session recording
items.detail: Privileged sessions are monitored and recorded for audit and forensics.

items.name: Least privilege / separation of duties
items.detail: Give only the access needed, and split sensitive tasks across people so no single person can complete fraud alone.

definition: An attack that tricks a server into making HTTP requests to destinations chosen by the attacker, often internal-only services or the cloud metadata endpoint, abusing the server's trust and network position (SSRF).
examContext: Mitigate with destination allow lists, blocking internal address ranges, network segmentation and cloud metadata protections. Do not confuse it with CSRF, which targets the user's browser.
analogy: Persuading a trusted employee to fetch documents from a locked internal room that you cannot enter yourself.
relatedTerms: CSRF, Input validation, Network segmentation, Directory traversal

detail.practicalScenario: A web app lets users supply an image URL to fetch. An attacker submits an internal address and retrieves cloud credentials from the metadata service. The fix is an allow list of permitted external hosts.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker submits a URL that makes a vulnerable web application fetch data from an internal-only service on the attacker's behalf. What attack is this?

definition: A cloud execution model in which the cloud provider dynamically allocates and manages the underlying servers, automatically scaling resources up or down, so developers deploy code (often as functions) without provisioning or maintaining infrastructure.
examContext: Remember 'serverless' doesn't mean no servers exist; it means the cloud provider manages and patches the underlying infrastructure under the shared responsibility model, while the customer is responsible only for the function code.
analogy: Like paying a taxi fare only for the exact ride you take, instead of owning and maintaining a car that sits in the garage most of the day.
relatedTerms: Virtualization, Containerization, Microservices, High availability

detail.practicalScenario: Maria rewrites a small image-resizing utility as a serverless function that triggers automatically whenever a file is uploaded to storage, so her team never has to patch or scale a dedicated server and only pays for the brief moments the function actually executes.
detail.quizQuestion: A startup wants to run short bursts of code in response to events without managing or patching any underlying servers, paying only for actual execution time. Which architecture model fits this need?

variants.title: Cloud service and deployment models compared

items.name: IaaS
items.detail: Infrastructure as a Service: the provider supplies virtual compute, storage and networking. YOU manage the OS, apps, data and patching (AWS EC2).

items.name: PaaS
items.detail: Platform as a Service: the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you deploy applications and data (Azure App Service).

items.name: SaaS
items.detail: Software as a Service: a complete application delivered over the web; you manage only your data, users and configuration (Microsoft 365).

items.name: XaaS
items.detail: Anything as a Service: the umbrella for delivering other capabilities (security, desktops, backup) as a service.

items.name: Public cloud
items.detail: Shared, multi-tenant infrastructure run by a provider.

items.name: Private cloud
items.detail: Infrastructure dedicated to ONE organization, on premises or hosted.

items.name: Hybrid cloud
items.detail: A mix of public and private (or on-premises) environments connected together.

items.name: Community cloud
items.detail: Shared by several organizations with common needs, such as compliance.

items.name: Shared responsibility
items.detail: The provider secures the cloud itself (facilities, hypervisor); you secure what you put IN it (data, identities, configuration). The more managed the service, the more the provider handles.

definition: An attack in which the attacker steals or guesses a valid session token (such as a cookie or session ID) and uses it to impersonate a logged-in user without knowing the password.
examContext: Defenses: TLS everywhere, Secure and HttpOnly cookies, short session lifetimes, re-authentication for sensitive actions and regenerating tokens after login. Related to on-path attacks and XSS.
analogy: Stealing the wristband of someone who already paid to enter, instead of buying a ticket yourself.
relatedTerms: Secure cookie, Man-in-the-middle attack, XSS, Replay attack

detail.practicalScenario: On an unsecured coffee-shop network, an attacker captures a user's session cookie for a web app and pastes it into their own browser, instantly gaining access to the account without logging in.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker steals a user's session cookie over unsecured Wi-Fi and uses it to access the user's account. What attack is this?

definition: A temporary symmetric key generated for a single communication session and discarded afterward. Asymmetric cryptography or a Diffie-Hellman exchange establishes it securely, then fast symmetric encryption protects the actual data.
examContext: Session keys are the symmetric half of hybrid encryption such as TLS. Because every session uses its own key, compromising one session does not expose the others, and ephemeral key exchange (DHE/ECDHE) adds perfect forward secrecy.
analogy: Like a hotel room key code created for your stay that stops working when you check out.
relatedTerms: Hybrid encryption, Symmetric encryption, Key exchange, Perfect forward secrecy

detail.practicalScenario: When a browser opens an HTTPS connection, the client and server run an ECDHE exchange to agree on a fresh AES session key. All page data is encrypted with that key, which is thrown away when the connection closes.
detail.quizQuestion: In a TLS connection, what is typically used to encrypt the bulk of the data once the handshake completes?
quizOptions: C) A hash of the certificate

definition: Hardware, software, or cloud services used by employees within an organization without the knowledge, approval, or oversight of the IT or security department.
examContext: The exam frames shadow IT as a governance and risk issue, since unapproved tools bypass security controls, patching, and data loss prevention policies, creating blind spots the security team cannot monitor or protect.
analogy: Like an employee building a private side door into the office that the building manager doesn't know exists: convenient for them, but a security blind spot for everyone else.
relatedTerms: Governance, Risk management, Data loss prevention, Attack surface

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's security audit discovers that the marketing team has been uploading customer data to a personal cloud storage account that IT never approved or secured, prompting a new policy requiring all cloud tools to go through formal review.
detail.quizQuestion: A security audit discovers an entire department has been using an unapproved cloud file-sharing tool that bypasses the organization's data loss prevention controls. What is this unapproved technology use called?

items.name: Nation-state
items.detail: Government-backed. Very high funding and sophistication, with patient long-term (APT) campaigns for espionage, sabotage and geopolitical goals.

items.name: Organized crime
items.detail: Structured criminal groups with high resources, driven by PROFIT: ransomware, fraud, theft and extortion.

items.name: Hacktivist
items.detail: Moderate skills, driven by ideology or politics. Typical acts: DDoS, website defacement, doxing and data leaks.

items.name: Unskilled attacker (script kiddie)
items.detail: Low skill and low resources. Runs pre-made tools and scripts for curiosity, bragging rights or chaos.

items.name: Insider threat
items.detail: An employee, contractor or partner with legitimate access. INTERNAL, and either malicious (revenge, profit) or unintentional (mistakes, negligence).

items.name: Shadow IT
items.detail: Staff using unapproved apps, devices or cloud services. Rarely malicious, but it creates unmanaged risk.

items.name: Attributes that separate actors
items.detail: Internal vs external; resources and funding (low to high); level of sophistication and capability (low to high).

definition: The act of covertly observing someone's screen, keyboard, or written material to capture sensitive information such as passwords or PINs.
examContext: Exam tests shoulder surfing as a low-tech observational attack, with mitigations like privacy screens and awareness training.
analogy: Like peeking over someone's shoulder at the ATM to catch their PIN as they type it.
relatedTerms: Social engineering, Dumpster diving

detail.practicalScenario: Priya notices a stranger lingering unusually close behind a coworker at the airport, apparently watching as the coworker types a corporate login password on a laptop.
detail.quizQuestion: A coworker at a coffee shop notices someone sitting unusually close, angling to view their laptop screen while they enter a password. What type of attack is occurring?

definition: The practice of installing an application onto a mobile device from a source other than the device's official, vetted app store, bypassing the store's security review and malware screening.
examContext: Know side loading as a mobile device vulnerability distinct from jailbreaking: it's the installation method that bypasses official app store vetting, which is why mobile device management policies commonly block installs from any source outside the approved store.
analogy: Like buying medication from an unlicensed street vendor instead of a pharmacy; nobody has checked that what's inside the package is actually safe.
relatedTerms: Jailbreaking, Supply chain attack, Zero-day

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's mobile device management policy blocks installation from any source except the approved corporate and official app stores, so when an employee tries to side load a cracked version of a paid app from a third-party website, the phone refuses the install and logs the attempt.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee downloads and installs an application directly from a third-party website instead of the official app store, bypassing the store's review process. What is this practice called?

items.name: Application
items.detail: Memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (TOCTOU) and malicious updates.

items.name: Operating system
items.detail: Unpatched or misconfigured OS components and services.

items.name: Web-based
items.detail: SQL injection, XSS and other flaws in web applications.

items.name: Hardware / firmware
items.detail: Flaws in firmware or silicon, plus end-of-life and legacy devices that can no longer be patched.

items.name: Virtualization
items.detail: VM escape (breaking out to the hypervisor or other VMs), resource reuse (data left in reassigned memory or storage), and VM sprawl.

items.name: Cloud-specific
items.detail: Misconfigured storage, over-permissive IAM roles, exposed APIs and weak tenant isolation.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Weaknesses introduced through a service provider, hardware provider or software provider.

items.name: Cryptographic
items.detail: Weak or outdated algorithms, short keys and poor key management.

items.name: Misconfiguration
items.detail: Open permissions, default settings and unnecessary services or protocols.

items.name: Mobile device
items.detail: Side loading and jailbreaking/rooting bypass the platform's security model.

items.name: Zero-day
items.detail: A flaw unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists yet.

definition: A component whose failure would stop the entire system or service because there is no redundancy or alternative path. Removing single points of failure is a core goal of high-availability design.
examContext: Seen with a lone firewall, a single internet link, a central automation server or one power feed. Fix with redundancy, clustering, load balancing and failover. Also a drawback of centralized automation.
analogy: The one bridge into town: if it collapses, nobody gets in or out.
relatedTerms: High availability, Redundancy, Failover, Fault tolerance, Load balancing

detail.practicalScenario: A company's only internet gateway router fails and every office loses connectivity. After the outage the team adds a second router and a second ISP link so one failure cannot take everything down.
detail.quizQuestion: A company's only internet gateway router fails and the whole office loses connectivity. What design weakness does this show?

items.name: Redundancy
items.detail: Duplicate components (disks, power supplies, links, servers) so a single failure does not stop service.

items.name: Fault tolerance
items.detail: The system keeps operating, with no interruption, when a component fails (RAID, dual power, clustering).

items.name: High availability
items.detail: Designing for maximum uptime (for example "five nines" = 99.999%), usually using redundancy, failover and load balancing.

items.name: Failover
items.detail: Switching automatically from a failed component to a standby.

items.name: Resilience
items.detail: The ability to absorb a disruption and recover quickly.

items.name: Scalability vs elasticity
items.detail: Scalability: the ability to handle growth. Elasticity: automatically adding and removing capacity as demand changes.

items.name: Single point of failure
items.detail: Any one component whose failure takes the whole service down. Redundancy exists to remove these.

variants.title: Automation and orchestration: benefits and drawbacks

items.name: Efficiency / time saving
items.detail: Routine work is done faster and with less manual effort.

items.name: Enforcing baselines
items.detail: Every system is configured the same way, every time.

items.name: Standard infrastructure configurations
items.detail: Consistent builds reduce errors and drift.

items.name: Scaling securely
items.detail: Security grows automatically with the environment.

items.name: Employee retention
items.detail: Staff spend less time on repetitive tasks.

items.name: Reaction time
items.detail: Machines respond to incidents in seconds.

items.name: Workforce multiplier
items.detail: A small team can do the work of a much larger one.

items.name: Drawbacks
items.detail: Complexity, cost, a single point of failure (a broken script breaks everything), technical debt, and ongoing supportability.

definition: An authentication scheme that allows a user to log in once with a single set of credentials and gain access to multiple independent applications or systems without re-authenticating for each one.
examContext: Know SSO improves user experience and centralizes authentication logging, but creates a single point of failure, since if the SSO credential is compromised, all connected systems are at risk; the exam often pairs this with MFA as a mitigation.
analogy: Like a single master key card that opens every door in an office building, so employees don't need a separate key for each room.
relatedTerms: Federation, Multifactor authentication, Authentication

detail.practicalScenario: Chen implements single sign-on across the company's email, HR portal, and file-sharing systems, so employees authenticate once in the morning and can move between all three applications without being prompted for credentials again.
detail.quizQuestion: Employees complain about having to log in separately to five different internal applications each day. Which solution would address this while centralizing authentication logs?

variants.title: SAML vs OAuth vs OpenID Connect vs Kerberos

items.name: SAML
items.detail: XML-based assertions passed between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP). Delivers authentication and authorization for browser SSO, mostly enterprise and B2B.

items.name: OAuth 2.0
items.detail: Delegated AUTHORIZATION: lets an app access resources at another service using an access token, without sharing your password ("allow this app to read your calendar"). Not authentication by itself.

items.name: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
items.detail: An AUTHENTICATION layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that returns an ID token (a JWT) saying who the user is. "Sign in with Google."

items.name: Kerberos
items.detail: Ticket-based SSO inside a Windows/Active Directory domain; a KDC issues tickets, with mutual authentication.

items.name: Roles
items.detail: The IdP authenticates the user and vouches for them; the SP / relying party trusts that assertion and grants access.

items.name: Trade-off of SSO
items.detail: One login reaches many apps, which is convenient, but a stolen SSO credential exposes all of them. Pair it with MFA.

definition: A physical assessment of a location, conducted before deploying wireless access points, that measures signal strength, interference, and coverage to determine optimal access point placement.
examContext: Know a site survey is performed before or during wireless network design to identify dead zones, interference sources, and ideal access point locations; it's commonly tested alongside heat maps as part of wireless deployment planning.
analogy: Like walking through a house with a signal meter before mounting any Wi-Fi routers, so you know exactly where the dead spots and walls that block signal are.
relatedTerms: Heat map

detail.practicalScenario: Priya walks through the new warehouse with a wireless scanning tool before installing any access points, mapping out areas where metal shelving blocks signal, and uses those findings to decide exactly where each access point needs to be mounted for full coverage.
detail.quizQuestion: Before installing wireless access points in a new office building, a technician walks the entire floor with signal-measuring equipment to identify interference sources and dead zones. What activity is the technician performing?

definition: Understanding the environment and threats around you, recognizing unusual people, requests or behavior, and knowing how to respond, such as noticing tailgating, shoulder surfing or a suspicious email.
examContext: A user-guidance topic in security awareness. It encourages reporting suspicious things instead of ignoring them.
analogy: Noticing the stranger in the hallway who is not wearing a badge.
relatedTerms: Security awareness training, Tailgating, Shoulder surfing, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: An employee notices a stranger without a badge following her toward the secure area. She stops, politely asks for credentials and reports the incident to security.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee notices an unbadged stranger following others through a secure door and reports it. Which security awareness concept is demonstrated?

items.name: Phishing campaigns
items.detail: Simulated phishing to teach users to recognize attacks and to measure click and report rates.

items.name: Reporting suspicious messages
items.detail: Give users an easy way to report (a report button), and respond to the reports.

items.name: Anomalous behavior recognition
items.detail: Recognize risky behavior (unsafe habits), unexpected behavior (out of pattern) and unintentional behavior (honest mistakes).

items.name: User guidance topics
items.detail: Policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threats, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, and hybrid/remote work.

items.name: Development and execution
items.detail: Create the content, deliver it (computer-based, in person, gamified), and keep it relevant.

items.name: Reporting and monitoring
items.detail: Initial training at onboarding, recurring refreshers, and tracking completion rates and metrics.

definition: A physical authentication token, something you have, embedded with a microprocessor chip that securely stores credentials or cryptographic certificates, used alongside a PIN for two-factor access to systems or facilities.
examContext: Know the Common Access Card and Personal Identity Verification card as classic government and military examples; smart cards are a something-you-have factor typically paired with a PIN for true MFA.
analogy: Like a hotel key card embedded with a chip that must be inserted and paired with a PIN at the safe inside the room, rather than a simple key that works alone.
relatedTerms: Multifactor authentication, Biometrics

detail.practicalScenario: Priya issues smart cards embedded with digital certificates to all employees, requiring them to insert the card into a reader and enter a PIN before they can log into any workstation, providing strong two-factor authentication for building and system access alike.
detail.quizQuestion: A government agency requires employees to insert a physical chip-embedded card and enter a PIN before accessing any workstation. What type of authentication factor does the card represent?

items.name: Something you know
items.detail: Knowledge: password, PIN, passphrase, security-question answers.

items.name: Something you have
items.detail: Possession: smart card, hardware token or security key, phone or authenticator app, certificate.

items.name: Something you are
items.detail: Inherence: biometrics such as fingerprint, iris, face, voice, vein.

items.name: Somewhere you are
items.detail: Location: GPS position, IP address or network location, geofencing.

items.name: Something you do
items.detail: Behavior: typing rhythm, gait, how you swipe or sign.

items.name: What counts as MFA
items.detail: Two or more DIFFERENT factor categories. A password plus a PIN is still single-factor (both are "know"), and a password plus a security question is not MFA.

definition: A social engineering attack delivered via SMS text messages that attempts to trick recipients into clicking malicious links or revealing information.
examContext: Exam tests smishing as the SMS or text-message variant of phishing, often involving fake delivery notifications or bank alerts.
analogy: Like a scam text claiming your package could not be delivered, hoping you tap the link without thinking.
relatedTerms: Phishing, Vishing, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Alex gets a text message claiming her bank account has been locked, with a link to a fake login page designed to steal her banking credentials.
detail.quizQuestion: Several employees receive a text message claiming to be from a parcel carrier, containing a link that leads to a credential-harvesting website. What is this attack called?

items.name: Phishing
items.detail: Mass, generic lures, usually email, that try to steal credentials or deliver malware.

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: A point-in-time image of a virtual machine, volume or file system that records its state so it can be rolled back quickly. Snapshots are fast and space-efficient but usually depend on the original storage, so they are not a substitute for real backups.
examContext: Handy for quick recovery before risky changes, but they are not offsite or independent of the source storage. Common with VMs and cloud volumes.
analogy: A save point in a video game: you can return to it quickly, but if the console breaks, the save goes with it.
relatedTerms: Backup, Replication, Backout plan, Virtualization

detail.practicalScenario: Before installing a risky update, an admin takes a snapshot of the VM. When the update breaks the application, he reverts to the snapshot in seconds.
detail.quizQuestion: Before a risky update, an admin captures a VM's state so it can be rolled back in seconds if the update fails. What did he create?

items.name: Full
items.detail: Copies everything. Slowest to take, but the fastest and simplest to restore (one set).

items.name: Incremental
items.detail: Copies only what changed since the LAST backup of any type. Fastest to take; slowest to restore (full plus every incremental, in order).

items.name: Differential
items.detail: Copies everything changed since the last FULL backup. Grows each day; restore needs the full plus the latest differential only.

items.name: Snapshot
items.detail: A point-in-time image of a VM or volume. Fast to take and roll back, but not a true backup if it lives on the same storage.

items.name: Replication
items.detail: Near-real-time copying to another system or site (synchronous or asynchronous). Improves availability but also copies corruption and deletions.

items.name: Journaling
items.detail: A running log of changes so a file system or database can replay or roll back to a consistent state after a crash.

items.name: Onsite vs offsite
items.detail: Onsite restores faster; offsite survives a site disaster. Keep both.

items.name: 3-2-1 rule
items.detail: Keep 3 copies, on 2 different media types, with 1 offsite (modern advice adds an offline or immutable copy against ransomware).

items.name: Protect the backups
items.detail: Encrypt them, test restores regularly, and keep at least one copy offline or immutable.

definition: The use of psychological manipulation to trick individuals into divulging confidential information or performing actions that compromise security.
examContext: Exam covers many social engineering subtypes and the underlying principles of persuasion, such as authority, urgency, scarcity, and social proof; expect you to identify the overarching category.
analogy: Like a con artist talking their way past a security guard instead of breaking down the door.
relatedTerms: Phishing, Pretexting, Vishing, Tailgating, Spear phishing

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's security awareness training teaches employees to recognize when a caller creates false urgency or authority to pressure them into bypassing normal verification steps.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker calls an employee pretending to be from IT, creating a sense of urgency to convince them to reveal their password over the phone. What broad category of attack does this represent?

items.name: Phishing
items.detail: Mass, generic lures, usually email, that try to steal credentials or deliver malware.

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

items.name: Authority
items.detail: People obey someone who appears to hold power (a CEO, an auditor, the police).

items.name: Intimidation
items.detail: Threats or pressure push a victim to comply ("your account will be closed").

items.name: Urgency / scarcity
items.detail: A deadline or limited supply stops people from thinking carefully.

items.name: Consensus / social proof
items.detail: People copy what others seem to be doing ("everyone else already completed this").

items.name: Familiarity / liking
items.detail: People help those they like or feel they know.

items.name: Trust
items.detail: Rapport built over time lowers suspicion.

items.name: Best defense
items.detail: Security awareness training, a no-exceptions verification process, and a culture where staff can safely say "let me check."

items.name: Phishing campaigns
items.detail: Simulated phishing to teach users to recognize attacks and to measure click and report rates.

items.name: Reporting suspicious messages
items.detail: Give users an easy way to report (a report button), and respond to the reports.

items.name: Anomalous behavior recognition
items.detail: Recognize risky behavior (unsafe habits), unexpected behavior (out of pattern) and unintentional behavior (honest mistakes).

items.name: User guidance topics
items.detail: Policies and handbooks, situational awareness, insider threats, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, and hybrid/remote work.

items.name: Development and execution
items.detail: Create the content, deliver it (computer-based, in person, gamified), and keep it relevant.

items.name: Reporting and monitoring
items.detail: Initial training at onboarding, recurring refreshers, and tracking completion rates and metrics.

definition: A targeted phishing attack directed at a specific individual or group, using personalized information to increase credibility.
examContext: Exam tests the distinction between generic phishing, which is mass and untargeted, and spear phishing, which is targeted and researched; watch for details like a named recipient or specific job reference.
analogy: Like a custom-crafted fake letter that mentions your actual boss's name and recent project to seem legitimate.
relatedTerms: Phishing, Whaling, Social engineering, Pretexting

detail.practicalScenario: Priya receives an email addressed by name, referencing her actual manager and a real ongoing project, asking her to urgently wire funds, a highly targeted attack crafted using information gathered about her specifically.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker researches an employee's role, manager's name, and recent projects, then crafts a highly personalized email to that one individual requesting a funds transfer. What type of attack is this?

items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.
