items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: Forging the identity of a source, such as an IP address, MAC address, email sender or caller ID, to impersonate a trusted party or hide the attacker's origin.
examContext: Common forms: IP spoofing (DDoS reflection), email spoofing in phishing (countered by SPF, DKIM and DMARC), MAC spoofing and caller ID spoofing. Ingress and egress filtering reduce IP spoofing.
analogy: Writing someone else's return address on an envelope.
relatedTerms: Phishing, ARP poisoning, DNS poisoning, SPF, DKIM, DMARC

detail.practicalScenario: An attacker sends emails that appear to come from the CEO's domain. Because the company published SPF, DKIM and DMARC records with a reject policy, receiving mail servers discard the forged messages.
detail.quizQuestion: Which combination of controls helps reduce spoofing of a company's email domain?

definition: Malware that covertly monitors and collects information about a user's activities, such as browsing habits or keystrokes, typically without consent.
examContext: Exam tests spyware as focused on surveillance and data collection rather than destruction; keyloggers are often categorized as a specific type of spyware.
analogy: Like a hidden camera secretly recording everything you do in your own home.
relatedTerms: Keylogger, Malware, Trojan horse

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's IT department discovers software secretly running on an executive's laptop that silently logs browsing history and sends it to an external server without the executive's knowledge.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee's laptop is found to be silently transmitting screenshots and browsing activity to a remote server without the user's knowledge or consent. What type of malware is responsible?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A downgrade attack by an on-path attacker who intercepts a user's initial HTTP request and keeps the victim on an unencrypted HTTP connection while speaking HTTPS to the real server, exposing everything the victim sends.
examContext: Mitigated by HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) and HSTS preload lists, plus users checking for HTTPS. Related to downgrade and on-path attacks.
analogy: A dishonest translator who talks to the foreign official in a secure room while keeping you in the open hallway.
relatedTerms: Downgrade attack, Man-in-the-middle attack, Perfect forward secrecy, Cipher suite

detail.practicalScenario: A user on public Wi-Fi types a site address without https. The attacker's device relays everything to the real site over HTTPS but shows the victim plain HTTP pages, capturing the password.
detail.quizQuestion: Which mechanism forces browsers to use HTTPS only and defeats SSL stripping?

definition: A documented, approved set of step-by-step instructions for performing a routine operation consistently and safely. In change management, SOPs describe how routine changes are carried out.
examContext: SOPs reduce errors and support audits and training. They are closely related to procedures and runbooks, and they define how a repeatable task is done the same way every time.
analogy: A recipe card the whole kitchen follows so every batch comes out the same.
relatedTerms: Security procedure, Change management, Runbook, Playbook

detail.practicalScenario: The operations team follows an SOP to deploy a standard server image: create the VM, apply the baseline, join the domain, register it in the CMDB and enable monitoring.
detail.quizQuestion: Which documented, repeatable set of instructions ensures staff perform routine tasks the same way every time?

items.name: Approval process
items.detail: A formal review (often by a Change Advisory Board) before any change is made.

items.name: Ownership
items.detail: A named person responsible for the change.

items.name: Stakeholders
items.detail: Everyone affected who must be informed or consulted.

items.name: Impact analysis
items.detail: What could break, and how risky is the change?

items.name: Test results
items.detail: Proof the change works in a non-production environment first.

items.name: Backout plan
items.detail: The steps to undo the change if it fails.

items.name: Maintenance window
items.detail: A scheduled time when changes are allowed so users are least affected.

items.name: Standard operating procedure
items.detail: The documented way routine changes are performed.

definition: A firewall technique that tracks the state of active network connections, such as TCP handshake status, and makes filtering decisions based on the context of traffic flows rather than just individual packets.
examContext: Know the contrast with simple packet filtering: stateful firewalls remember connection state so that return traffic for an established session is automatically permitted without needing a separate rule.
analogy: Like a receptionist who remembers which visitors already checked in, automatically letting them back through without re-verifying, unlike a guard who checks every person from scratch regardless of history.
relatedTerms: Firewall, Packet filtering

detail.practicalScenario: Sam replaces the company's old packet-filtering firewall with a stateful inspection firewall so that return traffic from legitimate outbound web requests is automatically allowed back in, without requiring a separate inbound rule for every possible response port.
detail.quizQuestion: A network engineer wants a firewall that automatically permits return traffic for established outbound connections without needing explicit inbound rules for each session. Which firewall technology provides this?

items.name: Packet filter (stateless)
items.detail: Checks each packet on its own against ACL rules (source/destination IP, port, protocol) with no memory of earlier packets. Fastest and simplest, but easiest to fool. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Stateful
items.detail: Tracks connection state in a state table, so return traffic for an established session is allowed automatically and unsolicited "replies" are dropped. Layers 3-4.

items.name: Application-layer / proxy
items.detail: Understands specific protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) and inspects the content. Acts as an intermediary, so it is slower but far deeper. Layer 7.

items.name: NGFW
items.detail: Next-generation firewall: stateful filtering plus deep packet inspection, application and user awareness, integrated IPS, TLS inspection and threat-intel feeds.

items.name: WAF
items.detail: Web application firewall: filters HTTP/HTTPS to block SQL injection, XSS and similar web attacks. Sits in front of web servers (Layer 7).

items.name: UTM
items.detail: Unified threat management: an all-in-one appliance (firewall, IPS, antivirus, web/content filter, VPN, spam filter). Simple for small sites, but a single point of failure.

items.name: Host-based vs network-based
items.detail: A host firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, iptables) protects one endpoint and can filter per application. A network firewall protects a whole segment.

items.name: Layer 4 vs Layer 7
items.detail: Layer 4 firewalls decide using IPs, ports and TCP/UDP state. Layer 7 firewalls decide using the application data itself (URLs, commands, file types).

definition: A method of reviewing an application's source code for security flaws and coding errors without actually executing the program, often performed automatically by scanning tools during development.
examContext: Know static analysis examines code at rest, before runtime, catching issues like hardcoded credentials or insecure function calls early in development; contrast this directly with dynamic code analysis, which tests the application while it's actually running.
analogy: Like proofreading a recipe on paper for mistakes before ever turning on the stove, catching errors in the instructions themselves rather than while the dish is cooking.
relatedTerms: Dynamic code analysis, Input validation, Sandboxing

detail.practicalScenario: Sam integrates a static code analysis tool into the development pipeline so that every code commit is automatically scanned for hardcoded passwords and known-insecure function calls before a human reviewer ever looks at it, catching several hardcoded API keys before they reached production.
detail.quizQuestion: A development team wants to automatically scan application source code for hardcoded secrets and insecure coding patterns before the application is ever compiled or run. What technique should they implement?

items.name: Development
items.detail: Where code is written. Least protected; should never contain real production data.

items.name: Test / QA
items.detail: Automated and manual testing. UAT (user acceptance testing) lets users confirm the software meets requirements.

items.name: Staging
items.detail: A production-like copy used for final validation before release.

items.name: Production
items.detail: The live system with real users and data and the strictest change control.

items.name: Static analysis (SAST)
items.detail: Examines source code or binaries WITHOUT running them.

items.name: Dynamic analysis (DAST)
items.detail: Tests the RUNNING application from the outside, such as with fuzzing and web scanners.

items.name: Code signing / SBOM
items.detail: Signing proves who published the code and that it is unaltered; a software bill of materials lists the components inside it.

definition: The practice of concealing a message, file, or data within another seemingly innocent file, such as hiding text inside an image, so its existence is not apparent.
examContext: Exam tests steganography as hiding the existence of data, as opposed to encryption, which scrambles data but does not hide that it exists.
analogy: Like writing a secret message in invisible ink inside an ordinary-looking postcard.
relatedTerms: Obfuscation, Exfiltration, Encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's data loss prevention tool flags an outbound image file that, upon closer analysis, contains an embedded hidden text file with proprietary source code concealed within its pixel data.
detail.quizQuestion: A forensic analyst discovers that an employee embedded a confidential spreadsheet's data inside the pixel data of an ordinary-looking vacation photo before emailing it externally. What technique was used to hide the data?

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Reversible with the right key. Protects confidentiality of data at rest and in transit.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: One-way. Used to verify integrity and store passwords; the original cannot be recovered.

items.name: Masking
items.detail: Replaces part of a value with placeholder characters (****-****-****-1234) for display, testing or training.

items.name: Tokenization
items.detail: Swaps a sensitive value for a random surrogate token; the real value lives only in a secured vault. Common for payment cards (shrinks PCI DSS scope).

items.name: Obfuscation
items.detail: Making data or code hard to understand (scrambling, renaming variables). Weak on its own: "security through obscurity."

items.name: Steganography
items.detail: Hides the very EXISTENCE of data inside another file such as an image or audio clip.

definition: A symmetric encryption algorithm that encrypts data one bit or byte at a time by combining it with a pseudorandom keystream, making it well-suited for continuous data streams like voice or video.
examContext: Know RC4 as a now largely deprecated example of a stream cipher, and that stream ciphers are typically faster but offer less error propagation protection than block ciphers.
analogy: Like a conveyor belt that encrypts each item individually as it passes by, rather than waiting to gather a full batch.
relatedTerms: Block cipher, Symmetric encryption, Cipher suite

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan's team evaluates encrypting a live video conferencing feed and chooses a stream cipher approach because it can encrypt the continuous flow of audio and video data in real time without waiting to fill fixed-size blocks.
detail.quizQuestion: An engineer needs to encrypt a continuous real-time voice call with minimal latency. Which cipher type is best suited for this use case?

items.name: DES
items.detail: 56-bit key, 64-bit block. Broken by brute force decades ago; obsolete. Know it only as the "weak legacy" answer.

items.name: 3DES
items.detail: Runs DES three times (up to 168-bit key, ~112 bits effective). Slow, 64-bit blocks make it vulnerable to birthday-style attacks; deprecated and being retired.

items.name: AES
items.detail: The standard. 128-bit block with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys. Fast, hardware-accelerated (AES-NI), and used everywhere: TLS, Wi-Fi (WPA2/3), disk encryption.

items.name: Blowfish
items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

definition: A subdivision of an IP network: a group of addresses that share the same network prefix, written in CIDR notation such as 192.168.1.0/24. Devices in the same subnet talk directly, while traffic to other subnets goes through a router or firewall.
examContext: Subnets keep broadcasts small and let you apply security controls between groups. Security+ expects you to read CIDR and masks (a /24 is 255.255.255.0 and gives 254 usable hosts), not to do heavy subnetting.
analogy: A neighborhood on a city map: neighbors can talk directly, but reaching another neighborhood means using the roads between them (a router).
relatedTerms: Subnet mask, CIDR, Default gateway, Network segmentation, VLAN, Router

detail.practicalScenario: A company gives each department its own subnet. A finance PC reaching an HR file server must go through the router, where an ACL decides whether the traffic is allowed.
detail.quizQuestion: Devices in two different subnets can communicate only through which kind of device?
quizOptions: A) A router or other Layer 3 device

definition: A 32-bit value that marks which part of an IPv4 address is the network and which part is the host, such as 255.255.255.0 (written /24). Devices use it to decide whether a destination is on the local subnet or must be sent to the default gateway.
examContext: Know the common masks: /8 is 255.0.0.0, /16 is 255.255.0.0, /24 is 255.255.255.0 and /30 is 255.255.255.252. A bigger prefix means a smaller network.
analogy: A stencil laid over the address that reveals which digits name the neighborhood and which name the house.
relatedTerms: Subnet, CIDR, VLSM, IP address, Default gateway

detail.practicalScenario: A host at 192.168.1.25 with the mask 255.255.255.0 wants to reach 192.168.1.80, which the mask shows is on its own subnet, so it sends the traffic directly. For 192.168.2.5 it uses the default gateway.
detail.quizQuestion: Which value tells a device which part of an IPv4 address identifies the network?

definition: An attack that targets vulnerabilities in a trusted third-party vendor, supplier, or software component to compromise the systems of their downstream customers.
examContext: Exam tests supply chain attacks with examples like compromised software updates or hardware tampering before delivery, a major real-world theme on SY0-701.
analogy: Like poisoning the water at the factory that bottles it, instead of attacking every store that sells the water.
relatedTerms: Watering hole attack, Threat actor, Vulnerability, Insider threat

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's organization discovers that a routine software update from a trusted third-party vendor had been tampered with at the source, silently installing a backdoor on every customer who applied the update.
detail.quizQuestion: A widely used IT management software vendor's update servers are compromised, causing malicious code to be pushed to thousands of the vendor's customers through a routine update. What type of attack is this?

variants.title: Common attack vectors and attack surfaces

items.name: Message-based
items.detail: Email, SMS and instant messaging carrying links, attachments or lures.

items.name: Image-based
items.detail: Malicious code or payloads hidden in image files (steganography) or malicious QR codes.

items.name: File-based
items.detail: Weaponized documents, PDFs, archives or macro-enabled Office files.

items.name: Voice call
items.detail: Vishing and pretext calls to the help desk.

items.name: Removable device
items.detail: USB drives dropped in a car park, or malicious cables.

items.name: Vulnerable software
items.detail: Unpatched client software (agent-based scanning sees it) or software that cannot host an agent (agentless scanning).

items.name: Unsupported systems
items.detail: End-of-life and end-of-support software receives no security patches.

items.name: Unsecure networks
items.detail: Open or poorly protected Wi-Fi, wired networks, and Bluetooth.

items.name: Open service ports
items.detail: Unneeded listening services that give attackers something to connect to.

items.name: Default credentials
items.detail: Factory usernames and passwords left unchanged.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Compromise through MSPs, vendors, suppliers, or tampered hardware and software updates.

items.name: Vendor selection
items.detail: Perform due diligence, check for conflicts of interest, and review financial stability and security posture.

items.name: Vendor assessment
items.detail: Penetration testing, a right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments and supply chain analysis.

items.name: Questionnaires
items.detail: Standardized security questionnaires the vendor completes.

items.name: Agreements
items.detail: SLA, MSA, SOW, NDA and similar contracts that set expectations and responsibilities.

items.name: Vendor monitoring
items.detail: Continual review of the vendor's performance, security and compliance throughout the relationship.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: Written limits on what testing a third party may do.

definition: A network device that connects devices on the same network and forwards Ethernet frames only to the port where the destination MAC address lives, using a MAC address table it learns from the traffic it sees. It works at Layer 2, and a Layer 3 switch can also route.
examContext: Switch means Layer 2 and forwarding by MAC address. Know the attacks and defenses: MAC flooding and port security, ARP poisoning and Dynamic ARP Inspection, rogue DHCP servers and DHCP snooping, VLAN hopping, and spanning tree attacks stopped by BPDU Guard. Contrast it with a hub (repeats to every port) and a router (uses IP addresses between networks).
analogy: A receptionist who knows which desk everyone sits at and walks each note straight to the right person.
relatedTerms: Hub, Router, Layer 3 switch, MAC address, Port security, MAC flooding, VLAN

detail.practicalScenario: An office connects 24 PCs to one switch. When PC1 sends a file to PC2, the switch looks up PC2's MAC address in its table and sends the frames only out of PC2's port, so the other 22 PCs never see the traffic.
detail.quizQuestion: Which device forwards frames to a specific port by looking up the destination MAC address in a table it has learned?

definition: An encryption method that uses a single shared secret key for both encrypting and decrypting data, offering high speed but requiring a secure way to distribute the key to all parties.
examContext: Exam questions often test whether you can identify symmetric algorithms such as AES and 3DES versus asymmetric ones, and the key-distribution problem is a classic scenario-based question.
analogy: Like a single house key that both locks and unlocks the same front door, so anyone with a copy can get in.
relatedTerms: Asymmetric encryption, Key exchange, Block cipher, Stream cipher, Hybrid encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Sam uses AES-256 to encrypt a large database backup before it is transferred to an offsite storage facility, because symmetric encryption is fast enough to handle the large file size without noticeable delay.
detail.quizQuestion: An administrator needs to encrypt a 500GB database backup quickly before transferring it offsite. Which type of encryption is most appropriate for this bulk operation?
