items.detail: 64-bit block, variable key (32-448 bits). Fast and unpatented; the basis of bcrypt. Its small block size limits it for big data.

items.name: Twofish
items.detail: 128-bit block, keys up to 256 bits. AES finalist, open and royalty-free; Blowfish's successor by the same designer.

items.name: RC4
items.detail: Stream cipher. Statistical biases made it unsafe; it caused WEP's failure and is now prohibited in TLS.

items.name: ChaCha20
items.detail: Modern stream cipher, paired with Poly1305 for authentication. Very fast in software, so it is preferred on devices without AES hardware (phones); supported in TLS 1.3.

items.name: IDEA
items.detail: 128-bit key, 64-bit block. Used by early PGP; patent-encumbered historically and largely replaced by AES.

items.name: Symmetric
items.detail: One shared secret key encrypts and decrypts. Very fast, so it does the bulk data encryption. Weakness: securely sharing the key. N users need N(N-1)/2 keys.

items.name: Asymmetric
items.detail: A mathematically linked public/private key pair. Slow, so it is used for key exchange, digital signatures and certificates. Solves key distribution. N users need only 2N keys.

items.name: Hybrid
items.detail: Asymmetric crypto securely exchanges a random symmetric session key, then symmetric crypto encrypts the actual data. This is how TLS and most real systems work.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: No key (unless it is an HMAC) and no way back: a one-way function giving a fixed-length digest. Used for integrity and password storage, not for confidentiality.

definition: A standard protocol (UDP 514, or TCP with TLS) and message format for sending log events from devices and servers to a central log collector, with facility and severity levels.
examContext: Used by network gear and Linux to forward logs to a SIEM. Plain syslog over UDP is unencrypted and unreliable, so use TLS where possible. Severity runs from 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug).
analogy: A postal service that carries every device's incident reports to one office.
relatedTerms: Log aggregation, SIEM, SNMP, NetFlow

detail.practicalScenario: Routers, switches and firewalls forward events to a central syslog server, which feeds the SIEM. When a switch reports repeated authentication failures, analysts see it alongside logs from other devices.
detail.quizQuestion: Which protocol do network devices commonly use to send log messages to a central collector?

variants.title: Log and data sources for investigations

items.name: Firewall logs
items.detail: Allowed and denied connections, source/destination IPs and ports.

items.name: Application logs
items.detail: Application events, errors and user actions.

items.name: Endpoint logs
items.detail: Events from EDR or the host: process starts, file and registry changes.

items.name: OS-specific security logs
items.detail: Windows Event Log (Security, System, Application) or Linux auth.log and syslog: logons, privilege use and policy changes.

items.name: IDS / IPS logs
items.detail: Detected and blocked attack signatures and anomalies.

items.name: Network logs
items.detail: Router and switch logs, NetFlow, DNS and proxy logs.

items.name: Metadata
items.detail: Data about data: file timestamps, EXIF in photos, email headers.

items.name: Vulnerability scans, automated reports, dashboards
items.detail: Aggregated views that spot trends and help prioritize.

items.name: Packet captures
items.detail: A full copy of traffic for deep analysis (PCAP files).

definition: A discussion-based incident response exercise in which stakeholders walk through a simulated scenario verbally, around a table, to evaluate and improve plans, roles, and decision-making without actually activating systems or performing hands-on technical actions.
examContext: Know a tabletop exercise is discussion-based only (no systems touched), making it the lowest-cost, lowest-disruption way to test and train on an incident response plan, compared to a full simulation or live exercise.
analogy: Like a fire drill where everyone sits in a conference room and talks through what they'd do if the alarm went off, instead of actually evacuating the building.
relatedTerms: Incident response, Business continuity, Disaster recovery, Change management

detail.practicalScenario: Maria facilitates a tabletop exercise where the incident response team talks through how they would handle a simulated ransomware outbreak, discovers that nobody actually knew who had authority to make the payment decision, and updates the incident response plan to assign that role clearly before a real attack happens.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to test its incident response plan by having key stakeholders discuss their roles and decisions during a simulated breach scenario, without taking any systems offline or performing technical actions. What type of exercise is this?

definition: The physical security breach of following an authorized person through a secured door or checkpoint without providing separate credentials.
examContext: Exam distinguishes tailgating, which happens without the authorized person's consent or knowledge, from piggybacking, which happens with consent; mitigations include mantraps and security guards.
analogy: Like slipping through a closing elevator door right behind someone who just badged in.
relatedTerms: Social engineering, Pretexting, Shoulder surfing

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's badge-access door closes slowly enough that an unauthorized visitor slips in right behind him without presenting any credentials, exploiting simple physical proximity rather than any technical flaw.
detail.quizQuestion: A visitor without a badge follows closely behind an employee through a secure badge-access door, entering without ever presenting credentials. What is this called?

items.name: Authority
items.detail: People obey someone who appears to hold power (a CEO, an auditor, the police).

items.name: Intimidation
items.detail: Threats or pressure push a victim to comply ("your account will be closed").

items.name: Urgency / scarcity
items.detail: A deadline or limited supply stops people from thinking carefully.

items.name: Consensus / social proof
items.detail: People copy what others seem to be doing ("everyone else already completed this").

items.name: Familiarity / liking
items.detail: People help those they like or feel they know.

items.name: Trust
items.detail: Rapport built over time lowers suspicion.

items.name: Best defense
items.detail: Security awareness training, a no-exceptions verification process, and a culture where staff can safely say "let me check."

definition: A control implemented with technology (hardware, software or firmware) to protect systems and data, such as firewalls, encryption, antivirus, access control lists, multifactor authentication and IDS/IPS. Also called a logical control.
examContext: Technical controls are often paired with a type: a firewall is preventive, an IDS is detective, and automated restoration from backup is corrective. If the thing doing the protecting is a machine or code, the category is technical.
analogy: The automatic sprinkler system and smoke detector of the digital world: machinery doing the protecting without a person having to act.
relatedTerms: Control categories, Preventive control, Detective control, Managerial control

detail.practicalScenario: The network team deploys an intrusion prevention system, enables full-disk encryption on laptops and enforces MFA on the VPN. All three are technical controls because technology performs the protection.
detail.quizQuestion: Which of the following is an example of a TECHNICAL control?
quizOptions: B) A badge reader on the server-room door
C) A signed acceptable use policy
D) A background check on new hires

variants.title: Control categories (WHAT the control is made of)

items.name: Technical
items.detail: Implemented with technology: firewalls, encryption, antivirus, ACLs, MFA, IDS/IPS.

items.name: Managerial (administrative)
items.detail: Policies, risk assessments, security planning and oversight: the "paperwork" that governs how security is managed.

items.name: Operational
items.detail: Carried out day to day by PEOPLE: security awareness training, guards, change and patch procedures, backups performed by staff.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tangible barriers and devices: locks, fences, bollards, cameras, badge readers, vestibules, lighting.

items.name: Tip
items.detail: The category describes what it is or who runs it. The TYPE (preventive, detective and so on) describes what it does. One control has both: a firewall is a technical, preventive control.

definition: The accumulated cost of shortcuts, quick fixes and outdated components in code or infrastructure that must eventually be repaid through rework. In security it expands the attack surface and makes patching and automation harder.
examContext: Listed as a drawback of automation and orchestration: poorly maintained scripts and ad-hoc integrations become technical debt, alongside complexity, cost and single point of failure.
analogy: Putting off home repairs: it feels free at first, but the bill keeps growing with interest.
relatedTerms: Single point of failure, Change management, Patch management, Attack surface

detail.practicalScenario: A team patched problems with undocumented scripts for years instead of fixing the underlying design. When a critical update arrives, nobody understands the scripts, so upgrades are slow and risky.
detail.quizQuestion: A team patches problems with undocumented scripts instead of fixing the underlying design, making future upgrades riskier and costlier. What is this called?

variants.title: Change management: technical implications and documentation

items.name: Allow lists / deny lists
items.detail: Changes may require editing the lists of approved or blocked applications, IPs or sites.

items.name: Restricted activities
items.detail: Some actions may be forbidden during a change window or freeze.

items.name: Downtime
items.detail: Planned outages that must be communicated.

items.name: Service / application restart
items.detail: A restart may be required for the change to take effect and can interrupt users.

items.name: Legacy applications
items.detail: Old software may break or not be supported after a change.

items.name: Dependencies
items.detail: Other systems and services that rely on the thing being changed.

items.name: Documentation
items.detail: Update network diagrams, policies and procedures after the change.

items.name: Version control
items.detail: Track every version of configurations and code so you can see what changed, who changed it, and roll back.

variants.title: Automation and orchestration: benefits and drawbacks

items.name: Efficiency / time saving
items.detail: Routine work is done faster and with less manual effort.

items.name: Enforcing baselines
items.detail: Every system is configured the same way, every time.

items.name: Standard infrastructure configurations
items.detail: Consistent builds reduce errors and drift.

items.name: Scaling securely
items.detail: Security grows automatically with the environment.

items.name: Employee retention
items.detail: Staff spend less time on repetitive tasks.

items.name: Reaction time
items.detail: Machines respond to incidents in seconds.

items.name: Workforce multiplier
items.detail: A small team can do the work of a much larger one.

items.name: Drawbacks
items.detail: Complexity, cost, a single point of failure (a broken script breaks everything), technical debt, and ongoing supportability.

definition: Any circumstance, event, or actor with the potential to cause harm to an asset by exploiting a vulnerability.
examContext: Exam tests the risk formula concept of risk being a function of threat and vulnerability; be ready to identify which element of a scenario is the threat versus the weakness it targets.
analogy: Like a storm that could damage your house, which is the potential danger, separate from the house's weak roof.
relatedTerms: Threat actor, Vulnerability, Risk, Advanced persistent threat

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's risk assessment lists ransomware campaigns targeting healthcare organizations as a threat facing the hospital, independent of whether the hospital's systems are currently vulnerable to it.
detail.quizQuestion: A risk assessment lists nation-state espionage groups targeting defense contractors as a potential danger to the company, separate from any specific technical weakness. What category does this entry represent?

definition: An individual or group responsible for carrying out, or having the potential to carry out, an attack against an organization's systems.
examContext: Exam tests classification of threat actor types, such as nation-state, hacktivist, organized crime, insider, and script kiddie, along with their typical motivations and sophistication levels.
analogy: Like naming the specific burglar, rather than just describing that a burglary could happen.
relatedTerms: Insider threat, Advanced persistent threat, Threat, Vulnerability

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's threat intelligence team identifies that a recent attack pattern matches the tactics of a known organized crime group rather than a nation-state actor, helping prioritize the incident response.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team attributes a sophisticated, well-funded, multi-year intrusion to a government-sponsored group rather than a lone hacker. Which term describes the entity behind the attack?

items.name: Nation-state
items.detail: Government-backed. Very high funding and sophistication, with patient long-term (APT) campaigns for espionage, sabotage and geopolitical goals.

items.name: Organized crime
items.detail: Structured criminal groups with high resources, driven by PROFIT: ransomware, fraud, theft and extortion.

items.name: Hacktivist
items.detail: Moderate skills, driven by ideology or politics. Typical acts: DDoS, website defacement, doxing and data leaks.

items.name: Unskilled attacker (script kiddie)
items.detail: Low skill and low resources. Runs pre-made tools and scripts for curiosity, bragging rights or chaos.

items.name: Insider threat
items.detail: An employee, contractor or partner with legitimate access. INTERNAL, and either malicious (revenge, profit) or unintentional (mistakes, negligence).

items.name: Shadow IT
items.detail: Staff using unapproved apps, devices or cloud services. Rarely malicious, but it creates unmanaged risk.

items.name: Attributes that separate actors
items.detail: Internal vs external; resources and funding (low to high); level of sophistication and capability (low to high).

items.name: Financial gain
items.detail: Ransom, fraud, theft of payment data or credentials to sell. The most common motive; organized crime.

items.name: Data exfiltration
items.detail: Stealing sensitive data to sell, leak or use for leverage.

items.name: Espionage
items.detail: Stealing government or corporate secrets. Nation-states and competitors.

items.name: Service disruption
items.detail: Taking systems offline (DDoS, wipers) to hurt a target or demand payment.

items.name: Blackmail
items.detail: Threatening to expose stolen or embarrassing data unless paid.

items.name: Philosophical / political beliefs
items.detail: Ideology-driven attacks. Hacktivists.

items.name: Ethical
items.detail: Authorized testing or responsible disclosure by "white hat" researchers and bug-bounty hunters.

items.name: Revenge
items.detail: Retaliation, classically a disgruntled insider.

items.name: Disruption / chaos
items.detail: Causing havoc for its own sake or for notoriety, often unskilled attackers.

items.name: War / geopolitical
items.detail: Cyber operations supporting military or state conflict.

definition: A proactive security practice where analysts actively search through networks and systems to detect threats that have evaded existing automated security tools, rather than waiting for an alert to be triggered.
examContext: Know threat hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven, often following an assume-breach mindset, contrasted with reactive alert-based monitoring; it often uses threat intelligence and indicators of compromise as starting hypotheses.
analogy: Like a detective who proactively looks for clues of a crime that hasn't been reported yet, rather than waiting for someone to call 911.
relatedTerms: Threat intelligence, Indicator of compromise, Blue team

detail.practicalScenario: Maria's threat hunting team forms a hypothesis that attackers may be using legitimate admin tools to move laterally, then proactively searches endpoint logs for unusual PowerShell activity and discovers a previously undetected intrusion that automated alerts had missed.
detail.quizQuestion: A security analyst proactively searches system logs for subtle signs of compromise based on a hypothesis, without waiting for an automated alert to fire. What activity is this?

items.name: Account lockout
items.detail: Many failed logins from one account or source suggest brute force or spraying.

items.name: Concurrent session usage
items.detail: The same account logged in from several places or devices at once.

items.name: Impossible travel
items.detail: Logins from locations too far apart for the elapsed time, suggesting stolen credentials.

items.name: Blocked content
items.detail: Spikes of blocked connections or filtered downloads, which can reveal malware phoning home or users hitting malicious sites.

items.name: Resource consumption
items.detail: Unexplained CPU, memory, disk or bandwidth use, such as cryptojacking or data exfiltration.

items.name: Resource inaccessibility
items.detail: Services, files or systems suddenly unavailable: DoS, ransomware or a wiper.

items.name: Out-of-cycle logging
items.detail: Log entries or activity at unusual times, such as a batch job or admin login at 3 a.m.

items.name: Missing logs
items.detail: Gaps or deleted logs, a sign that an attacker is covering their tracks.

items.name: Published / documented
items.detail: Known IoCs and attack patterns from threat intelligence, such as a documented IP, hash or domain.

definition: Evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging threats, including threat actor tactics, techniques, indicators, and motivations, that organizations collect and analyze to inform proactive security decisions.
examContext: Know sources include open-source intelligence, closed or commercial feeds, and information-sharing organizations such as ISACs; the exam may test identifying threat intelligence as the input that drives threat hunting and indicator-of-compromise detection.
analogy: Like a weather forecast compiled from many data sources that helps you prepare for a storm before it actually hits, rather than reacting after you're already soaked.
relatedTerms: Indicator of compromise, Threat hunting, Threat actor

detail.practicalScenario: Sam subscribes the organization to an industry ISAC threat intelligence feed, which provides early warning about a new ransomware campaign's indicators, allowing his team to proactively block the associated malicious IP addresses before any attack occurs.
detail.quizQuestion: An organization wants to proactively learn about emerging attacker tactics and indicators before those threats target its own network. What should it subscribe to?

items.name: Open-source (OSINT)
items.detail: Freely available: government advisories, vendor blogs, social media, paste sites, public feeds.

items.name: Proprietary / third-party
items.detail: Paid commercial feeds and research services, often more curated and timely.

items.name: Information-sharing organizations
items.detail: Industry communities such as ISACs and the Automated Indicator Sharing (AIS) service, which share indicators among members.

items.name: Dark web
items.detail: Hidden forums and markets where stolen credentials and exploits are traded; monitoring them gives early warning of leaks.

items.name: Responsible disclosure program
items.detail: A published, safe way for researchers to report a vulnerability privately so it can be fixed before it is public.

items.name: Bug bounty program
items.detail: A responsible-disclosure program that PAYS researchers for valid findings.

variants.title: MITRE ATT&CK vs Kill Chain vs Diamond Model

items.name: MITRE ATT&CK
items.detail: A knowledge base of real-world adversary TACTICS (the goal, such as persistence) and TECHNIQUES (how they do it), arranged as a matrix. Used for detection engineering and red/purple teaming.

items.name: Cyber Kill Chain
items.detail: Lockheed Martin's seven stages: Reconnaissance, Weaponization, Delivery, Exploitation, Installation, Command and Control, Actions on Objectives. Stop the attacker at ANY stage to break the chain.

items.name: Diamond Model
items.detail: Analyzes an intrusion through four linked features: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure and Victim.

items.name: TTPs / IoCs
items.detail: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures describe HOW an adversary behaves. Indicators of Compromise are the artifacts they leave (hashes, IPs, domains).

definition: A zero trust control-plane principle of limiting the number of resources, paths, and privileges any single subject can reach, shrinking the blast radius an attacker could exploit if that subject were compromised.
examContext: Listed as a control-plane element of zero trust; the exam frames this as the underlying reason for microsegmentation and least privilege, since it minimizes how far an attacker can move after an initial compromise.
analogy: Like dividing a submarine into watertight compartments so a single hull breach floods only one small section instead of sinking the whole ship.
relatedTerms: Zero trust, Microsegmentation, Least privilege, Network segmentation, Lateral movement

detail.practicalScenario: Maria redesigns network access policies so that a compromised marketing laptop can only ever reach the marketing file share, drastically reducing the number of systems an attacker could pivot to if that single account were breached.
detail.quizQuestion: A company restructures access policies so that every account and device can only reach the small set of resources it specifically needs, limiting how far an attacker could move after any single compromise. This directly supports which zero trust principle?

items.name: Segmentation
items.detail: Split the network so a compromise cannot spread freely.

items.name: Access control (ACLs and permissions)
items.detail: Restrict who and what can reach a resource.

items.name: Application allow list
items.detail: Only approved programs may run; everything else is blocked by default.

items.name: Isolation
items.detail: Separate or quarantine a risky or infected system from the rest of the environment.

items.name: Patching
items.detail: Fix known vulnerabilities.

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Protect data confidentiality at rest and in transit.

items.name: Monitoring
items.detail: Detect problems early through logging, SIEM and alerts.

items.name: Least privilege
items.detail: Grant only the access needed to do the job.

items.name: Configuration enforcement
items.detail: Automatically keep systems in line with the secure baseline.

items.name: Decommissioning
items.detail: Securely retire systems that are no longer needed, wiping data.

definition: The three messages (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) that establish a TCP connection before any data is sent. A SYN flood abuses it by sending many SYN packets and never completing the handshake, exhausting the server's resources.
examContext: Know the order SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, and that UDP has no handshake. Defenses against SYN floods: SYN cookies, rate limiting, shorter timeouts, and firewalls or an IPS in front of the server.
analogy: Opening a phone call: "Hello?" ... "Hello, I can hear you." ... "Great, let's talk."
relatedTerms: TCP, UDP, DoS, DDoS, Stateful inspection

detail.practicalScenario: A web server becomes unresponsive. Logs show thousands of connection attempts that sent a SYN but never replied to the server's SYN-ACK, so the server is holding half-open connections. Enabling SYN cookies restores service.
detail.quizQuestion: Which sequence of messages establishes a TCP connection?

definition: An access control that permits logins or resource use only during defined hours or days, such as business hours, and blocks activity outside them.
examContext: A rule-based control that reduces exposure to off-hours attacks. It may conflict with on-call staff, so exceptions need to be managed.
analogy: A building whose doors only unlock during opening hours.
relatedTerms: Rule-based access control, Least privilege, Out-of-cycle logging, Account lockout

detail.practicalScenario: A bank limits teller accounts to 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays. When a stolen teller credential is used at 2 a.m., the system denies the login and raises an alert.
detail.quizQuestion: A company allows its payroll accounts to log in only on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Which access control is this?

definition: A data protection method that replaces sensitive data, such as a credit card number, with a non-sensitive placeholder token that has no exploitable value, while the original data is stored securely in a separate token vault.
examContext: SY0-701 distinguishes tokenization from encryption and hashing, since the token has no mathematical relationship to the original data and cannot be reversed without access to the vault; common in PCI DSS compliance scenarios.
analogy: Like a coat-check ticket, the ticket itself is worthless to a thief, but it can be exchanged for your coat at the counter that holds the real item.
relatedTerms: Data masking, Encryption

detail.practicalScenario: Alex implements tokenization in the payment processing system so that credit card numbers are replaced with random tokens in the application database, meaning a breach of that database would expose no usable card data.
detail.quizQuestion: A retailer wants to reduce PCI DSS compliance scope by ensuring that stored transaction records contain no usable credit card numbers, even if the database is breached. Which technique best accomplishes this?

items.name: Encryption
items.detail: Reversible with the right key. Protects confidentiality of data at rest and in transit.

items.name: Hashing
items.detail: One-way. Used to verify integrity and store passwords; the original cannot be recovered.

items.name: Masking
items.detail: Replaces part of a value with placeholder characters (****-****-****-1234) for display, testing or training.

items.name: Tokenization
items.detail: Swaps a sensitive value for a random surrogate token; the real value lives only in a secured vault. Common for payment cards (shrinks PCI DSS scope).

items.name: Obfuscation
items.detail: Making data or code hard to understand (scrambling, renaming variables). Weak on its own: "security through obscurity."

items.name: Steganography
items.detail: Hides the very EXISTENCE of data inside another file such as an image or audio clip.

definition: Confidential business information that gives a company a competitive advantage because it is kept secret, such as a formula, process or customer list. Protection depends on the company actively keeping it confidential.
examContext: Unlike patents (public and time-limited), trade secrets have no registration and last as long as they stay secret. A leak can destroy the protection, so NDAs, least privilege and DLP matter.
analogy: The secret recipe locked in the restaurant's safe.
relatedTerms: Intellectual property, Data classification, Data loss prevention, NDA

detail.practicalScenario: A beverage company keeps its exact formula in a restricted vault, limits access to a handful of staff and requires NDAs. The formula is valuable precisely because competitors do not know it.
detail.quizQuestion: A beverage company never publishes its exact formula and guards it with strict access controls and NDAs. What type of data is the formula?

items.name: Public
items.detail: Safe to disclose; no harm.

items.name: Private / internal
items.detail: For internal use only.

items.name: Sensitive
items.detail: Disclosure could cause harm or embarrassment.

items.name: Confidential
items.detail: Disclosure would cause serious harm; protected by contract or law.

items.name: Restricted
items.detail: The most tightly controlled, with very limited access.

items.name: Critical
items.detail: Essential to operations; loss or alteration would be severe.

items.name: Government scheme
items.detail: Unclassified, then Confidential, Secret and Top Secret, in rising order of damage if disclosed.

items.name: Data types
items.detail: Regulated (PII, PHI, payment data), trade secrets, intellectual property, legal information and financial information. Data may be human-readable or non-human-readable (binary, encoded).

definition: Malware disguised as legitimate or desirable software that tricks users into installing it, often delivering a hidden malicious payload.
examContext: Exam tests trojans as relying on deception, appearing useful or legitimate, rather than self-replication; a common vector for installing backdoors or spyware.
analogy: Like the mythological wooden horse, which looks like a harmless gift but hides attackers inside.
relatedTerms: Backdoor, Malware, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan downloads what appears to be a free PDF converter tool from an untrusted website, not realizing it secretly installs a backdoor that gives attackers remote access to his laptop.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee downloads a free video converter utility from an unofficial website, and it later turns out to have secretly installed a remote access tool alongside the advertised program. What type of malware is this?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A switch port that carries traffic for multiple VLANs at once by adding an 802.1Q tag to each frame. It is used between switches or toward a router or firewall, while an access port carries a single VLAN without a tag.
examContext: VLAN hopping attacks aim to turn an access port into a trunk (switch spoofing) or to abuse the native VLAN (double tagging). Defenses: set user ports to access, disable trunk negotiation (DTP), move the native VLAN away from VLAN 1 and prune the VLANs a trunk carries.
analogy: A multi-lane highway between two cities where each car carries a tag saying which neighborhood it belongs to.
relatedTerms: VLAN, VLAN hopping, Network segmentation, Switch

detail.practicalScenario: Two switches are joined by a trunk that carries the staff, guest and server VLANs. Each frame carries a VLAN tag, so the switch at the other end delivers it into the right VLAN.
detail.quizQuestion: Which type of switch port carries traffic for multiple VLANs by using 802.1Q tags?

definition: A technique in which an attacker registers a domain name that is a common misspelling or slight variation of a legitimate website's domain, hoping to catch users who mistype the URL and lure them to a malicious site.
examContext: The exam tests recognizing typosquatting as domain-based deception, such as a single swapped or doubled letter, used to deliver malware or harvest credentials, distinct from brand impersonation, which can occur without owning a lookalike domain at all.
analogy: Like opening a store right next door with an almost identical sign, hoping customers wander in by mistake.
relatedTerms: Brand impersonation, Phishing, Social engineering

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's security team discovers that an attacker registered a near-identical misspelling of a legitimate vendor's domain and used it to host a fake login page targeting employees who mistype the real address.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker registers a domain that is a one-letter misspelling of a popular streaming service's real URL, hoping to catch users who mistype it, then serves them a fake login page. What is this technique called?

items.name: Phishing
items.detail: Mass, generic lures, usually email, that try to steal credentials or deliver malware.

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: A penetration test (black box) in which the tester starts with no prior information about the target and must perform reconnaissance like an external attacker.
examContext: The most realistic but slowest and most expensive. The findings reflect what an outsider could discover.
analogy: An inspector who walks up to the building with no keys or plans.
relatedTerms: Known environment, Partially known environment, Penetration testing, Active reconnaissance, Passive reconnaissance

detail.practicalScenario: The testers are given only the company name. They begin with public research and scanning to discover what is exposed, exactly as a real external attacker would.
detail.quizQuestion: A pentest team starts with only the company's name and must discover everything else itself. Which type of test is this?

items.name: Known environment (white box)
items.detail: The tester receives full information (network diagrams, source code, credentials). Fast and thorough; resembles an insider or post-breach scenario.

items.name: Partially known (gray box)
items.detail: Limited information, such as a user-level account or part of the architecture. A balance of realism and efficiency.

items.name: Unknown environment (black box)
items.detail: No prior information; the tester starts like an outside attacker and must do reconnaissance first. Most realistic, but slowest and costliest.

items.name: Offensive / defensive / integrated
items.detail: Offensive = red team attacks. Defensive = blue team detects and responds. Integrated (purple) = both collaborate and share findings.

items.name: Physical
items.detail: Tests locks, badges, tailgating and cameras by actually trying to get in.

items.name: Passive reconnaissance
items.detail: Gathers information WITHOUT touching the target: OSINT, WHOIS, DNS records, social media, job postings, Shodan. Hard to detect.

items.name: Active reconnaissance
items.detail: Interacts directly with the target: port scans, ping sweeps, banner grabbing. Detectable.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: The written authorization: scope, timing, allowed techniques, contacts and escalation. Never test without it.

items.name: Typical flow
items.detail: Planning and rules of engagement, reconnaissance, scanning and enumeration, exploitation, post-exploitation (persistence, pivoting), reporting and clean-up.

definition: A low-skill attacker, often called a script kiddie, who relies on pre-made tools, scripts and exploits written by others, usually for curiosity, bragging rights or chaos rather than a sophisticated goal.
examContext: Lowest sophistication and resources. These attacks tend to be noisy and easy to detect, but automated tools can still do real damage, so keep systems patched against known exploits.
analogy: Someone who buys a lock-pick set online and tries it on random doors without understanding how locks work.
relatedTerms: Threat actor, Hacktivist, Organized crime, Exploit

detail.practicalScenario: A teenager downloads a ready-made DDoS tool and points it at a school website just to see if it works. He did not write the tool and has no deeper plan.
detail.quizQuestion: A teenager uses a downloaded attack tool he does not understand to take down a small website for fun. What is the BEST classification of this actor?

definition: Evaluating a supplier's security posture and risk before and during the relationship using questionnaires, penetration test results, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments, supply chain analysis and the right to audit.
examContext: Part of third-party risk management along with vendor selection (due diligence, conflict of interest), agreements and ongoing monitoring.
analogy: Checking a contractor's references and licenses before letting them into your house.
relatedTerms: Right-to-audit clause, Due diligence, Supply chain attack, Conflict of interest

detail.practicalScenario: Before signing with a payroll provider, the company sends a security questionnaire, reviews its SOC 2 report and asks for penetration test results. It then monitors the vendor throughout the contract.
detail.quizQuestion: A company reviews a supplier's questionnaire answers, SOC 2 report and penetration test results before signing a contract. Which activity is this?

items.name: Vendor selection
items.detail: Perform due diligence, check for conflicts of interest, and review financial stability and security posture.

items.name: Vendor assessment
items.detail: Penetration testing, a right-to-audit clause, evidence of internal audits, independent assessments and supply chain analysis.

items.name: Questionnaires
items.detail: Standardized security questionnaires the vendor completes.

items.name: Agreements
items.detail: SLA, MSA, SOW, NDA and similar contracts that set expectations and responsibilities.

items.name: Vendor monitoring
items.detail: Continual review of the vendor's performance, security and compliance throughout the relationship.

items.name: Rules of engagement
items.detail: Written limits on what testing a third party may do.

definition: A system that tracks and stores every change to files such as source code, configurations and documentation, recording who changed what and when so changes can be compared, audited and rolled back.
examContext: Supports change management, secure development (Git) and recovery from bad changes. Protect repositories from leaked credentials and unauthorized commits, and require reviews for changes.
analogy: The undo history of a document that never forgets who made each edit.
relatedTerms: Change management, Backout plan, IaC, Baseline configuration

detail.practicalScenario: A network team keeps firewall configurations in a Git repository. When a rule change breaks an application, they see who changed what and revert to the last good version in minutes.
detail.quizQuestion: Which practice lets a team see exactly who changed a firewall configuration file and revert to the previous version?

variants.title: Change management: technical implications and documentation

items.name: Allow lists / deny lists
items.detail: Changes may require editing the lists of approved or blocked applications, IPs or sites.

items.name: Restricted activities
items.detail: Some actions may be forbidden during a change window or freeze.

items.name: Downtime
items.detail: Planned outages that must be communicated.

items.name: Service / application restart
items.detail: A restart may be required for the change to take effect and can interrupt users.

items.name: Legacy applications
items.detail: Old software may break or not be supported after a change.

items.name: Dependencies
items.detail: Other systems and services that rely on the thing being changed.

items.name: Documentation
items.detail: Update network diagrams, policies and procedures after the change.

items.name: Version control
items.detail: Track every version of configurations and code so you can see what changed, who changed it, and roll back.

definition: The use of cameras, often recording continuously, to monitor and capture activity in and around a physical facility for deterrence, detection, and post-incident investigation.
examContext: The exam distinguishes video surveillance as primarily a detective control and deterrent rather than a preventive one; footage also supports incident investigations and establishing a chain of custody for physical evidence.
analogy: Like a store's security cameras that may not stop a theft in the moment, but record exactly what happened and who did it.
relatedTerms: Security guard, Lighting, Incident response, Chain of custody

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team installs video surveillance cameras covering every entrance and the parking lot, allowing the security team to review footage after an after-hours door alarm to confirm whether the access was authorized.
detail.quizQuestion: After an unauthorized entry is suspected at a secured facility overnight, which existing control would best help investigators confirm who entered and when?

items.name: Perimeter
items.detail: Fencing, bollards, lighting, guards, signage and gates. Deters and delays.

items.name: Building
items.detail: Access badges, locks, access control vestibules (mantraps) and turnstiles.

items.name: Interior
items.detail: Video surveillance, motion sensors, locked rooms, cages and racks.

items.name: Device
items.detail: Cable locks, USB port blockers, tamper seals and privacy screens.

items.name: Deter vs prevent vs detect
items.detail: Signs and visible guards deter; locks, bollards and vestibules prevent; cameras and sensors detect.

items.name: Infrared (PIR)
items.detail: Detects the body heat of a person moving through its field of view. Common in motion-activated lights and alarms.

items.name: Pressure
items.detail: Detects weight or force on a floor mat, tile or fence line, so it triggers when someone steps or climbs.

items.name: Microwave
items.detail: Emits microwave energy and detects changes in the reflection caused by movement. Covers a large area and can sense through thin walls.

items.name: Ultrasonic
items.detail: Emits high-frequency sound and detects movement from changes in the reflected waves. Good for enclosed rooms.

items.name: Video / camera
items.detail: Records or analyzes images; paired with motion detection to alert on activity.

items.name: Role in security
items.detail: All of these are DETECTIVE controls. The response (alarm, lights, recording) can add a deterrent or corrective effect.

definition: Technology that uses a hypervisor to create and run multiple virtual machines, each with its own virtual hardware, operating system, and applications, on a single piece of physical hardware.
examContext: Know that virtualization risks include VM escape (an attacker breaking out of a guest VM to reach the hypervisor or host) and VM sprawl, and that virtualization underlies most cloud computing.
analogy: Like dividing one large office building into fully separate apartments, each with its own kitchen and plumbing, even though they all sit on the same foundation.
relatedTerms: Containerization, Microservices, Serverless computing, High availability, Fault tolerance

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan consolidates ten aging physical servers onto a single powerful host running a hypervisor, creating ten isolated virtual machines that each run a different legacy application, reducing hardware costs while keeping the applications logically separated from one another.
detail.quizQuestion: A security concern specific to running multiple virtual machines on a single hypervisor is that an attacker who compromises one VM could potentially break out and access other VMs or the host. What is this risk called?

definition: Malicious code that attaches itself to a legitimate host file or program and requires user action, such as opening the file, to execute and spread.
examContext: Exam tests viruses as requiring a host file and human interaction to propagate, unlike self-spreading worms; know variants like macro viruses and polymorphic viruses.
analogy: Like a seed that only sprouts once someone plants it, needing both a host and an action to take root.
relatedTerms: Worm, Malware, Trojan horse

detail.practicalScenario: Priya's team traces an infection back to a macro-enabled spreadsheet attachment that, once an employee opened it and enabled macros, attached malicious code to other documents on the shared drive.
detail.quizQuestion: Malicious code only begins executing after a user opens an infected spreadsheet attachment and enables macros, and then it attaches itself to other documents. What type of malware is this?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A social engineering attack conducted over voice calls, including VoIP, to trick victims into revealing sensitive information or taking harmful actions.
examContext: Exam tests vishing as the voice or phone-call variant of phishing, often combined with caller ID spoofing.
analogy: Like a scammer calling pretending to be a government agency, demanding payment over the phone.
relatedTerms: Phishing, Smishing, Social engineering, Pretexting

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's elderly relative receives a phone call from someone claiming to be from the bank's fraud department, pressuring her to read back her one-time passcode over the phone.
detail.quizQuestion: An employee receives a phone call from someone claiming to be from the IT help desk, asking them to verbally confirm their password to resolve a system issue. What type of attack is this?

items.name: Phishing
items.detail: Mass, generic lures, usually email, that try to steal credentials or deliver malware.

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: An attack that lets an attacker send traffic into a VLAN they should not reach, either by switch spoofing (tricking a port into trunk mode) or by double tagging frames.
examContext: Mitigations: disable unused ports, disable DTP/trunk auto-negotiation, set access ports explicitly, and do not use VLAN 1 or the native VLAN for user traffic.
analogy: A guest tricking a staff-only elevator into thinking he is a staff member.
relatedTerms: Network segmentation, MAC flooding, ARP poisoning, VLAN

detail.practicalScenario: An attacker plugs into a wall port and negotiates a trunk with the switch, gaining access to the server VLAN. The team disables trunk negotiation on all access ports to stop it.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker tricks a switch port into trunking and gains access to other VLANs. What attack is this?

definition: An attack in which code running inside a virtual machine breaks out of its isolation to interact with the hypervisor or other VMs on the same host, defeating virtualization's isolation boundary.
examContext: Rare but severe because one compromised VM can expose the host and its neighbors. Mitigate by patching the hypervisor, minimizing host features, segmenting workloads and monitoring.
analogy: A prisoner who tunnels out of a cell into the guards' corridor.
relatedTerms: Virtualization, Sandboxing, Containerization, VM sprawl

detail.practicalScenario: A researcher demonstrates malware in a guest VM exploiting a hypervisor flaw to read memory belonging to other tenants on the host. The cloud provider patches the hypervisor to fix it.
detail.quizQuestion: Malicious code in one virtual machine exploits a hypervisor flaw to reach other VMs on the same host. What is this called?

definition: The uncontrolled growth of virtual machines that are easy to create but never tracked, patched or retired, leaving unmanaged systems that expand the attack surface.
examContext: Prevent with lifecycle management, ownership and tagging, regular audits and automated decommissioning. Related to shadow IT.
analogy: Rental storage units you keep forgetting to cancel and never check.
relatedTerms: Virtualization, Attack surface, Shadow IT, Patch management

detail.practicalScenario: An audit finds 140 forgotten test VMs, many unpatched and still joined to the corporate network. The team adds owner tags and automatic expiry dates to stop it happening again.
detail.quizQuestion: An audit finds hundreds of forgotten, unpatched virtual machines that were created for tests and never retired. What problem is this?

definition: A weakness in a system, process, or control that could be exploited by a threat to cause harm.
examContext: Exam distinguishes vulnerability, the weakness itself, from threat and exploit, the danger and method used against it; vulnerability scanning questions are common.
analogy: Like an unlocked window on a house, which is a weakness whether or not a burglar ever notices it.
relatedTerms: Threat, Risk, Exploit, Vulnerability scanning, Zero-day

detail.practicalScenario: Alex runs a vulnerability scan and discovers that a web server is running an outdated TLS version, creating a weakness that could be targeted even though no attack has occurred yet.
detail.quizQuestion: A scan reveals that a server is missing a critical security patch, though no attacker has yet targeted it. What does this unpatched weakness represent?

items.name: Application
items.detail: Memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (TOCTOU) and malicious updates.

items.name: Operating system
items.detail: Unpatched or misconfigured OS components and services.

items.name: Web-based
items.detail: SQL injection, XSS and other flaws in web applications.

items.name: Hardware / firmware
items.detail: Flaws in firmware or silicon, plus end-of-life and legacy devices that can no longer be patched.

items.name: Virtualization
items.detail: VM escape (breaking out to the hypervisor or other VMs), resource reuse (data left in reassigned memory or storage), and VM sprawl.

items.name: Cloud-specific
items.detail: Misconfigured storage, over-permissive IAM roles, exposed APIs and weak tenant isolation.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Weaknesses introduced through a service provider, hardware provider or software provider.

items.name: Cryptographic
items.detail: Weak or outdated algorithms, short keys and poor key management.

items.name: Misconfiguration
items.detail: Open permissions, default settings and unnecessary services or protocols.

items.name: Mobile device
items.detail: Side loading and jailbreaking/rooting bypass the platform's security model.

items.name: Zero-day
items.detail: A flaw unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists yet.

items.name: Credentialed
items.detail: The scanner logs in with an account, so it sees patch levels, configuration and local vulnerabilities. More accurate, with fewer false positives.

items.name: Non-credentialed
items.detail: An outside-in view, like an attacker. Finds exposed services but may miss internal weaknesses and produces more false positives.

items.name: Intrusive vs non-intrusive
items.detail: Intrusive scans actively try to exploit and can disrupt systems; non-intrusive scans only probe and identify.

items.name: Agent-based vs agentless
items.detail: Agent-based: software on the host reports continuously, even for roaming devices. Agentless: the scanner connects over the network.

items.name: Active vs passive
items.detail: Active sends probes; passive listens to traffic and infers what exists without touching it.

items.name: Scan vs pen test
items.detail: A scan is automated and lists KNOWN weaknesses without exploiting them. A pen test is largely manual and exploits weaknesses to prove real impact.

items.name: False positive / false negative
items.detail: False positive: reported but not real (wastes time). False negative: a real flaw that was missed (dangerous).

items.name: Confirmation
items.detail: Verify findings and weed out false positives and false negatives.

items.name: Prioritization
items.detail: Rank by CVSS, exploitability, asset criticality, exposure and business impact.

items.name: Remediation
items.detail: Patch, change configuration, or segment the system.

items.name: Compensating control
items.detail: When you cannot fix the flaw (legacy system, patch unavailable), add another control that reduces the risk.

items.name: Exception / exemption
items.detail: A documented, approved decision to leave a vulnerability unfixed for a stated reason and period.

items.name: Insurance / transfer
items.detail: Shift part of the financial impact to a third party.

items.name: Validation
items.detail: Rescan, audit, and verify that the fix worked and nothing broke.

items.name: Reporting
items.detail: Share trends and metrics with owners and leadership.

definition: An automated process that examines systems, networks, and applications for known weaknesses, such as missing patches or misconfigurations, by comparing them against a database of known vulnerabilities, producing a report ranked by severity.
examContext: Know vulnerability scanning is non-intrusive and automated, unlike penetration testing which actively exploits findings; exam scenarios test recognizing scanning as the discovery phase before remediation or deeper testing.
analogy: Like a home inspector checking a house against a standard checklist for code violations, without actually trying to break in through any of the issues found.
relatedTerms: Penetration testing, Patch management, Threat intelligence

detail.practicalScenario: Sam schedules a weekly automated vulnerability scan of all production servers, generating a prioritized report of missing patches and misconfigurations that the operations team then works through based on severity.
detail.quizQuestion: A security team wants an automated, non-intrusive way to identify missing patches and misconfigurations across hundreds of servers on a recurring basis. What should they implement?

items.name: Credentialed
items.detail: The scanner logs in with an account, so it sees patch levels, configuration and local vulnerabilities. More accurate, with fewer false positives.

items.name: Non-credentialed
items.detail: An outside-in view, like an attacker. Finds exposed services but may miss internal weaknesses and produces more false positives.

items.detail: False positive: reported but not real (wastes time). False negative: a real flaw that was missed (dangerous).

items.name: Confirmation
items.detail: Verify findings and weed out false positives and false negatives.

items.name: Prioritization
items.detail: Rank by CVSS, exploitability, asset criticality, exposure and business impact.

items.name: Remediation
items.detail: Patch, change configuration, or segment the system.

items.name: Compensating control
items.detail: When you cannot fix the flaw (legacy system, patch unavailable), add another control that reduces the risk.

items.name: Exception / exemption
items.detail: A documented, approved decision to leave a vulnerability unfixed for a stated reason and period.

items.name: Insurance / transfer
items.detail: Shift part of the financial impact to a third party.

items.name: Validation
items.detail: Rescan, audit, and verify that the fix worked and nothing broke.

items.name: Reporting
items.detail: Share trends and metrics with owners and leadership.

definition: Driving or walking around with a laptop or phone to locate and map wireless networks, often noting which are open or weakly secured. The related practice war chalking marks discoveries with symbols.
examContext: Reconnaissance for wireless attacks. Mitigated by strong encryption (WPA3), disabling WPS and limiting signal leakage outside the building.
analogy: Cruising neighborhoods noting which houses have unlocked windows.
relatedTerms: Evil twin, Rogue access point, Site survey, WPA3

detail.practicalScenario: A pentester drives around a business park with a laptop and GPS, mapping every Wi-Fi network and noting two that still use WEP. The findings go into the report as high-risk.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker drives through a business park mapping Wi-Fi networks with a laptop. What is this activity called?

definition: A recovery site with hardware, power and network connectivity in place but without current data or fully configured systems. Data and applications must be restored from backups before it is usable, which takes hours to days.
examContext: A middle ground on cost and recovery time between hot and cold sites. Expect to restore from recent backups, so RPO depends on the backup schedule.
analogy: A furnished apartment waiting for your clothes: the basics are there, but you must move your things in.
relatedTerms: Hot site, Cold site, Disaster recovery, Backup

detail.practicalScenario: A logistics firm keeps a second facility with servers installed and live connectivity. After a flood, the team restores the previous night's backups and brings it online within a day.
detail.quizQuestion: Which recovery site has equipment installed but needs data restored from backups before it can be used?

items.name: Hot site
items.detail: A fully equipped duplicate with current data, ready almost immediately (minutes to hours). Most expensive; the lowest RTO.

items.name: Warm site
items.detail: Hardware and connectivity are in place but data must be restored and systems configured (hours to days). A middle ground on cost.

items.name: Cold site
items.detail: Empty space with power and cooling only; you bring the equipment and data (days to weeks). Cheapest; the highest RTO.

items.name: Geographic dispersion
items.detail: Spreading systems and data across distant regions so one regional disaster cannot take everything out.

items.name: Platform diversity
items.detail: Using different operating systems, vendors or technologies so one flaw does not take down every system.

items.name: Multi-cloud
items.detail: Using more than one cloud provider to avoid lock-in and single-provider outages (more complexity to secure).

definition: An attack strategy in which a threat actor compromises a website frequently visited by a specific target group, infecting visitors with malware.
examContext: Exam tests watering hole attacks as targeting a trusted third-party site rather than the victim directly, often used by advanced persistent threats against specific industries.
analogy: Like a predator poisoning the one watering hole that all the zebras in the area are known to drink from.
relatedTerms: Advanced persistent threat, Supply chain attack, Threat actor

detail.practicalScenario: Chen's threat intel team discovers that attackers compromised a niche industry forum frequently visited by employees of defense contractors, planting malware to infect only visitors from targeted companies.
detail.quizQuestion: Attackers compromise a popular industry-specific news website, knowing that employees of their target organization regularly visit it, in order to infect those specific visitors with malware. What is this technique called?

items.name: Spear phishing
items.detail: Targeted at a specific person or group, using researched, personalized details to look credible.

items.name: Whaling
items.detail: Spear phishing aimed at senior executives (the "big fish").

items.name: Vishing
items.detail: Voice phishing by phone call, often with spoofed caller ID or an AI-cloned voice.

items.name: Smishing
items.detail: Phishing by SMS or text message.

items.name: Pharming
items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: A control that blocks or allows web access based on URL, domain, content category, reputation or keywords, implemented as an endpoint agent, a centralized proxy or a cloud service.
examContext: Know the methods: agent-based versus centralized proxy, URL scanning, content categorization, block rules and reputation. It also blocks known malware and phishing sites.
analogy: A school librarian who decides which websites the children may visit.
relatedTerms: Proxy server, DNS filtering, Allow list and deny list, Firewall

detail.practicalScenario: A company routes all web traffic through a cloud web filter. It blocks gambling and known malicious sites by category and reputation, and an agent applies the same policy to laptops working from home.
detail.quizQuestion: Which control blocks users from visiting sites in categories such as gambling or known malicious domains?

items.name: URL / domain block and allow lists
items.detail: Explicitly permit or deny named sites. Precise, but must be maintained.

items.name: Content categorization
items.detail: Sites are sorted into categories (gambling, adult, malware) and whole categories are blocked.

items.name: Reputation filtering
items.detail: Blocks sites with a poor trust score based on threat intelligence, newly registered domains and past abuse.

items.name: Agent-based
items.detail: Software on the endpoint enforces policy wherever the device is, even off the corporate network.

items.name: Centralized proxy
items.detail: All web traffic is forced through one gateway that applies the policy; users on the network are covered without agents.

items.name: DNS filtering
items.detail: Blocks malicious or unwanted domains at name resolution, before a connection is made.

definition: A spear phishing attack specifically targeting high-profile individuals such as executives or senior leadership within an organization.
examContext: Exam tests recognizing whaling as targeting senior executives, often involving fraudulent wire transfer requests known as business email compromise or CEO fraud.
analogy: Like a con artist who skips the regular customers and goes straight for the bank manager.
relatedTerms: Spear phishing, Phishing, Social engineering, Pretexting

detail.practicalScenario: Jordan, the CFO, receives a spoofed email appearing to come from the CEO urgently requesting an international wire transfer, a classic whaling attempt aimed squarely at executive leadership.
detail.quizQuestion: An attacker crafts a fraudulent email specifically impersonating the CEO and sends it only to the company's CFO, requesting an urgent wire transfer. What specific type of attack is this?

items.detail: Silently redirects victims to a fake site (through DNS poisoning or a changed hosts file) without them clicking a lure.

items.name: Business email compromise
items.detail: Impersonating an executive or vendor to trick staff into wire transfers or payment changes. Often no link or malware at all.

items.name: Typosquatting
items.detail: Registering look-alike domains that rely on typing mistakes (gogle.com).

items.name: Brand impersonation
items.detail: Posing as a trusted brand in email, sites or social media.

items.name: Watering hole
items.detail: Compromising a site that the target group already visits, rather than attacking them directly.

items.name: Pretexting
items.detail: Inventing a believable scenario (an IT help-desk call, an auditor) to get information or access.

items.name: Impersonation
items.detail: Pretending to be someone with authority or a legitimate need (employee, contractor, delivery driver), in person or remotely.

definition: A single digital certificate that uses an asterisk in its common name, such as *.example.com, to secure an unlimited number of subdomains under one domain, rather than issuing a separate certificate for each subdomain.
examContext: The exam tests the tradeoff: wildcard certificates simplify management and reduce cost across many subdomains, but if the private key is ever compromised, every subdomain covered by that certificate is at risk simultaneously.
analogy: Like a single master key that opens every apartment in a building: convenient, but if it's ever stolen, every unit is exposed at once.
relatedTerms: Certificate, Certificate authority, Public key, Private key, Chain of trust

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's company purchases a wildcard certificate for *.company.com so that mail.company.com, shop.company.com, and dozens of other subdomains can all use HTTPS without purchasing and managing a separate certificate for each one.
detail.quizQuestion: A company wants to secure dozens of subdomains, such as mail.company.com and shop.company.com, using a single purchased certificate rather than issuing one per subdomain. What should they use?

items.name: Self-signed
items.detail: Signed by its own private key, so no third party vouches for it. Free and fine for labs or internal dev, but browsers warn users and it cannot be revoked by a public CA.

items.name: Public CA-issued
items.detail: Signed by a CA that browsers and operating systems already trust. Required for public-facing sites.

items.name: Wildcard
items.detail: One certificate for *.example.com, covering every first-level subdomain. Convenient, but one stolen key exposes all of them.

items.name: SAN (Subject Alternative Name)
items.detail: One certificate that lists several specific hostnames or domains. Not to be confused with a SAN as a Storage Area Network; the exam uses both meanings.

items.name: DV / OV / EV
items.detail: Domain Validation proves only control of the domain; Organization Validation vets the company; Extended Validation is the strictest vetting.

items.name: Code signing
items.detail: Proves who published software and that it has not been altered since signing.

items.name: Machine / user / email
items.detail: Certificates that authenticate a device or a person, or sign and encrypt email (S/MIME).

items.name: Root certificate
items.detail: Self-signed certificate at the top of a chain, pre-installed in the OS/browser trust store.

definition: A denial-of-service attack that transmits radio noise on the same frequency as a wireless network so legitimate signals cannot get through.
examContext: A physical-layer attack. Detect with spectrum analysis; mitigate by locating and removing the source, changing channels, or using wired links for critical systems.
analogy: Someone with a loud speaker drowning out a conversation.
relatedTerms: Deauthentication attack, DoS, WIDS, Site survey

detail.practicalScenario: The office Wi-Fi becomes unusable every afternoon. A spectrum analyzer shows strong noise across the 2.4 GHz band coming from a device in a neighboring unit, which is then removed.
detail.quizQuestion: A device floods the 2.4 GHz band with noise so the office Wi-Fi is unusable. What attack is this?

definition: A self-replicating type of malware that spreads independently across networks without needing to attach itself to a host file or require user interaction.
examContext: Exam distinguishes worms, which self-propagate without a host file, from viruses, which require a host file and often user action; a classic example involves exploiting a network service vulnerability.
analogy: Like a contagious illness that spreads from person to person on its own, without needing someone to deliberately pass it along.
relatedTerms: Virus, Malware, Botnet, Exploit

detail.practicalScenario: Sam's network monitoring detects a piece of malicious code automatically spreading from server to server overnight by exploiting an unpatched network service, with no user ever clicking a file.
detail.quizQuestion: Malicious code spreads automatically across an entire corporate network overnight by exploiting a vulnerable network service, without any user opening a file or clicking a link. What type of malware is this?

items.name: Virus
items.detail: Attaches itself to a host file or program and needs the user to run it. Spreads by infecting other files.

items.name: Worm
items.detail: Self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, exploiting vulnerabilities, with no user action needed. Often consumes bandwidth.

items.name: Trojan
items.detail: Disguised as legitimate software. Does not self-replicate; delivers a payload such as a backdoor, RAT or banking stealer.

items.name: Ransomware
items.detail: Encrypts data (or locks the system) and demands payment. Offline, tested backups are the best defense.

items.name: Spyware
items.detail: Secretly collects information about user activity, such as browsing, credentials and screenshots.

items.name: Keylogger
items.detail: Records keystrokes to capture passwords and messages. It can be hardware or software.

items.name: Rootkit
items.detail: Hides itself, and other malware, by modifying the OS, kernel or firmware to keep privileged persistence. Very hard to detect; often needs a rebuild.

items.name: Logic bomb
items.detail: Dormant malicious code that fires when a condition is met (a date, an event, an account being disabled). A classic insider tool.

items.name: RAT
items.detail: Remote Access Trojan: gives an attacker interactive remote control of the victim system.

items.name: Botnet
items.detail: A group of infected devices controlled through command and control for DDoS, spam, or cryptomining.

items.name: Fileless malware
items.detail: Runs in memory using legitimate tools (PowerShell, WMI), leaving little on disk to scan. Detect it with behavior-based EDR.

items.name: Bloatware / PUP / adware
items.detail: Unwanted bundled software that wastes resources, shows ads or widens the attack surface.

definition: A security model that assumes no user, device, or network segment is inherently trusted, requiring continuous verification for every access request regardless of location.
examContext: SY0-701 heavily emphasizes zero trust architecture, including the never trust, always verify philosophy and concepts like policy enforcement points.
analogy: Like a building where you must badge in at every single door, even ones you just walked through minutes ago.
relatedTerms: Least privilege, Network segmentation, Microsegmentation, Authentication, Defense in depth

detail.practicalScenario: Maria redesigns the corporate network so that internal employees must authenticate and be authorized at every application boundary, rather than being automatically trusted once inside the VPN.
detail.quizQuestion: A company stops assuming that devices inside its corporate network are automatically safe and instead requires continuous verification for every resource request. Which model is being adopted?

definition: A vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor or public and has no available patch, making it exploitable until discovered and fixed.
examContext: Exam frequently tests zero-day as the most dangerous vulnerability type because no signature or patch exists yet; often paired with advanced persistent threat scenarios.
analogy: Like a secret flaw in a lock that even the locksmith does not know about yet.
relatedTerms: Vulnerability, Exploit, Advanced persistent threat, Patch management

detail.practicalScenario: Alex's security team detects unusual outbound traffic from a server and later learns it was caused by attackers exploiting a previously undisclosed flaw in the web server software, with no vendor patch yet available.
detail.quizQuestion: Attackers compromise a company's mail server using a flaw that the software vendor has never publicly acknowledged or patched. What type of vulnerability was exploited?

items.name: Application
items.detail: Memory injection, buffer overflow, race conditions (TOCTOU) and malicious updates.

items.name: Operating system
items.detail: Unpatched or misconfigured OS components and services.

items.name: Web-based
items.detail: SQL injection, XSS and other flaws in web applications.

items.name: Hardware / firmware
items.detail: Flaws in firmware or silicon, plus end-of-life and legacy devices that can no longer be patched.

items.name: Virtualization
items.detail: VM escape (breaking out to the hypervisor or other VMs), resource reuse (data left in reassigned memory or storage), and VM sprawl.

items.name: Cloud-specific
items.detail: Misconfigured storage, over-permissive IAM roles, exposed APIs and weak tenant isolation.

items.name: Supply chain
items.detail: Weaknesses introduced through a service provider, hardware provider or software provider.

items.name: Cryptographic
items.detail: Weak or outdated algorithms, short keys and poor key management.

items.name: Misconfiguration
items.detail: Open permissions, default settings and unnecessary services or protocols.

items.name: Mobile device
items.detail: Side loading and jailbreaking/rooting bypass the platform's security model.

items.name: Zero-day
items.detail: A flaw unknown to the vendor, so no patch exists yet.
